# Majmu' al-Fatawa - Tome 17

## Page 8609

Volume Seventeen
The Book of Quranic Exegesis
Part Four
Commentary on Sūrat al-Ikhlās and the Two Surahs of Refuge

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy. All praise belongs to Allah alone, and may blessings and peace be upon him after whom there is no prophet.

Sūrat al-Ikhlās

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah be pleased with him—was asked:

Concerning the report that the surah “Say, ‘He is Allah, the One’” is equivalent to one-third of the Quran, and similar reports concerning the surahs (The Earthquake), “Say, ‘O disbelievers’” and (The Opening): Are these reports of equivalence established for all these surahs or only some of them? Who narrated them, and which of them are authentic? What does this equivalence mean, given that Allah’s speech is one in relation to Him, Mighty and Majestic? And does this difference in merit—assuming

---

## Page 8610

it is established—extend to the names and attributes, or not? Is it permissible to regard some eternal attributes and eternal names as superior to others, even though they are eternal? Who has held this view, and in which of his books did he state it? What grounds support the preferred view, with whatever rational and transmitted evidence can be provided?

He replied—may Allah be pleased with him:

All praise belongs to Allah. The compilers of the authentic collections, such as al-Bukhārī and Muslim, recorded reports concerning the excellence of “Say, ‘He is Allah, the One.’” It is reported that al-Dāraqutnī said: “No surah has more authentic reports concerning its excellence than this one.”

They likewise recorded reports concerning the excellence of the Opening of the Book. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said of it:

“Nothing like it has been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, or the Quran.”

He did not state that it was equivalent to a portion of the Quran, as he said of “Say, ‘He is Allah, the One’” that it was equivalent to one-third of the Quran.

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, al-Dahhāk al-Mashriqī narrated from Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, who said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to his Companions, ‘Is any one of you unable to recite one-third of the Quran in a night?’ They found this difficult and said, ‘Which of us could manage that, O Messenger of Allah?’ He said, ‘“Allah, the One, the Eternal Refuge” is one-third of the Quran.’”

In Sahīh Muslim, Ma‘dān ibn Abī Talhah narrated from Abū al-Dardā’:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Is any one of you unable to recite one-third of the Quran in a night?’

---

## Page 8611

They asked, ‘How can one recite one-third of the Quran?’ He replied, ‘“Say: He is Allah, the One” is equivalent to one-third of the Quran.’”

Muslim also narrated from Abū al-Dardā’ that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah divided the Quran into three parts and made ‘Say: He is Allah, the One’ one of those parts.”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Abd Allāh ibn Abī Sa‘sa‘ah narrated from Abū Sa‘īd:

“A man heard another man repeatedly reciting ‘Say: He is Allah, the One.’ In the morning, he went to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and mentioned this to him, regarding that recitation as little. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘By Him in whose hand is my soul, it is indeed equivalent to one-third of the Quran.’”

Al-Bukhārī also recorded from Abū Sa‘īd, who said: “My brother Qatādah ibn al-Nu‘mān informed me that a man stood in prayer during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, reciting ‘Say: He is Allah, the One’ before dawn, without reciting anything else…” The rest of the hadith follows in similar wording.

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayrah said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Gather together, for I shall recite to you one-third of the Quran.’ So people gathered. Then the Prophet of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came out, recited ‘Say: He is Allah, the One,’ and went back inside. We said to one another, ‘I think some news has come to him from heaven, and that is what made him go inside.’ Then the Prophet of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came out and said, ‘I told you that I would recite to you one-third of the Quran. Indeed, it is equivalent to one-third of the Quran.’”

In another wording recorded by Muslim, he said: “The Messenger of Allah came out to us

---

## Page 8612

, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said, ‘I shall recite to you one-third of the Quran.’ He then recited, ‘Say: He is Allah, the One; Allah, the Eternal Refuge,’ continuing to the end of the surah.”

As for the hadith concerning “The Earthquake” and “Say: O disbelievers,” al-Tirmidhī narrated from Anas ibn Mālik, who said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Whoever recites “When the earth is shaken,” it is equivalent for him to half the Quran. Whoever recites “Say: O disbelievers,” it is equivalent for him to one-quarter of the Quran.’”

Ibn ‘Abbās said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘“When the earth is shaken” is equivalent to half the Quran, and “Say: O disbelievers” is equivalent to one-quarter of the Quran.’”

Al-Tirmidhī narrated both reports and described each as singular.

As for the hadith concerning al-Fātihah, al-Bukhārī narrated in his Sahīh from Abū Sa‘īd ibn al-Mu‘allā, who said:

“I was praying in the mosque when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, called me, but I did not answer him. I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, I was praying.’ He said, ‘Has Allah not said, “Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you”?’ Then he said, ‘I shall surely teach you a surah that is the greatest surah in the Quran.’ He said, ‘“All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds” is the seven oft-repeated verses and the glorious Quran.’”

In the Sunan and Musnad collections, al-‘Alā’ ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān narrated from his father, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Ubayy ibn Ka‘b:

“Shall I teach you a surah the like of which has not been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, or the Criterion?” He said, “I hope

---

## Page 8613

that you will not leave through this door before you have learned it.” The report also states: “He asked, ‘How do you recite in prayer?’ I recited the Mother of the Quran to him, and he said, ‘By Him in Whose hand is my soul, nothing like it has been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, or the Quran. It is the seven oft-repeated verses and the glorious Quran that I have been given.’” Mālik also narrated it in al-Muwatta’, from al-‘Alā’ ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān, from Abū Sa‘īd, the freedman of ‘Āmir ibn Kurayz, with an interrupted chain of transmission.

In Sahīh Muslim, ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Āmir said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Have you not considered the verses revealed tonight, the like of which has never been seen: “Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak” and “Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind”?’”

Another wording reads:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to me, ‘Verses have been revealed to me, the like of which has never been seen: the two surahs of refuge.’”

In this authentic hadith, he stated that nothing like the two surahs of refuge had ever been seen, just as he stated that nothing like al-Fātihah had been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, or the Quran. This demonstrates that some portions of the Quran are superior to others.

Section

As for the question about the meaning of this equivalence, given that all of it is equally the speech of Allah, this question encompasses two matters:

First: Are some portions of Allah’s speech superior to others, or not?

Second: What does it mean that “Say: He is Allah, the One” is equivalent to one-third of the Quran? And what is the reason for that?

---

## Page 8614

We say in response:

As for the first, it is “a major question” over which there is widespread disagreement. Some groups maintain that certain portions of Allah’s speech are superior to others, as the prophetic texts explicitly state. The Prophet said that nothing like al-Fātihah had been revealed in the three scriptures, and that Sūrat al-Ikhlās is equivalent to one-third of the Quran. Its equivalence to one-third of the Quran precludes its being equal in merit to other passages containing the same number of letters.

He also declared Āyat al-Kursī to be the greatest verse in the Quran, as is established in the Sahīh. It is likewise established in Sahīh Muslim that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Ubayy ibn Ka‘b:

“Abū al-Mundhir, do you know which of the verses of Allah’s Book that you know is the greatest?”

He said: “I replied, ‘Allah and His Messenger know best.’ He said, ‘Abū al-Mundhir, do you know which verse in Allah’s Book is the greatest?’ I replied, ‘Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all.’ He then struck my chest and said, ‘May your knowledge bring you joy, Abū al-Mundhir!’”

Ibn Abī Shaybah also narrated it in his Musnad through Muslim’s chain of transmission, adding:

“By Him in Whose hand is my soul, this verse has a tongue and two lips with which it glorifies the Sovereign at the foot of the Throne.”

It has also been reported that it is “the foremost of the verses of the Quran.” Concerning the two surahs of refuge, he said:

“The like of them has never been seen.”

Allah Most High has said:

“Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it.”

He thus states that He brings one better than it or similar to it. This is Allah’s declaration that He may sometimes bring a verse similar to that one, and at other times one better than it. This indicates that

---

## Page 8615

the verses are sometimes equal in merit and at other times differ in merit. Moreover, the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran are all Allah’s speech, yet Muslims know that the Quran is the best of the three books.

Allah Most High says:

“And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming the Scripture that came before it and as a guardian over it.”

He also says:

“Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will preserve it.”

And He says:

“Say: If mankind and jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce its like, even if they supported one another.”

And He says:

“Allah has sent down the finest discourse—a Book consistent in its parts and oft-repeated—at which the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver; then their skins and hearts soften at the remembrance of Allah.”

He thus declares it to be the finest discourse, indicating that it is better than all other discourse, whether revealed by Allah or not.

Allah Most High also says:

“And We have certainly given you the seven oft-repeated verses and the magnificent Quran.”

Whether this refers to al-Fātihah or to the Quran in its entirety, it indicates that the magnificent Quran is distinguished by this description above what does not share it. Allah has also described the entire Quran as glorious, noble, and mighty.

He has challenged creation to produce its like, or the like of ten of its surahs, or the like of a single surah of it. He says:

“Then let them produce a discourse like it, if they are truthful.”

And He says:

“Then produce ten fabricated surahs like it.”

And He says:

“Then produce a surah like it.”

He has further distinguished it in that nothing but it is to be recited in prayer. No one may recite anything else, whether alongside it or without it, nor may one pray without reciting the Quran. Thus, nothing else can take

---

## Page 8616

its place when one is able to recite it. Likewise, Muslims agree that no other passage can take the place of al-Fātihah in every respect, whether it is considered an obligation whose omission requires the prayer to be repeated, a duty whose omission is sinful but does not require repetition, or a sunnah. No one has said that reciting another passage is equal in every respect to reciting it.

The Quran is also distinguished by the requirement that only someone in a state of purity may touch a written copy of it. This is established from the Companions—such as Saʿd, Salmān, and Ibn ʿUmar—and from the vast majority of earlier and later scholars, including the four imams of jurisprudence and others. This was also prescribed in the Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the letter he wrote to ʿAmr ibn Hazm, which he undoubtedly wrote to him. Allah’s Book also indicates this. Likewise, according to the vast majority of scholars, including the four imams of jurisprudence and others, someone in a state of janābah (major ritual impurity) may not recite the Quran, as the Sunnah indicates.

Distinguishing one of two discourses through rulings that confer honor upon it indicates that it is intrinsically superior, even if this were to amount to preferring one of two identical things without any grounds for preference. This is contrary to what is known of the way of the Lord Most High in His legislation, and indeed in His creation, and contrary to what both rational and scriptural evidence indicate.

Furthermore, Allah Most High says:

“And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord.”

And He says:

“So give good tidings to My servants who listen to what is said and follow the best of it.”

And He says:

“Hold firmly to them, and command your people to follow the best of them.”

This thus indicates

---

## Page 8617

that among what has been revealed, some is good and some is better, whether the better is the abrogating passage that must be followed rather than the abrogated passage—since He does not abrogate a verse without bringing one better than it or equal to it—or something else.

The view that some of Allah’s speech is superior to other parts is the view transmitted from the early generations. It is also the position of the leading jurists of the four schools and others. Statements affirming this are numerous and widespread in many books. One example is the explanation of this hadith by Abū al-ʿAbbās ibn Surayj, which will be mentioned below: Allah revealed the Quran in three divisions, one third consisting of rulings, one third of promises and warnings, and one third of the divine names and attributes. This surah brings together the names and attributes.

Another example is what the followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad mentioned concerning the specific prescription of al-Fātihah in prayer. Abū al-Muzaffar Mansūr ibn Muhammad al-Samʿānī al-Shāfiʿī said in his book al-Istilām:

“As for their statement that the other rulings relating to the Quran are not exclusive to al-Fātihah, I reply: The other rulings apply to the Quran generally, whereas this ruling applies specifically to al-Fātihah. The evidence is that, according to us, reciting al-Fātihah specifically is prescribed as an obligation, while according to you it is prescribed as a sunnah.”

He said:

“Our fellow scholars have said: Since reciting al-Fātihah is obligatory in prayer, al-Fātihah must be specifically prescribed. This is because the Quran is distinguished from all other speech by its inimitability, and the smallest portion through which its inimitability is established is a surah. This surah is the noblest of the surahs because it is the seven oft-repeated verses, and because it can take the place of all the surahs, but not

---

## Page 8618

all the surahs together can take its place; and because it contains what no other surah of comparable length contains: praise and glorification of the Lord, and the servant’s seeking help and refuge and offering supplication. Since this surah is the noblest of surahs, and prayer is the noblest of states, the noblest surah is specifically prescribed in the noblest state.”

These are his words. Thus, it has been transmitted from the followers of al-Shāfi'ī that this surah is the noblest of surahs, just as prayer is the noblest of states. They explained its superiority over other surahs in the terms just mentioned.

Likewise, some followers of Ahmad stated this, including Judge Abū Ya'lā, son of Judge Abū Khāzim, son of Judge Abū Ya'lā ibn al-Farrā'. In his commentary—from which I copied in his own handwriting—he said, discussing whether reciting al-Fātihah is an essential pillar of prayer:

“The principal argument in this matter is as follows: Prayer is the noblest act of worship, and recitation is obligatory within it. Therefore, the noblest surah must be specifically prescribed for it. Al-Fātihah is the noblest surah, so it must be specifically prescribed.”

He said:

“Know that establishing this argument requires us to demonstrate two things: first, that prayer is the noblest act of worship; and second, that al-Hamd (Praise) is the noblest surah.”

He supported this with the evidence he cited, saying:

“As for the evidence that the Opening of the Book is the noblest, it consists of textual evidence, substantive considerations, and the legal ruling. The textual evidence is what was previously mentioned: that it takes the place of other surahs. And from Abū Sa'īd

---

## Page 8619

al-Khudrī, who reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘The Opening of the Book is a cure for poison.’

“Al-Hasan al-Basrī said: ‘Allah sent down one hundred and four books from heaven and placed their knowledge within four of them: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and al-Furqān (the Criterion). He then placed the knowledge of these four within al-Furqān, then the knowledge of the Quran within al-Mufassal, then the knowledge of al-Mufassal within the Opening of the Book. Whoever knows its interpretation is therefore like one who knows the interpretation of all Allah’s revealed books, and whoever recites it is as though he has recited the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Quran.’

“As for the substantive consideration, Allah set it alongside the entire Quran, saying:

‘We have certainly given you seven oft-repeated verses and the glorious Quran.’

“This is a distinction in which no other surah comes close to it.”

I say: This follows the interpretation of those who identify it as the seven oft-repeated verses and understand ‘the glorious Quran’ to mean the entire Quran.

He said: “Furthermore, it is called ‘the Mother of the Quran’; the mother of a thing is its source and substance. Thus Allah called Mecca ‘the Mother of Cities’ because of its superiority over them. Moreover, it is the seven oft-repeated verses, and it contains what no other surah contains: praise and glorification of the Lord Most High, and the servant’s seeking His help and refuge and offering supplication, as in the well-known hadith in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said that Allah Most High says: ‘I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant.’”

He said: “Furthermore, He has revealed nothing like it in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, or any of the revealed books. Evidence of this is that its recitation has been made easy for everyone in a way that is not the case with other parts of the Quran.

---

## Page 8620

And it is used as a proverbial comparison; thus people say, ‘So-and-so knows something by heart as well as he knows al-Fātiha.’ Since it holds this position, no other surah equals it in this respect, and it therefore enjoys a unique distinction. Moreover, it is the seven oft-repeated verses. The Quran commentators said that this means its recitation is repeated in every unit of prayer. Some said, ‘It was revealed to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, twice.’”

I say: There are other interpretations as well.

He said: “As for the legal ruling, its recitation is recommended in every unit of prayer, and omitting it is disliked. Were it not superior, it would not have been singled out in this way. Supporting this is the position of those who disagree—meaning the followers of Abū Hanīfa—that whoever omits its recitation must perform the prostrations of forgetfulness.

“We therefore say: Either it is a pillar of prayer or it is not. If it is a pillar, its omission cannot be made up for by prostration; if it is not a pillar, prostration should not be obligatory for omitting it.”

I say: He means that prostration is required only for omitting an act that is obligatory when one is acting deliberately; if one forgets it, prostration becomes obligatory. If an act is obligatory, deliberately omitting it must invalidate one’s prayer, because one has not done what one was commanded to do. This differs from forgetting some obligatory acts, since their omission can be made up for by the prostrations of forgetfulness.

The position of Mālik, Ahmad, and Abū Hanīfa is that the prostrations of forgetfulness are obligatory, because they hold that some obligatory acts may be omitted forgetfully without invalidating the prayer. Likewise, according to the scholars’ consensus, the prayer is not invalidated by a forgetful addition, whereas a deliberate addition would invalidate it.

However, according to the well-known position reported from Mālik and Ahmad, they say:

---

## Page 8621

“Deliberately omitting an obligatory act invalidates one’s prayer. If it is omitted forgetfully, some such omissions invalidate the prayer, while others can be made up for by the prostrations of forgetfulness. Thus, omitting bowing, prostration, or recitation invalidates the prayer in either case. According to both of them, deliberately omitting the first tashahhud invalidates the prayer, whereas forgetting it requires the prostrations of forgetfulness.”

Abū Hanīfa, however, says: “If someone omits an obligatory act (wājib) that is not a strict obligation (fard)—such as reciting al-Fātiha—he has acted wrongly, but his prayer is not invalidated.” Al-Shāfi‘ī makes no distinction in prayer between a pillar and an obligatory act, although he and all the other imams distinguish between them in Hajj. The purpose here is to mention some of those who said that al-Fātiha is more excellent than other surahs.

Abū Umar ibn Abd al-Barr said:

“As for the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to Ubayy:

‘Do you know a surah the like of which Allah has not revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, or the Quran?’

“The meaning is that none equals it in encompassing the meanings of goodness. It praises Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as He deserves, with the praise that truly belongs to Him alone, for every blessing and every good comes from Him and no other. He is the Creator, the Provider. None can withhold what He gives, and none can give what He withholds. He is praised for this, and even when another is praised, the praise ultimately returns to Him.

“It also magnifies Him, declaring that He is the Lord of all creation and the Sovereign of this world and the Hereafter, the One who is worshipped and whose help is sought. It teaches supplication and right guidance, and avoidance of the path of those who have strayed and gone astray. Supplication is the very essence of worship. Thus, it is the surah that most comprehensively encompasses goodness; nothing in the scriptures equals it in these

---

## Page 8622

respects.”

He continued:

“It has also been said that this means prayer is valid through its recitation, but not through that of another surah, and that no other surah can take its place. This interpretation, however, is not unanimously accepted.”

I say:

He means that scholars disagree over this point—namely, that prayer is valid only with its recitation. This indicates that scholars agree on the first description: that it is the most excellent surah.

The same applies to what the Quran and Sunnah state concerning the Quran’s superiority to the rest of Allah’s speech—the Torah, the Gospel, and all the other scriptures. All the early Muslim generations acknowledged this. None of them said, “It is all Allah’s speech,” and therefore refused to regard the Quran as superior to the others. Allah Most High says:

“Allah has sent down the best discourse: a Book consistent in its parts, repeating its teachings.”

He thus declares that it is the best discourse. He also says:

“We relate to you the best of narratives through Our revelation to you of this Quran, although before it you were among the unaware.”

Regarding “the best of narratives,” some have said that it is a verbal noun, while others have said that it is a direct object.

According to the first interpretation, the meaning is: “We narrate to you in the finest manner,” just as one might say, “We speak to you in the finest manner,” or, “We explain to you in the clearest manner.”

Al-Zajjāj said:

“We explain to you in the clearest manner. A narrator is someone who relates a story as it truly happened.”

He explained that His words,

“through Our revelation to you of this Quran,”

mean, “by Our revealing this Quran to you.” Whoever holds this view says, “through Our revelation to you of this Quran.” According to this interpretation, it is like saying, “We recite

---

## Page 8623

to you in the finest manner, and recite to you in the finest way.”

The second interpretation is that the meaning is: “We relate to you the best of what can be related”—that is, the finest accounts and narratives—as He says in another surah:

“Allah has sent down the best discourse.”

He also says:

“And who is more truthful than Allah in speech?”

This is supported by His words in the account of Moses:

“When he came to him and related his story,”

and His words:

“There was certainly a lesson in their narratives for people of understanding.”

What is meant is their accounts, reports, and stories, not merely the act of narration. The two interpretations necessarily imply one another in meaning, as we shall explain. Thus, this accusative expression may combine the sense of a verbal noun with that of a direct object, since it contains both meanings. This differs from cases in which the action is distinct from its object: there, construing the accusative in one sense precludes the other.

The grammarians who preferred the first interpretation—such as al-Zajjāj and others—said that qasas is a verbal noun. One says, qassa atharahu, yaqussuhu qasasan, meaning that he traced someone’s footsteps. Hence the words of Allah Most High:

“So they turned back, retracing their footsteps.”

The expressions iqtassa atharahu and taqassasa have the same meaning. One also says, iqtasastu al-hadītha, meaning, “I related the account as it actually happened,” and iqtassa ‘alayhi al-khabara qasasan, meaning, “He related the news to him.”

Qasas, with an a, is not the plural of qissah, as some ordinary people suppose. Rather, the plural is qisas, with an i, and its singular is qissah. A qissah is an event or account that is related; it follows the pattern fi‘lah with a passive meaning. Its plural is qisas, with an i.

In His words,

“We relate to you the best of narratives,”

the word is qasas, with an a. He did not say qisas, with an i. Yet

---

## Page 8624

some people thought that what was meant was “the best of stories”—qisas, with an i—and that the story in question was that of Joseph. A number of Quran commentators mentioned this.

They then asked: Why was it called the best of narratives? One answer was that no other story in the Quran contains as many lessons, wise teachings, and subtle insights as this story. Another was that a long period of time separates its beginning from its end. Another was the excellence of the dialogue between Joseph and his brothers, his patience in bearing their mistreatment, his refraining from mentioning what they had done when they met again, and his generous forgiveness.

Another explanation was that it mentions prophets, righteous people, angels, devils, humans, jinn, livestock, and birds; the lives of kings, slaves, merchants, scholars, the ignorant, men, and women; and women’s scheming and stratagems. It also discusses Allah’s oneness, jurisprudence, history, dream interpretation, governance, social relations, and the management of one’s livelihood. It is therefore the best of narratives because of the meanings and benefits it contains that serve both religious and worldly life. Another explanation was that it mentions the lover and the beloved. Yet another was that “best” means “most remarkable.”

Among those who regard Joseph’s story as the best of narratives are some who know that qasas, with an a, means an account or report, and who say that it is the finest of all accounts and reports. Many of them, however, think that what is meant is “the best of stories”—qisas, with an i. These people are ignorant of Arabic. Both views are mistaken. His words, “the best of narratives,” do not refer to Joseph’s story alone. Rather, it is one of the accounts Allah has related and is included among the best of narratives.

---

## Page 8625

and for this reason Allah Most High says at the end of the surah:

“We sent before you only men from the towns, to whom We revealed. Have they not travelled through the land and seen what became of those before them? The home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah. Will you not then use reason?”

“Until, when the messengers had lost hope and their people thought they had been lied to, Our help came to them, and those We willed were saved. Our punishment cannot be averted from the criminal people.”

“There is certainly a lesson in their accounts for people of understanding. This is no fabricated tale, but a confirmation of what came before it, a detailed explanation of all things, and guidance and mercy for people who believe.”

Thus He explains that the lesson lies in the accounts of the messengers. He commands us to consider the fate of those who rejected them, and how the messengers themselves ultimately attained victory. It is well known that the story of Moses, including what happened between him and Pharaoh and others, is far, far greater and nobler than the story of Joseph. It is therefore the greatest of the accounts of the prophets related in the Quran. Allah repeats it more often than any other and recounts it at greater length and in greater detail. Indeed, the accounts of the other prophets—such as Noah, Hūd, Sālih, Shuʿayb, and the other messengers—are greater than the story of Joseph. For this reason, Allah repeats those accounts in the Quran but does not repeat the story of Joseph.

This is because those who opposed Joseph did not oppose him on account of religion. Rather, their hostility arose from worldly concerns: they envied him for his father’s love and wronged him, but he remained patient and feared Allah. He—may Allah’s blessings be upon him—was tested both by those who wronged him and by someone who invited him to sexual immorality. In both trials, he remained patient and feared Allah. He was also tested with sovereignty, and thus underwent trials in prosperity as well as adversity. In both circumstances, he remained patient and feared Allah. His story was therefore among the best of narratives, and it is

---

## Page 8626

better than the accounts not related in the Quran. People may wrong others, envy them, invite them to immorality, and be tested with sovereignty. and their obedience, piety, and patient perseverance in what they did were greater than Joseph’s obedience, worship, and piety. Those are the messengers of firm resolve whom Allah singled out for mention in His words:

The point here is that, concerning His words, “the best of narratives,” some have said that the expression is a verbal noun, while others have said that it is a direct object. The two interpretations entail one another.

The correct view, however, is that al-qasas (“narrative”) functions as a direct object. Although originally a verbal noun, it came to be used predominantly for what is recounted, as with khabar (“report”) and naba’ (“tidings”). Usage indicates this, as explained earlier, and lexicographers have acknowledged it. Al-Jawharī said:

“One says, ‘He recounted the report to him,’ using qasas as the verbal noun. The noun is also qasas, with a short a vowel; it was used in place of the verbal noun until it came to predominate.”

Thus His words, “the best of narratives,” are like saying, “We tell you the best of reports,” and “We inform you of the best of tidings,”

---

## Page 8637

and “We relate to you the finest discourse.”

The word kalām (“speech”) may denote the act expressed by kallamahu taklīman (“he spoke to him”), or it may denote the utterance itself. An utterance involves an act on the speaker’s part, which is what the verbal noun denotes, and the utterance arises from that act. Thus, an utterance is sometimes regarded as a kind of action, because it results from an activity, and sometimes as a separate category alongside action, as when one says, “speech and action.” The same distinction may apply to qasas (“narrative”), bayān (“explanation”), hadīth (“discourse”), khabar (“report”), and similar words.

When qasas and similar words are intended as verbal nouns denoting the act, that act necessarily entails an utterance, which follows from it. When they denote the speech or utterance itself, this necessarily entails an act and follows from that act.

Verbal nouns formed according to the regular patterns of their verbs denote the act, as in kallamtuhu taklīman (“I spoke to him”) and akhbartuhu ikhbāran (“I informed him”). By contrast, forms that do not follow the regular patterns of their verbs—such as kalām (“speech”), khabar (“report”), and the like—denote the utterance when used without qualification. The same may be said of qasas, since the regular verbal noun of its verb is qass, just as one says ‘addahu ‘addan (“he counted it”), maddahu maddan (“he extended it”), and likewise qassahu qassan (“he recounted it”).

Qasas, however, is not the regular verbal-noun form of a verb whose second and third root consonants are identical. The only evidence they have cited for its being a verbal noun is His statement:

“So they retraced their footsteps.”

Yet this does not establish that it is a verbal noun. Rather, it may be an action noun used in place of the verbal noun, as in His statement:

“And Allah has caused you to grow as a growth from the earth.”

Even if qasas is taken to be the verbal noun of qassa al-athar (“he followed the tracks”), it does not follow that it is the verbal noun of qassa al-hadīth (“he recounted the discourse”). For a discourse is a report and tidings; thus, qasas is like khabar (“report”), naba’ (“tidings”), and kalām (“speech”).

---

## Page 8638

In matters of speech, action nouns encompass the utterance itself and indicate the speaker’s act by inclusion and necessary implication. Thus, saying kalām (“speech”), khabar (“report”), hadīth (“discourse”), naba’ (“tidings”), and qasas (“narrative”) is not like saying taklīm (“speaking to someone”), inbā’ (“giving tidings”), ikhbār (“informing”), and tahdīth (“relating”). Hence it is said to be accusative as a direct object. An action noun can also be accusative in the role of a verbal noun, as in His statement:

“And Allah has caused you to grow as a growth from the earth.”

When someone says, “I spoke good words to him” (kallamtuhu kalāman hasanan), “I related a pleasant account to him” (haddathtuhu hadīthan tayyiban), “I conveyed glad news to him” (akhbartuhu akhbāran sārratan), “I recounted true stories to him” (qasastu ‘alayhi qisasan sādiqatan), and similar expressions, these nouns are accusative as direct objects. This is unlike saying kallamtuhu taklīman (“I spoke to him”) or anba’tuhu inbā’an (“I informed him”).

It is therefore clear that His words “the best of stories” are accusative as a direct object. Everything Allah recounts is the best of stories. However, since such an expression encompasses both the meaning of the verbal noun and that of the direct object, its accusative case may be understood in both senses, for they necessarily entail one another. You say, “I uttered good words” (qultu qawlan hasanan), and “I made him hear an utterance” (asma‘tuhu qawlan). He did not hear the act denoted by the verbal noun; rather, he heard the sound. You also say, qāla, yaqūlu, qawlan (“he said; he says; saying”), thus treating qawl as a verbal noun. Yet the sound itself is not what the verbal noun denotes. What it denotes is the act that necessarily entails the sound, though the two are inseparable.

For this reason, the people of the Sunnah and hadith disagreed concerning recitation and the Quran: is recitation the Quran being recited, or not? Ibn Qutaybah and others noted a point relevant to this meaning and discussed it. The confusion arises because what is recited is the Quran itself, which is speech. “Recitation” may refer to this, or it may refer to the reciter’s actual movement

---

## Page 8639

and action, or it may refer to both together. Whoever says, “Recitation is what is recited,” means by “recitation” the Quran itself as heard, which is indeed what is recited. Whoever says that it is something different means by “recitation” the servant’s movement and action, which are not the Quran. Those who prohibit saying either “Recitation is what is recited” or “Recitation is different from what is recited” do so because the term “recitation” encompasses both meanings. Likewise, Imam Ahmad and others prohibited saying, “My utterance of the Quran is created,” or “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” This is because “utterance” may mean the words uttered themselves, which are Allah’s speech, or it may mean the act expressed by the verbal noun of “to utter,” which is the servant’s action.

Some of the people of hadith stated without qualification, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated,” while others stated without qualification, “My utterance of it is created.” Ibn Qutaybah said, “The people of hadith have not disagreed over any of their positions except on the question of utterance.” This was the disagreement among the people of hadith and the Sunnah who lived in the time of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and his companions who knew him.

After them came a group who said, “Recitation is different from what is recited.” By “recitation” they meant Allah’s actual Arabic speech, which is the Quran, while by “what is recited” they meant a single meaning subsisting in Allah’s essence.

Others said, “Recitation is what is recited.” By “recitation” they meant the actual sounds heard when the Quran is recited. They regarded those audible sounds as the very speech that is uncreated, failing to distinguish between hearing speech from its speaker and hearing it from someone conveying it on his behalf. Each of these two groups thus introduced innovations that none of the people of the Sunnah and knowledge had previously asserted. There was therefore no one among the people of

They differed, however, concerning the servants’ recitation of it: is it the Quran itself, or the act by which one recites the Quran? ## Page 8641

what the verbal noun denotes—namely, the act itself—for that cannot be heard. His saying,

is of this kind: it means “We read to you the best of accounts” or “We recite to you the best of accounts,” as He Most High says:

The well-known grammatical analysis of His saying, “When you recite the Quran,” is that “the Quran” is in the accusative as the direct object. The same applies to “the best of accounts.” Yet both also carry the meaning of a verbal noun, as explained above. Thus, both the direct-object sense and the verbal-noun sense are present. Sometimes the verbal-noun sense predominates, as in His saying:

“It is for Us to gather it and to recite it.”

Here, what is intended is the very act denoted by the verbal noun. At other times, the other sense predominates, as in His saying:

“Listen to it and remain silent,”

and His saying:

“Say: If mankind and jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce its like,”

and His saying:

“Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.”

In most occurrences, the word “Quran” denotes the speech itself, not the act of uttering that speech, which is what the verbal noun denotes.

Such usage is common in language: two things are invariably or usually inseparable, so the same name is applied to both. Sometimes one sense predominates, and sometimes the other; the name may also refer to either one alone. Examples include “river,” “village,” “rainspout,” and similar terms involving something contained and its container. Thus, the name encompasses both the watercourse and the flowing water. Likewise, the word

---

## Page 8642

“Allah sets forth the example of a village that was safe and secure, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place. Yet it denied Allah’s blessings, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger.”

“Or like the one who passed by a village that had fallen in upon its roofs.”

Since a village’s inhabitants are the focus of interest, it is more often they who are meant in the Book of Allah. Likewise, since water is the focus of interest in a river, it is more often what is meant, as in His saying:

“And We made rivers flow beneath them,”

and His saying:

“And We caused a river to flow between them.”

This usage is common—more common than saying, “We dug the river.” Likewise, the word “Quran” is applied more often to the speech itself than to the act of speaking. The same applies to the terms “speech,” “saying,” and “accounts,” and all other forms of

---

## Page 8643

speech: these terms refer more often to the speech itself than to the speaker’s act. These matters can be discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that His saying, Most High:

“We relate to you the best of narratives,”

refers to the speech that constitutes the best of narratives. It encompasses everything Allah has related; He did not restrict it to Surah Yūsuf. Hence He said:

“Through Our revelation to you of this Quran,”

and did not say, “Through Our revelation to you of this surah.” All the reports transmitted from the early generations on this matter support this understanding. They also show that they believed the Quran to be superior to all other scriptures, which is the point at issue.

The intended conclusion holds whichever interpretation is adopted. Whether “the best of narratives” denotes the act of narration, what is narrated, or both, it indicates that the Quran and the narratives it contains are better than others. We have already explained that the two are inseparable: whichever is better, the other must also be better. Thus, His saying, Most High:

“The best of narratives,”

is like His saying:

“Allah has sent down the best of speech.”

The reports from the early generations support this.

The early generations acknowledged that the Quran is the best of speech and the best of narratives, just as it is the guardian over the heavenly scriptures that preceded it. How, then, can it be said that, throughout Allah’s speech, no part is superior to any other?

Ibn Abī Hātim narrated from al-Masʿūdī, on the authority of al-Qāsim:

“The Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, grew weary and said, ‘Speak to us, O Messenger of Allah.’ So Allah revealed:

‘We relate to you the best of narratives.’

Then they grew weary again and said, ‘Speak to us, O Messenger of Allah.’ Then the following was revealed:

‘Allah has sent down the best of speech.’

---

## Page 8644

Then they grew weary once more and said, ‘Speak to us, O Messenger of Allah.’ So Allah revealed:

‘Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humbly submit to the remembrance of Allah and the truth that has been revealed?’”

‘These are the verses of the clear Book.’

and he recited it to them for some time.”

Since the Quran is the best of speech, they were forbidden to follow anything else. Allah Most High said:

Al-Nasā’ī and others reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saw a portion of the Torah in ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb’s hand and said:

For this reason, the Companions were forbidden to follow books other than the Quran. ʿUmar benefited from this lesson, so much so that when Alexandria was conquered and many books of the Romans were found there, they wrote to ʿUmar about them. He ordered that they be burned, saying, “The Book of Allah is sufficient for us.”

Ibn Abī Hātim reported: My father narrated to us; Ismāʿīl ibn Khalīl narrated to us; ʿAlī ibn Mushir narrated to us; ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Ishāq narrated to us, from Khalīfah ibn Qays, from Khālid ibn ʿUrfutah, who said:

“He replied, ‘Yes.’

“He asked, ‘And are you the one residing in al-Sūs?’

This indicates that “the best of accounts” encompasses all of this. Indeed, the word “accounts” includes what the prophets related of Allah’s verses, beyond accounts of past nations, as in His words, Most High:

“Did there not come to you messengers from among yourselves, relating My verses to you and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours? They will say, ‘We bear witness against ourselves.’”

Elsewhere He says:

“Reciting to you the verses of your Lord.”

And He, Most High, has said: “And We have sent down to you
