## Page 8647

the Book in truth, confirming the Scriptures that came before it and as a guardian over them.”

Ibn Abī Hātim reported through the well-known chain of transmission that Ibn 'Abbās said: “Entrusted with them.” He said: “It is also reported from 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan, Sa'īd ibn Jubayr and 'Atā' al-Khurāsānī that it means ‘the trustworthy one.’”

In al-Wālibī’s commentary, Ibn 'Abbās is reported to have said: “The guardian is the trustworthy one,” adding: “Over every Book that preceded it.” Likewise, al-Hasan said: “Confirming these Books and entrusted with them.”

Also in al-Wālibī’s commentary, Ibn 'Abbās explained “and as a guardian over them” as meaning “a witness.” Al-Suddī likewise reported this from Ibn 'Abbās. Concerning the words “and as a guardian over them,” he said: “Over every Book that preceded it.”

He said: “Similar explanations are reported from Sa'īd ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, 'Atiyyah, 'Atā' al-Khurāsānī, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Qatādah, al-Suddī and 'Abd al-Rahmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.”

At the beginning of his commentary, Ibn Abī Hātim mentioned that he had been asked to compile a concise commentary on the Quran using the soundest chains of transmission. He stated that he sought to include reports with the soundest chains and the fullest texts, and he provided his chain of transmission to everyone from whom he quoted anything.

Thus, all the early generations agree that the Quran is the guardian, the trustworthy custodian and the witness over the Scriptures that preceded it. It is well known that a guardian over something is higher in rank than it. Among Allah’s names is “al-Muhaymin” (the Overseer). A ruler who manages people’s affairs is also called a guardian.

Al-Mubarrid, al-Jawharī and others said: “In the language, al-muhaymin means the one entrusted with something.” Al-Khalīl said: “The watchful protector.” Al-Khattābī said: “Al-Muhaymin is

---

## Page 8648

the Witness.”

He added that some linguists defined guardianship as overseeing something and caring for it. He cited the verse:

“Indeed, the best of people after their Prophet
Is their guardian, who follows him in good and ill.”

He means the one who oversees people and cares for them.

There are two views concerning the word muhaymin (guardian). According to one, its original form is mu’aymin, with the letter h replacing the hamzah; according to the other, the h is an original root letter.

Such is the Quran: it affirms what the earlier Scriptures contain of accounts concerning Allah and the Last Day, while providing further clarification and detail. It sets out the evidence and proofs for these matters, affirms the prophethood of all the Prophets and the missions of the Messengers, and confirms the universal laws with which all the Messengers were sent.

It argues against those who deny the Scriptures and the Messengers, using various arguments and proofs. It explains Allah’s punishments of them and His support for those who followed the Scriptures and adhered to them. It makes clear what has been distorted and altered in those Scriptures, and what the People of the Book have done to the earlier Scriptures. It also makes clear what they concealed of that which Allah commanded them to disclose, as well as everything brought by the prophetic revelations, through the finest laws and ways revealed in the Quran.

Thus, the Quran has guardianship over the Scriptures that preceded it in numerous respects. It bears witness to their truth and to the falsehood of what has been distorted in them. It judges by upholding what Allah has upheld and abrogating what He has abrogated. Thus, it is a witness in matters of fact and a judge in matters of command.

---

## Page 8649

Likewise, “bearing witness” and “judging” entail affirming what Allah has affirmed as true and as remaining in force, and invalidating what He has declared false or abrogated. Neither the Gospel nor the Psalms occupy this position in relation to the Torah. Rather, they follow the Torah’s law, apart from the few provisions Allah abrogated through the Gospel. The Quran, however, is different.

Moreover, the Quran is itself miraculous: created beings cannot produce anything like it. It contains the Messenger’s call and is itself his sign and proof of his truthfulness and prophethood. It contains what the Messenger brought and is itself proof of what he brought. It also presents parables and explains signs demonstrating the superiority of what the Messenger brought, such that, were the knowledge of all scholars gathered together and compared with it, their knowledge would amount to only part of what the Quran contains.

Whoever reflects on what earlier and later generations have said concerning the foundations of religion, knowledge of divine matters, the Hereafter, prophethood, ethics, governance, worship, and everything else through which souls attain perfection, righteousness, happiness, and salvation will find that earlier and later generations—whether followers of prophetic revelation or proponents of reason, such as philosophers and others—possess only part of what the Quran has brought.

Thus, with its Messenger and its Book, this community has had no need of another prophet or another book, much less of anything else that cannot stand on its own—whether the knowledge of those granted inspired insight and those who receive inspiration, or the knowledge of those who engage in rational inquiry and analogy without also holding fast to a Book sent down from heaven. This is why the Prophet said

---

## Page 8650

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—in an authentic hadith:

“Among the nations before you were men granted inspired insight. If there is anyone of this kind in my community, it is Umar.”

He thus made their presence in his own community conditional, while affirming it decisively of earlier communities. This is because the communities before us needed people granted inspired insight, just as they needed one prophet after another. As for the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Allah has made their Messenger and their Book sufficient for them, leaving them in no need of anything else. Thus, even from someone among them granted inspired insight, such as Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, only what accords with the Book and the Sunnah is accepted. If something is conveyed to his heart, he may not accept it until he has tested it against the Book and the Sunnah. Nor may he accept it unless it accords with the Book and the Sunnah. This is an extensive subject concerning the merits of the Quran over everything else.

The point is to show that matters such as this were firmly established in the minds of the community’s earliest generations and those who followed them. No one among the early generations was ever known to reject such a thing or to say, “No part of Allah’s speech can be nobler than another, for all of it belongs to Allah’s attributes,” or anything similar. Such rejection arose only when the innovations of the Jahmiyyah appeared—those who differed concerning the Book and divided it into parts.

Among those who discussed “the intrinsic superiority of some parts of the Quran over others” were followers of al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others, including Shaykh Abū Hāmid al-Isfarāyīnī, Judge Abū al-Tayyib, Abū Ishāq al-Shīrāzī, and others; likewise, Judge Abū Ya‘lā, al-Halwānī the Elder and his son ‘Abd al-Rahmān, and Ibn ‘Aqīl. Abū al-Wafā’ Ibn ‘Aqīl said in

---

## Page 8651

*al-Wādih fī Usūl al-Fiqh* (The Clear Exposition of the Principles of Jurisprudence), in his argument that the Quran cannot be abrogated by the Sunnah:

“One such proof is His saying:

‘Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or like it.’

The Sunnah is neither like the Quran nor better than it. Abrogation by the Sunnah is therefore ruled out, since it would entail an impossibility: His statement would not correspond to what it reports. That is impossible for Allah, and whatever entails it is likewise impossible.”

He said:

“If it is objected: ‘Your argument rests on the premise that “better” means superior in excellence. Yet that is not what is intended. Rather, the meaning is: “We bring one better than it for you.” For us, this amounts to one of two things: either an easier obligation, which is an immediate benefit, or a greater reward because the obligation is more burdensome and difficult, which brings benefit in the Hereafter and in the final outcome. Both may be brought about through the Sunnah.

‘Another possible meaning is: “We bring something better than it,” not as an abrogating replacement, but as an entirely new obligation that is better for you, even if it is conveyed neither through an abrogating Quranic passage nor through an abrogating Sunnah.’

They say: ‘These interpretations are supported by the fact that no part of the Quran itself is better than another. Thus, they must interpret the expression beyond its apparent meaning, so that “better” refers to the obligation rather than to the means by which it is conveyed.’”

In reply, he said:

“Their contention that ‘better’ refers to an ease or reward specific to us is unsound. Had He intended that, He would have said, ‘for you.’ His omission of those words therefore indicates the unrestricted meaning of the expression: that the abrogating passage is better both in itself, intrinsically, and in the benefit derived from it in this life and the Hereafter. Moreover, its apparent meaning requires

---

## Page 8652

verses better than those abrogated, for the comparison concerns things of the same kind. Thus, if someone says, ‘I never take a dinar from you without giving you something better than it,’ the unqualified statement can only be understood to mean a better dinar. Superiority is thus sought first within the same kind, and then in the benefit it offers. It cannot refer instead to a garment or some commodity other than a dinar.

The end of the verse also indicates that He intended the Quran, for He says:

‘Do you not know that Allah has power over all things?’

His description of Himself as powerful indicates that what He brings is something that belongs to Him alone, to the exclusion of others. Likewise, His words,

‘or like it,’

support what we have stated, because an unqualified comparison of likeness entails likeness in every respect. This is especially so since He uses a feminine pronoun referring to a verse. It is as though He said: ‘We bring a verse better than it, or a verse like it.’”

I say:

Furthermore, ‘better’ cannot mean that the prescribed action is easier, or that it is more difficult and carries a greater reward. These two descriptions apply to everything Allah commands, whether as an initial prescription or as an abrogating replacement. It is either easier than something else in this world, or more difficult and therefore greater in reward. Since this characteristic necessarily applies to all rulings, it would not be apt to say: ‘Whatever ruling We abrogate, We bring one better than it or like it.’ For, on this understanding, the abrogated ruling could likewise be better or equal. If they interpret ‘better’ as meaning easier, the abrogated ruling might be easier and thus better. If they interpret it as meaning greater in reward because of its difficulty, the abrogated ruling might also fit that description. Yet Allah has declared that He will necessarily bring something better than what He abrogates, or something like it; He does not bring something inferior to it.

---

## Page 8653

Furthermore, on their interpretation, nothing would be better than anything else: if one thing were better in being easier, the other would be better in carrying a greater reward.

Ibn ʿAqīl said:

“As for their claim that the Quran itself admits no differences in excellence or superiority, and that ‘better’ therefore cannot mean superior, this is not so. The affirmation of Allah’s oneness in Sūrat al-Ikhlās, including its denial that He can be partitioned or divided, is superior to Sūrat Tabbat, which condemns Abū Lahab and his wife. You may consider this in terms of praise being superior to censure, or in terms of inimitability: reciting other verses whose eloquence and clarity are manifest is superior. The fact that the Speaker is one does not preclude differences in excellence on another level, for reasons pertaining to the speech itself. Likewise, the One who sent Jonah and Abraham is one, yet Abraham is superior to Jonah.”

He said:

“As for their claim that ‘We bring one better than it’ refers not to an abrogating replacement but to an independent prescription, this is incorrect. The verb occurs in the jussive as the consequence of a condition, which conveys substitution and reciprocity. This is like saying, ‘If you honour me, I will honour you,’ or ‘If you obey me, I will obey you.’ Such wording requires the consequence to be a corresponding response and replacement, not an independently initiated act.”

I say:

The purpose here is to mention the position he defended—that some parts of the Quran are, in themselves, better than others—not to discuss the question of abrogation. Others besides these scholars have also explicitly stated that some parts of the Quran may be better than others. Among those who mentioned this was Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī in his book Jawāhir al-Qurʾān (The Jewels of the Quran). He said:

---

## Page 8654

“Perhaps you will say: ‘These observations of yours aim to establish the superiority of some Quranic verses over others. Yet all of it is Allah’s speech. How, then, can its verses differ from one another? How can some be nobler than others?’

“Know that if the light of insight does not guide you to the distinction between the Verse of the Throne and the verse on debts, or between Sūrat al-Ikhlās and Sūrat Tabbat, and your fainthearted soul, steeped in blind imitation, recoils from acknowledging such distinctions, then follow the bearer of the revealed Law—Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him. It was to him that the Quran was revealed, and he said:

‘Yā Sīn is the heart of the Quran.’

“The reports establish that some parts are nobler than others. He said:

‘The Opening of the Book is the best surah of the Quran.’

“He also said:

‘The Verse of the Throne is the foremost verse of the Quran.’

“And he said:

‘“Say: He is Allah, One” equals one-third of the Quran.’

“The reports concerning the merits of the Quran’s powerful passages, and the particular excellence of certain surahs and verses and the abundant reward for reciting them, are innumerable. Consult the books of hadith for them if you wish. We shall now draw your attention to the meaning of these four reports concerning the superiority of these surahs.”

I say:

Allah willing, we shall mention his explanation of the superiority of “Say: He is Allah, One.” Among those who discussed the scholars’ views on this subject and attributed this position to certain early scholars was al-Qādī ‘Iyād in his Commentary on Sahīh Muslim. Commenting on the Prophet’s words to Ubayy—“Do you know which verse in Allah’s Book is the greatest?”—and his mention of the Verse of the Throne, he said:

“This provides evidence that some parts of the Quran are superior to others

---

## Page 8655

and that the Quran is superior to Allah’s other Books, according to those who hold this view, including Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh and other scholars and theologians.”

He said:

“This refers to the great reward granted to those who recite these passages, and to the more abundant recompense for some parts than for others.”

He said:

“This is a matter on which the scholars have differed. Al-Ash‘arī, Ibn al-Bāqillānī, and a number of jurists and scholars rejected this, because superiority implies that the less excellent falls short of the more excellent, whereas Allah’s speech is indivisible. They said: ‘Where certain verses and surahs are described as “best” or “greatest,” the meaning is that they are excellent and great.’”

He said:

“It has also been said that the Verse of the Throne is the greatest because it encompasses the fundamental divine names and attributes: divinity, life, oneness, knowledge, dominion, power, and will. These seven, they said, are the foundations of the divine names and attributes.”

I say:

What concerns us here is his account of the scholars’ statements. As for the assertion that these seven are the foundations of the divine names, many theologians regard these seven as those known through reason, while maintaining that all others are known only through revelation. This, however, concerns how we come to know them, not an objective reality inherent in them. How, then, can this be so, when the majority hold that other attributes can also be known through reason, such as love, pleasure, commanding, and forbidding?

The position of Ibn Kullāb and most early scholars who affirmed the divine attributes is that Allah’s being above is among the attributes knowable through reason. This is also the position of Abū al-‘Abbās al-Qalānisī and al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī, as well as various groups of theologians, hadith scholars, and jurists. It was also the later of the two views held by al-Qādī

---

## Page 8656

Abū Ya‘lā and Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī, among others, as well as the position of Ibn Karrām and his followers. It is also the view of the general body of leading scholars of hadith, jurisprudence, and Sufism.

Likewise, al-Qādī ‘Iyād’s explanation that those who affirm superiority mean a greater reward concerns something that al-Ash‘arī and Ibn al-Bāqillānī do not dispute. Reward is, after all, one of the things Allah Most High has created, and no one disputes that some of it is better than other parts. The disagreement concerns Allah’s speech itself, which is His speech. Thus, his account of the disagreement contradicts his explanation of the position of those who affirm superiority.

He has explained the reasoning of those who reject such superiority. Some deny any degrees of superiority among the attributes whatsoever, on the grounds that what is eternal admits no degrees of superiority, and the Quran is one of the attributes. Others single out the Quran on the grounds that, according to their fundamental premise, it is one indivisible whole: two distinct meanings cannot be conceived within it, let alone anything superior or inferior. This is the fundamental premise of Abū al-Hasan and those who agree with him, as we shall explain, if Allah Most High wills.

None of those whose statements we have cited affirming that some of Allah’s speech is superior to other parts holds that Allah’s speech is created, as is maintained by certain adherents of innovation, such as the Jahmiyyah and the Mu‘tazilah. Rather, all of them say:

“Allah’s speech is uncreated.”

Were all those who held this view to be listed, they would be numerous, for this is the position of the vast majority of Muslims, earlier and later, both adherents of the Sunnah and adherents of innovation. As for the early generations—such as the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness—no disagreement among them is known concerning this principle. Rather, it is affirmed by mass-transmitted reports from them.

---

## Page 8657

The denial that some of Allah’s speech is superior to other parts became widespread after the year 200 AH, when the Jahmiyyah openly proclaimed that the Quran was created. The leading scholars of the Sunnah and the vast majority of the Muslim community agreed in rejecting and refuting this claim. A large group—including Abū Muhammad ibn Kullāb and those who agreed with him—thought that this claim could only be refuted by maintaining that Allah has not spoken by His will and power; that He did not speak to Moses when Moses came to Him, nor say to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” after creating him; that He does not become angry with anyone after that person disbelieves in Him, nor become pleased with him after he obeys Him, nor love him after he draws near to Him through voluntary acts of worship; and that He does not utter one speech after another, such that His words would be without end—along with other things they thought must be denied of Allah.

They said that these people could only be opposed by maintaining that the Quran and all His other speech are inseparable from Allah Most High’s essence, and that He has always been, and will always be, uttering every utterance of His, such as:

“O Adam! O Noah!”

They divided into two groups. One group says that His speech is a single meaning subsisting in His essence. The other says that it consists of letters, or letters and sounds, conjoined with one another from all eternity and for all eternity, although they have an intrinsic sequence, not a sequence in which they come into existence. The various views concerning Allah’s speech have been explained elsewhere. According to the first group, Allah’s speech is a single thing with no parts, so there can be no question of some parts being superior to others.

The other group says:

“It is eternal and inseparable from His essence, and what is eternal admits no degrees of superiority.”

It is sometimes reported from some of the early generations, concerning the words of the Most High,

“We bring forth one better than it,”

---

## Page 8658

that he said:

“Better for you than it, or more beneficial to you.”

Someone might therefore suppose that the person who said this agreed with those people. But that is not so. Rather, his purpose was to explain in what respect it is better: namely, that it is more beneficial to people. For speech that is more beneficial to people is also intrinsically superior, as explained elsewhere.

Those among the later followers of Ahmad, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī and others who followed the path of the Kullābiyyah came to think that affirming the superiority of some of Allah’s speech over other parts was possible only according to the position of the Mu‘tazilah and others like them who say that it is created. Those who say it is created regard the superiority of some parts over others as the superiority of one created thing over another; and no one denies that some created things are superior to others.

Thus, when those people supposed that affirming the superiority of some of Allah’s speech over other parts necessarily implied that the Quran was created, they recoiled from this affirmation and rejected it because of the necessary connection they imagined. Yet the matter is not as they supposed. Rather, the early generations of the Muslim community and its vast majority say:

“The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated; likewise, all the rest of Allah’s speech is uncreated.”

At the same time, they say:

“Some of Allah’s speech is superior to other parts,”

as expressly stated in the Book, the Sunnah, and the reports from the Companions and their Successors, with no known disagreement among them concerning this.

My father related to us, on the authority of our grandfather Abū al-Barakāt and his companion Abū Abd Allāh ibn Abd al-Wahhāb, that they had examined the views mentioned by one of the Quran commentators concerning His words:

“We bring forth one better than it or similar to it.”

I believe they were consulting the Quran commentary of Abū Abd

---

## Page 8659

Allāh Muhammad ibn Taymiyyah. When they saw those views, they said, “This is consistent only with the position of the Mu‘tazilah.”

This same Abū Abd Allāh ibn Abd al-Wahhāb once visited our shaykh Abū Zakariyyā ibn al-Sayrafī while the latter was ill. Abū Zakariyyā offered a supplication transmitted from Imam Ahmad, which included these words:

“I ask You—by Your power through which You were able to say to the heavens and the earth, ‘Come, willingly or unwillingly,’ and they said, ‘We come willingly’—to do such and such for us.”

When the people had left, he said to him, “What is this supplication you have offered? This is consistent only with the position of the Mu‘tazilah, who say that the Quran is created. As for Ahl al-Sunnah, according to them, it is not said that He was able to speak or say something, for His speech is eternal, inseparable from His essence, and unconnected to His will and power.”

Abū Abd Allāh ibn Abd al-Wahhāb—may Allah have mercy on him—had derived this from the discussions presented by Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī and others like him; before him, by Abū al-Wafā’ ibn ‘Aqīl and others like him; and before them both, by al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā and others of his kind. These men, their counterparts among the followers of Mālik and al-Shāfi‘ī—such as Abū al-Walīd al-Bājī and Abū al-Ma‘ālī al-Juwaynī—and a group of Abū Hanīfah’s followers agree with Ibn Kullāb’s assertion that Allah does not speak by His will and power, and with his assertion that the Quran is inseparable from Allah’s essence. Indeed, they suppose that this is the position of the early generations—the position of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and all the other early scholars—who say that the Quran is uncreated. This goes so far that those among them who followed the path of the Sālimiyyah—such as al-Qādī, Ibn ‘Aqīl, and Ibn

---

## Page 8660

al-Zāghūnī—explicitly assert that Ahmad’s position is that the Quran is eternal and consists of letters and sounds. Yet Ahmad ibn Hanbal and the other three imams never said this or argued in its defense. Rather, these men and other followers of the four imams were unfamiliar with their positions on certain issues.

Those who supposed that the position of Ibn Kullāb and his followers represented the position of the early generations and their affirmation that the Quran is uncreated were the ones who began to say:

“The view that some of Allah’s speech is superior to other parts is consistent only with the position of the people of innovation—the Jahmiyyah and the Mu‘tazilah.”

Various groups among the imams’ followers likewise came to say this, as we shall show by citing statements from some followers of Mālik and al-Shāfi‘ī. They did not know that none of the early generations had held this position. Rather, they rejected this principle of Ibn Kullāb, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others instructed people to shun the Kullābiyyah on account of it. Even al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī was shunned because he was an associate of Ibn Kullāb and had agreed with him on this principle. It was subsequently reported, however, that he retracted that view. Ahmad used to warn against the Kullābiyyah.

A dispute over this principle also arose between Abū Bakr ibn Khuzaymah, known as the Imam of Imams, and some of his associates, because they held Ibn Kullāb’s position. Al-Hākim Abū Abd Allāh al-Naysābūrī related their account in The History of Nishapur.

A detailed discussion of this principle belongs elsewhere. Here we have merely drawn attention to the underlying grounds through which the true nature of these positions can be understood.

---

## Page 8661

Section

In sum, the evidence from the prophetic texts, reports from the early generations, rulings of Islamic law, and rational arguments that some of Allah’s speech is superior to other parts is clear and well known.

Moreover, the Quran is entirely Allah’s speech, as are the Torah, the Gospel, and the divine hadiths that the Messenger relates from Allah, blessed and exalted is He, such as His words:

“O My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another”—and the rest of the hadith;

and His words:

“Whoever remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself.”

Although these and similar texts are alike in being Allah’s speech, it is well known that speech has two relationships: a relationship to the speaker and a relationship to its subject matter. Speech thus varies in excellence with respect to both relationships, and also in itself. Declarative speech, for example, has two relationships: one to the speaker who conveys the information, and another to the subject about which that information is conveyed.

Thus, “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” and “May the hands of Abū Lahab perish” are both Allah’s speech and are alike in this respect. Yet they differ in excellence with respect to their subject matter. The former is Allah’s speech, His account of Himself, and His description of Himself

---

## Page 8662

and His speech in which He speaks about Himself. The latter is Allah’s speech in which He speaks about some of His creation, gives an account of them, and describes their condition. In this respect, the two differ in excellence according to the relative excellence of the meanings intended by each.

Do you not see that a created being utters words that are all his own speech, yet his words mentioning his Lord are greater than his words mentioning some created things, although all are his speech? Thus, the fact that two utterances share the same relationship to their speaker does not preclude their differing in excellence with respect to their subject matter, whether both relationships, or either one of them, entail superiority or not.

Thus, some of the speech of the prophets—and then of scholars, orators, and poets—is superior to other parts, even when the speaker is the same. The same applies to the speech of angels and jinn. Whether ‘speech’ means the meanings alone, the words alone, both together, or each separately, there is no doubt that the words and meanings expressed by a single speaker differ in excellence. This shows that the mere fact that two utterances have the same speaker does not require them to be alike in every other respect.

That speech differs in excellence according to its subject matter, whether declarative or non-declarative, is known through both innate human nature and revealed law. A statement containing praise of Allah and extolling Him by His most beautiful names is not like a statement mentioning Abū Lahab, Pharaoh, and Iblīs, even though the latter is great and revered speech spoken by Allah. Nor is the command to affirm Allah’s oneness, to believe in Allah and His Messenger, and to uphold other fundamentals of religion enjoined

---

## Page 8663

by all revealed laws, along with other commands to perform great duties and prohibitions against associating partners with Allah, taking a life, unlawful sexual intercourse, and similar acts forbidden by all revealed laws and entailing grave corruption, like the command to lick one’s fingers and remove any dirt from a fallen morsel, or the prohibition against eating dates two at a time. Even if both commands are obligatory, the command to believe in Allah and His Messenger is not like the command to dress properly for every prayer, or the command to provide for a pregnant woman and pay her wages if she breastfeeds.

For this reason, the majority of jurists hold that obligations and prohibitions vary in degree. They say:

“Making one of two acts obligatory may be more emphatic than making the other obligatory, and prohibiting one may be more stringent than prohibiting the other. Thus, this act is more strongly obligatory, and that act more strictly prohibited.”

However, a group of speculative theologians, including Ibn ʿAqīl and others, disputed this, saying: “The difference in degree does not lie in obligation and prohibition themselves, but in what is associated with them: the magnitude of reward and punishment.”

The majority say:

“Rather, the difference in degree exists in both respects. Differences in effects indicate differences in their causes. That the reward and punishment associated with one of two acts are greater shows that the command or prohibition concerning it is more emphatic. No rational person doubts that one of two commands or prohibitions may receive particular emphasis that the other does not. Were they equal in every respect, neither could be singled out for emphasis or any other factor giving it precedence, for equality and superiority are mutually opposed.”

The majority of leading jurists hold that obligation and prohibition vary in degree, and the unqualified affirmation of

---

## Page 8664

this is the view held by the vast majority of later followers of the four imams. It is the view of Judge Abū Yaʿlā, Abū al-Khattāb, Judge Yaʿqūb al-Barzabīnī, ʿAbd al-Rahmān al-Halwānī, Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī, and others. Some of them, however, explain this variation in degree as differences in reward and punishment and similar matters that those who deny such variation do not dispute. The correct understanding is that love, pleasure, hatred, will, honor, demand, requirement, and similar meanings themselves vary in degree, as do the expressions that signify them.

The servants’ love for their Lord itself varies in degree, as Allah Most High says:

“But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah.”

Allah’s love for them likewise varies in degree. His two intimate friends, Abraham and Muhammad, are dearer to Him than anyone else, and some deeds are dearer to Allah than others. Statements such as “This deed is dearer to me than that one” are well known and widely reported in prophetic traditions and the words of the best of creation. For example, some of the Companions said:

“If we knew which deeds were dearest to Allah, we would perform them.”

Allah then revealed Sūrat al-Saff. This is a well-known, established report, narrated by al-Tirmidhī and others. That one thing is dearer to Allah than another falls under the favoring of some deeds and people over others, and of some places and times over others. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Mecca:

“By Allah, you are the best of Allah’s lands and the dearest of Allah’s lands to Allah. Had my people not driven me out of you, I would not have left.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “A good, authentic hadith.” He narrated it from

---

## Page 8665

the report of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAdī ibn al-Hamrā’. Likewise, His love and hatred surpass those of others, as related in the two Sahīh collections from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“No one loves praise more than Allah; for that reason He praised Himself. No one loves accepting an excuse more than Allah; for that reason He sent messengers bearing glad tidings and warnings.”

He also said:

“No one has greater protective jealousy than Allah.”

This too is in the two Sahīh collections. Allah Most High says:

“Allah’s hatred is indeed greater than your hatred of yourselves,”

to the end of the verse.

It is self-evident that commanded acts differ in excellence: some are better than others, and some prohibited acts are worse than others. Accordingly, the demand for what is superior is itself more perfect than the demand for what is inferior. If the one making the demand is wise, his demand for the former will be more emphatic.

In short, it is firmly established in the natural disposition of rational people that both statements and commands vary in excellence according to what is reported and what is commanded. When what is reported is more perfect and excellent, the statement conveying it is more excellent; and when what is commanded is more excellent, the command enjoining it is more excellent.

Thus, information concerning what delivers souls from punishment and brings eternal happiness is more excellent than information concerning what brings rank or a sum of money. A dream conveying the better of these two kinds of news is greater than a dream conveying the lesser. This is firmly established in the natural disposition of all rational people.

If we suppose two rulers, one of whom commands comprehensive justice through which he brings prosperity to the land and wards off corruption, this command is greater than the command of a ruler who

---

## Page 8666

administers justice between two disputants over a deceased person’s estate.

Furthermore, a statement entails knowledge of what is reported, while a command entails a demand and a will for what is commanded, even if this does not entail willing its actual execution. Allah Most High commanded His servants to do what He commanded them, but He aided the obedient and thus willed to create their performance of those acts. He did not aid the disobedient and thus did not will to create their performance of them. This creative, decretive will does not necessarily entail a command. As for will in the sense that He loves the performance of what He commands, approves of it when it is performed, and wills that the person commanded perform it insofar as that person is commanded, this is indispensable to a command. Accordingly, Allah affirmed this kind of will in relation to His commands, but not the former kind. Some people, however, erred and denied will altogether. Neither group distinguished between creative will and prescriptive will.

The Quran distinguishes between these two kinds of will. Concerning the first, Allah says:

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted.”

Noah said:

“My counsel will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray.”

Allah says:

“If Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another, but Allah does whatever He wills.”

And He says:

“Why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, ‘What Allah wills comes to pass; there is no power except through Allah’?”

Hence the Muslims say: “Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.”

Concerning the second kind, He says:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

And He says:

“Allah intends only to remove impurity from you, people of the Household, and to purify you thoroughly.”

And He says:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favour upon you.”

---

## Page 8667

And He says:

“Allah intends to make things clear to you, guide you to the ways of those before you, and accept your repentance. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

“Allah intends to accept your repentance, whereas those who follow their desires want you to deviate greatly.”

“Allah intends to lighten your burden, for mankind was created weak.”

This is discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that a command necessarily involves a request, a call for action, and a demand. This holds whether one maintains that there is a prescriptive will and that the Lord has no other will concerning His servants’ actions—as the Mu‘tazilah and similar groups among the Qadariyyah maintain—or maintains that the Lord has no will other than the creative, decretive will, concerning which it is said, “Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.”

According to this latter position, His will is identical to His love and approval; His will, love, and approval relate to everything that actually occurs, whether faith or disbelief, and do not relate to anything that does not occur, whether faith or disbelief. It also holds that a servant has no power that affects the actual occurrence of what lies within his capacity; that created things contain no powers or causes through which Allah creates; and that Allah has no wise purpose for which He creates and commands.

These and similar views are maintained by Jahm ibn Safwān, the leading figure of the Jabriyyah, and by those who agree with him on all or some of these matters: various groups of speculative theologians, some later jurists, and others who affirm divine decree in this manner rather than in the manner of the early generations and the imams, such as Abū al-Hasan and others. Their opposition to the Mu‘tazilī Qadariyyah drove them to deny the reality of commands and prohibitions, promises and threats. Yet those who hold some of these views fall into inconsistency, and one of them may affirm something in these matters that has no substantive reality.

---

## Page 8668

As for the early generations, the leading jurists, and the majority of Muslims, they affirm both creation and command: the creative, decretive will encompassing everything that occurs, and the prescriptive, legislative will encompassing everything Allah loves and approves for His servants. The latter comprises what the Messengers commanded: what benefits people, sets them right, and brings a praiseworthy, beneficial outcome in the Hereafter that wards off ruin. This prescriptive, legislative will relates to His divinity, which entails His lordship, just as the creative, decretive will relates to His lordship.

Thus, whoever considers only the latter, attending to the creative, universal, decretive will while disregarding the former, has a beginning but no culmination. He is therefore among those whose deeds bring the greatest loss. They attain some of their worldly aims by seeking Allah’s aid, since they recognize His lordship, but they have no share in the Hereafter, since they did not worship Allah with sincere devotion to Him alone. Various groups among the Sufis and speculative theologians have fallen into this.

Whoever considers the prescriptive, legislative reality while disregarding the other may attain a praiseworthy outcome and may observe the command. Yet he remains powerless and bereft of divine support, since he does not recognize Allah’s lordship and his own need of Him, so as to rely upon Him and acknowledge that he has no might or power except through Him.

Such a person may intend to worship Him without intending truly to seek His aid. This is the condition of the Qadariyyah among the Muʿtazilah and others like them, who maintain that Allah neither creates His servants’ actions nor wills the things that occur. Hence Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said:

“Only a Qadarī admires his own action, because he does not recognize that it is He who creates his action. As for the people of the Sunnah, who

---

## Page 8669

acknowledge that Allah creates their actions and that they owe Him gratitude for this—how could they admire themselves for them?” Or words to that effect.

The former may seek His help, call upon Him, rely upon Him, and disclaim any might or power except through Him. Yet he does not intend to worship Him by doing what He commanded and abandoning what He prohibited through His Messengers. Nor does he recognize that Allah loves to be worshipped and obeyed, rejoices in the repentance of those who repent, loves the righteous, and is angry with the disbelievers and hypocrites. Rather, he sheds the religion, or part of it, especially in the final stages of his path. If he follows this approach consistently, his condition becomes worse than that of the Muʿtazilī Qadariyyah. Indeed, if he follows it through to its full implications, it takes him out of the religion as completely as a hair is drawn out of dough. This is the condition of the polytheists.

As for someone whom Allah guides, he truly lives by His words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

He knows that every deed that is not done seeking Allah’s Face and does not accord with His command is rejected, and that anyone pursuing an aim without Allah’s help is thwarted in attaining it. He testifies that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah, and so worships Allah with sincere devotion to Him alone, seeking Allah’s help in doing so and believing in His creation and command: His decree and His revealed law. He seeks Allah’s help in obeying Him and thanks Him for that obedience, knowing that it is a favor Allah has bestowed upon him. He seeks refuge in Allah from the evil of his own soul and his evil deeds. He knows that whatever evil befalls him comes from himself, while also knowing that everything occurs by Allah’s decree and predestination, that Allah’s conclusive argument stands against His creation, and that His creation and command embody consummate wisdom and abundant mercy. These matters are fundamental principles of great importance, whose detailed exposition belongs elsewhere.

---

## Page 8670

The point here is that all rational people agree that a truthful statement involves knowledge and belief, while a command involves a demand. But does a statement signify a category of meaning distinct from knowledge, and a command a category of meaning distinct from will, as maintained by a group of speculative theologians such as Ibn Kullāb and those who agree with him? Or do they signify meanings belonging to knowledge and will, as maintained by the majority of the speculative theologians of Ahl al-Sunnah who affirm the divine attributes and predestination—saying, “The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated,” and, “Allah is the Creator of people’s actions”—and also by the Muʿtazilah and others who oppose Ahl al-Sunnah on these two fundamentals? These latter disagree with Ibn Kullāb and those who agree with him on those two fundamentals.

Hence it is said that none of the other groups agreed with him on the views he introduced concerning speech and the divine attributes, even though his position was better than that of the Muʿtazilah and the pure Jahmiyyah. As for the majority of Muslims—the jurists, hadith scholars, Sufis, and various groups of speculative theologians—they hold neither the position of the Muʿtazilah nor that of the Kullābiyyah. This has been stated by jurists of the various schools, including the followers of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others, in their works on the principles of jurisprudence, let alone their other books.

The point here is that people agree that every kind of statement and command conveys meanings, whether these are called demand, will, knowledge, judgment, or inward speech. These meanings differ in excellence in themselves. For our knowledge of Allah and His names is not

---

## Page 8671

like our knowledge of the state of Abū Lahab. Nor is the demand within us when we are commanded to believe in Allah and His Messenger like the demand within us when we are commanded to raise our hands in prayer, eat with the right hand, or give a dirham in zakat. This shows that the meanings conveyed by speech may differ in excellence in themselves, just as they may be equal. It also makes clear that the meanings contained in commands and prohibitions and indicated by the imperative form—whether called demand, requirement, request, will, love, approval, or something else—differ in excellence according to the relative excellence of what is commanded. Likewise, the kinds of knowledge, beliefs, and inward judgments contained in statements differ in excellence in themselves according to the relative excellence of their subject matter. This is one way in which speech differs in excellence according to its subject matter, even when the speaker is the same.

Speech also differs in excellence according to the one who utters it, even when its subject matter is the same. As the Most High says:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger to reveal, by His permission, whatever He wills.”

It is well known that His speaking from behind a veil is superior to His speaking through revelation or by sending a messenger. Thus, one of the distinctions of Moses, peace be upon him, was that Allah spoke to him directly. He said:

“I have chosen you above the people with My messages and My speaking to you.”

And He said:

“Those messengers—We favored some of them over others. Among them were those to whom Allah spoke, and He raised some of them in rank.”

What people find within themselves is that the states of one and the same person differ in excellence

---

## Page 8672

in different kinds of speech. Indeed, even within a single utterance, the meanings present in his heart and the words uttered by his tongue may differ in excellence. When making a request, he may desire, love, and seek one of two things more intensely than the other; his voice may be stronger, his wording more eloquent, and his manner of requesting more forceful and effective. Thus, when the same admonition—or even the same verse—is heard from two different people, the difference in excellence may be unmistakable to any rational person. This is too evident and well known to require an example.

Likewise, when conveying information, the recognition, knowledge, conception of what is known, and awareness of it within his heart, together with the excellence of his expression in words and voice, may far surpass what is present in his heart and on his tongue when he speaks about something else. This briefly indicates the position of those who hold that some of Allah’s speech is superior to other parts, in accordance with what the Book, the Sunnah, and the statements of the early generations and the imams indicate.

The second group maintains that no part of Allah’s speech is superior to another. They offer two interpretations of the texts that mention such superiority. The first is that differences in excellence concern only what His speech relates to: for example, some of it may be more beneficial to people than other parts because it brings greater reward, or because acting upon it is easier while the reward remains the same. They interpret His words:

“We bring one better than it”

to mean: We bring one that is better for you, not that it is intrinsically better than the other. This is the position of a group of Quran commentators, including Muhammad ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī, who said:

“We bring a ruling better for you than the ruling of the abrogated verse: either in this life, because it is less burdensome

---

## Page 8673

for you, or in the Hereafter, because its reward is greater on account of the hardship of bearing it.”

He said: “What is meant is: ‘Whatever ruling of a verse We abrogate,’ just as in His words, ‘Their hearts were imbued with the calf because of their disbelief’—meaning, love of it.” He said: “That this is so is indicated by His words, ‘We bring one better than it or similar to it.’ It is not possible for any part of the Quran to be better than another, because all of it is Allah’s speech. Nor is it permissible to say of Allah’s attributes that some are more excellent or better than others.”

He extended this reasoning to Allah’s names, denying that any of His names could be greater, more excellent, or grander than another. He said: “The ‘greatest name’ means the ‘great name’; all His names are equal in greatness. Rather, it is people’s states when supplicating that differ in excellence. Thus, a name is ‘greatest’ in relation to the circumstances of the supplication, not because it is intrinsically greater.”

What he said concerning Allah’s names parallels the second interpretation concerning the superiority of some of Allah’s speech over other parts. This second interpretation, offered by those who deny such superiority, is that describing something as ‘more excellent’ or ‘better’ means that it is excellent in itself, not that it is more excellent than something else.

This view is reported from Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī and those who agreed with him. They said: “It means that it is great and excellent.” They also said: “Calling something ‘more excellent’ entails that what is less excellent falls short of it, whereas Allah’s speech cannot be divided into parts.”

They say this concerning His speech because, in their view, it is a single entity within which neither equivalence nor differences in excellence are possible. As for their denial that some attributes are superior to others, this rests on their view that the attributes cannot be distinct from one another. They do not say this concerning the Arabic Quran, for in their view the Arabic Quran is created and, according to the majority of them, is not Allah’s speech. They said: “For speech

---

## Page 8674

cannot subsist in anyone other than the speaker, just like all other attributes.” In their view, however, the Arabic Quran cannot subsist in Allah’s essence, exalted is He. Were they to allow Allah’s speech to subsist in another, this would invalidate the principle upon which they and the rest of Ahl al-Sunnah agreed, and by which they refuted the Muʿtazilah’s assertion that the Quran is created. These people acknowledge that some parts of the Arabic Quran are superior to others, since they regard it as created; according to the great majority of them, however, it is not Allah’s speech.

Some of their later scholars say that the expression “Allah’s speech” is used in two distinct senses: the meaning subsisting within the self, and the created Arabic speech that signifies it. As for Allah’s speech which they regard as uncreated, it is that meaning, within which, they maintain, differences in excellence are impossible. Their fundamental position is that Allah’s speech consists of meanings—indeed, of only a single meaning—and that the meanings of Allah’s Book are one single thing, admitting neither multiplicity nor division.

Thus, the meaning of the Throne Verse, the verse concerning debt, al-Fātihah, the surahs beginning “Say: He is Allah, One” and “Perish,” the Torah and the Gospel, every divine saying, everything the Lord says to His servants on the Day of Resurrection, and everything He says to the angels and prophets—all these are numerically one and the same meaning, not merely one in kind. It admits neither multiplicity nor division. They also hold that the Arabic Quran is not Allah’s speech, but the speech of another—Gabriel or Muhammad—or a created thing among His creations through which that single meaning is expressed. That single meaning is the command to do everything He has commanded, the prohibition of everything He has forbidden, and the declaration of everything He has declared. They hold that command, prohibition, and declaration are not kinds or divisions of speech, for what is numerically one does not admit

---

## Page 8675

differentiation into kinds or division, whereas what is one in kind admits both. Rather, these are attributes of that numerically single meaning—relational attributes. When it relates to actions required of servants, it is a command; when it relates to what is forbidden, it is a prohibition; and when it relates to something being declared, it is a declaration.

The great majority of rational thinkers say:

The falsity of this is necessarily known. We know that the meanings of “Say: He is Allah, One” are not the meanings of “May the hands of Abū Lahab perish”; that the meanings of the verse concerning debt are not those of the Throne Verse; and that the meanings of statements about Allah’s attributes are not those of statements about His creations.

Moreover, if the relation of that meaning to the realities being described and the actions to which commands and prohibitions pertain has actual existence, it must have a subject in which to subsist. If it subsists in Allah’s essence, then the meanings of the speech subsisting in His essence are multiple. If it subsists in the essence of another, it is an attribute of that other, not of Allah. If it subsists without a subject, that is impossible, for meanings do not subsist independently. But if that meaning’s relation to those realities has no actual existence, there would be nothing to distinguish declaration, command, and prohibition. Indeed, nothing would distinguish Allah’s statements about Himself from His statements about the people of Noah and ʿĀd, since that single meaning contains no multiplicity, let alone parts distinguishable from one another.

The realities about which statements are made, and which are commanded or forbidden, do not, in and of themselves, acquire the status of being stated, commanded, or forbidden. Rather, statements about them, commands to perform them, and prohibitions against them are distinct from the things themselves. Thus, if there were nothing existent apart from that meaning, within which there is neither distinction nor multiplicity, and apart from the created things, which do not distinguish between command, prohibition, and declaration, then there would not

---

## Page 8676

be anything here to distinguish prohibition from declaration, or to make the meanings of the verse concerning ablution different from those of the verse concerning debt. For if the created letters signifying that meaning signify nothing but it, then it contains neither multiplicity nor differentiation. If they signify relations that have no existence, then nonexistence is not a thing that could constitute a command, a prohibition, or a declaration.

According to these thinkers, there is nothing but that meaning and its relation to the realities spoken of or commanded. The Arabic Quran itself, which they hold to be created, signifies that meaning. If what it signifies is that meaning, then within it no command is distinguishable from a declaration, no command to pray from a command to give zakah, and no prohibition of disbelief from a declaration of Allah’s oneness.

If those relations have no existence, then what is nonexistent is not a thing, and nonexistence cannot constitute a command, a prohibition, or a declaration. Nor can what the Torah, the Gospel, the Quran, and all Allah’s other Books signify be nonexistent things with no reality. Nor can nonexistent things be what makes prayer obligatory and wrongdoing forbidden. By virtue of those nonexistent things, that single meaning could have only relational attributes, which are of the nature of negation: if they do not negate something existent, then they are a relation that does not exist.

The reality of the matter, according to their position, is therefore that Allah has no speech—neither meanings nor letters—except in the sense of a single meaning that has no existent or knowable reality.

Among their arguments is that, if some of His speech is said to be superior to other parts, then the less excellent would fall short of the more excellent. Yet Allah’s attributes are perfect, without deficiency, and the Quran

---

## Page 8677

is one of His attributes.

These thinkers say:

Allah’s attributes are all fully perfect, reaching the utmost completeness; no deficiency can affect any of them under any circumstances. Believing that differences in excellence among Allah’s attributes were impossible, they then supposed that affirming the superiority of some of His speech over other parts was possible only according to the position of the Jahmiyyah—the Muʿtazilah and others—who say that it is created. For if it is said to be created, then some created things may be deemed superior to others, and thus some of it may be superior to other parts.

They say:

But according to Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah, who unanimously agree that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated, differences in excellence among Allah’s attributes subsisting in His Essence are impossible.

Because of this belief, those who hold it have come to claim that Ahl al-Sunnah unanimously agree that no part of the Quran can be deemed superior to another. Thus Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Darrāj stated in a work he composed on this question:

“Ahl al-Sunnah unanimously agree that whatever occurs in the revealed texts apparently indicating differences in excellence among the Quran’s verses and surahs is not intended to mean that some are intrinsically superior to others. For it is all Allah’s speech and one of His attributes. Rather, all of it is excellent, belonging to Allah like His other attributes, which necessarily possess perfection.”

This claim of consensus rests on what he supposed necessarily followed from the position of Ahl al-Sunnah. Knowing that they say, ‘The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated,’ and supposing that differences in excellence occur only among created things, not among the divine attributes, he made this statement. Otherwise, it is not reported of any of the early generations or the imams that he denied the superiority of some of Allah’s speech

---

## Page 8678

over other parts, whether intrinsically or in its implications and connections—let alone that there was a consensus on denying this superiority. Nor does this denial necessarily follow from the position of Ibn Kullāb and those who agree with him, such as al-Ashʿarī and his followers. They allow differences in excellence within the Arabic Quran, which they regard as created. This created Quran is called “the Book of Allah,” whereas the eternal meaning is called “the speech of Allah.” They use the term “Quran” to refer both to that eternal meaning and to the created Arabic Quran. Accordingly, they interpret the transmitted statements about the superiority of some parts of the Quran over others as referring to what they regard as the created Quran.

Rather, what has been transmitted through numerous independent chains from the imams of the early generations is their statement that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated, and their rejection of the doctrine of the Jahmiyyah, who held that the Quran was something created and separate from Allah. and (Refutation of the Jahmiyyah) by ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd al-Dārimī; (ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd’s Rebuttal of the Stubborn, Lying Jahmī concerning His Fabrications against Allah regarding Divine Oneness); (The Book of Divine Oneness) by Ibn Khuzaymah; (The Sunnah) by al-Tabarānī and by Abū al-Shaykh al-Asbahānī; (Explanation of the Foundations of the Sunnah) by Abū al-Qāsim al-Lālakā’ī; (The Elucidation) by Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Battah; the books of Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mandah; (The Sunnah) by Abū Dharr al-Harawī; (The Names and Attributes) by al-Bayhaqī; (The Foundations) by Abū ʿUmar al-Talamankī; (The Criterion) by Abū Ismāʿīl al-Ansārī; and (The Proof) by Abū al-Qāsim al-Taymī.

Those who introduced into Islam the doctrine that the Quran is created were al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham, al-Jahm ibn Safwān, and those who followed him among the Muʿtazilah and the other groups of the Jahmiyyah. None of the Companions, nor those who followed them in righteousness, held this doctrine.

Thus, the position known to be that of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah is that the Quran

## Page 8680

is Allah’s speech and is uncreated. As for the claim that no part of it is superior to another, this has not been transmitted from any of the early generations of the Muslim community or the imams of the Sunnah who led the way during the trial, such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal and his peers, nor from anyone before them. How, then, could it be so treated when it has not been transmitted from any of them? their exact words. Rather, what is reliably transmitted from them—or from many of them—indicates that they held that Allah’s attributes differ in excellence. He said:

The reply is as follows: As for the statement, “Were it not for the excuse of ignorance, anyone who affirmed differences in excellence would be judged a disbeliever,” his opponents counter him with the same claim, and their argument is stronger. This is because disbelief is a judgment established by revelation and can only be established through revealed evidence. Someone who denies something that revelation does not establish, but which is known through reason alone, is not thereby a disbeliever. Rather, only someone who denies what the Messenger brought is a disbeliever. It is well known that neither the Book nor the Sunnah contains any text precluding some of Allah’s speech from being superior to other parts, or even precluding differences in excellence among His attributes

---

## Page 8683

—exalted is He. Nor has this negation been transmitted from any of the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, or the imams of the Muslims whose good standing in the community has made them beacons of the Sunnah and leaders of the community.

As for some of Allah’s speech being superior to other parts—indeed, some of His attributes being superior to others—there is abundant evidence for this in the Book, the Sunnah, the rulings of revelation, and the reports from the early generations. If we were to suppose that, in reality, His attributes do not differ in excellence, this absence of differences could be known only through reason, not through revealed evidence. If, however, we suppose that they do differ in excellence, this is supported by both revealed and rational evidence. Thus, supposing that such superiority is indeed true, there would be stronger grounds for judging someone who denies it a disbeliever than for judging someone who affirms it a disbeliever on the supposition that it is not actually true. For the former has denied what the revealed evidence entails without any revealed proof, relying instead on his own reasoning, in which he has erred—as we are speaking within this hypothetical case. It is well known that someone who opposes what the Messengers brought from Allah merely on the basis of his own reasoning is more deserving of being judged a disbeliever than someone who does not oppose what the Messengers brought from Allah, but opposes only what is known through reason—assuming that it is true.

A parallel to this is the statement of one of those who deny the divine attributes. Having reflected on the condition of his companions and that of those who affirm the attributes, he said:

“There is no doubt that these people’s standing before Allah is better than ours. If they are right, they will have attained the highest ranks and the greatest divine pleasure. If they are mistaken, they will say: ‘Our Lord, we believed what Your Book indicated

and the Sunnah of Your Messenger indicated. For You did not make clear to us through the Book and the Sunnah that the attributes should be denied, whereas Your words indicated that they should be affirmed. We therefore affirmed what Your words and the words of Your Messenger indicated. Rather, even supposing it to be true, only a few individuals would know it. What, then, when most of those who have pursued that contrary position to its furthest limits acknowledge bewilderment and doubt?’”

The denier said:

“Even if we are right, we will be told: ‘You said something I did not command you to say, and sought knowledge I did not command you to seek. Reward is only for those who obey, and you did not comply with My command.’”

He said:

Such is the situation of those who affirm differences in excellence within Allah’s speech and attributes, and those who deny them. Those who affirm them hold fast to the Book, the Sunnah, and the reports of the early generations. They also have clear rational proofs demonstrating the soundness of their position and the falsity of their opponents’ position—proofs against which no valid objection can be raised. Those who deny them, however, have neither a verse from Allah’s Book, nor a hadith from Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—nor a statement from any of the early generations of this community. They have nothing but an opinion which they claim their reason supports. Their opponents demonstrate that reason actually supports the opposite, and that the error of their position is established by clear reason just as it is established by authentic transmitted evidence.

It is utterly unsound to argue against differences in excellence on the basis of His words:

“They divided the Quran into portions.”

For the verse does not indicate this in any way whatsoever

whether it refers to those who believed in some of it and disbelieved in some, or to those who slandered it, saying, “It is magic, poetry,” and the like. Rather, whoever denies the superiority of “Say: He is Allah, One” over “May the hands of Abū Lahab perish” is more deserving of being counted among those who divided it into portions—if the verse has any bearing on this question.

For whoever believes in the descriptions Allah has given of His speech acknowledges that all of it is Allah’s speech and affirms it in its entirety, without disbelieving in a single letter of it. He knows that Allah’s speech is superior to all other speech, that the best speech is Allah’s speech, and that none speaks better or more truthfully than Allah. He also acknowledges what Allah and His Messenger have related concerning the excellence of particular parts of His speech: the Opening of the Book, the Verse of the Throne, “Say: He is Allah, One,” and the like; indeed, also the special excellence of Yā Sīn, “Blessed is He,” and the last two verses of the surah “The Cow”; and likewise the excellence of “The Cow,” “The Family of ‘Imrān,” and other surahs and verses whose excellence is expressly affirmed in the scriptural texts. He acknowledges that it is Allah’s speech and that none of it—neither its meanings nor its letters—is the speech of anyone else.

Such a person is further removed from dividing it into portions than someone who does not believe in the excellence by which Allah has made some of it superior to the rest, but believes only in its excellence on account of the One who speaks it, without believing in its excellence on account of its subject matter. In reality, the latter believes in it in one respect but not in another.

Likewise, whoever says that it is a single meaning, and that Allah did not speak the Arabic Quran, but that it is created—Allah having created it in the air, or Gabriel or Muhammad having brought it into being—then such a person

## Page 8686

is more deserving of being counted among those who slander the Quran, accuse it of falsehood, and make the Arabic Quran the speech of a created being—whether a human, an angel, or something else.

As for whoever holds that the Quran in its entirety is Allah’s speech—that neither it nor any part of it is created or brought into being by any creature, whether Gabriel or Muhammad—Gabriel is, rather, an angelic messenger, and Muhammad a human messenger. Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind. He thus chose the angelic messenger to convey His speech, and he brought it down to the human messenger whom He had chosen. He attributed it to each of the two messengers because each conveyed and delivered it, not because either composed or originated it. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, this is the word of a noble messenger, endowed with power and held in honor by the Lord of the Throne, obeyed there and trustworthy.”

This describes Gabriel, of whom He says:

“Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel—it is he who brought it down upon your heart by Allah’s permission.”

He also says:

“The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down upon your heart, so that you might be one of those who warn, in a clear Arabic tongue.”

And He says:

“When We replace one verse with another—and Allah knows best what He sends down—they say, ‘You are only a fabricator.’ But most of them do not know. Say, ‘The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth.’”

In the other passage, He says:

“Indeed, this is the word of a noble messenger. It is not the word of a poet—how little you believe! Nor is it the word of a soothsayer—how little you take heed! It is a revelation from the Lord of all worlds. Had he falsely attributed any statements to Us, We would have seized him by the right hand, then severed his aorta, and none of you could have protected him from Us.”

This describes Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He attributed the speech to each of them by referring to him as a messenger, saying:

“The word of a messenger”

because a messenger points to the one who sent him. This indicates that it is the word of a messenger who conveyed it from his sender. He did not say, “It is the word of an angel” or “of a human being.” Rather, He declared whoever regarded it as the word of a human being to be a disbeliever, saying:

“Leave Me to deal with the one I created alone,
and granted abundant wealth,
and sons always by his side,
and made life easy for him.

then frowned and scowled,
then turned away in arrogance,

Whoever says that it is the word of a human being, or of a creature other than a human being, has disbelieved. But whoever regards it as the word of a human messenger has spoken the truth, because the messenger’s role in it is only to convey and deliver it. As Allah Most High says:

“O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord.”

In Abū Dāwūd’s Sunan, Jābir ibn Abd Allāh reported:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to present himself to people during the pilgrimage season, saying, ‘Is there any man who will take me to his people so that I may convey my Lord’s speech? For Quraysh have prevented me from conveying my Lord’s speech.’”

The early generations agreed that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated. A number of them said, “From Him it originated, and to Him it will return.” Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others said, “From Him it originated”—meaning that He is the One who spoke it; it did not originate from anyone else, as claimed by the Jahmiyyah, who say that the Quran is created. They said that He created it in something other than Himself, so that it originated from that created locus. Their position necessarily entails that it is the speech of that created locus, not of Allah

---

## Page 8688

Most High—especially since all the Jahmiyyah hold that Allah creates people’s actions, and are extreme proponents of determinism. The Mu‘tazilah agree with them in denying the divine attributes and declaring the Quran created, but differ from them concerning divine decree, religious designations, and rulings. If Allah creates everything other than Himself, their position necessarily entails that all speech is His speech, because He created it. Hence Ibn Arabī al-Tā’ī—an extremist among these Jahmiyyah who professed the oneness of existence—said:

All speech in existence is His speech;
To us, its prose and verse are all the same.

For this reason, Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd al-Hāshimī—a peer of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, concerning whom al-Shāfi‘ī said, “I have never seen anyone more intelligent than these two men: Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd al-Hāshimī”—said:

“Whoever says that ‘Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me’ is created is a disbeliever. If the Quran were created, as they claim, why should Pharaoh be more deserving of remaining in the Fire forever for saying, ‘I am your most exalted lord,’ when they claim that this is created?”

The meaning is that Pharaoh’s statement, “I am your most exalted lord,” was speech subsisting in Pharaoh himself. If His statement, “Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me,” were speech that He created in the tree, then the tree would be the one saying it, just as Pharaoh was the one who spoke his words. In that case, making the tree a deity would be greater disbelief than making Pharaoh a deity.

---

## Page 8689

According to the Jahmiyyah and the Mu‘tazilah, no demand, will, love, pleasure, anger, or anything else understood to be signified by created sounds subsists in Allah’s essence. Nor, according to them, does any imposition of obligation or duty, prohibition or restriction subsist in His essence. Thus, speech created in something other than Him would signify no meaning subsisting in His essence by which to distinguish what He created in inanimate objects from what He created in living beings.

The point made by the early generations—may Allah be pleased with them—was that Allah Himself spoke the Quran and all His other speech, and that it came down from Him, not from anyone else. As the Most High says:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth.”

And the Most High says:

“Say, ‘The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth.’”

None of the early generations said that the Quran is eternal. Rather, they said that it is Allah’s speech, uncreated. They said that Allah has always spoken if He wills, whenever He wills, however He wills, and as He wills. Nor did any of them say that Allah called Moses in pre-eternity, or that Allah has always been and will always be saying, “O Adam,” “O Noah,” “O Moses,” “O Iblīs,” and similar words that He has informed us He said.

However, a group among those who followed the early generations believed that if it is uncreated, it must necessarily be eternal, since they recognized only these two possibilities. These people deny that Allah speaks by His will and power, becomes angry with the disbelievers when they disobey Him, is pleased with the believers when they obey Him, rejoices at the repentance of those who repent when they turn to Him, or called Moses when he came to the tree, and other such matters indicated by

---

the Book and the Sunnah, as in His words:

“That is because they followed what angered Allah and disliked His pleasure, so He rendered their deeds worthless.”

And His words, Most High:

“So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them.”

And His words:

“When he came to it, he was called, ‘O Moses!’”

And the Most High said:

“We created you, then fashioned you, then said to the angels, ‘Prostrate before Adam.’”

And the Most High said:
