He has also informed us that His words are inexhaustible, saying:

“If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought another like it as a supplement.”

And the Most High said:

“If all the trees on earth were pens, and the sea, replenished by seven more seas, were ink, Allah’s words would not be exhausted. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”

The followers of the early generations say that Allah’s speech is eternal, meaning that He has always spoken if He wills. They do not say that any particular utterance itself is eternal, such as His call to Moses and the like. These people, however, believed that the Quran and every other particular instance of Allah’s speech are eternal, and that Allah does not speak by His will and power.

They then differed. Some said that what is eternal is a single meaning constituting all the meanings of the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran; that the Torah, when expressed in Arabic, becomes the Quran; and that the Quran, when expressed in Hebrew, becomes the Torah. They said that Allah did not speak the Arabic Quran. Rather, either He created it in some physical body, or Gabriel or Muhammad brought it into being. In that case, it would be the speech of that messenger, by which he conveyed the single meaning subsisting in the Lord’s essence, which is

---

## Page 8691

all the meanings of speech.

Others among them said: Rather, the eternal Quran consists of letters, or letters and sounds, which are eternal and beginningless, subsisting in the Lord’s essence without beginning or end. They occur in succession in their intrinsic nature and essence, but not in their existence, for no part of what is eternal can precede another. They thus distinguished between speech itself and its existence, locating succession in speech itself rather than in its existence—just as those among the Mu'tazilah and the philosophers who hold such a view distinguish things’ existence from their individual realities and essences.

Both groups maintain that when He speaks to Moses, the angels, or His servants on the Day of Resurrection, He does not address them with speech that He utters by His will and power at the time He addresses them. Rather, He creates in the one addressed a perception through which that person perceives the eternal speech inseparable from Allah’s essence, without beginning or end. According to them, He has always been, and will always be, saying:

“O Adam, dwell, you and your wife,”

and:

“O Noah, disembark in peace from Us and with blessings upon you,”

and:

“O Iblīs, what prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?”

and similar statements. These views and others have been discussed at length elsewhere.

The point is that no one can transmit either of these two views from any of the early generations—meaning the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, and the other leading Muslim scholars renowned for knowledge and religious devotion, who are spoken of with honour within the Muslim community—in the time of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Shāfi'ī, or Abū Hanīfah, or before them. The first to introduce this principle was Abū Muhammad 'Abd Allāh ibn Sa'īd ibn Kullāb. He recognized that letters occur in succession and therefore cannot be eternal as individual entities, for that which comes later

---

## Page 8692

has been preceded by something else, whereas nothing precedes that which is eternal. Moreover, a particular sound does not endure for two successive moments, so how could it be eternal? He therefore held that what is eternal is the meaning. He then held this meaning to be one, admitting neither multiplicity nor division, on the grounds that it could not be restricted to a particular number of meanings, nor could infinitely many meanings exist at a single instant. He held that the Arabic Quran is not Allah’s speech.

When his view became widespread and the majority of Muslims recognized its invalidity in terms of both revelation and reason, another group—who agreed with him both on the position of the early generations, that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated, and on the principle he had introduced, namely that the Quran is eternal—said that the Quran is eternal, yet consists of successive letters and composed sounds.

Their position thus combined the views of the Mu'tazilah and the Kullābiyyah. When they debated the Mu'tazilah in defence of the position that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated, they used Ibn Kullāb’s method. When the Kullābiyyah disputed with them over the position that the Arabic Quran is Allah’s speech and that the Quran recited by Muslims is Allah’s speech, they argued against them using the arguments of the Mu'tazilah.

None of these views was held by anyone among the early generations, as has been explained at length elsewhere. Neither the four imams nor their companions who lived in their time held any of these views. Among those affiliated with them, only some later scholars held these views, having received them from the speculative theologians who advocated them. They were familiar neither with the views of the early generations, which are supported by the Book, the Sunnah, and sound reason

---

## Page 8693

nor with the true nature of the views of the speculative theologians whose discipline the early generations condemned, why they adopted these views, or what compelled them to do so.

It had become widely known among ordinary people and scholars alike that the Quran is uncreated, and that declaring it created is an innovated position condemned by the early generations and the imams. Thus, someone reading works of speculative theology in which he finds only the position of the Mu'tazilah and that of those who refuted them and claimed adherence to the Sunnah comes to imagine that these are the only two positions on the issue. Knowing that the former was condemned by the early generations, he assumes that the other must be their position. Something similar happens in many other questions: a person knows only two or three positions on an issue and assumes that one of them must be correct, whereas there is another position, unknown to him, which alone is correct. This is a widespread phenomenon affecting many issues.

May Allah guide us and all our fellow Muslims to the words and deeds He loves and is pleased with. Whoever strives to the best of his ability with the intention of obeying Allah and His Messenger is not burdened by Allah beyond his capacity. Rather, Allah rewards him for his obedience and forgives his errors concerning matters he was unable to ascertain.

Section

There are numerous scriptural texts and transmitted reports establishing the superiority of some of Allah’s speech over other parts—indeed, even of some of His attributes over others. As for the statement, “All of Allah’s attributes are excellent

---

## Page 8694

and possess the utmost completeness and perfection, with no deficiency,” this is correct. However, his assumption that, if some attributes are superior to others, the latter must be flawed or deficient is mistaken. The scriptural texts indicate that some of His names are superior to others; hence the expression, “He called upon Allah by His greatest name.” They also indicate that some of His attributes are superior to others, and some of His acts are superior to others. Thus, the transmitted reports mention His mighty name and His mightiest name, and His great name and His greatest name, as in the Sunan collections and in the report narrated by Ahmad and by Ibn Hibbān in his Sahīh, from Ibn Buraydah, from his father, who said:

“I entered the mosque with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and there was a man praying and supplicating: ‘O Allah, I ask You by my testimony that You are Allah: there is no god but You, the One, the Self-Sufficient, who neither begets nor is born, and to whom none is equal.’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘By Him in whose hand is my soul, he has indeed asked Allah by His greatest name, by which, when He is asked, He gives, and when He is called upon, He answers.’”

Anas said:

“I was sitting in the circle with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, while a man stood praying. After bowing and prostrating, he recited the testimony of faith and supplicated, saying in his supplication: ‘O Allah, I ask You, for all praise belongs to You. There is no god but You, the Bestower of favors, the Originator of the heavens and the earth. O Possessor of Majesty and Honor, O Ever-Living, O Self-Subsisting Sustainer of all!’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘By Him in whose hand is my soul, he has indeed called upon Allah by His greatest name, by which, when He is called upon, He answers, and when He is asked, He gives.’”

It is also established in the Sahīh

---

## Page 8695

from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah wrote in a book, which is kept with Him above the Throne: ‘My mercy prevails over My wrath.’”

In another narration: “My mercy preceded My wrath.”

He thus described His mercy as prevailing over and preceding His wrath. This indicates the superiority of His mercy over His wrath in respect of its precedence and its prevailing over it. It is also established in Sahīh Muslim, from Ā’ishah, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say while prostrating:

“O Allah, I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your displeasure, and in Your sparing me from Your punishment. I seek refuge in You from You.”

Al-Tirmidhī narrated that he used to say this in his witr prayer, but this requires scrutiny. Seeking refuge in His perfect words is also established through multiple routes in the Sahīh, Sunan, and Musnad collections, as in his saying:

“I seek refuge in Allah’s perfect words from His wrath and punishment, from the evil of His servants, and from the incitements of the devils and their presence.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Khawlah reports that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever stops at a place and says, ‘I seek refuge in Allah’s perfect words,’ will not be harmed by anything until he departs from it.”

It is also related in the Sahīh that he said to Uthmān ibn Abī al-Ās:

“Say: ‘I seek refuge in Allah’s might and power from the evil of what I feel and fear.’”

It is well known that that in which refuge is sought is superior to that from which refuge is sought. He sought refuge in His pleasure from His displeasure, and in His sparing him from His punishment.

As for his seeking refuge in Him from Him, this must be understood in terms of two aspects: he seeks refuge in Him with regard to one aspect, and from Him with regard to the other, so that the one in whom refuge is sought differs from the one

---

## Page 8696

from whom refuge is sought, since the one from whom refuge is sought is feared and dreaded, whereas the one in whom refuge is sought is invoked, appealed to for protection, and turned to for shelter. One and the same aspect cannot be both sought and fled from; this is possible, however, when two different aspects are considered. Thus, in the hadith narrated in the two Sahīh collections from al-Barā’ ibn Āzib, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, taught a man to say at bedtime:

“O Allah, I submit myself to You, turn my face toward You, place my back in Your protection, and entrust my affairs to You, in hope of You and fear of You. There is no escape and no refuge from You except with You. I believe in Your Book which You have revealed and in Your Prophet whom You have sent.”

He thus made clear that none but He can deliver anyone from Him, and that refuge from Him can be sought only with Him. Where the two verbs competed to govern the same complement, he made the second verb govern it. It is well known that the respect in which He delivers differs from the respect in which deliverance is sought from Him. Likewise, the respect in which refuge is sought with Him differs from the respect in which refuge is sought from Him—whether this is said to relate to what He brings into being, His acts that subsist in Him, His attributes, or His Essence considered in two different respects.

In Sahīh Muslim, Abdullāh ibn Umar reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Those who act justly will be with Allah on pulpits of light, to the right of the Most Merciful—and both of His hands are right hands—those who are just in their judgments, with their families, and in whatever is entrusted to their care.”

The two hands are mentioned in several hadiths, which state that both are right hands while also affirming the superiority of the right hand. A number of scholars have said: Since the attributes of created beings involve imperfection, and a person’s left hand is deficient in strength and deficient in action

---

## Page 8697

such that they use their left hands for everything considered objectionable—as when a person handles impurities and filth with his left hand—the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made clear that both of the Lord’s right hands are blessed, without any deficiency or defect whatsoever such as is found in the attributes of created beings. Nevertheless, the right hand is the superior of the two, as in the hadith concerning Adam, who said:

“I have chosen my Lord’s right hand, and both my Lord’s hands are blessed right hands.”

There is no deficiency in His attributes and nothing blameworthy in His acts. Rather, all His acts are either acts of bounty or acts of justice.

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Mūsā reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah’s right hand is full; no expenditure diminishes it, as it pours forth night and day. Have you considered how much He has spent since He created the heavens and the earth? It has not diminished what is in His right hand. Justice is in His other hand; He raises and lowers.”

Thus, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made clear that bounty is in His right hand and justice in His other hand. It is well known that, although both His hands are right hands, bounty is higher than justice. Every mercy from Him, glory be to Him, is bounty, and every punishment from Him is justice; His mercy is superior to His punishment. For this reason, those who act justly will be on pulpits of light to the right of the Most Merciful, not beside His other hand. Placing them to the right of the Most Merciful is an honour bestowed upon them, just as in the Quran He favours the people of the right hand and those of the right side over the companions of the left hand and those of the left side, even though He punishes the latter only in accordance with His justice. Likewise, the hadiths and transmitted reports state that those in the grasp of His right hand are the blessed, while those in the grasp of His other hand are the wretched.

---

## Page 8698

This is further clarified by the fact that evil does not occur in His names, but only in what He brings into being. It is attributed to Him only in general terms; otherwise, it is attributed to a created cause, or its agent is left unmentioned. Examples include His words, Most High:

“Allah is the Creator of all things,”

and:

“From the evil of what He has created.”

Likewise, His names occur in pairs, such as the Giver and the Withholder, the One who causes harm and the One who grants benefit, the One who honours and the One who abases, the One who lowers and the One who raises. Other examples include His words:

“And when I am ill, it is He who cures me.”

“The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have incurred wrath, nor of those who have gone astray.”

And the words of the jinn:

“We do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends right guidance for them.”

It is authentically reported in Sahīh Muslim that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would say in the opening supplication of prayer:

“All good is in Your hands, and evil is not ascribed to You.”

Whether this means that evil is not ascribed to You and cannot be a means of drawing near to You, or whether evil is said to be either nonexistence or a necessary consequence of nonexistence, neither of which is attributable to Allah, this makes clear that only good is ascribed to Him, glory be to Him. His names signify His attributes, all of which are good, excellent and beautiful, containing no evil. Evil occurs only in created things. Allah Most High says:

“Tell My servants that I am indeed the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful,”

“and that My punishment is indeed the painful punishment.”

He, Most High, also says:

“Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, and He is certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

Thus He made forgiveness and mercy part of the meanings of His most beautiful names by which He names Himself. Hence forgiveness

---

## Page 8699

and mercy are among His attributes. As for the punishment that befalls His servants, it is something He creates, and it is this that is painful. He did not say, “And I am the Punisher.” Nor is “the Avenger” among His names established through the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, vengeance is mentioned in the Quran with a qualification, as in His words:

“Indeed, We will exact vengeance upon the criminals.”

Its meaning is also attributed to Allah in His words:

“Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Possessor of vengeance.”

This is an indefinite expression in an affirmative context. An indefinite expression in an affirmative context is unrestricted; it does not denote generality encompassing all instances.

That is because Allah, glory be to Him, is Wise and Merciful. He has stated that He created all things only in accordance with His wisdom, as in His words, Most High:

“We did not create the heaven and the earth and all that is between them without purpose. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve.”

He, Most High, also says:

“Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for people of understanding.”

“Those who remember Allah while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: ‘Our Lord, You have not created this without purpose.’”

He, Most High, also says:

“We did not create the heaven and the earth and all that is between them in play.”

“Had We wished to take a diversion, We would have taken it from Our own presence, if We were to do so.”

And He says in the other surah:

“We created them only in truth, but most of them do not know.”

This makes clear that His expression “in truth” in the other verses carries this meaning, which encompasses His wisdom, as in His words:

“It is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth, and on the Day He says, ‘Be,’ it comes to be.”

And His words:

“We did not create the heavens and the earth and all that is between them except

---

## Page 8700

in truth. And indeed, the Hour is coming, so pardon graciously.”

“Indeed, your Lord is the All-Creating, the All-Knowing.”

Some people think that His words, “He is the All-Creating,” indicate that He creates His servants’ deeds, and that one should therefore not be severe in condemning them, but rather pardon them graciously on account of divine decree. This is among the greatest forms of ignorance. For He, glory be to Him, has punished those who oppose Him and His messengers, has been angry with them, has commanded that they be punished, and has prepared for them a punishment that contradicts the claims of these people who nullify His commands and prohibitions, His promises and threats.

His words, “So pardon graciously,” are connected to what precedes them, namely:

“And indeed, the Hour is coming, so pardon graciously.”

For they have an appointed time at which they will be recompensed, as He, Most High, says in similar passages:

“Your duty is only to convey the message, and Ours is to call them to account.”

“So remind them; you are only a reminder. You are not a controller over them. But whoever turns away and disbelieves—Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment. Indeed, to Us is their return. Then it is for Us to call them to account.”

And His words:

“So turn away from them for a time.”

And His words:

“So pardon them and say, ‘Peace.’ They will come to know.”

Allah has never excused anyone on the grounds of divine decree. Had He accepted it as an excuse, His prophets and His close servants would have been more entitled to it. Adam only prevailed over Moses in argument because Moses blamed him for the calamity that befell his descendants, saying to him, “Why did you cause us and yourself to be expelled from Paradise?”

Whatever calamities befall a servant, he must submit to Allah concerning them and know that they have been decreed for him, as He says

---

## Page 8701

Most High:

“No calamity befalls except by Allah’s permission. And whoever believes in Allah, He will guide his heart.”

Alqamah said—and this has also been reported from Ibn Mas‘ūd—“This is a man who suffers a calamity, knows that it is from Allah, and so accepts it contentedly and submits.” The servant is commanded to fear Allah and to be patient. Fearing Allah means doing what He has commanded, while patience includes patiently bearing whatever befalls one. Such a person will have a praiseworthy outcome, as Joseph, peace be upon him, said:

“Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient—Allah does not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

And He, Most High, says:

“And if you are patient and fear Allah, that is indeed a matter requiring firm resolve.”

And He says:

“And if you are patient and fear Allah, their schemes will not harm you at all.”

And He says:

“Yes, if you are patient and fear Allah, and they come upon you suddenly, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels bearing marks.”

Every servant inevitably does things that require repentance and seeking forgiveness, and undergoes trials that require patience. For this reason, he is commanded to be patient and to seek forgiveness, as the best of creation was told:

“So be patient; indeed, Allah’s promise is true. Ask forgiveness for your sin, and glorify your Lord with praise in the evening and the morning.”

The debate between Adam and Moses has been discussed at length elsewhere. Many people have interpreted it in ways contrary to the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Muslim community. Some have rejected the hadith because they did not understand it. Yet the hadith is true and establishes that, if a person suffers a calamity through someone else’s action, whether his father or another—especially if his father has repented of that action and therefore no longer bears any liability before Allah, as was the case with Adam, Allah’s blessings be upon him—Allah, Most High, says:

“And Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray.”

“Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him.”

---

## Page 8702

and He says:

“Then Adam received words from his Lord, and He accepted his repentance.”

Adam and Moses knew Allah far too well for either of them to invoke divine decree to excuse his sin and for the other to agree. Had that been so, Adam would not have needed to repent, nor would he have been sent down from Paradise. Moses himself said:

“My Lord, I have indeed wronged myself, so forgive me.”

He also said:

“My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.”

And he said:

“You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, for You are the best of those who forgive.”

And he said to his people:

“So repent to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is better for you in the sight of your Creator.”

If divine decree excused the sinner, he would not have needed any of this. Rather, the appeal to divine decree was in response to Moses’ reproach concerning the calamity decreed to befall him, which Allah had written and ordained.

Part of believing in divine decree is knowing that whatever befalls a servant could never have missed him, and whatever misses him could never have befallen him. The believer therefore patiently bears calamities and seeks forgiveness for sins and faults. The ignorant wrongdoer, however, invokes divine decree to excuse his own sins and misdeeds, yet does not excuse those who wrong him on the grounds of divine decree. Nor does he acknowledge divine decree when Allah enables him to do good. He thus reverses the matter.

Rather, when he does a good deed, he ought to recognize it as a blessing from Allah, who enabled him to perform it and graciously bestowed it upon him. He should not claim credit for it or attribute it to himself as though he were its creator. When he does an evil deed, he should seek forgiveness and repent of it. And when a calamity befalls him, whether through natural causes or human actions, he should know that it had been destined and decreed for him.

---

## Page 8703

and this is discussed at length in its proper place.

The point here is that He, glorified be He, has explained that He created all things only for a wise purpose. This is the meaning of His words:

“in truth.”

He has condemned those who suppose that He created them in vain and without purpose, saying:

“Did you think that We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?”

And He says:

“Does man think that he will be left unchecked?”

And He says:

“Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for those of understanding—”

“those who remember Allah while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth: ‘Our Lord, You have not created this in vain. Glory be to You! Protect us, then, from the punishment of the Fire.’”

People must therefore be recompensed for their deeds. Hence it was said:

“So pardon with gracious forbearance.”

In everything Allah creates, glorified be He, there is a wise purpose that He loves and is pleased with. He, glorified be He, has made everything He created good and perfected everything He has made. Whatever evil exists among created things has come into being for the sake of that intended wise purpose which He loves and is pleased with. Thus, as an act of Allah, it is good and beautiful, and He, glorified be He, is praised for it. All praise belongs to Him in every circumstance, even though it may be evil in relation to certain individuals.

This is a momentous subject that has been discussed at length elsewhere. Concerning the Lord’s creation and commands, and why He acts as He does, people occupy two extremes and a middle position.

The Qadariyyah among the Mu‘tazilah and others sought to exalt the Lord and declare Him free of actions they considered evil or unjust. They therefore denied the all-encompassing nature of His power and will, and did not regard Him as the Creator

---

## Page 8704

of all things, nor did they affirm that whatever He wills comes to pass and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. Rather, they said: “He wills what does not happen, and things happen that He does not will.” They then prescribed a law for their Lord concerning what is obligatory and forbidden for Him—by analogy with themselves. They discussed what is just and what is permissible on the basis of this false analogy, likening the Creator to His creation. Thus they went astray and led others astray.

At the opposite extreme were the Jahmiyyah, who carried their belief in compulsion to excess. They denied Allah’s wisdom and mercy, saying: “He did not create for a wise purpose, nor did He command for a wise purpose. There is no ‘lām of purpose’ in the Quran, whether concerning His creation or His commands.” They claimed that in His words:

“And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth—all of it,”

and:

“He created for you all that is on the earth,”

and His words:

“To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, so that He may recompense those who do evil for what they have done and reward those who do good with the best reward,”

and His words:

“and so that you may complete the prescribed period and glorify Allah for guiding you,”

and His words:

“so that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers,”

—and in similar passages—the particle lām merely denotes an eventual outcome, as in His words:

“Then Pharaoh’s household picked him up, so that he would become an enemy to them and a source of grief,”

and the poet’s words:

“Bear children for death, and build for ruin.”

They failed to understand that the lām of outcome applies only to someone who is ignorant of the outcome of his action, such as Pharaoh, who did not know how matters concerning Moses would end; or to someone unable to avert the outcome of his action, just as human beings cannot ward off death from themselves or ruin from their homes. As for the One who knows all things, has power over all things, and wills all

---

## Page 8705

that He has created, the lām of outcome cannot apply to Him, since it entails either a lack of knowledge or a lack of power.

These people denied that Allah loves and approves of some things but not others. They said: “Love and approval have the same meaning as will. Allah wills everything He has created, so He approves of it and loves it.”

They claimed that the Quran’s denial that He loves or approves of disbelief and sins, as in His words:

“Allah does not love corruption,”

and:

“He does not approve of disbelief for His servants,”

refers only to those of His servants who have not committed such things, or means that He did not will them as a religion for which He would reward them. They also claimed that Allah does not love or approve of the acts of worship He has commanded unless they actually occur; then He wills them, just as He then wills whatever disbelief and sins have occurred. These and other views of theirs are discussed at length elsewhere.

Many later scholars suppose that this is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah, yet none of the early generations of this Muslim community or its leading scholars ever held it. Rather, all the early scholars who affirmed divine decree distinguished love and approval from will. Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī, however, followed Jahm in this regard.

Abū al-Maʿālī al-Juwaynī said:

“Among the matters concerning which the people of truth differed over whether the terms may or may not be applied are love and approval. The earlier scholars held that He, glorified be He, neither loves nor approves of disbelief, and likewise every sin.

“Our shaykh Abū al-Hasan said: ‘Love is will itself, as are approval and choosing. He, glorified be He, wills disbelief

---

## Page 8706

and approves of it as reprehensible disbelief for which He exacts punishment.’”

The matter is as Abū al-Ma‘ālī stated: the earlier scholars of all Ahl al-Sunnah upheld what the Quran and Sunnah indicate—that He, glorified be He, neither approves of nor loves what He has forbidden. This was also the position of the early followers of the four imams—Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad—including Abū Bakr ‘Abd al-‘Azīz and others among their early followers. Some later scholars, however, equated all these meanings, as Abū al-Hasan did. This was originally Jahm’s position: he advocated compulsion in matters of divine decree and held views contrary to Ahl al-Sunnah. He denied Allah Most High’s mercy and would go out to people afflicted with leprosy and say:

“Would the Most Merciful of the merciful do this?”

Thus he denied that Allah is the Most Merciful of the merciful, whereas the truthful and trusted Messenger said:

“Allah is surely more merciful to His servants than a mother is to her child.”

These are weighty matters, and this is not the place to discuss them at length.

The purpose here is simply to draw attention to the broad principles. Many people read works on the foundations of religion and the principles of jurisprudence—even commentaries on the Quran and hadith—without finding in them the position that accords with the Quran and Sunnah and was upheld by the early generations of this community and its leading scholars: the position consistent with authentic transmitted evidence and clear reason. Instead, they find views each containing some error and contradiction. They are consequently bewildered about what to believe concerning these matters, what the Messenger brought, and what is true and sound, since none of those views provides them with the answer. Guidance lies only in what the Messenger brought—the Messenger concerning whom Allah said:

“And indeed, you guide to a straight path—the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Unquestionably, to Allah do all matters return.”

## Page 8707

Section

Once it is established by revelation, reason and the agreement of the early generations that some parts of the Quran are superior to others, and likewise that some of His attributes are superior to others, it remains to discuss how “Say: He is Allah, the One” is equivalent to one-third of the Quran. What does this mean? Is the reward for reciting it equal to the reward for reciting one-third of the Quran? Assuming that it is, what purpose does reciting the rest of the Quran serve?

The answer is as follows:

Regarding the first question, several explanations have been offered. The best of them—and Allah knows best—is the answer transmitted from Imam Abū al-‘Abbās Ibn Surayj. Abū al-Walīd al-Qurashī reported that he asked Abū al-‘Abbās Ibn Surayj about the meaning of the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“‘Say: He is Allah, the One’ is equivalent to one-third of the Quran.”

He replied: “It means that the Quran was revealed in three divisions: one-third consists of rulings, one-third of promises and warnings, and one-third of the divine names and attributes. This surah brings together the names and attributes.”

Abū al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzī mentioned three explanations of this hadith. He began with this explanation, transmitting Ibn Surayj’s statement through his chain of transmission from Zāhid, from al-Sābūnī and al-Bayhaqī, from al-Hākim Abū ‘Abd Allāh, the hadith master, who said: “I heard Abū al-Walīd

---

## Page 8708

Hassān ibn Muhammad, the jurist, say: ‘I asked Abū al-‘Abbās Ibn Surayj what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, meant by saying: “‘Say: He is Allah, the One’ is equivalent to one-third of the Quran.” He replied: “The Quran was revealed in three divisions: one-third consists of rulings, one-third of promises and warnings, and one-third of names and attributes. ‘Say: He is Allah, the One’ brings together one of these thirds, namely the attributes. Thus, it was said to be equivalent to one-third of the Quran.”’”

The second of the three explanations mentioned by Abū al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzī is that knowledge of Allah consists of knowledge of His essence, knowledge of His names and attributes, and knowledge of His actions. This surah encompasses knowledge of His essence, since everything that exists originates from something else, except Allah: He has no equal and nothing is like Him.

Abū al-Faraj said: “Some jurists of the early generations mentioned this.”

He continued: “The third explanation is that whoever acts upon what this surah contains—acknowledging Allah’s oneness and submitting to the Creator—is like someone who recites one-third of the Quran without acting upon what it contains. Ibn ‘Aqīl mentioned this.”

Ibn ‘Aqīl said: “It cannot mean that whoever recites it receives the reward of reciting one-third of the Quran, because the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

‘Whoever recites the Quran receives ten good deeds for every letter.’”

I say: Both explanations are weak. As for the first of these, its weakness is evident in several respects. First, we say that the Quran is not

---

## Page 8709

entirely concerned with the knowledge just mentioned. Rather, it also contains commands to perform obligatory deeds and prohibitions against unlawful acts. What is required of Allah’s servants is both obligatory knowledge and obligatory action. The entire Muslim community agrees that the deeds Allah has prescribed are obligatory; no one has said that they are not. Although some people have disputed whether deeds form part of faith, they have not disputed that Allah has prescribed the five daily prayers and the other ordinances of Islam, and has forbidden shameful deeds:

“Whether open or secret, sin, unjust aggression, associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about Allah what you do not know.”

Since this is so, even supposing that a surah encompasses one-third of this knowledge, that would not constitute one-third of the Quran.

Second, we may say: When someone speaks of knowledge of His essence, knowledge of His names and attributes, and knowledge of His actions, if he means that His essence can be known without knowing any of His names or attributes, whether affirmative or negative, this is impossible. Even if he supposed this possible, or a servant imagined an essence abstracted from all negative and affirmative qualifications, that would certainly not constitute knowledge of Allah. Nor is the Lord of the worlds an essence abstracted from every negative or affirmative qualification.

Thus, no rational person has maintained this except the esotericist Qarmatians. They say: “Every affirmative and privative predicate is denied of Him. He is not described as existent or nonexistent, knowing or not knowing, powerful or not powerful, or anything of the kind.” Although their position is self-evidently false to reason, these people are

---

## Page 8710

self-contradictory. As for the first point, denying both contradictories is impossible, just as affirming both together is impossible: nothing can be neither existent nor nonexistent. As for their self-contradiction, they must use some distinguishing feature to identify the One of whom they claim that both contradictories are denied, in order to predicate this denial of Him. Whatever they say must entail a negation or an affirmation; indeed, it must entail an affirmation. We have refuted them at length elsewhere. For this reason, many heretics do not go this far.

Rather, they say, as Abū Yaʿqūb al-Sijistānī and other heretics have said:

“We do not deny both contradictories; rather, we refrain from attributing either of them to Him. Thus, we do not say that He is existent or nonexistent, living or dead, knowing or ignorant.”

They should be told:

“Your hearts’ turning away from knowing Him and your tongues’ refraining from mentioning Him do not mean that He Himself is devoid of both contradictories. Rather, this reveals your disbelief in Allah and your aversion to knowing Him, mentioning Him, and worshipping Him. This is the true nature of your doctrine.”

Those heretics who claim adherence to Sufism and the realization of truth, such as Ibn Sabʿīn, al-Sadr al-Qūnawī, and others, and who say that He is absolute existence, on condition of being unrestricted by any affirmative or negative attribute, belong to the same category as these people. Yet they say that He is absolute existence, thus ascribing existence to Him rather than nonexistence. Then they say that He is absolute; but that which is absolute, on condition of being unrestricted by any negative or affirmative qualification, exists only

---

## Page 8711

in the mind, not in external reality.

These people say:

Universal existence, divided into necessary and contingent existence, which the philosophers make the subject matter of metaphysics—also called “the highest wisdom” and “first philosophy”—is universal only in the mind, not in external reality. In external reality, there is never one and the same existence that is both necessary and contingent, nor one and the same existence that characterizes both the Necessary Being and a contingent being. Rather, the attributes of the Necessary Being are peculiar to Him, and those of a contingent being are peculiar to it. The existence of the Necessary Being is His alone, shared by no other; likewise, the existence of a contingent being is its alone, shared by no other.

Thus, every attribute with which the Lord has described Himself is peculiar to Him: it is impossible for anyone to share it with Him or resemble Him in it. His holy Essence resembles no other essence, and His attributes are peculiar to Him and resemble no other attributes. Rather, He—glorified be He—is One, the Self-Sufficient:

“He neither begets nor is born,”

“and there is none comparable to Him.”

His name al-Ahad (the One) indicates that none shares in His attributes or resembles Him, while His name al-Samad (the Self-Sufficient) indicates that He is entitled to every attribute of perfection. This has been explained at length in the extensive commentary devoted to this surah. All attributes declaring Him free of imperfection—indeed, all affirmative attributes as well—are encompassed by these two meanings.

Tawhīd (affirming Allah’s oneness) has been discussed at length, including its division into two kinds: one pertaining to knowledge and declaration, the other to practice and intention. Thus, Surah “Say, O disbelievers” explicitly sets forth tawhīd in practice and also indicates tawhīd in knowledge

---

## Page 8712

by necessary implication. Surah “Say, He is Allah, One” explicitly sets forth tawhīd pertaining to knowledge and declaration, and indicates tawhīd in practice by necessary implication. For this reason, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—would recite these two surahs in the two units of prayer of Fajr, the two units of prayer associated with circumambulation, and on other occasions. It is also established that, in the two units of prayer of Fajr, he would recite the verse of faith from al-Baqarah in the first unit:

“Say, ‘We believe in Allah,’”

and the verse of submission from Āl ‘Imrān:

“Say, ‘O People of the Scripture, come to a common word between us and you: that we worship none but Allah, associate nothing with Him, and do not take one another as lords besides Allah.’ But if they turn away, then say, ‘Bear witness that we are Muslims.’”

The point here is that the attributes declaring Him free of imperfection are encompassed by these two meanings mentioned in this surah.

The first is the denial of imperfections in Him. This necessarily follows from affirming the attributes of perfection: whoever possesses absolute perfection is free of the deficiency that contradicts it. Perfection is among the meanings conveyed by His name al-Samad (the Self-Sufficient).

The second is that nothing is like Him in the attributes of perfection affirmed of Him. This is among the meanings conveyed by His name al-Ahad (the One). These two magnificent names—al-Ahad and al-Samad—thus declare Him free of every deficiency and defect, and affirm that He has no equal in any of His attributes of perfection. His name al-Samad entails the affirmation of all

---

## Page 8713

attributes of perfection. This thus entails affirming every attribute of perfection and denying every attribute of deficiency. The surah therefore encompasses everything that must be denied of Allah, as well as everything that must be affirmed of Him, in two ways: through His name al-Samad, and because denying that He has ancestors, offspring, or equals also entails affirming His attributes of perfection.

Every negation by which the Lord is praised must imply an affirmation. Indeed, the same applies to every negation by which any existing thing is praised: it must imply an affirmation. Otherwise, pure negation amounts to sheer nonexistence, and sheer nonexistence is nothing at all, let alone an attribute of perfection.

This is illustrated by what He, glorified be He, mentions in the Verse of the Throne, such as His words:

“Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep.”

Denying that drowsiness or sleep overtakes Him necessarily implies the perfection of His life and His sustaining of all existence. Sleep is incompatible with sustaining all existence, and sleep is the brother of death. For this reason, the people of Paradise do not sleep.

Then He says:

“To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?”

Denying intercession without His permission necessarily implies the perfection of His sovereignty. For anyone who accepts an intercession made to him without his permission has been influenced by that intercessor: the intercession has affected him, prompting him to act after he had not done so. That intercessor would thus be a partner of the one petitioned in the matter sought through intercession, since the intercession took place without his permission. In particular, when a created being accepts an intercession made to him without his permission, he accepts it only out of hope or fear, whether from

---

## Page 8714

the intercessor or someone else. Otherwise, if his own motivation were complete and he possessed the ability, he would have no need of intercession. Allah Most High is exalted above all of this, as He says in the divine hadith:

“O My servants, you can never confer any benefit upon Me, nor can you inflict any harm upon Me.”

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would instruct his Companions to intercede with him. When someone came to him seeking something, he would say:

“Intercede, and you will be rewarded; Allah will decree through the tongue of His Prophet whatever He wills.”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded this in their Sahīh collections. His purpose was that they should be rewarded for interceding, while he himself would do only what Allah commanded him to do.

Likewise, He says:

“He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills.”

He makes clear that they know nothing of His knowledge except what He has taught them, just as the angels said:

“We have no knowledge except what You have taught us.”

This negation thus affirms that His servants know only what He has taught them. It affirms that He is the One who taught them, and that they acquire knowledge only from Him. For He is:

“the One who created—created man from a clinging substance,”

and who

“taught by the pen—taught man that which he knew not.”

Then He says:

“His Kursī extends over the heavens and the earth, and their preservation does not burden Him.”

That is, it neither troubles Him nor weighs upon Him. This negation implies the perfection of His power: although He preserves the heavens and the earth, doing so does not weigh upon Him as it would upon someone whose strength is deficient.

This is like His saying, Most High:

“We certainly created the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us.”

He thus declares Himself free from being touched by weariness. The lexicographers say:

---

## Page 8715

“Weariness means exhaustion and fatigue.”

Likewise, He says:

“Vision does not encompass Him.”

According to the early generations and the majority, “encompassing” here means comprehending something in its entirety. Some have said that it means seeing, but this is a weak interpretation, because denying that He can be seen entails no praise: what does not exist cannot be seen either. Any description common to both existence and nonexistence entails no positive attribute and therefore offers no praise, since it is pure negation. By contrast, saying that He cannot be encompassed indicates the greatness of the Lord—majestic is His glory. Although His servants see Him, their vision does not encompass Him, just as, although they know Him, their knowledge does not encompass Him. Likewise, although they praise and extol Him, their praise cannot encompass Him. Rather, He is as He has praised His own holy Self.

For this reason, the best and most knowledgeable of creation said:

“I cannot enumerate Your praises; You are as You have praised Yourself.”

These matters are discussed at length elsewhere. The purpose here is to explain what it means for the surah “Say: He is Allah, the One” to equal one-third of the Quran, and to demonstrate that the first view is correct.

The third argument demonstrating the invalidity of the second view is as follows:

When someone speaks of “knowledge of His acts,” if he means knowledge of His signs that point to Him, this forms part of complete knowledge of Him. Yet he has left unmentioned knowledge of His promises and warnings and the accounts of believing and disbelieving nations—which constitute the second category of the Quran’s meanings—just as he has left unmentioned His commands and prohibitions. If, however, he includes these among the effects of His actions, then it is well known that the purpose of knowing the promises, warnings, and accounts is belief in the Last Day and the recompense of deeds

---

## Page 8716

just as the purpose of commands and prohibitions is obedience to Him. Every community must have faith in Allah and the Last Day and perform righteous deeds, as the Most High says:

“Indeed, those who believed, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians—whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteous deeds—will have their reward with their Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.”

The fourth argument is as follows:

The negation of any likeness to Him and of begetting, which he mentioned, also appears outside this surah. Thus, this meaning is not unique to it.

The fifth argument is as follows:

Granted that it declares His freedom from imperfection, as Allah has stated, knowledge of Allah does not consist in knowing attributes of negation. Rather, its foundation is the attributes affirmed of Him; negation is subordinate and serves to complete that affirmation. As we have indicated, every declaration of the Lord’s freedom from imperfection by which He is praised includes an affirmation. Thus, saying “Glory be to Allah” both declares the Lord free from imperfection and extols His greatness: it declares Him free from faults and deficiencies and magnifies Him, glorified and exalted is He. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

As for the third view—that what is meant is that whoever acts upon its contents is like someone who recites one-third of the Quran without acting upon its contents—this too is weak. His denial of equivalence rests on the view of those who measure the amount of reward by the number of letters. That view is false, as has been explained in its proper place. For if, by acting upon it, he means

---

## Page 8717

the obligatory action of affirming its contents and affirming Allah’s oneness, then the reward for this is greater than the reward of someone who recites the entire Quran without acting accordingly. For if he lacks faith in the contents of the Quran, he is a hypocrite; and if he fails to perform the deeds obligatory upon him, he is a sinful transgressor. It is well known that even if such a person recited the Quran ten times, his reward would not equal that of a believer who fears Allah. Moreover, this reward is for believing in its contents, whether he recites it or not, whereas the reward mentioned in the hadith is for someone who recites it. Thus, he must have recited it while believing in what it contains.

Furthermore, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, declared that reciting it was equivalent to one-third of the Quran. He recited it to his Companions and told them that he had recited one-third of the Quran to them. His recitation of it was therefore equivalent to his own recitation of a third. The same applies to the man who kept repeating it. Likewise, when he told them that it was equivalent to one-third of the Quran, he meant a third as recited by them. He did not mean a third in the case of a hypocrite who recites it without believing in the meaning of:

“Say: He is Allah, One.”

Moreover, the interpretation that this refers to someone who recites a third without believing in this surah has no basis in the wording; rather, the wording indicates the opposite. This interpretation and others like it constitute the distortion of words from their proper places for which Allah condemned those among the People of the Book who did so. It is a form of deviation concerning the words of Allah and His Messenger.

Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī mentioned another explanation besides these three. He said in his book Jawāhir al-Qur’ān wa-Duraruhu (The Jewels and Pearls of the Quran):

“As for his statement, ‘“Say: He is Allah, One”

---

## Page 8718

is equivalent to one-third of the Quran,’ I do not think you understand why this is so. Sometimes you say, ‘He said this to encourage recitation, without intending an exact equivalence.’ Yet the office of prophethood is far above such a thing.

“At other times you say, ‘This defies understanding and interpretation. The Quran contains more than six thousand verses; how can so short a passage constitute a third of them?’ This stems from your limited knowledge of the truths of the Quran and your attention to its outward wording. You imagine that its meanings grow greater and more numerous as its wording grows longer, and diminish as it grows shorter. This is like preferring many silver coins to a single jewel merely because they are numerous.

“Know, then, that Surah al-Ikhlās is certainly equivalent to one-third of the Quran. This relates to the three categories we mentioned concerning the Quran’s essential subjects: knowledge of Allah, knowledge of the Hereafter, and knowledge of the straight path. These three kinds of knowledge are what matters most; the rest is subsidiary. Surah al-Ikhlās encompasses one of these three: knowledge of Allah, declaring Him free of imperfection, and affirming His oneness, with none sharing with Him in genus or species. This is what is meant by denying that He has any parent, offspring, or equal. Describing Him as al-Samad (the Self-Sufficient Master) indicates that He is the Master, the only one in existence to whom one turns for one’s needs. It does not, however, discuss the Hereafter or the straight path. That is why it is equivalent to one-third of the Quran—that is, one-third of the Quran’s fundamental subjects. This is like his statement:

“‘Hajj is Arafah.’

“That is, it is the essential part, while the rest is subsidiary.”

I say: The verses of the Quran are of two kinds: those concerned with knowledge and those concerned with practice. Some verses combine both. Abū Hāmid collected the verses concerned with knowledge relating to Allah’s essence, attributes, and actions, excluding those relating to

---

## Page 8719

the Last Day and the narratives, and called them “The Jewels of the Quran.” He also collected the verses concerned with practice and called them “The Pearls of the Quran.” He placed the first half of al-Fātihah among the jewels and the second among the pearls. Verses combining both meanings he assigns to whichever category predominates in them. Together, the verses he included in these two categories constitute a quarter of the Quran’s verses—approximately fifteen hundred verses.

He divided the meanings of the Quran into six categories: three fundamental subjects and three subsidiary ones. He described the Quran as the all-encompassing ocean from which the knowledge of earlier and later generations branches out.

He said:

“The secret of the Quran, its purest essence, and its ultimate purpose is to call people to the Most High, the All-Compelling, Lord of this world and the Hereafter, Creator of the lofty heavens and the earths below.

“The three essential subjects are: making known the One to whom people are called; making known the straight path that must be followed in journeying to Him; and making known their condition upon reaching Him.

“As for the three remaining subjects, the first concerns the circumstances of those who respond to the call and the subtleties of Allah’s dealings with them. Its inner meaning and purpose are to inspire longing and desire. It also makes known the circumstances of those who turn aside and shrink from responding, and how Allah subdues them and makes an example of them. Its inner meaning and purpose are to provide a lesson and inspire fear.

“The second recounts the statements of those who deny the truth and exposes their shameful failings and ignorance through debate and argument in support of the truth. With regard to falsehood, its purpose and inner meaning are to lay it bare, warn against it, and make it repellent; with regard to truth, to clarify, confirm, and establish it.

“The third explains how to maintain the way stations along the path, and how to obtain provisions, a mount, and the equipment needed to prepare.”

I say: What he has stated—that the foundations of faith are three—is indeed true, just as he has said.

---

## Page 8720

and all three are indispensable in every faith and religion, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, the believers, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabeans—whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds—will have their reward with their Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.”

Something similar appears in Sūrat al-Mā’idah.

Thus, He mentions these three foundations: belief in Allah, belief in the Last Day, and righteous deeds. The other three, subsidiary subjects are included within these. The Quran’s accounts of the conditions of the blessed and the wretched in the Hereafter elaborate upon belief in the Last Day. Its discussion of maintaining the path falls under righteous deeds. Its debates and arguments complete its exposition of these three foundations: when it sets them forth, it presents the signs and proofs that establish them, mentions the specious arguments of those who deny them, and exposes their unsoundness.

Abū Hāmid himself mentioned this, saying:

“The section devoted to disputing and debating with the unbelievers, exposing their shameful failings through clear proof, and laying bare their falsehoods and illusory notions.

“Their falsehoods are of three kinds:

“First: speaking of Allah in ways unbefitting Him, claiming that the angels are His daughters, that He has a child as a partner, and that He is the third of three.

“Second: describing the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as a sorcerer, a soothsayer, and a poet, and denying his prophethood.

“Third: denying the Last Day and rejecting the resurrection, the rising of the dead, Paradise, and Hell, and denying the consequences of obedience and disobedience.”

As for its accounts of the circumstances of believers and unbelievers in this world—which is what Abū Hāmid meant by mentioning the circumstances of those who respond and those who turn aside—this forms part of

---

## Page 8721

the full presentation of the proofs and signs. For this is something witnessed in this world: its effects have been seen, and reports of it have been transmitted through numerous independent sources. It is not among the events after death that remain unseen by Allah’s servants.

For this reason, He—glory be to Him—mentions such accounts as evidence and proof, alongside the admonition they contain, as in His words:

“Certainly, in their stories there is a lesson for people of understanding.”

“There was certainly a sign for you in the two armies that met: one fighting in the cause of Allah and the other disbelieving. They saw them with their own eyes as twice their number. Allah strengthens with His victory whom He wills. Indeed, in that is a lesson for those with insight.”

And His words:

“It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture from their homes at the first gathering. You did not think they would leave, and they thought their fortresses would protect them against Allah. But Allah came upon them from where they had not expected and cast terror into their hearts. They destroyed their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers. So take heed, O people of insight.”

And His words:

“Say: Travel through the land, then see what was the fate of those who denied the truth.”

And His words:

“How many a town We destroyed while it was doing wrong! It lies collapsed upon its roofs; how many an abandoned well and lofty palace!”

“Have they not travelled through the land so that they may have hearts with which to understand or ears with which to hear? For it is not the eyes that become blind, but the hearts within the breasts.”

And His words:

“Have they not travelled through the land and seen what was the fate of those before them? They were greater than them in strength, and they tilled the land and developed it more than these have developed it. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs”—and the following verses.

---

## Page 8722

And His words, exalted is He, after mentioning the account of the people of Lot:

“We turned it upside down and rained upon them stones of baked clay.”

“Indeed, in that are signs for those who discern.”

“And indeed, it lies on an established road.”

One who discerns is someone who draws inferences from marks and distinguishing signs. The Most High says:

“If We willed, We could show them to you, and you would recognize them by their marks; and you will surely recognize them by the tenor of their speech.”

Recognizing the hypocrites by the tenor of their speech is thus affirmed by an oath, but this occurs when they speak. Recognizing them by their marks, however, depends upon Allah’s will, for that is more subtle.

In the hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhī, who graded it sound, Abū Sa‘īd reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Beware of the believer’s discernment, for he sees by the light of Allah.”

He then recited the words of the Most High:

“Indeed, in that are signs for those who discern.”

Mujāhid and Ibn Qutaybah explained this as referring to those endowed with perceptive insight. Ibn Qutaybah said: “One says, ‘I discerned goodness in so-and-so,’ meaning, ‘I perceived it.’” Al-Zajjāj said: “In Arabic, those who discern are observers who keep their gaze fixed until they recognize the true distinguishing mark of a thing. One says, ‘I discerned such-and-such in so-and-so,’ meaning, ‘I recognized it.’”

His words, “who keep their gaze fixed,” refer to looking with their eyes until they recognize the distinguishing marks, unlike those of whom it is said:

“How many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by, yet turn away from it!”

Al-Dahhāk said: “Those who observe.” Ibn Zayd said: “Those who scrutinize.” Qatādah said: “Those who draw lessons.” All of this is correct, for one who discerns combines all these qualities.

Then the Most High said:

“And indeed, it lies on an established road.”

He then mentioned the account of the people of the thicket, and then said:

“And indeed, both lie on a clear highway.”

That is, on a road evident and clear to people.

---

## Page 8723

Likewise, in another passage, He says:

“So We brought out whoever was there of the believers.

“But We found there only a single household of Muslims.

“And We left therein a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.”

And He says concerning Noah’s Ark:

“And We certainly left it as a sign. Is there, then, anyone who will take heed?”

He thus tells us that He left signs—that is, marks and proofs. This shows that the particular accounts of the believers and their good outcome in this world, and of the disbelievers and their evil outcome in this world, constitute signs and proofs from which evidence and lessons may be drawn, yielding both knowledge and admonition. They establish the truth of what the messengers conveyed and provide encouragement and warning. They also demonstrate that Allah is pleased with those who obey Him and honors them, and that He is angry with those who disobey Him and punishes them.

Similarly, His creation in general provides evidence of His power, for an act necessarily entails power on the part of its agent. The perfection of His acts provides evidence of His knowledge, for a perfectly executed act necessarily entails knowledge on the part of its agent. His determining things in their particulars provides evidence of His will, for such determination necessarily entails His willing it. Likewise, His choosing what leads to the most praiseworthy outcome provides evidence of His wisdom, for directing an act toward a praiseworthy outcome necessarily entails wisdom.

His singling out the prophets and their followers for victory and a good outcome, and singling out those who deny them for disgrace and an evil outcome, provides evidence that He commands, loves, and is pleased with what the prophets brought, and that He dislikes and is displeased with the ways of those who denied them. For singling out one of these two groups for honor, deliverance, a good name, and prayers on their behalf, while singling out the other for punishment, destruction, an evil name, and curses, necessarily entails His love for what the first group did and His hatred of what the second group did.

---

## Page 8724

As for the will said to single out one of two equivalent things rather than the other without a reason, there is disagreement over whether Allah is to be described as possessing such a will.

If it is said that He is not, there is nothing further to discuss. If it is said that He is, it is nevertheless known that singling out the prophets—peace be upon them—for one treatment and their enemies for the other did not occur without a determining reason. Rather, it is known that He intended to single out the former for honor and the latter for punishment, and that the faith of the former was the reason for their treatment, while the disbelief of the latter was the reason for theirs. A fuller discussion of these matters belongs elsewhere. The point here, however, is that these three are included within the first three.

But Abū Hāmid identifies argumentation with the craft of speculative theology, maintaining the path with the science of jurisprudence, and accounts of the prophets with the science of narratives. He says that speculative theology and disputation do not establish any truth through evidence, but merely repel innovations by exposing their contradictions. He likens their practitioners to guards who protect pilgrims, and holds that the sole purpose of jurisprudence is worldly welfare. Most people have disputed his views on this and discussed them at a length that would be out of place here.

Likewise, they have criticized the philosophical ideas he presents in this book (Jawāhir al-Qur’ān, The Jewels of the Quran) and in his other books, which he regards as the Quran’s esoteric meaning. Muslim scholars have written more in refutation of this than in refutation of the foregoing, for it contains grave matters that contradict the Messenger’s intent. They have also criticized what he says about prophethood, which resembles the philosophers’ discourse on the subject.

---

## Page 8725

The point is that what he says about “Say: He is Allah, One” is better than what many people have said about it, and closer to the view we cited from Ibn Surayj and defended. Yet that view is undoubtedly correct, for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, stated that Allah divided the Quran into three parts, making “Say: He is Allah, One” one of those parts. This entails that the Quran as a whole consists of three parts, not six: three fundamental categories and three subsidiary ones.

Likewise, he stated that “Say: He is Allah, One” is equivalent to a third of the Quran. He did not say a third of its important content, of the greater part of it, or of its fundamental teachings. The entire Quran must therefore comprise three categories. According to Abū Hāmid’s account, however, it comprises six: three important categories and three supplementary ones, with this surah constituting one of the three important categories. This contradicts the hadith.

Moreover, dividing the Quran into three categories rests on a demonstrable basis: the Quran is speech, and speech is either informative or performative. Informative speech concerns either the Creator or creation. This is a clear division.

As for placing the science of jurisprudence outside the straight path and righteous action, and placing the science of proofs and arguments outside faith in and knowledge of Allah and the Last Day, this is rejected by the overwhelming majority of earlier and later scholars. Abū Hāmid only said this because he maintains that the meanings of these matters can be known solely through purification, not through prophetic reports or inferential reasoning.

---

## Page 8726

so these matters cannot be known through either transmitted revelation or reason. This is among the views for which people criticized him and which groups of scholars wrote books to refute. Yet Abū Hāmid’s excuse is that, in what he knew of the methods of the philosophers and speculative theologians, he found nothing that clarified the truth concerning these matters. He knew of no other rational methods, and therefore denied that the truth could be known through rational inquiry.

As for methods based on prophetic reports, he lacked familiarity with the authentically transmitted words of the Messenger and with how those words convey his intended meanings. Sharing certain assumptions with some speculative theologians and philosophers, he supposed that the Messenger had not made his meaning clear through his words. Together, these two positions closed off the paths of reason and transmitted revelation. He thought that the desired end could be attained, not through purification and practice, so he pursued that course, but still failed to attain his objective. Thus, toward the end of his life, he returned to reading al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

Qādī ‘Iyād mentioned several explanations of how “Say: He is Allah, One” is equivalent to a third of the Quran, as did al-Māzirī before him. He reports the Imam—meaning Abū ‘Abd Allah al-Māzirī—as saying:

“It has been said that this means the Quran comprises three kinds of content: narratives, rulings, and descriptions of Allah—exalted is His power. ‘Say: He is Allah, One’ contains mention of His attributes, and thus constitutes a third in this respect.”

He said: “This interpretation may accord with the apparent meaning of the hadith which mentions that Allah divided the Quran into parts.”

I say: This is Ibn Surayj’s view—the one we have defended. Al-Māzirī mentioned it in his discussion of Ibn Battāl’s remarks, as will follow.

He said: “It has also been said that it means a third of the Quran for a person

---

## Page 8727

in particular whom the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had in mind.”

Ibn Battāl also mentioned this. He said:

“It has also been said that Allah graciously multiplies the reward of whoever recites it, with this multiplication reaching an amount equal to one third of the reward he would merit for reciting the Quran without any multiplication of that reward.”

He said: “Some versions of this hadith report that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gathered the people and said, ‘I shall recite to you a third of the Quran.’ He then recited ‘Say: He is Allah, One.’”

Al-Māzirī said: “This version undermines the interpretation that makes this specific to a particular person.”

Qādī ‘Iyād said:

“Some have said: Allah Most High says, ‘Alif Lām Rā. A Book whose verses have been perfected and then explained in detail, from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware.’ He then sets out this detail, saying, ‘That you worship none but Allah.’ This is the section on divinity. Then He says, ‘Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bearer of good tidings.’ This is the section on prophethood. Then He says, ‘And seek your Lord’s forgiveness, then turn to Him in repentance.’ This is the section on religious obligation and the promises and warnings that follow it. As for the narratives found throughout much of the Quran, they belong to the section on prophethood, since they provide evidence for it and an understanding of it as well. This indicates that ‘Say: He is Allah, One’ encompasses the first section.”

I say:

The substance of this view is that the meanings of the Quran fall into three categories: matters concerning Allah, prophethood, and religious laws; and that this surah covers the matters concerning Allah. The proponent of this view placed promises, warnings, and narratives under the category of

---

## Page 8728

prophethood, because these are matters reported by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or matters that attest to his prophethood.

This view too is weak, for it may be objected that commands and prohibitions are also part of what the Prophet brought, just as he brought promises and warnings.

It may also be said that the narratives attest to commands and prohibitions just as they attest to prophethood. They show that Allah honors those who obey Him and punishes those who disobey Him, thereby reinforcing commands and prohibitions, as explained earlier. Moreover, the purpose of prophethood is to convey what Allah has commanded and what He has made known. Whatever in the narratives establishes prophethood also establishes the truth of what the Prophet brought; and whatever establishes the truth of what the Prophet brought establishes the commands and prohibitions he brought. The two are thus inseparably connected.

Furthermore, matters concerning Allah are also part of what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought. He explained the rational proofs for what can be known through reason and reported matters of the unseen wholly beyond the reach of reason. There is therefore no reason to include the narratives under prophethood but not matters concerning Allah. If what is meant is that the narratives attest to his prophethood, they do so because he reported them, just as he reported other matters of the unseen. Among his reports concerning Allah and future events are those that serve this purpose just as effectively as the narratives, and even more powerfully. If, however, what is meant is that the punishment of those who rejected the messengers attests to prophethood, then these narratives attest to prophethood in general and to

---

## Page 8729

the prophethood of the one whose people He punished; they do not establish the prophethood of a later prophet unless what he reports is of the same kind as what the earlier prophet reported.

All these considerations, and more, apply to matters concerning Allah, for the Prophet reported concerning Him the same things that the prophets before him had reported. Allah has mentioned this in several places, as in His words:

“Ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: Did We appoint any gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?”

And His words:

“We never sent a messenger before you without revealing to him: There is no deity but Me, so worship Me.”

And His words:

“We certainly sent a messenger to every nation, saying: Worship Allah and shun false gods.”

Allah has also told us that the prophets whose accounts He related—such as Noah, Hūd, Sālih, and Shuayb, may Allah’s blessings be upon them all—each said to his people:

“My people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him.”

Indeed, each began his call with this. The Most High also stated that the prophets and their communities, from Noah to the disciples, were Muslims, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Furthermore, it is through matters concerning Allah, by which the Lord’s power, will, wisdom, and actions are known, that a true prophet is distinguished from a pretender and a prophet’s truthfulness is established. These matters therefore provide stronger evidence of a prophet’s truthfulness than the narratives alone. Whatever evidence the narratives contain of his truthfulness has force only in conjunction with matters concerning Allah; taken in isolation, it would establish nothing. Prophethood is thus more closely connected with matters concerning Allah than with anything else, and the prophets were sent only to call people to Allah

---

## Page 8730

alone. They may describe the Hereafter both generally and in detail, while some of them may recount certain narratives only in general terms.

Matters concerning Allah, however, are the foundation. The command to worship Allah alone, to the exclusion of all others, must be explained in detail. Every prophet must therefore teach the three foundations: belief in Allah, belief in the Last Day, and righteous deeds. Allah mentions the universal foundations shared by the prophets in the Meccan surahs, such as al-Anʿām, al-Aʿrāf, the surahs beginning with “Alif Lām Rā,” “Tā Sīn Mīm,” and “Hā Mīm,” most of the Mufassal surahs, and others of this kind. The Medinan surahs include addresses to those who believe in messengers in general, from among the People of the Book, from among those who believe in the revealed laws with which the Seal of the Messengers was sent.

As for the claim that this concerns one particular individual, it is utterly untenable, both in wording and in meaning. Moreover, Allah singles out a particular case for a ruling peculiar to it only because of a consideration peculiar to that case. An example is what the Prophet said to Abū Burdah ibn Niyār. He had slaughtered his sacrifice on Eid before the prayer, before the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had prescribed for them that slaughtering should take place after the prayer. When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The first thing we do on this day of ours is pray; then we slaughter our sacrifices. Whoever slaughtered before the prayer must offer another sacrifice, for his animal was merely a sheep slaughtered for meat that he provided for his family,”

Abū Burdah told him that he had slaughtered before the prayer, not knowing that this was impermissible. He also told him that he had a young she-goat better than a jadhaʿah. He said:

“It will suffice for you, but it will not suffice for anyone after you.”

He singled him out for this ruling because he was excused for slaughtering before the prayer: he had done so before the ruling was instituted, so it was not

---

## Page 8731

yet prohibited. Moreover, the only animal he had was of that age. As for his instruction to the wife of Abū Hudhayfah ibn ‘Utbah to breastfeed Sālim, her husband’s freedman, five times so that he would become a relative she was permanently forbidden to marry, the early generations differed over this: was the ruling exclusive to him, or did it also apply to others? If it is said that it applies to anyone who needs it—as she did—this reconciles the evidence.

In short, the Lawgiver is wise. He does not distinguish between two like cases unless one has a particular feature warranting that distinction, nor does He treat as equal things that differ and are unequal.
