Indeed, He—glory be to Him—has rebuked those who attribute this to Him and condemned those who judge in this way. He, Most High, says:

“Or should We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like those who spread corruption on earth? Or should We treat the God-fearing like the wicked?”

He, Most High, also says:

“Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds, alike in their life and their death? How evil is their judgment!”

He, Most High, says:

“Shall We then treat those who submit to Us like the criminals?”

“What is the matter with you? How do you judge?”

He, Most High, says:

“Are your disbelievers better than those, or do you have immunity in the Scriptures?”

He, Most High, says:

“They destroy their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers. So take heed, O people of insight.”

Such a lesson can only be drawn if like cases are treated alike. But if it is said, “That is not how things actually are,” then no lesson can be drawn. People have differed over this principle, namely, whether He singles someone out with a command

---

## Page 8732

or prohibition without any cause or wisdom whatsoever, simply singling out one of two like cases rather than the other? Jahm ibn Safwān and those among the Jabriyyah (determinists) who agreed with him affirmed this, as did many speculative theologians who affirm divine decree.

The early generations, however, along with the leading scholars of jurisprudence, hadith, and Sufism, and most schools of speculative theology—both those who affirm divine decree, such as the Karrāmiyyah and others, and those who deny it, such as the Mu‘tazilah and others—do not accept this principle. Rather, they say that He—glory be to Him—makes particular distinctions in His creation and His commands for reasons and wisdom that He has in doing so. This principle has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Likewise, some say: “He multiplies its reciter’s reward to equal the unmultiplied reward given to someone who recites a third of the Quran.” This claim is supported neither by the hadith nor by reason, and there is no fitting rationale or wisdom in it. The text states that reciting it is equivalent to a third of the Quran, and that whoever recites it is as though he had recited a third of the Quran. If the reward is multiplied in one case, it is multiplied in the other; if it is not multiplied in one, neither is it multiplied in the other. To single out one of them for multiplication is therefore arbitrary.

Furthermore, assigning a multiplied reward equivalent to that of a third of the Quran can only be because of the surah’s distinctive merit. Its merit, then, accounts for this valuation, without any need to diminish the reward of the rest of the Quran. Moreover, this is sheer arbitrariness: no evidence supports it, no cause warrants it, and there is no wisdom in it.

People often err because of their deficient knowledge of, and faith in, the words of Allah and His Messenger, their worth, and what they contain

---

## Page 8733

of knowledge that surpasses the knowledge of all who came before and all who come after.

Whoever knows that the Messenger is the most knowledgeable of all creation concerning the truth, the most eloquent in explaining it, and the most sincere in seeking the good of creation knows that he combines perfect knowledge of the truth, perfect ability to explain it, and perfect willingness to do so. When knowledge, ability, and willingness are all complete, the intended result must be achieved in the most perfect manner. It is therefore clear that his words explain the religious matters he addressed—concerning Allah and other subjects—with the utmost eloquence, completeness, and clarity.

Whoever takes this firmly to heart cannot distort the texts through interpretations such as these. Upon reflection, he will find that anyone who intended such meanings by those words would be far removed from the qualities that the Messenger must possess. He will also know that whoever follows this path does so only because of a deficiency in the knowledge and faith he has been given. Allah Most High has said:

“Allah will raise those who have believed among you and those who were given knowledge, by degrees.”

We therefore ask Allah to make us and our brothers among the people of knowledge and faith whose ranks He has raised.

Now that the weakness of these views has become clear—apart from the first view, which we defended, held by Ibn Surayj and others such as al-Muhallab, al-Asīlī, and others—we say:

It is known that differences in excellence within the Quran and the rest of Allah’s speech are not based on their attribution to the Speaker, for He—glory be to Him—is One. Rather, they are based on the meanings He expresses and on His words that convey those meanings.

It is authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, singled out Sūrat al-Fātihah for superiority among the surahs, saying:

“There has never been revealed in

---

## Page 8734

the Torah, the Gospel, or the Quran anything like it.” The rulings of Islamic law support this, and its meanings have been discussed at length elsewhere.

Among the verses, he singled out the Verse of the Throne for superiority. In an authentic hadith, he said to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb:

“Do you know which verse in Allah’s Book that you know is the greatest?”

He replied: “Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence.”

He then struck him on the chest with his hand and said: “May your knowledge bring you joy, Abū al-Mundhir!”

No other single verse in the Quran contains all that the Verse of the Throne contains. What Allah mentions at the beginning of Sūrat al-Hadīd and the end of Sūrat al-Hashr extends over several verses, not just one.

We shall explain, if Allah wills, that even though “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” equals one-third of the Quran, it does not follow that it is superior to al-Fātihah, nor that reciting it three times suffices in place of reciting the Quran. Indeed, the early generations disapproved of reciting it more than once when reciting the entire Quran, just as it appears once in the written Quran. The Quran is to be recited as it is written in the written copy, without addition or omission.

The takbīr (declaration that Allah is the Greatest) transmitted from Ibn Kathīr is not traced through a chain of transmission to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. No one traced it through such a chain to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, except al-Bazzī, who thereby differed from everyone else who transmitted it. They transmitted it only as a practice chosen by someone below the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, whereas he alone traced it back to him. His weakness has been reported by scholars versed in hadith and its transmitters, among both scholars of Quranic recitation and scholars of hadith, as noted by more than

---

## Page 8735

one scholar. The point is that the Sunnah is to recite the Quran as it appears in the written copies. However, when “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” is recited on its own, it may be recited three times or more. Whoever recites it receives a reward equivalent to one-third of the reward for reciting the Quran. Yet a thing’s equivalent—ʿadl, pronounced with a short a—is of a different kind from it, as we shall explain, if Allah wills.

Rewards are of different kinds, just as wealth is of different kinds: food, drink, clothing, housing, money, and so forth. If a man possesses, for example, a thousand dinars’ worth of one kind of wealth, it does not follow that he can dispense with all the other kinds. If his wealth consists of food, he still needs clothing, housing, and other things. Likewise, if it consists of some kind other than money, he needs other kinds; and if he possesses nothing but money, he needs all the various goods themselves and the benefits they provide.

Al-Fātihah contains benefits in the form of praise and supplication that people need, for which “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” cannot substitute, even though its reward is immense. A person benefits from that immense reward only alongside the reward of reciting the Opening of the Book. Thus, if he were to recite that surah alone in prayer, without al-Fātihah, his prayer would not be valid. Even if he were to recite the entire Quran except al-Fātihah, his prayer would not be valid, because the meanings of al-Fātihah encompass the fundamental needs that Allah’s servants cannot do without. This has been discussed at length elsewhere, and it has been explained that the praise contained in al-Fātihah

---

## Page 8736

and supplication—namely, the words:

“Guide us to the straight path.”

“The path of those You have blessed, not those who have incurred Your anger, nor those who have gone astray.”

—constitute the finest, most binding, and most beneficial supplication a servant can address to his Lord. It encompasses all that benefits him in his religion, his worldly life, and the Hereafter. The servant constantly needs it, and nothing else can take its place. Even if he received the reward for reciting nine-tenths of the Quran—let alone one-third—but did not attain what this supplication seeks, that reward would neither replace it nor fulfil its purpose.

This is like a man who, hypothetically, gives immense sums in charity and undertakes great efforts in jihad, surpassing in merit repeated recitations of the Quran, yet has not performed the five prayers that day. The reward for these deeds would not take the place of those prayers. Likewise, a man might possess immense wealth in gold, silver, slaves, livestock, and real estate, yet have no food for his morning and evening meals. He would remain hungry, suffering, and in distress; all that immense wealth would not take the place of the food he needs. Hence Shaykh Abū Madyan, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

“The noblest knowledge is knowledge of Allah’s oneness;
the most beneficial knowledge is knowledge of the rulings governing His servants.”

Thus, what is superior and nobler is not necessarily what benefits a person at a particular time. Rather, what is most beneficial at any given time is what the servant needs then: doing what Allah has commanded and refraining from what He has forbidden. Hence it is said:

“What is generally less meritorious is, in its proper place and time, better than what is generally more meritorious.”

For the revealed law indicates that prayer is superior to Quran recitation, Quran recitation is superior to remembrance of Allah, and remembrance of Allah is superior to

---

## Page 8737

supplication. This is a general principle. Yet prayer may be forbidden at certain times, making Quran recitation superior to prayer at those times. Likewise, glorifying Allah is commanded during bowing and prostration, whereas Quran recitation is forbidden. There are many similar examples.

The merit of “Say: He is Allah, One” and other surahs should be understood accordingly. Reciting al-Fātihah at the beginning of prayer is better than reciting that surah; indeed, it is obligatory. That surah alone cannot suffice; rather, the prayer is invalid if one relies on it alone.

Thus, drawing near to Allah through obligatory deeds must precede drawing near through voluntary deeds. Voluntary deeds constitute a means of drawing near only when the obligatory deeds are performed. This contradicts what some proponents of union maintain, such as the author of al-Futūhāt al-Makkiyyah (The Meccan Revelations) and others like him: that nearness through obligatory deeds follows nearness through voluntary deeds, and that voluntary deeds make the Real his covering, whereas obligatory deeds make the Real his very self. This rests upon his corrupt doctrine of union, as explained.

It has also been explained that the hadith contradicts his doctrine in several respects. Al-Bukhārī narrated it in his Sahīh from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah says: ‘Whoever shows enmity towards a devoted servant of Mine has openly declared war against Me. My servant draws near to Me through nothing comparable to fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues drawing near to Me through voluntary deeds until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he grasps, and through Me he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him, and if he seeks refuge in Me, I will surely grant him refuge.

---

## Page 8738

and I have never hesitated over anything I am going to do as I hesitate over taking the soul of My believing servant: he hates death, and I hate to distress him, yet he must inevitably face it.’”

This hadith makes clear that the one drawing near is not the One to whom he draws near; rather, he is distinct from Him. It also makes clear that His servant draws near to Him through nothing comparable to fulfilling the obligatory duties, and thereafter continues drawing near through voluntary deeds until he becomes beloved to Allah. He then hears through Him, sees through Him, grasps through Him, and walks through Him. Then He says:

“If he asks Me, I will surely give him, and if he seeks refuge in Me, I will surely grant him refuge.”

Thus He distinguishes between the one asking and the One being asked, and between the one seeking refuge and the One in whom refuge is sought. He describes the servant as asking his Lord and seeking refuge in Him. This is a noble hadith encompassing great purposes, which this is not the place to discuss. Our purpose here is to discuss “Say: He is Allah, One.”

We have explained that the best explanation is that the meanings of the Quran fall into three categories: affirmation of Allah’s oneness, narratives, and rulings. This surah describes the Most Merciful and contains only the affirmation of His oneness. This is because the Quran is Allah’s speech.

Speech is of two kinds: prescriptions and reports. Reports concern either the Creator or created beings. Prescriptions are rulings, such as commands and prohibitions. Reports concerning created beings are narratives, while reports concerning the Creator consist of the mention of His names and attributes. No surah in the Quran is devoted purely to describing the Most Merciful except this surah. In the two Sahīhs, ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah Most High be pleased with her, reported: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, appointed a man to command a military detachment

---

## Page 8739

and, when leading his companions in prayer, he would conclude his recitation with ‘Say: He is Allah, One.’ When they returned, they mentioned this to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He said, ‘Ask him why he does that.’ They asked him, and he replied, ‘Because it describes the Most Merciful, and I love to recite it.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Tell him that Allah loves him.’”

Al-Bukhārī also stated in the chapter “Combining Two Surahs in One Unit of Prayer”:

‘Ubayd Allāh reported from Thābit, from Anas:

“A man from the Ansār used to lead them in prayer in the mosque of Qubā’. Whenever he was about to recite a surah for them in prayer, he would first recite ‘Say: He is Allah, One’ in full, then recite another surah along with it. He did this in every unit of prayer. His companions spoke to him, saying, ‘You begin with this surah, but then you do not consider it sufficient without reciting another. Either recite it alone, or leave it and recite another.’

“He replied, ‘I will not give it up. If you would like me to lead you in prayer in this way, I will do so; but if you dislike it, I will stop leading you.’ They considered him one of the best among them and were reluctant to have anyone else lead them.

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came to them, they told him what had happened. He said, ‘So-and-so, what prevents you from doing what your companions ask of you, and what makes you adhere to this surah in every unit of prayer?’

“He replied, ‘I love it.’ He said, ‘Your love for it has admitted you to Paradise.’”

The Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “It is equivalent to one-third of the Quran,” is true, just as he said. For he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the truthful one whose truthfulness is confirmed, who does not speak from his own desire. Nothing but the truth ever passed his lips.

---

## Page 8740

Those who find this statement problematic base their objections on two grounds:

The first is their denial that some of Allah’s speech is superior to other parts—a position whose weakness has already been demonstrated. The second is their belief that reward depends on the number of letters: the more letters a passage contains, the greater the reward for reciting it.

They argue that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever recites the Quran will have ten good deeds credited to him for every letter. I do not say that ‘Alif Lām Mīm’ is one letter; rather, alif is a letter, lām is a letter, and mīm is a letter.”

Al-Tirmidhī said, “An authentic hadith.” They argue, “It is well known that one-third of the Quran contains far more letters, so the good deeds credited for it must be more numerous.”

The response to them is:

This is true, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stated. Yet good deeds vary in magnitude: some are great and others small. The Prophet’s point, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was that Allah rewards His servant tenfold for every good deed, as He, Most High, says:

“Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold.”

Thus, reciting a letter constitutes a good deed, and Allah grants the reciter ten times the value of that good deed. But he did not say that the good deeds credited for reciting different letters are equal in value. Likewise, someone who gives a dinar in charity receives ten times the reward for that good deed.

If someone who came after the earliest forerunners were to spend gold equal to Mount Uhud, it would not equal a mudd given by any one of them, nor even half of it, as is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the two Sahīh collections. Thus, if that person gives a mudd, he receives ten times the reward for this good deed. But

---

## Page 8741

that good deed is not equal in value to the good deed of one of the earliest Companions who gave a mudd. There are many similar examples. Likewise, the letters of the Quran differ in merit because their meanings differ in excellence, and for other reasons. For each letter of al-Fātihah, the reciter earns a good deed greater than those earned for letters of “May the hands of Abū Lahab perish.”

When one thing is equivalent to another, its ʿadl—with the vowel a—is its equal, even if it is of a different kind. As Allah, Most High, says:

“Or the equivalent of that in fasting.”

Fasting is not of the same kind as food or the compensatory offering, but it is equivalent to them in measure. Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah will accept from him neither sarf nor ʿadl.”

And Allah, Most High, says:

“Nor will any ransom be accepted from it.”

Here, ʿadl means a ransom: something equivalent to what is being redeemed, even if it is of a different kind.

“Yet those who disbelieve set up equals to their Lord.”

That is, they assign Him an equal—a rival in divinity—even though they know that it is not of the same kind as the Lord, glory be to Him.

If one man possessed various kinds of wealth, and another possessed gold of the same value, the wealth of the one would be equivalent to that of the other, even though they were of different kinds. Thus, a man may possess gold and other assets of immense value, yet if he needs medicine, a compound preparation, a dwelling, or something similar, and is unable to purchase it, that immense wealth will not benefit him.

People need the commands, prohibitions, and narratives contained in the Quran, even though the affirmation of Allah’s oneness is greater than these. If a person needs to know which actions He has commanded and which He has forbidden, or

---

## Page 8742

needs the instruction and lessons conveyed by the narratives, promises, and warnings, nothing else can take their place. The affirmation of Allah’s oneness cannot replace these, nor can the narratives replace the commands and prohibitions, or the commands and prohibitions replace the narratives. Rather, people benefit from and need everything Allah has revealed.

When a person recites “Say: He is Allah, One,” he receives a reward equal in measure to the reward for a third of the Quran. Yet this reward need not be of the same kind as that obtained through the rest of the Quran. He may need the kind of reward obtained through its commands, prohibitions, and narratives, and “Say: He is Allah, One” neither replaces these nor serves in their stead.

Thus, if he does not recite “Say: He is Allah, One,” then, even if he receives a great reward, he does not obtain by reciting it the kind of reward obtained by reciting other parts of the Quran. Rather, he remains in need of the knowledge of commands, prohibitions, promises, and warnings through which his faith is perfected, even if he fulfills his obligations. The knowledge gained by reciting the rest of the Quran cannot be gained merely by reciting this surah.

In this respect, one who recites the entire Quran is better than one who recites this surah three times, because of the variety of rewards. Although someone who recites “Say: He is Allah, One” three times receives a reward equal in measure to that reward, it is of a single kind, lacking the various kinds that the servant needs. This is like one person possessing three thousand dinars, while another possesses food, clothing, dwellings, and money together worth three thousand dinars. The latter possesses what benefits him in all his affairs, whereas the former needs what the latter possesses, even though their possessions are equal in value. Likewise, if he possessed

---

## Page 8743

food of the finest quality worth three thousand dinars, he would still need clothing, dwellings, and means of warding off harm, such as weapons, medicines, and other things that food alone cannot provide.

It should also be understood that the merit of recitation, remembrance of Allah, supplication, prayer, and other acts may vary according to a person’s condition. Recitation with reflection is better than recitation without reflection, and prayer with humility and an attentive heart is better than prayer without them. A report states:

“Two men may stand together in the same row, yet the difference between their prayers is as great as the distance between heaven and earth.”

One of the shaykhs used to recite “Say: He is Allah, One” for healing, and this brought great blessing. Others would recite it for healing without obtaining that result, so he would say: “Not everyone’s recitation of ‘Say: He is Allah, One’ benefits everyone.”

Once this is understood, one person’s glorification of Allah may be better than another’s recitation, and one person’s recitation of certain surahs may be better than another’s recitation of “Say: He is Allah, One” or other surahs. A single person’s condition also varies. He may perform an act of lesser merit in a perfect manner and thereby attain greater merit than through his other, more excellent deeds.

Allah forgave a prostitute for giving a dog water, as established in the two Sahīh collections. This was because of the acts of the heart and other factors that accompanied her deed. A man may spend many times as much yet not be forgiven, because the factors that purify a deed are absent. For Allah accepts only from those who are mindful of Him. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said

---

## Page 8744

in an authentic hadith:

“Were any of you to spend as much gold as Mount Uhud, it would not equal one mudd (a measure) given by any one of them, nor even half of it.”

He said this concerning his earliest and foremost Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Thus, when it is said that the reward for “Say: He is Allah, One” equals the reward for one-third of the Quran, equality in all other respects must be taken into account. Otherwise, if reciting other passages with reflection and humility is compared with reciting this surah in heedlessness and ignorance, that equivalence does not hold.

Indeed, a servant’s saying:

“Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is the Greatest,”

with an attentive heart imbued with these meanings may be better than reciting this surah in ignorance and heedlessness. People differ in their understanding of this surah and what it contains, just as they differ in their understanding of the rest of the Quran.

Section

The foundation of this issue is to understand that differences in excellence and equality can exist only between two or more things. Within that which is one in every respect, it is inconceivable that one thing should be better than another. Differences in excellence among His attributes, exalted is He, are therefore conceivable only if multiple attributes are affirmed for Him, such as knowledge, power, will, love, hatred, pleasure, and anger. Likewise, multiple names denoting multiple meanings are affirmed for Him, and multiple words are affirmed for Him

---

## Page 8745

that subsist in His Essence, so that one may ask: “Are some of them superior to others, or not?” Every position in this matter other than that of the early generations and the leading scholars is erroneous and self-contradictory. Whatever answer its proponent gives to this question will be erroneous; he cannot give a sound answer.

Thus, whoever says that He has no positive attributes, but only negative or relational attributes—as do the thoroughgoing Jahmiyyah among the philosophers and speculative theologians, the followers of Jahm ibn Safwān—cannot, on the basis of his false premise, give a sound answer when asked: “Which is superior: His relation to the heavens and the earth—namely, creating them—or His relation to a mosquito? Or which is superior: denying that He is ignorant of anything or incapable of anything, or denying that He is ignorant of universals?”

If he says, “Creating the heavens is equivalent to creating a mosquito,” this is an obstinate denial of both reason and revelation. Allah, Most High, says:

“The creation of the heavens and the earth is indeed greater than the creation of mankind, but most people do not know.”

But if he says, “Rather, the former is mightier and greater, as stated in the Quran,” he is told: “You acknowledge no two existing realities, one of which surpasses the other, since, according to you, creation is nothing beyond the created thing itself. Thus, nothing remains but sheer nonexistence. How, then, can one conceive of one of two things that are nonexistent in every respect being superior to the other, when there is no existent reality in which such a difference in excellence could occur?”

Likewise, to say that negating ignorance and inability with regard to some things is equivalent to negating them with regard to other things is an obstinate denial. But if he says, “Rather, negating ignorance generally is more perfect than negating ignorance in particular cases,” he is told: “If it does not

---

## Page 8746

follow from the negation of ignorance that knowledge of anything is affirmed, but rather both negations are pure nonexistence, how can differences in excellence be conceived in something that is identical in every respect? Such differences cannot be conceived in pure nonexistence and sheer negation, for that is nothing at all: it has no reality in existence and contains neither perfection nor anything praiseworthy. Differences in excellence arise only through attributes of perfection, and perfection must consist either in a self-subsisting existent or in an existing attribute subsisting in something else. Pure nonexistence contains no perfection whatsoever.”

This is why Allah describes Himself with attributes declaring His freedom from imperfection, not with merely negative attributes of nonexistence: they imply positive realities that constitute perfections by which He—glorified be He—praises Himself. This has been explained at length elsewhere. For example, He, Most High, says:

“Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep.”

Negating these things implies the perfection of His life and of His self-subsistence and sustaining of all things. Likewise, His words:

“Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?”

imply the perfection of His sovereignty and lordship, and that these belong to Him alone. His exclusive possession of sovereignty, guidance, teaching, and all other attributes of perfection is itself an attribute of perfection. This is why the surah contains the two names al-Ahad (the One) and al-Samad, each of which indicates perfection. His word “Ahad” indicates that He has no equal, while His word “al-Samad,” with the definite article, indicates that the quality denoted by this name belongs exclusively to Him. This is why the definite article appears in His name al-Samad but not in Ahad: no one other than Him is described affirmatively as ahad, unlike samad, for the Arabs call a chief samad.

Yahyā ibn Abī Kathīr said: “The angels are called samad, whereas the human being is hollow.” Thus, His word

---

## Page 8747

“al-Samad” indicates that the perfection denoted by this name belongs exclusively to Him.

We have already explained the meaning of al-Samad and how it encompasses every attribute of perfection, as the scholars transmitted from Ibn Abī Talha’s account of Ibn ʿAbbās’s explanation. Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Hātim, al-Bayhaqī and others cited it. Explaining His word “al-Samad,” he says:

“The Master whose mastery is perfect; the Noble One whose nobility is perfect; the Great One whose greatness is perfect; the Wise One whose wisdom is perfect; the All-Knowing One whose knowledge is perfect; and the Forbearing One whose forbearance is perfect. He is perfect in every aspect of nobility and mastery. Such is His description—glorified be He—and it befits Him alone. He has no equal, and there is nothing like Him. Glorified be He, the One, the All-Subduing.”

Likewise, it is established through the narration of al-Aʿmash from Abū Wāʾil, cited by al-Bukhārī in his Sahīh and transmitted by many scholars in their books, that he said:

“Al-Samad is the Master whose mastery has reached its utmost perfection.”

Several of the early generations, including Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and others, also said:

“Al-Samad is the One who has no hollow interior.”

Both explanations are true and accord with the Arabic language, as has been explained at length in its proper place. That al-samad means “the master” is well known; the other meaning is also recognized in the language. Al-Jawharī and others mentioned that al-samad is a variant of al-samt (that which is solid, without a hollow interior). This is not a case of substituting the letter t for d, as some have supposed; rather, the forms samada, yasmudu, samadan themselves indicate this meaning.

The point here is that attributes of perfection pertain only to things that exist

---

## Page 8748

and negative attributes constitute perfection only when they imply positive realities. Thus, glorifying the Lord involves both declaring Him free of imperfection and magnifying Him. When a servant says, “Glory be to Allah,” this declares Allah’s freedom from all evil and imperfection. This meaning entails His intrinsic greatness; it is not mere negation devoid of any positive reality, for that would convey neither praise nor magnification.

The same applies to everything else from which the Lord is declared free, including partners, offspring and other things. Thus, He, Most High, says:

“Has your Lord, then, favoured you with sons and taken females from among the angels for Himself? You are indeed making an outrageous claim!”

—up to His words—

“Then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne.”

“Glory be to Him! Exalted is He far above what they say!”

“The seven heavens, the earth, and all those within them glorify Him. There is nothing that does not glorify Him with praise, but you do not understand their glorification. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing, All-Forgiving.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, far above what they ascribe to Him!”

“And peace be upon the messengers.”

There are other such passages. Negating faults and deficiencies necessarily entails affirming perfection, while denying partners entails oneness, which is part of complete perfection. For when something has a counterpart, the attributes and acts of perfection are divided between it and its counterpart, so it possesses some attributes of perfection, not all of them. Thus, the One who alone possesses every attribute of perfection is more perfect than one who has a partner sharing those attributes with him.

This is why those who affirm Allah’s oneness and devote themselves sincerely to Him love Allah more perfectly than the polytheists who love others besides Him—those who have taken rivals besides Him, loving them as they love Him. He says:

---

## Page 8749

Most High:

“Among people are those who take rivals besides Allah, loving them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

This has been discussed at length elsewhere, where it has been explained that this constitutes major polytheism, which Allah Most High does not forgive. In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn Masʿūd reported:

“I asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, which sin is greatest?’ He replied, ‘To set up a rival to Allah when it is He who created you.’ I asked, ‘Then which?’ He replied, ‘To kill your child for fear that he will share your food.’ I asked, ‘Then which?’ He replied, ‘To commit adultery with your neighbour’s wife.’”

Allah Most High revealed confirmation of this:

“And those who do not invoke another god besides Allah, nor kill a soul whom Allah has forbidden to be killed except by right, nor commit adultery”—to the end of the verse.

Whoever sets up a rival to Allah, loving it as he loves Allah, is among those who invoke another god besides Allah. This constitutes major polytheism. The point here is that when something is divided and shared, the portion each receives is diminished; when all of it belongs to one, it is more complete. This is why the love for Allah of believers who affirm His oneness and devote themselves sincerely to Him is more perfect.

Likewise, refraining from the other major sins and indecencies they have been forbidden brings the positive realities of their worship, obedience, knowledge and love to perfection. This contributes to their purification and growth, just as removing weeds from a crop makes it flourish more fully and brings its positive attributes of perfection to greater fulfilment. Allah Most High says:

“Woe to the polytheists,”

“who do not give zakah.”

The foundation of zakah is affirming Allah’s oneness

---

## Page 8750

and sincere devotion to Him, as the foremost scholars of the early generations explained it.

Allah Most High says:

“Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their chastity. That is purer for them.”

He also says:

“Take charity from their wealth to purify and cleanse them thereby.”

All this has been discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that whoever denies imperfections of Allah—such as death, ignorance, inability, deafness, blindness and muteness—without affirming attributes that have real existence, such as life, knowledge, power, hearing, sight and speech, but instead claims that His attributes are purely negative and that He cannot be described by anything positively existent, has established no attribute of perfection for Him whatsoever, let alone any basis for asking which of two attributes is superior. Comparing two things in excellence presupposes that each possesses some perfection; only then can one consider which is more perfect. If, however, both are assumed to be pure nonexistence, there is neither perfection nor excellence there at all.

The same applies to someone who affirms His names but not His attributes, saying, “He is Living, All-Knowing, All-Powerful, All-Hearing, All-Seeing, Almighty and All-Wise—but these names do not entail that He possesses life, knowledge, power, hearing, sight, might or wisdom.”

If he is then asked, “Which of the two names is superior?” he cannot give a sound answer. For if he says, for example, “The All-Knowing is greater than the All-Hearing because its scope is universal,” or, “The Almighty is more perfect than the All-Powerful because it necessarily entails power, whereas the reverse does not hold,” he would be told: “If, in your view, the names have no

---

## Page 8751

real meanings subsisting in Him, then there is no knowledge, hearing, sight, might or power. There is nothing but an essence stripped of attributes, and created things. Within this bare essence, there is nothing that admits of comparison in either excellence or equality. As for created things, the question was not whether some are superior to others: everyone knows that they are, and no rational person is in doubt about it.”

The same applies to anyone who identifies some of His attributes with others, or identifies an attribute with the One possessing it—for example, someone who says, “Knowledge is power, and knowledge and power are themselves the One who knows and has power,” as some of the Jahmī philosophers and others maintain.

Or someone may say:

“All His speech is a single meaning subsisting in His essence. It is the command enjoining everything commanded and the report of everything reported. If expressed in Arabic, it is the Quran; if expressed in Hebrew, it is the Torah; and if expressed in Syriac, it is the Gospel. The meaning of the Verse of the Throne and the verse on debt is one and the same. Command and prohibition are relational attributes of speech, not distinct kinds of it. Rather, the very speech that is a command is the very speech that is a prohibition; only the relation differs.”

Such is the doctrine professed by the Kullābiyyah. Although most rational people say that merely conceiving it is enough to recognize its falsity, on this view one cannot answer that some of Allah’s speech is superior to other parts, or that some is equal to others, because, according to them, speech is one and the same entity

---

## Page 8752

that admits neither multiplicity nor division. How, then, can one ask, “Are some parts of it superior to others, or are they equal?” when, according to them, it has no parts?

If they say, “Equality and superiority concern the expressions that signify it,” the reply is: “According to the foundational principle of this doctrine, and according to their leading authorities, those expressions are not Allah’s speech. Rather, they are among His created things, and there is no difficulty in acknowledging differences in excellence among created things.”

Any of their followers who says that these expressions are literally called Allah’s speech, and that the term ‘speech’ applies both to them and to that meaning subsisting within the self by way of homonymy, has not understood the true nature of their doctrine. Indeed, this claim of his undermines their foundational principle.

For their foundational principle is that speech subsists only in the speaker, not in anyone else. If speech could subsist in someone other than the speaker, Allah’s speech could be created and subsist in someone other than Him while still being Allah’s speech.

This is the foundational principle of the outright Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah, on which the Kullābiyyah and all others who affirm the divine attributes opposed them. They said: “A speaker cannot be a speaker unless speech subsists in him.” They said the same concerning the other attributes: “A knower cannot be a knower unless knowledge subsists in him, nor can one who wills be such unless will subsists in him.” Thus, if they allowed Allah to have speech that is His while being created and separate from Him, this foundational principle would be invalidated.

The foundational principle of those among the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah who negate and deny the divine attributes is that they describe Allah by what does not subsist in Him, but instead subsists in something other than Him, or by what does not exist. They say, “These are relations, not attributes.” Thus they say that He is merciful and shows mercy, yet mercy does not subsist in Him; rather, it is

---

## Page 8753

created, and is His bounty.

They say: “He is pleased and becomes angry, but pleasure and anger do not subsist in Him; rather, they are created, and are His reward and punishment.” They say: “He is a speaker and speaks, but speech does not subsist in Him; rather, it is created and subsists in something other than Him.” They may also say: “He possesses will and wills.” Then they may say that will is not something existent; or they may say that it consists of created things and the created command. They may also say: “He brought into being a will that subsists in no subject.”

This false foundational principle, established by those who negate the attributes—the outright Jahmiyyah among the Muʿtazilah and others—is precisely the point on which all who affirm the attributes parted ways with them. These include the early generations, the imams, the scholars of jurisprudence, hadith, Sufism, and Quranic exegesis, and the various speculative thinkers who affirm the attributes: the Kullābiyyah and their followers among the Ashʿariyyah and others, as well as the Hishāmiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, and other groups of speculative thinkers who affirm the attributes. This is also the position of the recognized leading imams of the Muslims and the leading jurists among their followers—the adherents of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, Abū Hanīfah, and others.

Thus, the claim that the term ‘speech’ applies literally to the expression, while that expression is nevertheless created, contradicts the foundational principle distinguishing those who affirm the attributes from those who deny them—unless that to which an attribute relates is given the name of the attribute itself. Thus, what is commanded is called a ‘command’; that through which mercy is shown is called ‘mercy’; a created thing is called ‘creation’; what is decreed is called ‘power’; and what is known is called ‘knowledge’. But the reply to him is: “None of these is the literal meaning when the term is used without qualification.”

---

## Page 8754

Moreover, these things are entities that subsist in their own right. When they are ascribed to Allah, the ascription is understood to denote ownership, not an attribute. An expression, by contrast, does not subsist in its own right, just as a meaning does not. This is the fundamental distinction between ascribing attributes to Allah and ascribing created things to Him.

Those who negate and deny the attributes among the Sabians, philosophers, Muʿtazilah, and other Jahmiyyah, together with their followers—such as Ibn ʿAqīl and Ibn al-Jawzī in some of their writings, although elsewhere they state the opposite—say: “The texts merely ascribe these things to Allah. These are called texts concerning ascriptions, not texts concerning attributes.” They speak of “texts concerning ascriptions” and “hadiths concerning ascriptions,” rather than “verses concerning the attributes” and “hadiths concerning the attributes.”

An ascription may relate a created thing to Allah because it has a particular connection to Him in some respect, as with the House, the she-camel, and the spirit in His words:

“And purify My House,”

and His words:

“Allah’s she-camel,”

and His words:

“Then We sent to her Our Spirit, and he appeared to her as a well-proportioned man.”

The proponents of divine indwelling among the Christians, the extremist Shīʿah, and the Sufis, together with their followers who hold that the spirit—that is, the souls of human beings—has no beginning, and who claim affiliation with Muslim imams such as al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others—including a group from Jīlān and elsewhere—say: “Rather, ascribing the spirit to Allah is like ascribing speech and power to Him. Speech and power are His attributes, and so too is the spirit.”

They also say that His words:

“When I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit”

provide evidence that the human soul is a beginningless attribute of Allah.

The Christians said:

---

## Page 8755

“Jesus is the Word of Allah, and Allah’s speech is uncreated; therefore Jesus is uncreated.”

The Sabians and the Jahmiyyah said:

“Jesus is the Word of Allah, and he is created. The Quran is Allah’s speech, so it too is created.”

These matters have confused many people. The imams, such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others, discussed them, addressing the ascription of speech and spirit to Allah and debating the Jahmiyyah and the Christians.

I have been asked about this, sometimes in connection with the proponents of divine indwelling and sometimes in connection with those who negate the attributes. The questioners have sometimes been Muslims and sometimes non-Muslims. The answer has been set out at length in several places. Here, however, the point is to distinguish between the two kinds of things ascribed to Allah:

If what is ascribed to Him is something that subsists in its own right, or something that inheres in such a self-subsisting entity, it cannot be an attribute of Allah, because an attribute subsists in that which it describes. The entities Allah has created subsist in their own right, and the attributes subsisting in them cannot be attributes of Allah. Ascribing them to Him therefore entails that they are created and owned by Him. They are ascribed to Him because of a particular connection that warrants this ascription, not because they are His attributes.

The Spirit, who is Gabriel, belongs to this category, as do the Kaaba and the she-camel. Wealth belonging to Allah also falls into this category, as do the souls of Adam’s descendants. Examples include His words:

“Then We sent to her Our Spirit, and he appeared to her as a well-proportioned man.”

“When I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit.”

“And purify My House.”

“Allah’s she-camel and her turn to drink!”

“Whatever Allah has granted His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah and to the Messenger.”

---

## Page 8756

But if what is ascribed to Him does not subsist in its own right, but can only be an attribute—such as knowledge, power, speech, pleasure, or anger—then this can only be the ascription of an attribute to Him, one that subsists in Him, glorified is He. Thus, when one says:

“I seek Your guidance through Your knowledge, and seek ability through Your power,”

His knowledge is an attribute subsisting in Him, and His power is an attribute subsisting in Him. Likewise, when one says:

“I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your wrath, and in Your pardon from Your punishment,”

His pleasure and wrath subsist in Him, as do His pardon and punishment. Their effects, however—the blessings that reach the servant and the afflictions averted from him—are created, separate from Him, and are not His attributes. The effect may be called by the name of the attribute, as in the authentic hadith:

“Allah says to Paradise: ‘You are My mercy; through you I show mercy to whomever I will among My servants.’”

Here, mercy is a self-subsisting entity and cannot be an attribute of something else. This, then, is the distinction between ascribing something as an attribute and ascribing it as a possession.

When it is said, “The Messiah is the Word of Allah,” this means that he was created through the word, for the Messiah himself is not speech. This is unlike the Quran, which is itself speech. Speech does not subsist in its own right, but only in the speaker. Its ascription to the speaker is therefore the ascription of an attribute to the one it describes, even though the speaker speaks through his power and will. Even if it is called an act in this respect, it is an attribute insofar as it subsists in the speaker.

Since this is so, whoever says that speech is a single meaning subsisting in the speaker’s essence cannot give a sound answer to this question. Thus, if it is said

---

## Page 8757

to him, “Are some parts of Allah’s speech superior to others?” he cannot, on his own premises, answer either yes or no, since he considers it indivisible and does not regard its verbal expression as Allah’s speech.

But suppose “speech” means the verbal expression, or he is asked, “Are some parts of the Quran superior to others?”—meaning by “Quran” the Arabic speech brought down by Gabriel, which he considers created, not spoken by Allah, but composed by Gabriel or someone else. Or suppose he is asked, “Are some of Allah’s scriptures superior to others?”—while Allah’s Book, according to him, is the Arabic Quran, which he considers created. Such a question would appear applicable to his position. In reality, however, both are impossible on his premises, because verbal expressions signify meanings: the meanings subsisting within the self are conveyed by verbal expressions. It is known that verbal expressions signify diverse meanings, whereas his premise allows only a single meaning. It is therefore necessarily impossible, as a matter of reason, for the entire Arabic Quran, the Torah, the Gospel, and all other verbal expressions attributed to Allah to signify only one meaning admitting neither multiplicity nor division. Thus, verbal expressions signifying meanings cannot be divisible unless those meanings are divisible as well.

For this reason, they have been asked: “When Moses, peace be upon him, heard Allah’s speech, did he hear all of it or only part of it?” If you say, “All of it,” then he knew everything Allah has communicated and everything He has commanded. Yet it is authentically reported that al-Khidr said to him:

“My knowledge and yours have diminished Allah’s knowledge only as much as this sparrow has diminished this sea.”

And indeed,

---

## Page 8758

He, the Exalted, says:

“Say, ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought another like it to replenish it.’”

If you say, “He heard part of it,” then it is divisible, whereas according to you it is indivisible. Moreover, Allah distinguished between His speaking to Moses, blessings and peace be upon him, and His revealing to the other prophets. He also distinguished between revelation and speaking from behind a veil. If the meaning were one and the same, all of this would be revelation, and there would be no distinct speaking beyond that. Nor is it impossible for the Lord Most High to call out to someone, since a meaning subsisting within the self does not constitute a call. Allah Most High has stated in several places in the Quran that He called out.

Accordingly, when any of these people says that no part of Allah’s speech is superior to another, what his position actually entails is that the question itself is impossible: there are not two things such that one could be said to equal the other or be superior to it. Equality and superiority are conceivable only between two or more things. They hold the same position concerning His will, knowledge, hearing, and sight. For anyone who regards an attribute as a single entity, it is impossible—on his own premises—to ask whether some parts of it are superior to others, since he holds that it has no parts.

The same applies to anyone who agrees with them that these attributes are each a single entity, yet says that Allah’s speech consists of letters that are individually beginningless, or of letters and sounds that are individually beginningless—whether he also says that they are the very sounds heard from reciters, or that they are some of the sounds heard from reciters—even though the falsity of this is self-evident,

---

## Page 8759

and says that these sounds are distinct from those.

Whoever maintains that speech consists of letters, or letters and sounds, conjoined with one another without beginning or end, yet constituting a single entity, holds a position whose falsity is recognized by the great majority of rational people. Likewise, the position of anyone who regards them as a single utterance is recognized as false by the great majority of rational people. In any event, if something is held to be a single entity, it is impossible to ask whether some of it is superior to the rest.

As for someone who affirms multiplicity in meanings and letters, or in either of them, his position makes the question of equality and superiority intelligible. The question then arises: can there be degrees of superiority within Allah’s speech, attributes, and names, or can such differences exist only among created things?

Accordingly, Ibn Battāl’s account in his commentary on al-Bukhārī, when discussing this hadith, reads:

“Al-Muhallab said—and he related this from al-Asīlī; it is also the position of al-Ash'arī, Abū Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, Ibn Abī Zayd, al-Dāwūdī, Abū al-Hasan al-Qābisī, and a group of Sunni scholars—that no part of the Quran is superior to another, since all of it is the speech of Allah Most High and His attribute, and it is uncreated. Degrees of superiority are possible only among created things.”

This presents these scholars’ views according to what he supposed their positions entailed, since he believed that degrees of superiority could exist only among created things, whereas these scholars held the Quran to be uncreated. Yet we have already explained that none of the early generations who declared it uncreated is reported to have said that no part of it is superior to another. Rather, what is reported from them is

---

## Page 8760

the opposite. As for attributing this position to al-Ash'arī and those who agree with him, this misrepresents them. In their view, Allah’s speech has neither a whole nor parts, and it is therefore inadmissible to ask whether some of it is superior to the rest. For him, degrees of superiority within it are impossible just as likeness is impossible. It cannot be described as having either mutually alike or mutually superior parts, since such relations require two things.

However, on his view, this question is conceivable with respect to multiple attributes, such as knowledge and power: which is superior? If he did say, “The Lord’s attributes do not differ in excellence, because the superiority of one implies that the other falls short of it,” this answer would apply only to these multiple attributes, not to speech itself. Moreover, this attribution to al-Ash'arī of a denial of degrees of superiority among the attributes has not been properly established. Al-Ash'arī did not say that the attributes do not differ in excellence; rather, attributing this to him is an error. What he does say is that speech admits neither degrees of superiority nor likeness because, in his view, it is one—not for the reason mentioned.

As for the multiple attributes, he explicitly stated that they are not mutually alike. His position is that the Essence is not like the attributes, nor is each attribute like the others. Thus, he does not affirm likeness among the meanings he regards as eternal. How, then, can anything entailing their likeness be asserted on the basis of his principles? If he refrains from applying the term “degrees of superiority,” this is like his refraining from applying the terms “likeness” and “mutual distinctness.” In short, anyone who reports that he denied degrees of superiority and affirmed likeness has erred.

---

## Page 8761

but he may refrain from using the term “degrees of superiority,” just as he refrains from using the term “likeness”—not because he considers the attributes alike. Rather, he denies likeness because there is no multiplicity, and because he does not apply the term “mutual distinctness.” Similar questions arise: Should the attributes be described as different or not? Are they mutually distinct or not? Should each attribute be said to be the Essence itself or other than it? Or should these two negations not be combined, but each be stated separately? Or should none of these expressions be used? These matters are not peculiar to this question—the question of superiority.

There is no doubt that likeness or degrees of superiority can be conceived only where there is multiplicity. The multiplicity of Allah’s names, attributes, and words is the position held by the majority of Muslims, and was the position of the early generations of this community and its leading scholars. It accords with the natural disposition Allah has instilled in His servants. Thus, people speak to one another in accordance with this natural disposition and the revealed law, even though some of them hold other views that contradict both and entail the invalidity of what they themselves say in accordance with them. The Quran and Sunnah indicate in numerous places that Allah’s words are multiple. The Exalted has said:

“Say, ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought its like as a supplement.’”

The Exalted has also said:

“If all the trees on earth were pens, and the sea, replenished by seven more seas, were ink, Allah’s words would not be exhausted.”

Elsewhere, we have presented the position of the early generations and shown that they affirmed that Allah has words without end. We have also explained the dispute over whether knowledge and will are multiple, and explained that

---

## Page 8762

many speculative theologians share the majority view that these are multiple, and that those who maintain that He wills everything He wills through a single will merely adopted this view from Ibn Kullāb. Most rational people consider its invalidity self-evident. Indeed, some distinguished scholars of rational inquiry deny that any rational person could hold such a view, because they find it so plainly contrary to reason, unaware that a group of speculative thinkers have maintained it.

Likewise, according to someone who identifies His will itself with both His mercy and His anger, the Prophet’s saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—

“I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your wrath”

would mean seeking refuge in will itself from will itself. This is impossible, for, in his view, will has no positive attribute by virtue of which refuge could be sought in it in one respect and from it in another. Rather, in his view, will merely has a relation to created beings, and that relation has no real existence. This differs from seeking refuge in Him from Him, for He, glorified be He, possesses diverse attributes: refuge is therefore sought in Him in one respect and from Him in another.

As for anyone who says that He is an essence without attributes, or an absolute existent possessing no positive attribute, such a thing cannot exist in external reality. It can only be conceived in the mind, just as impossibilities can be conceived—let alone be a Lord and Creator of creatures—as has been explained at length in its proper place.

These people were driven to such positions by the pressure that the Jahmiyyah and Muʿtazilah brought to bear on them concerning the attributes. They began saying to them:

“Is Allah’s speech Allah Himself or other than Allah? If you say that it is other than Him, then whatever is other than Allah is created. But if you say that it is

---

## Page 8763

He Himself, that is wilful denial of the obvious.”

This was the first argument they put to Imam Ahmad during the ordeal. When al-Muʿtasim told them, “Debate with him,” ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Ishāq said to him, “Abū ʿAbd Allāh, what do you say about the Quran”—or he said, “about Allah’s speech”—meaning, “Is it Allah Himself or other than Him?”

Ahmad replied, “What do you say about Allah’s knowledge? Is it Allah Himself or other than Him?” Ahmad thus countered his argument by invoking Allah’s knowledge, and ʿAbd al-Rahmān fell silent. This illustrates Abū ʿAbd Allāh’s skill in debate—may Allah have mercy on him.

When an innovator has built his doctrine upon a corrupt premise, presenting the truth you hold at the outset will prompt him to dispute it because of the specious argument lodged in his mind. Thus, when an opponent in debate claims to possess the truth, one should begin by dismantling his position. Once he has been defeated and seeks the truth, give it to him. Otherwise, as long as he believes the opposite of the truth, the truth will not enter his heart. It is like a tablet inscribed with falsehood: first erase it, then write the truth upon it.

These people intended to argue in support of their innovation, so Imam Ahmad—may Allah have mercy on him—presented counterarguments and refutations that invalidated it. In his refutation of the Jahmiyyah, Imam Ahmad addressed this argument and explained that revelation does not use the term “other,” either affirmatively or negatively. Accordingly, no binding conclusion follows as to whether it falls within the term “other” in the Lawgiver’s speech or not; thus there is no scriptural proof that it is created.

Furthermore, it is an ambiguous term: “other” may mean something separate from a thing, or it may mean something that is not that thing itself.

---

## Page 8764

For this reason, one should not state without qualification that Allah’s speech, Allah’s knowledge, and the like are He Himself, for this is false. Nor should one state without qualification that they are other than Him, lest this be understood to mean that they are separate and detached from Him. This position, explained by Imam Ahmad, is upheld by the most discerning imams of the Sunnah. They neither state without qualification that an attribute is He Himself, nor that it is other than Him. Nor do they say, “It is neither He Himself nor other than Him,” for this too establishes a third category, which is mistaken. There is a difference between refraining from using either expression without qualification because of their ambiguity, and categorically denying what both expressions signify while affirming a third meaning outside the scope of either.

After them came Abū al-Hasan, who was more discerning than those who followed him. He said: “We negate each separately, not both together. We say separately, ‘The attribute is not the one who possesses it,’ and separately, ‘It is not other than Him.’ The two should not be combined by saying, ‘It is neither He Himself nor other than Him,’ because combining the two negations creates a misleading impression that does not arise when they are stated separately.”

Others came after him and said: “Rather, we negate both together, saying, ‘It is neither He Himself nor other than Him.’” Yet many of these, when examining the matter, say that this meaning is other than Him, thereby contradicting themselves. The reason is that the term “other” is ambiguous: it may mean something separate and detached, or it may mean something that is not the very thing itself. The first sense is sometimes expressed by saying that two things are “other” when one of them may exist or not exist, or when one may be separate from the other in time, place, or existence. The second is expressed by saying that one of the two may be known while

---

## Page 8765

the other is not known. There is a clear difference between these two senses. The Lord’s inseparable attributes never depart from Him, so they are not “other” in the first sense. Yet one may know some attributes without knowing others, and know the essence without knowing an attribute; thus, they are “other” in the second sense. For this reason, many who affirm the attributes have described them as other than the essence.

Some of them have said: “We say that they are other than the essence, but we do not say that they are other than Allah, because the term ‘essence’ does not include the attributes, whereas the name ‘Allah’ encompasses them.” Accordingly, the correct position—according to Ahl al-Sunnah—is not to say that the attributes are additional to what the name “Allah” denotes. Whoever attributes that statement to them has misrepresented their position.

If it is asked, “Are they additional to the essence or not?” the answer is that the essence as it exists in reality necessarily entails the attributes. The essence cannot exist stripped of its attributes; indeed, no entity exists devoid of all attributes. Moreover, the word dhāt (essence) is the feminine form of dhū (possessor of), and dhū necessarily requires a genitive complement.

This usage arose later. Originally, the word occurred in expressions such as “possessing knowledge,” “possessing power,” and “possessing hearing,” just as Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah and set matters right between you.”

One also says, “Such-and-such a woman possesses wealth” or “possesses beauty.” Then, when they understood that the Lord Himself possesses knowledge, power, hearing, and sight—in refutation of those who denied His attributes—they made the word dhāt definite, so that the definite article took the place of the genitive complement. Thus, wherever the expression “the essence” is used, it means an essence possessing such-and-such. The essence, therefore, can only be an essence possessing knowledge and power

---

## Page 8766

and other such attributes, both in wording and in meaning. When the discerning scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah say, “The attributes are additional to the essence,” they mean only that they are additional to what those who deny the attributes have affirmed concerning the essence. For the latter affirm a bare essence devoid of attributes, whereas Ahl al-Sunnah affirm attributes beyond what those people have affirmed. This is an addition in knowledge, belief, and description—not an addition to Allah Himself, exalted be His majesty and holy be His names. Rather, His holy Self possesses these attributes inseparably: the attributes cannot exist without the essence, nor the essence without the attributes. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere.

The point is that if al-Ashʿarī or any other affirmer of the attributes who followed the approach of Ibn Kullāb says that the attributes are equivalent to one another, this is something no rational person would say. Two things are equivalent when either can fulfil the function of the other and take its place. Knowledge is not equivalent to power, nor is power equivalent to will. Speech, however, is in his view one single thing, and a single thing cannot admit of degrees of excellence or equivalence.

In sum, those who deny that some of Allah’s speech is better than other parts base their position on two grounds:

The first is that none of the Lord’s attributes is better than another. They sometimes express this by saying that what is eternal admits no degrees of excellence.

---

## Page 8767

The second is that it is one, and a single thing cannot admit of degrees of excellence or equivalence. This follows the position of those who say that it is one single entity.

Among those who hold that it is one single entity, some nevertheless regard it as letters, or as letters and sounds, whose individual entities are eternal, while maintaining that it is a single thing. This appears in the statements of some later scholars who adopted from the Kullābiyyah the view that Allah has only one will, one knowledge, one power, and one speech, and that the Quran is eternal. From the Mu'tazilah and others, they adopted the view that it consists solely of letters and sounds. They committed themselves to holding that the individual letters and sounds are eternal, although they have an intrinsic order in existence, and that they have existed from eternity, always coexisting with one another. They distinguished between a thing’s essence and its external existence, agreeing with those among the Mu'tazilah who make this distinction. Many who hold that it is eternal and consists of letters and sounds do not say that it is a single thing. Rather, they regard it as multiple, while maintaining the eternity of the Quran and of the individual letters and sounds.

The other position held by those who say that it is one single entity is that what is eternal is a single meaning admitting neither multiplicity nor division, as has already been explained in setting out the true nature of their position. This is the position attributed to Ibn Kullāb and al-Ash'arī. The first person known to have expressed this position in Islam was Ibn Kullāb. No Companion, Successor, or other leading scholar of the Muslims preceded him in it, despite the extensive discussions of Allah’s speech by the Companions and Successors, and despite its being among the greatest and most important matters of religion, to which are devoted

---

## Page 8768

people’s efforts to understand and discuss it, and despite the mass-transmitted texts of the Book and the Sunnah and reports from the Companions that contradict this view.

The Book, the Sunnah, and the reports from the early generations contradict every one of these views. Moreover, the majority of rational people who understand these views agree that their falsity is self-evident to reason. A group of rational people may agree upon a statement whose falsity is self-evident to reason if this results from prior agreement, just as they may conspire to agree upon a lie. Without such agreement, however, this is not possible. Thus, a doctrine that people have adopted from one another—such as the doctrines of the Christians, the Rāfidah, the Jahmiyyah, the Dahriyyah, and others—may contain something whose falsity is self-evident to reason, even though a group of rational people have affirmed it in this manner. But for them to affirm it independently, without prior agreement, does not occur. Most people who unquestioningly adopt false views do not conceive of them fully; a full conception of them would necessarily reveal their falsity. Then, when a view becomes widespread among a group who know of no other view attributed to Ahl al-Sunnah, they assume that it is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah.

Since it is widely known among Muslims that Ahl al-Sunnah do not say that the Quran is created, anyone who sees a group rejecting the claim that the Quran is created comes to suppose that everything that group says on this subject is the position of the early generations and the leading scholars of the Sunnah—and those who said that the Quran is uncreated, but rather subsists in Allah’s essence, and agreed with

## Page 8769

the early generations and the leading scholars on this point. When the Jahmiyyah’s inquisition arose—and Imam Ahmad, through whom Allah strengthened and supported the Sunnah, stood firm throughout it—the hallmark of Ahl al-Sunnah became the affirmation that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated, and that Allah will be seen in the Hereafter. In common parlance, anyone who denied this was counted among the people of innovation. Consequently, many came to agree with the adherents of the Sunnah and hadith on these matters without understanding their actual position. Rather, they retained certain principles of the Jahmī innovators and sought to reconcile them with the position of Ahl al-Sunnah, just as an adherent of philosophy seeks to reconcile the statements of philosophers who oppose the messengers with what the messengers brought.

Thus, those who affiliate themselves with the Sunnah and affirm that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated, came to hold several views:

One is the view of those who say that the Quran is beginningless in its individual existence, that Allah does not speak by His will and power, and that He does not speak one utterance after another. These people, in turn, hold two views. Some say that this beginningless speech is a single meaning eternally inseparable from Allah’s essence, or five meanings.

Others say that it consists instead of letters and sounds, each individually beginningless and eternally inseparable from Allah’s essence.

The third (1) is the view of those who say that, in the Lord’s beginningless eternity, speech was not possible for Him, just as, according to them, action was not possible for Him. This is because speech and action occur only through His will and choice, while they hold that anything occurring through will and choice cannot have existed perpetually.

The view commonly reported from these people is that of those who say:

## Page 8770

He came to speak, in the eternity to come, with letters and sounds subsisting in His essence, as several groups maintain, including the Karrāmiyyah. Some people make statements implying that the speech which subsisted in Him successively was nothing but instances of knowledge and volition. Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī inclines toward this in some of his books.

The fifth (1) is the view of those who say: He has always spoken however He wills. This is the position known from the early generations and the leading scholars of the Sunnah, such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and the other adherents of hadith and the Sunnah.

Among these scholars, some say: He has always spoken and is never silent; rather, He continually speaks by His will and power. Ibn Hāmid identified this as the well-known position of Ahmad and his followers, although it has been reported that Ahmad’s statements consistently affirm that He has always spoken however He wills and as He wills.

The second view is that He speaks when He wills and is silent when He wills. Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz reported this view from a group of Ahmad’s followers. Ibn Hāmid likewise inferred it as a position within the school, while stating that Ahmad’s position had never varied concerning His having always spoken however He wills and as He wills, and that He could not have always been silent and then begun to speak, as the Karrāmiyyah maintain.

These views and their implications are discussed at length elsewhere. The point here is that those who said, “Allah’s speech is uncreated,” disagreed

## Page 8771

thereafter along the lines of these views, although most of those who adopted some of these views do not know what others have said. Indeed, even their leading scholars who have written on this subject know, at most, two, three, or four of these views—such as those of the Mu'tazilah, the Kullābiyyah, the Sālimiyyah, and the Karrāmiyyah. They do not know that anyone within Islam has held any other view. One of them may compile a large book on “the doctrines of Muslims” and “religions and sects,” mentioning most of the innovated views on this subject, yet neither knowing nor transmitting the view handed down from the early generations and the leading scholars.
