The point here is that someone may regard, for example, the view of the Mu'tazilah—or the views of the Mu'tazilah and the Karrāmiyyah, or those views together with that of the Kullābiyyah, or those views together with that of the Sālimiyyah—as false doctrines held by the people of innovation. He then believes that the only remaining position that could represent Ahl al-Sunnah is the other view, even though it too is an innovated position contrary to sound reason and authentic transmitted evidence. He derives further conclusions from that view and attributes them to the Sunnah. Then, when he reflects on the texts of the Quran and the Sunnah and the reports from the early generations, he finds that they contradict that view in both its foundations and its implications.

This is what happened to those who denied the superiority of “the Opening of the Book,” “the Verse of the Throne,” and “Say: He is Allah, One” over other portions of the Quran. Their mainstay is the unsound principle I mentioned earlier. As for speech being one, it is inconceivable that it should admit

---

## Page 8772

differences in excellence, equivalence, or multiplicity. As for the assertion that the Lord’s attributes do not differ in excellence—sometimes expressed as “What is beginningless does not admit differences in excellence,” which resembles the assertion of the Jahmiyyah, the Mu'tazilah, and others that “What is beginningless does not admit multiplicity”—this is an ambiguous expression. If “what is beginningless” means the Lord of the worlds, then the Lord of the worlds is indeed one God, without partner. But if it means His attributes, then whoever says that the Lord’s attributes do not admit multiplicity is saying that knowledge is power, power is will, and hearing and sight are knowledge. Some of them may also say that knowledge is speech, while others say that knowledge and power are will. They may then say that the attribute is identical with the one possessing it: knowledge is the one who knows, and power is the one who possesses power.

These assertions have been explicitly made by those philosophers, Jahmiyyah, and others who deny the divine attributes, as I have quoted their actual words elsewhere. These assertions plainly contradict sound reason and authentic transmitted evidence—indeed, they contradict what rational people know self-evidently and what is necessarily known in the religion of Islam and the religion of the messengers—to such an extent that their utter invalidity, both in revelation and in reason, is clear.

These people then interpreted the texts of the Quran and the Sunnah in invalid ways. Some said that describing it as greater, more excellent, and better merely means that it is great in itself. They refused to understand these descriptions as expressing superiority. This position has been attributed to al-Ash'arī, Ibn al-Bāqillānī, and a number of others. Anyone who reflects on the wording of the Quran and the Sunnah will plainly see that it cannot bear this meaning; rather, this is a form of Qarmatian interpretation. For Allah

---

## Page 8773

Most High says:

“He has sent down the best of speech.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Ubayy, “Do you know which verse that you know from Allah’s Book is the greatest?” He also said, “I shall certainly teach you a surah the like of which has not been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, or the Quran.” There are other examples already mentioned.

Some of them said: Rather, what is meant by His words “better than it” is “better for you”—that is, bringing greater reward or involving less hardship. They said that whatever indicates that some of it is more excellent than the rest does not establish the superiority of the speech itself, but of what relates to it: reciting this passage and acting upon it brings greater reward than reciting and acting upon another.

The response to these people is: What you have mentioned is evidence against you, besides contradicting the text. For the reward for one of two utterances or deeds is greater than that for the other only because it is intrinsically more excellent. This is why the texts speak of the excellence of the utterance or deed itself. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked on more than one occasion, “Which deed is most excellent?” He would answer by declaring one deed superior to another, which necessarily entails its greater reward. As for a greater reward when the two deeds are equal, this is contrary to both revelation and reason.

The same applies to speech. In Sahīh Muslim, Samurah reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The most excellent utterances after the Quran are four—and they are part of the Quran: Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; none has the right to be worshipped but Allah; and Allah is the Greatest.”

---

## Page 8774

Thus he stated that these are the most excellent utterances after the Quran, even though they are themselves part of the Quran. He therefore declared these utterances themselves superior to all others apart from the Quran. Likewise, Sahīh Muslim relates that he was asked:

“Which utterance is most excellent?”

He replied, “What Allah has chosen for His angels: Glory and praise be to Allah.”

Al-Muwatta’ and other works report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The most excellent thing that I and the prophets before me have said is: None has the right to be worshipped but Allah alone, with no partner. His is the dominion, and His is all praise, and He has power over all things.”

He thus stated that these words are the most excellent thing that he and the prophets before him have said.

Sunan Ibn Mājah reports that he said:

“The most excellent remembrance is: None has the right to be worshipped but Allah. And the most excellent supplication is: Praise be to Allah.”

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā also narrated this. In Sahīh al-Bukhārī and Sahīh Muslim, he is reported to have said:

“Faith has sixty-odd—or seventy-odd—branches, the highest of which is saying: None has the right to be worshipped but Allah.”

There are many such examples in the revealed texts, declaring one deed superior to another and one utterance superior to another. From this, we know that the reward for one is greater than that for the other. But a greater reward without any superiority in the utterance or deed itself is neither established by any transmitted text nor warranted by reason. For if two utterances, or two deeds, are identical in every respect, assigning a greater reward to one than to the other would mean favoring one of two identical things over the other without any grounds for preference.

This is the fundamental premise of the Qadariyyah and the Jahmiyyah, who say that one who has power gives preference to one of two things within his power without any determining factor. They imagined that through this premise they were supporting Islam. Yet neither for Islam

---

## Page 8775

did they secure victory, nor did they crush its enemy. Rather, the early generations and leading scholars of the Muslim community assailed them with charges of religious innovation, misguidance, disbelief, and ignorance. Their opponents—the eternalists and others—also assailed them by demonstrating that their position contradicted reason, and used this as a pretext for departing still further from revelation and reason, as happened between the heretics and the religious innovators.

Furthermore, to say:

“One part is no better than another; rather, one brings a greater reward,”

is to reject Allah’s explicit statement, for Allah says:

“We bring one better than it or similar to it.”

How, then, can it be said that no part is better than another? If all are identical in themselves, none can be better than another. To interpret “better” as meaning “greater in reward,” while maintaining that they are identical in themselves, is supported by the wording neither literally nor figuratively. It is therefore impermissible to interpret it in this way. It is entirely unknown for someone to say, “This is better than that,” or “This is superior to that,” when the two things and their attributes are equal in every respect. Rather, using such an expression necessarily implies a difference in excellence, even if only in some attributes.

Suppose, however, that an agent exercising choice assigned to one of two identical things something not assigned to the other, despite their being equal in their attributes in every respect. Such a situation is inconceivable. Even if it were conceivable, one would not say that one is better or superior to the other on account of something that is not an attribute of either at all.

Furthermore, an authentic hadith reports that he said concerning al-Fātiha:

“Nothing like it has been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, or the Quran.”

Thus the Messenger explicitly stated

---

## Page 8776

that Allah has revealed nothing like it. Whoever says, “Everything revealed of Allah’s speech is like it in every respect,” has therefore contradicted what the Messenger reported.

Furthermore, His words have already been cited:

“The best of speech.”

Yet if all of Allah’s speech were identical, the Quran would not be better than the Torah and the Gospel. The rulings with which Allah has singled out the Quran have likewise already been discussed.

If it is said:

“We concede that Allah has assigned certain parts of His speech rewards and rulings that others do not share. In our view, however, this is solely by His will, not because that speech possesses an attribute distinguishing it from the rest.”

The reply is:

First, this contradicts the explicit texts of the Quran and Sunnah and the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community, as well as contradicting sound reason. Moreover, it rests upon a principle held by the Jahmiyyah and Qadariyyah: that an agent possessing power and exercising choice can give preference to one of two identical things over the other without any determining factor.

Having admitted this possibility, they said:

“The Lord had always been inactive, and in the eternal past it was not possible for Him either to speak or to act. Then speech and action became possible without anything arising that would account for their transition from impossibility to possibility.”

They also said:

“An agent with the power to give preference can do so without any determining factor.”

The Jahmiyyah then said:

“The servant has no real power and therefore gives preference to nothing. Rather, Allah performs the servant’s act, and the servant’s act is itself the Lord’s act.”

And it was said by

---

## Page 8777

the Qadariyyah:

“The servant possesses complete power and gives preference to one of two possible acts over the other without any newly arising cause, and without any need for Allah to bring about something that determines the performance of one rather than the other. Although he stands in the same relation to the two opposites—faith and disbelief—one is preferred over the other without any determining factor, whether from Allah or from the servant. He needs neither Allah’s help nor for Him to make him willing, make him establish prayer, or make him a Muslim.”

Sound reason establishes the contrary. Allah Most High does whatever He wills and decrees whatever He wishes. Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. The praise expressed in these words, however, means that His will is unrestricted: nothing can obstruct Him when He wills something. As the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“None of you should say, ‘O Allah, forgive me if You will; O Allah, have mercy on me if You will.’ Rather, let him be firm in his request, for no one can compel Allah.”

He thus explained that Allah acts only by His will. No one can compel Him such that He should be told, “Do it if You will,” nor does He act if He does not will. When He, glorified be He, wills something, He has the power to do it, and nothing can prevent Him.

This does not mean that He acts merely by a will unaccompanied by wisdom. Yet, according to them, He performs acts whose performance and nonperformance are, in relation to Him, alike in every respect. This is no praise; rather, reason recognizes it as a blameworthy attribute. Whoever acts merely because he wishes to act, with no wisdom behind his action and no abstract end that it serves, would be better off not acting. Allah, glorified be He, has condemned in His Book those who attribute this to Him. He Most High said:

## Page 8780

by divine decree, is not unjust. For if one person punishes another for his misdeeds and secures redress for the wronged against the wrongdoer, all rational people agree that this is not injustice on his part. Rather, it is praiseworthy, and no one says that the wrongdoer is excused on account of divine decree. So when the Lord of all worlds secures justice for some of His servants against others and recovers the rights of the wronged from their wrongdoers, how could this be injustice on His part on account of divine decree?

Likewise, when a servant puts everything in its proper place, placing the pure with the pure in a place suited to it, and the impure with the impure in a place suited to it, this is justice and wisdom on his part. The same applies when the Lord of all worlds puts everything in its proper place and does not treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like those who spread corruption on earth, nor the God-fearing like the wicked, nor Muslims like criminals.

Paradise is pure, and only one who is pure is fit to enter it. Hence, no one enters it until after the settling of claims that cleanses them of impurity, as authentically reported from Abū Sa‘īd, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“When the believers have crossed the bridge—that is, the Sirāt stretched across Hell—they will be stopped on a bridge between Paradise and Hell. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that the Qadariyyah’s assertions concerning injustice and justice, by which they draw an analogy between the Lord and His servants, are among the innovations through which they have gone astray and contravened the Book and the Sunnah

and the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community. These causes are attested by revelation, reason, and sensory experience, and affirmed by the early generations of the Muslim community and the leading scholars of the religion. This is why those who agreed with his position while professing adherence to the way of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah fall into contradiction. When they discuss the revealed law, they need to follow the approach of the leading scholars of the religion in affirming the merits of the Sharī‘ah: its commands to pursue what serves people’s welfare and benefits them, its prohibitions against what corrupts their affairs and harms them, and the fact that the Messenger sent with it was sent as a mercy. As Allah Most High says:

“We have sent you only as a mercy to all the worlds.”

“Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find described in the Torah and the Gospel they possess, who commands them to do what is right and forbids them

---

## Page 8782

from what is wrong, makes lawful for them what is wholesome, and forbids them what is foul.” Thus, He states that the Messenger commands what is right, forbids what is wrong, makes lawful what is wholesome, and prohibits what is foul.

If “right” meant nothing more than what is commanded, and “wrong” meant nothing more than what is prohibited, this would be like saying: “He commands them to do what he commands them, forbids them what he forbids them, makes lawful for them what he makes lawful, and prohibits for them what he prohibits.” Such words convey nothing of benefit, let alone establish his superiority over others. Clearly, anyone who issues a command can be described in this way, and the same is true of every prophet who was sent.

Allah Most High says:

“Because of the wrongdoing of the Jews, We forbade them wholesome things which had been lawful to them.”

This establishes that wholesomeness is a quality of the thing itself, and that Allah may nevertheless prohibit it as a punishment for His servants. Thus, after mentioning what He prohibited for the Children of Israel, Allah Most High says:

“That is how We recompensed them for their transgression, and We are indeed truthful.”

Allah Most High also says:

“They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say, ‘Wholesome things have been made lawful for you.’”

If “wholesome” meant merely what is lawful, these words would convey nothing of benefit. It is therefore clear that wholesomeness and foulness are qualities inherent in things themselves. What is meant is not merely the pleasure derived from eating, for a person may enjoy harmful poisons and things a physician tells him to avoid. Nor does it mean that a particular people, such as the Arabs, find something pleasurable, or that the Arabs are accustomed to it. For the mere fact that a people are accustomed to eating something and find it agreeable, or dislike it because it is not found in their land

---

## Page 8783

does not mean that Allah must forbid all believers whatever these people are unaccustomed to, or permit all believers whatever they are accustomed to. How could it, when the Arabs were accustomed to eating blood, carrion, and other things that Allah Most High has forbidden?

An Arab was once asked, “What do you eat?”

He replied, “Everything that crawls or walks, except Umm Hubayn (a small lizard-like creature).”

The questioner said, “Then may Umm Hubayn enjoy being spared!”

Quraysh themselves used to eat foul things that Allah has forbidden, while finding repugnant foods that Allah has not forbidden. The two Sahīh collections relate:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was served spiny-tailed lizard meat, but he withdrew his hand and did not eat. He was asked, ‘Is it forbidden, Messenger of Allah?’ He replied, ‘No, but it is not found in the land of my people, so I find myself averse to it.’”

It is therefore clear that the aversion of Quraysh or others to a particular food does not warrant prohibiting it for believers among all other Arabs and non-Arabs. Moreover, neither the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor any of his Companions prohibited whatever the Arabs disliked or permitted everything the Arabs ate.

Allah Most High says:

“He makes lawful for them what is wholesome and forbids them what is foul.”

This foretells that he would do so. Accordingly, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, permitted wholesome things and prohibited foul things, such as every fanged beast of prey and every bird with talons. These creatures are aggressive and predatory. When people eat them—and food resembles the one who consumes it—their character becomes tinged with the traits of these beasts, namely oppression and aggression. Likewise, he prohibited blood poured forth, because it is where the appetitive and irascible faculties of the soul are concentrated, and an increase in it causes these faculties to run rampant

## Page 8784

and blood is Satan’s pathway through the body, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Satan flows through the son of Adam as blood flows.”

For this reason, when Ramadan begins, the devils are chained, for fasting is a shield. The wholesome things he permitted are foods that benefit the mind and character, while foul things are those that harm the mind and character. Likewise, wine is the mother of all evils because it corrupts the mind and character.

Allah has therefore permitted the God-fearing wholesome things that help them worship their Lord—the purpose for which they were created—and forbidden them foul things that hinder them from fulfilling that purpose. Along with consuming these wholesome things, He commanded them to give thanks and forbade them to declare such things unlawful. Whoever consumes them without giving thanks neglects what Allah has commanded and deserves punishment. Whoever declares them unlawful—as monks do—has transgressed Allah’s limits and deserves punishment. Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, eat of the wholesome things We have provided for you, and give thanks to Allah, if it is Him that you worship.”

In an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah is indeed pleased with a servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, or takes a drink and praises Him for it.”

Another hadith states:

“The grateful person who eats is like the patient person who fasts.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Then, on that Day, you will surely be questioned about your blessings.”

That is, about giving thanks for them. For He does not permit something and then punish someone for doing it. Rather, He questions the person about the duty He prescribed alongside it and about what He prohibited: whether that person fell short by neglecting a command or committing a forbidden act. As Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, do not forbid the wholesome things

---

## Page 8785

that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”

He thus forbade them to declare wholesome things unlawful. A group of the Companions had resolved to adopt monasticism, so Allah revealed this verse. The two Sahīh collections relate that some Companions made the following statements. One said, “As for me, I will fast without taking a day off.” Another said, “As for me, I will pray all night and never sleep.” Another said, “As for me, I will not approach women.” Another said, “As for me, I will not eat meat.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“What is the matter with men who say such-and-such? Yet I fast and refrain from fasting, pray at night and sleep, marry women, and eat meat. Whoever turns away from my sunnah is not of me.”

A fuller discussion of these matters belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that Allah has explained, in His Book and through His Messenger, His wisdom in His creation and His commands. For example, He says:

“Do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse. It is indeed an immorality and an evil way.”

He thus explains its prohibition by the fact that it is an immorality independently of the prohibition, and that this is the reason for forbidding it. He also says:

“When they commit an immoral act, they say, ‘We found our fathers doing it, and Allah has commanded us to do it.’ Say, ‘Allah does not command immorality.’”

He thus declares Himself free of this, presenting it as grounds for praising Him and affirming that He is exalted above it. This shows that there are things that cannot be ascribed to Allah as His commands. Things are not all equal in themselves or in His sight. He does not distinguish what is commanded from what is forbidden merely by arbitrary choice. Rather, He assigns commands to what He commands and prohibitions to what He forbids in accordance with the requirements of His wisdom.

---

## Page 8786

I have reflected on most of the statements of the early generations that I have encountered—having researched them extensively and read a great many—to see whether the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness, or any one of them, held the views I have mentioned, which I found in the books of the speculative theologians: the Jahmiyyah, the Qadariyyah, and those who adopted these views from them.

These include the Jahmiyyah’s claim that, of two identical things, Allah commands one and forbids the other without any reason or wisdom; or that, of statements and deeds identical in every respect, Allah makes some more richly rewarded than others without any reason or wisdom. Similar claims include their assertion that all of Allah’s speech is alike, even though the reward for some of it is greater.

I have found nothing in the statements of the early generations that agrees with this. Rather, they explicitly discuss the wisdom and reasons involved, explaining the good qualities in what is commanded that make it fitting to command it, and the bad qualities in what is forbidden that make it fitting to forbid it. They also explain that some statements and deeds are intrinsically superior to others. I have never seen any report from any of them contradicting the scriptural texts that indicate this, finding it problematic, or interpreting it according to his own understanding. Yet they are reported to have found difficulties and ambiguities in many verses and hadiths and to have interpreted them in different ways, some of which may be mistaken, while another interpretation is correct.

Nor have I found them, regarding such statements as Allah’s words:

“Allah has sent down the best statement: a consistent Book wherein is reiteration,”

and the Prophet’s question to Ubayy, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Which verse in the Book of Allah is the greatest?”

and his statement concerning al-Fātihah:

“Nothing like it has been sent down in the Torah, the Gospel, or the Quran,”

---

## Page 8787

and similar statements, doing anything other than affirming them and accepting what they entail.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, asked Ubayy, “Which verse in the Book of Allah is the greatest?” Ubayy answered that it was the Verse of the Throne. He then struck Ubayy on the chest with his hand and said, “May your knowledge bring you joy, Abū al-Mundhir!”

Neither Ubayy nor anyone else found anything problematic in the question of some parts of the Quran being greater than others. Rather, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, attested to the knowledge of someone who recognized the superiority of some parts over others and knew which verse was the most excellent. The same applies to Allah’s words:

“Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten.”

I have not seen them disagree over the interpretation of “with one better than it.”

This verse has two well-known readings. The majority read aw nunsihā (“or cause it to be forgotten”), from ansāhu–yunsīhi, meaning to cause someone to forget. Ibn Kathīr and Abū Amr read aw nansaʾhā (“or defer it”), with a hamzah, from nasaʾahu–yansaʾuhu. The first derives from forgetting, while the second derives from nasaʾa, meaning to defer.

The linguists say: “Nasaʾtuhu nasʾan means ‘I deferred it,’ as does ansaʾtuhu. One says nasaʾtuhu al-bayʿa and ansaʾtuhu, meaning ‘I allowed him to defer payment for the sale.’” Al-Asmaʿī said: “Ansaʾa Allāhu fī ajalihi and nasaʾa fī ajalihi have the same meaning: ‘May Allah prolong his life.’” The expression bayʿ al-nasīʾah (sale on deferred payment) derives from this same root.

Among the sayings of the Arabs is:

“Whoever desires a prolonged life—though there is no prolongation—should eat early, keep his debts light, and have intercourse with women less often.”

As for the first reading, its meaning is clear to most Quran commentators. They say that it refers to what Allah caused to be forgotten of the Quran, as the transmitted reports indicate. For whatever is removed

---

## Page 8788

from the Quran may be withdrawn through divine legislation by being erased from people’s hearts; this is causing it to be forgotten. Allah Most High thus states that whatever He abrogates or causes to be forgotten, He replaces with something better or similar. This demonstrates His bounty and mercy toward His believing servants, for He says immediately before this:

“O you who believe, do not say, ‘Rāʿinā (Attend to us),’ but say, ‘Unzurnā (Look upon us),’ and listen. And for the disbelievers there is a painful punishment.”

“Neither the disbelievers among the People of the Book nor the polytheists wish for any good to be sent down to you from your Lord. But Allah singles out for His mercy whomever He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of immense bounty.”

He thus forbade them to imitate the People of the Book in their disrespect toward the Messenger and what he brought. He explained that, because of their envy, they did not wish Allah to send down to him any of the Book or wisdom. He then described His favor toward the believers: some of the Quran was abrogated, and some was caused to be forgotten—as the transmitted reports indicate. What He, glorified be He, caused to be forgotten belongs to those passages whose rulings and recitation He abrogated. This differs from abrogated passages that are still recited, though their rulings have been abrogated, or passages whose recitation He abrogated but which were not forgotten. Abrogation and causing passages to be forgotten involve a reduction in what He revealed to His servants.

He, glorified be He, therefore explained that there is no diminution in this. Rather, whatever is abrogated or caused to be forgotten, Allah replaces with something better or similar. The believers thus continually enjoy a blessing from Allah that does not diminish but increases: when He brings something better, the blessing increases, and when He brings something similar, the blessing remains. Allah Most High says:

“Or cause it to be forgotten.”

He thus attributes the act of causing it to be forgotten to Himself, for this is not blameworthy, unlike forgetting what must be retained, which is blameworthy.

## Page 8789

for this is being made to forget what Allah has withdrawn. Forgetting what He has commanded one to retain, however, is blameworthy. Allah Most High says:

“Thus did Our signs come to you, but you forgot them; and thus will you be forgotten today.”

Although this forgetting includes neglecting to act upon them while retaining them in memory, forgetting the verses altogether, so that their contents are no longer known, entails an even greater neglect of acting upon them. This, therefore, is blameworthy. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith recorded in the Sunan collections:

“Whoever recites the Quran and then forgets it will meet Allah maimed.”

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, disliked a person attributing forgetfulness to himself. He said in the hadith recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“How bad it is for someone to say, ‘I have forgotten such-and-such a verse!’ Rather, he has been made to forget it. Keep reviewing the Quran, for it escapes from people’s hearts more readily than camels escape their tethers.”

Some interpreters understood “Whatever verse We abrogate” to refer to a verse whose recitation and written text Allah retained while abrogating its ruling, and what He caused to be forgotten to refer to what He withdrew, so that it is no longer recited. Others included in the first category verses whose recitation was abrogated, even if they remained memorized.

The first interpretation is that of Mujāhid and the companions of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd. Scholars have transmitted through sound chains, from Ibn Abī Najīh, that Mujāhid explained “Whatever verse We abrogate” as follows: “We retain its written text and change its ruling.” He said: “This is also the view of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd.” “Or cause it to be forgotten” means “We erase it,” for what has been forgotten has not been retained.

Ibn Abī Hātim narrated through his chain of transmission, from ʿIkrimah, that Ibn ʿAbbās said:

“Revelation would sometimes come down to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, at night

## Page 8790

and he would forget it during the day. So Allah revealed:

‘Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it.’”

The same was also reported from Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, Qatādah, and ʿIkrimah.

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās used to recite it as aw tunsihā (“or you forget it”), in the second person—that is, “you forget it, O Muhammad.” He recited Allah’s words, “We will make you recite, and you will not forget,” and His words:

“Remember your Lord when you forget.”

Reports also relate that one of them would memorize passages of the Quran and then forget them. They would mention this to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he would say, “It has been withdrawn.” An example is the sound report transmitted by al-Zuhrī: Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf told me, in the gathering of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib:

“A man had memorized a surah and rose during the night to recite it, but could not. Another rose to recite it, but could not, and another rose to recite it, but could not.
