---

## Page 8830

I say:

Etymology supports both views: that al-Samad is the One who has no cavity, and that He is the Master. It points more clearly to the first, however, for the first meaning underlies the second. In Arabic, the word samad is used of that which has no cavity.

Yahyā ibn Abī Kathīr said: “The angels have no cavities, whereas human beings are hollow.” In the hadith concerning Adam, Iblīs is reported to have said of him: “He is hollow, not solid.” Al-Jawharī said: “Musammad is a variant of musmat, meaning that which has no cavity.” He also said: “Simād is the covering over a bottle’s mouth,” and: “Samad denotes high, solid ground.” Abū al-Najm said:

“It leaves the high ground like the back of a saddle-sore camel.”

The fundamental meaning of this root is gathering together and strength. Thus, one says yasmudu al-māl, meaning “he gathers wealth together.” Likewise, sayyid (master) was originally saywid: the letters yā’ and wāw came together, with the first unvowelled, so the wāw was changed into yā’ and the two were assimilated. Similarly, mayyit (dead) was originally maywit. The root, as found in sawād (blackness) and su’dud (mastery), conveys the sense of gathering together, and black is the color that concentrates the gaze.

Allah Most High has said:

“Noble and chaste.”

Most of the early generations interpreted sayyidan (“noble”) as “forbearing.” This is also reported from al-Hasan, Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr, ‘Ikrimah, ‘Atā’, Abū al-Sha‘thā’, al-Rabī‘ ibn Anas, and Muqātil. Abū Rawq reported from al-Dahhāk that it means “one of good character.” Sālim reported from Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr that it means “the God-fearing.” A man does not become a master over others until he is himself self-possessed and steadfast in character.

---

## Page 8831

‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar said:

“After the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, I have seen no one who surpassed Mu‘āwiyah in the qualities of leadership.” He was asked, “Not even Abū Bakr or ‘Umar?” He replied, “Abū Bakr and ‘Umar were better than him, but after the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, I have seen no one who surpassed Mu‘āwiyah in the qualities of leadership.”

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: “He meant forbearing”—or he said, “generous.” Hence the saying:

“If ever you wish to lead a tribe,
Lead with forbearance, not haste and abuse.”

For this reason, a group of the early generations explained sayyid as one who leads his people in religion. Ibn Zayd said, “It means the noble.” Al-Zajjāj said, “One who surpasses his people in goodness.”

Ibn al-Anbārī said: “Sayyid here means a chief and a leader in goodness.” Ibn ‘Abbās and Mujāhid explained it as “one held in honour by his Lord,” while Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib explained it as “a jurist and scholar.”

It has already been mentioned that they call a bottle’s covering simād. Al-Jawharī said: “The ‘ifās is a piece of leather fitted over the head of a bottle. What goes inside its mouth, however, is the simām. The expression ‘afastu al-qārūrah means: ‘I fastened the covering over the bottle.’”

(I say:

In the authentic hadith from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning lost property, he said:

“Then familiarize yourself with its container and its tie.”

The ‘ifās here means whatever holds the dirhams, such as a cloth in which they are tied. The wikā’ is something like the string used to tie it. This is of the same kind as the covering of a bottle. The words ‘afs, sadd, and samad

---

## Page 8832

and jam‘ (gathering) and su’dud (leadership) are similar in meaning: they all convey gathering together and strength. Food is described as ‘afs (astringent), possessing ‘ufūsah (astringency), meaning that it causes contraction. From this comes ‘afs, the gallnuts used to make ink.

Al-Jawharī said:

“It is a later coinage, not part of the speech of the desert Arabs.”

This does not detract from it, for they had no gallnuts to call by this name. Nevertheless, the designation accords with the principles of Arabic speech. The same applies to their calling what is inserted into a bottle’s mouth a simām (stopper), for this root conveys gathering together and sealing.

Al-Jawharī said: A bottle’s simām is its stopper. An asamm stone is hard and solid. An asamm man is one who cannot hear because his hearing is obstructed. A man described as simmah is brave; simmah also means a male snake. The samīm of something is its pure essence, into which nothing has entered to break it apart or weaken it. Thus one says samīm al-harr (the height of the heat), samīm al-bard (the depth of the cold), and “So-and-so is of the pure stock of his people.” A samsām is a sharp, cutting sword that does not bend. The expression sammama, used of travelling or other pursuits, means “he pressed on.” A man described as summ is stout.

Sawm (abstention) is related to this through broader etymological affinity, for sawm means refraining.

Abū ‘Ubaydah said:

“Anyone who refrains from food, speech, or travelling is sā’im.”

This is because refraining involves holding together, and nothing enters the interior of one who is fasting. One says sāma al-faras when a horse stands without feeding.

Al-Nābighah said:

“Some horses stand, others move beneath the dust,
And others champ their bits.”

---

## Page 8833

The same applies to sadd (blocking), sadād (soundness), su’dud (leadership), and sawād (a mass). Likewise, the word samad conveys gathering together, and gathering together entails strength: the more closely something’s parts are joined, without gaps between them, the stronger it is compared with something containing empty spaces.

Thus, firm, elevated ground is called samad because of its strength, cohesion, and compactness. A man described as samad is a leader who is sought out. One may say qasadtuhu, qasadtu lahu, or qasadtu ilayhi, all meaning “I sought him out”; likewise, one may say masmūd, masmūd lahu, or masmūd ilayhi, meaning “one who is sought out.” People seek help with their needs only from someone who can meet them. Only someone who is composed, strong, and steadfast in himself can do this: a noble, generous leader. This contrasts with someone who is anxious and fretful, becoming distracted, agitated, and overwhelmed by the number and burden of their needs. Such a person is not a leader upon whom they can depend and to whom they turn for their needs.

They therefore called a human leader samad because he possesses the quality for which people seek him out to meet their needs. In their language, leadership does not have a merely relational meaning—as nearness and distance do. Rather, it denotes a quality inherent in the leader, on account of which people seek him out. Sayyid (leader) derives from su’dud (leadership) and sawād (a mass). Through broader etymological affinity, this belongs to the same family as sadād, for the Arabs interchange a weak letter and a doubled consonant.

For example, they say taqaddā al-bāzī and taqaddada, both meaning “the hawk swooped down.” A sādd is something that blocks or fills something else, leaving no empty space in it. From this come sidād al-qārūrah (a bottle’s stopper) and sidād al-thaghr (what closes an opening), both pronounced with an i vowel: that which closes the thing in question. From it also comes sadād, with an a vowel, meaning correctness, and hence the expression “sound speech.” As stated by

---

## Page 8834

Allah Most High:

“Fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.”

They explained this as “upright and true.” Ibn ‘Abbās explained it as “correct”; Qatādah and Muqātil as “just”; and al-Suddī as “straight.” All these explanations are correct, for sound speech accords with what is right. If it conveys information, it is truthful, corresponding to what it reports without addition or omission. If it gives a command, it commands justice without excess or deficiency. Hence they explain sadād (soundness) in terms of qasd (uprightness), and qasd in terms of justice.

Al-Jawharī said:

“Tasdīd means enabling someone to attain sadād: correctness and uprightness in speech and action. A man is described as musaddad when he acts correctly and uprightly. Musaddad also means ‘straightened’; one says saddada rumhahu, ‘he straightened his spear.’ An affair described as sadīd or asadd is rightly directed. Istadda, said of something, means that it became straight.

“The poet said:

‘I teach him archery every day;
Then, when his arm aimed true, he shot at me.’

“Al-Asma‘ī said: ‘The reading ishtadda [grew strong], with the dotted sh, is of no account.’”

Their explanation of sadd (blocking) in terms of qasd shows that the word qasd carries the sense of gathering together and strength. Qasd means justice, just as it means soundness and correctness: exact correspondence and agreement, without excess or deficiency. This combines completeness with exact correspondence. From this comes the statement of Allah Most High:

“And upon Allah is the direction of the way.”

That is, the way characterized by qasd—the just way. This means that the just way leads to Him, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, upon Us is guidance.”

That is, guidance leads to Us.

---

## Page 8835

This is the soundest interpretation of the two verses. The same applies to His statement, Most High:

“He said, ‘This is a straight path leading to Me.’”

Related to this through intermediate derivation is sidq (truthfulness), whose root letters are the same as those of qasd. This includes truthfulness in speech, because it corresponds to what is reported, as explained concerning sadād (soundness). Sadq, pronounced with a short a, describes a solid spear; it is also said to mean a straight one. Thus, it is straight and solid, with neither defect nor crookedness. A sundūq (box), whose plural is sanādīq, gathers together whatever is placed inside it.

Something that should be understood concerning derivation is that the statement “This is derived from that” has two meanings.

The first is that the two expressions correspond in wording and meaning, regardless of which expression the speakers of the language used first. In this sense, each expression is derived from the other, since what is meant is that they correspond in wording and meaning. This resembles saying, “This water is from that water,” or “This speech is from that speech.” Accordingly, whether one says that the verb is derived from the verbal noun or that the verbal noun is derived from the verb, both statements are correct. This is the sense of derivation supported by morphological evidence.

As for the second sense of derivation—namely, that one is the source of the other—

---

## Page 8836

if by this one means that one expression was used before the other, there is no evidence for this in most cases. If, however, one means that one has conceptual priority over the other, because one is simple and the other composite, then the verb is derived from the verbal noun.

Minor derivation involves two expressions sharing the same letters in the same order; intermediate derivation involves their sharing the same letters, but not their order; and major derivation involves their sharing some identical letters, while the remaining letters agree in their class rather than their identity—for example, both being guttural letters. Thus, hazara, ʿazzara, and azara all convey strength and firmness. They also share with rā’, zāy, and hā’ the feature that the three are guttural letters.

Accordingly, if it is said that al-Samad means musmat (solid, without a cavity), and that it is derived from it in this sense, this is correct, since dāl is closely related to tā’. For samt means silence: refraining from speech and keeping the mouth closed.

Abū ʿUbayd said: “Musmat means something without a cavity. Asmattuhu means ‘I made it solid.’ A bāb musmat is a door that has been completely shut.”

A musmat horse is one of a single color, with no other color mixed into it. This is also the sense of Ibn ʿAbbās’s statement: “Only pure silk has been forbidden.”

Thus, musmad and musmat correspond through major derivation. The dāl has not changed from a tā’; rather, dāl is stronger, and musmad expresses its meaning more fully than musmat. The stronger the letter, the stronger its meaning, for the language of the Lord displays the utmost precision and harmony. This is why samt means refraining from speech despite

---

## Page 8837

being able to speak. A human being has an internal cavity and produces speech through his mouth, yet he may remain silent. Samad, by contrast, is used only of that in which there is no fragmentation, as in al-Samad, al-sayyid (the master), samad as applied to land, simād (a bottle stopper), and the like.

Among these related expressions, none is more complete than those formed from samad. It contains sād, mīm, and dāl, and each of these three letters possesses a distinction over its corresponding letters. The meanings conveyed by such letters are likewise more complete.

Related to these meanings is that of sabr (patience), for patience involves gathering oneself together and exercising restraint. Hence the definition: “Patience is restraining oneself from anguish.” One says sabara (“he was patient”) and sabbartuhu (“I made him patient”). This is also the sense of the Most High’s words:

“And keep yourself patient.”

Likewise, the meaning of “the master, al-Samad” is the opposite of being fretful and withholding. Related to this is subra, a heap of food, because it is gathered and piled together. Subāra means stones, while the sabr of something is its thickness.

Its opposite is jaza‘ (anguish), which carries the sense of being cut apart and dispersed. One says jaza‘a lahu jiz‘atan min al-māl, meaning that he cut off a portion of the property for him. A juzay‘a is a portion of a flock of sheep. Ijtaza‘tu min al-shajari ‘ūdan means “I cut and broke a stick off a tree.” Jaza‘tu al-wādī means “I crossed the valley from side to side,” while jaz‘ denotes a bend in a valley. Related to this is jaz‘, the Yemeni beads containing both white and black. Similarly, jazza‘a al-busr is said when the unripe date has become half or two-thirds ripe. This contrasts with their use of musmat for a single color: the latter involves unity, whereas the former involves division.

The Most High has said:

“Indeed, mankind was created anxious.”
“When evil touches him

---

## Page 8838

he is fretful.”
“And when good touches him, he is withholding.”

Al-Jawharī said: “Hala‘ (anxiety) is the most extreme form of anguish.” Others said: “In linguistic usage, it means the most intense greed and the worst anguish.” Hence the Prophet’s saying (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“The worst traits in a person are panic-stricken avarice and unnerving cowardice.”

A she-camel is described as halū‘ when she is swift and nimble. A wolf is described as hali‘ bali‘: hali‘ refers to its greed, and bali‘ to its swallowing.

Thus, the explanations given by the early generations encompass these meanings. Ibn ‘Abbās is reported to have said: “It describes someone who is fretful when evil touches him and withholding when good touches him.” He is also reported to have said: “It describes someone who covets what is unlawful for him.” Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr explained it as “avaricious”; ‘Ikrima, “fretful”; Ja‘far, “greedy”; al-Hasan and al-Dahhāk, “stingy”; and Mujāhid, “voracious.” Al-Dahhāk also said: “The halū‘ is someone who is never satisfied.” Muqātil explained it as “constricted in heart,” and ‘Atā’ as “hasty.”

All these meanings are contrary to steadfastness, strength, collectedness, self-restraint, and patience. The Most High has said:

“The building they built will remain a source of doubt in their hearts, unless their hearts are torn apart.”

Although this has been interpreted to mean that their hearts split apart and they die, it resembles expressions used in such circumstances: “His heart has split apart,” “My heart has become divided,” “My heart has become scattered,” and “My heart has been torn in different directions.” Hence it is said of fear: “It has scattered his heart.” Conversely, one says: “He is firm of heart,” “His heart is collected,” and “His heart is gathered together.”

---

## Page 8839

Section

Allah Most High says:

“Say: He is Allah, One.”
“Allah, the Eternal Refuge.”

He prefixed the definite article al- to Samad (the Eternal Refuge), but not to ahad (One), because no existing being other than Allah Most High is called ahad in an affirmative statement when the word stands alone, without being joined to a following noun in a genitive construction. This differs from negative statements and constructions that function similarly, such as conditions and questions. Thus one says: “Is anyone with you?” and “If anyone comes to me from you, I will honour him.”

Otherwise, it is used only in simple counting: ahad, ithnān (one, two), and ahad ‘ashr (eleven). The first day is called yawm al-ahad (Sunday), for—according to the more correct of the two views—it was on that day that Allah began creating the heavens, the earth, and everything between them, as indicated by the Quran and authentic hadiths.

The Quran states in several places that He created the heavens, the earth, and everything between them in six days. It is established in an authentic hadith, whose authenticity is agreed upon, that Adam was the last creature to be created and that he was created on Friday. Since creation ended on Friday, it follows that it began on Sunday, because the days were six.

As for the hadith narrated by Muslim, which states:

“Allah created the soil on Saturday,”

it is a defective hadith whose authenticity was challenged by leading hadith scholars, including al-Bukhārī and others.

---

## Page 8840

Al-Bukhārī said: “The correct account is that the report goes back only to Ka‘b.” Al-Bayhaqī also discussed its defects. They explained that it is an error, not something Abū Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is among the reports whose inclusion by Muslim was criticized by expert hadith scholars, just as they criticized his inclusion of a few other reports. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Abū al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzī, commenting on the words of Allah Most High,

“created the earth in two days,”

mentioned that Ibn ‘Abbās said: “He created the earth on Sunday and Monday.” This was also the view of ‘Abd Allāh ibn Salām, al-Dahhāk, Mujāhid, Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddī, and the majority. Muqātil said: “On Tuesday and Wednesday.”

Ibn al-Jawzī said: “Muslim included the hadith of Abū Hurayrah:

‘Allah created the soil on Saturday.’”

He said: “This hadith contradicts what preceded, and it is more authentic.”

He thus judged this account authentic because he assumed the hadith was authentic, since Muslim had narrated it. Yet there are other instances of this: Muslim narrated hadiths known to contain errors, such as Abū Sufyān’s statement upon accepting Islam: “I wish to marry Umm Habībah to you.” There is no disagreement that the Prophet had married her before Abū Sufyān accepted Islam. Such instances, however, are exceedingly few.

Another example is what Muslim narrated through some chains of transmission of the hadith concerning the eclipse prayer: that the Prophet performed it with three or four bowings. The correct account is that he performed it only once, with two bowings. This is why al-Bukhārī included only this account, as did al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal—according to one of the two reports from him—and others. Al-Bukhārī avoided errors of this kind; for whenever there occurred in some of the

---

## Page 8841

narrations an error, he would cite the reliably preserved narrations that exposed the narrator’s mistake. He was more knowledgeable about hadith and their hidden defects, and understood their meanings more deeply, than Muslim and others like him.

Elsewhere, Ibn al-Jawzī mentioned that this was the view of Ibn Ishāq. He said: “Ibn al-Anbārī said: ‘This is the consensus of the scholars.’”

He also mentioned a third view concerning the beginning of creation: that it began on Monday, attributing this too to Ibn Ishāq. This is contradictory. He mentioned that this was the view of the People of the Gospel, whereas beginning on Sunday was the view of the People of the Torah. This attribution to the People of the Gospel is mistaken, just as it was mistaken to claim that the first view represented the consensus of Muslim scholars. It seems that these people supposed that every community holds its gathering on the seventh of the seven days in which Allah created the world. This is mistaken: the Muslims gather on the last day on which Allah created the world, namely Friday, as established in authentic hadiths.

The point here is that the term ahad (One) has not been used to describe any individual being except Allah alone. When used of anyone other than Allah, it occurs only in negation. Linguists say that one may use it in “There is no one in the house,” but not in “There is someone in it.”

Thus, it occurs in the Quran only in non-affirmative contexts, as in the words of the Most High:

“And none of you could have shielded him from Us.”

And His words:

“You are not like any other woman.”

And His words: “And if anyone from among the

---

## Page 8842

polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection.” It also occurs in a possessive construction, as in His words:

“Then send one of you.”

“We gave one of them two gardens.”

As for the name al-Samad (the Self-Sufficient One upon whom all depend), linguists have used it of created beings, as noted earlier. Thus, He did not say, “Allah is a samad,” but rather:

“Allah is al-Samad.”

He thereby made clear that He alone, to the exclusion of all others, deserves to be al-Samad, for He is entitled to this attribute in its fullest perfection. Although a created being may be samad in certain respects, it does not truly possess this attribute: it is susceptible to fragmentation and division, and it also needs others. Everything besides Allah needs Him in every respect. None is sought by everything while himself needing nothing except Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

Everything created is capable of division, fragmentation, partition, and separation of its parts. Allah, glorified is He, is al-Samad, to whom none of these things can apply. Rather, this attribute in its reality and perfection belongs necessarily and inseparably to Him alone. He cannot lack it in any respect, just as His oneness cannot admit of a second in any respect. He is One: nothing resembles Him in any way, as He says at the end of the surah:

“And there is none comparable to Him.”

Here He uses ahad in a negative statement: nothing whatsoever is comparable to Him in any respect, because He is One.

“A man said to the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), ‘You are our master.’ He replied:

---

## Page 8843

‘The Master is Allah.’” His words, “the One, the Self-Sufficient One upon whom all depend,” indicate that He neither begets nor was begotten, and there is none comparable to Him. For al-Samad is the One who has neither an internal cavity nor internal organs. Nothing enters Him, so He neither eats nor drinks—glorified and exalted is He—as He says:

“Shall I take as protector anyone other than Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who feeds but is not fed?”

In the reading of al-A‘mash and others, it is wa-lā yat‘amu (“and He does not eat”), with a fathah.

He, Exalted, also says:

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

“I seek no provision from them, nor do I ask that they feed Me.”

“Indeed, Allah alone is the Provider.”

Among His creatures are the angels, who are samad and neither eat nor drink. Their Creator—majestic is His glory—is all the more entitled to every form of self-sufficiency and perfection that He has granted to some of His creatures. Hence some of the early generations explained al-Samad as the One who neither eats nor drinks. Al-Samad is the One who is not hollow, who has no internal cavity; no distinct entity therefore issues from Him, and so He does not beget.

For this reason, some of the early generations said, “He is the One from whom nothing issues.” They did not mean that He does not speak, even though speech may be described as issuing from Him, as stated in the hadith:

“The servants draw near to Allah through nothing better than that which has issued from Him.”

This means the Quran. When Abū Bakr al-Siddīq heard Musaylimah’s purported Quran, he said, “This has certainly not issued from God.”

Speech issuing from a speaker means that he speaks it, so it is heard from him and reaches another. It is not something created in another, as the Jahmiyyah claim. It does not mean that anything subsisting in Him separates from Him and moves from Him to another

---

## Page 8844

, for this is impossible even with the attributes of created beings: an attribute cannot leave the subject in which it subsists and pass to another. How much more so with the attributes of the Creator—majestic is His glory.

He, Exalted, says concerning the speech of created beings:

“Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths; they speak nothing but a lie.”

That utterance subsists in the speaker and is heard from him. Its coming out of his mouth does not mean that the speech subsisting in him leaves him and passes to someone else. Rather, each thing issues forth in a manner appropriate to it. Knowledge and speech, when received from a scholar or speaker, do not diminish in their source. Hence they are likened to a light from which everyone draws illumination, while it remains unchanged and undiminished. Thus, the statement of some of the early generations, “Al-Samad is the One from whom nothing issues,” is sound in the sense that nothing of Him separates from Him.

For this reason, it is impossible for Him to beget or to be begotten. Begetting, generation, and everything denoted by such expressions require two sources. Whatever is generated as a self-subsisting entity must have material from which it emerges; whatever is an accident subsisting in another must have a subject in which it subsists. He rules out the first by His word, “One,” for the One is He who has neither an equal nor a counterpart. It is therefore impossible for Him to have a consort, whereas generation occurs only between two things. He, Exalted, says:

“How could He have a child when He has no consort? He created all things, and He has knowledge of everything.”

Thus He, glorified be He, denies having a child because its necessary prerequisite is impossible for Him, for the absence of a necessary prerequisite indicates

---

## Page 8845

the absence of that which depends upon it. He also denies having a child on the grounds that He is the Creator of all things: everything other than Him is His creation, and nothing among it is begotten of Him.

As for the second, He rules it out by being, glorified be He, Al-Samad. Whatever is generated from two sources comes from two portions that separate from those sources, as an animal is generated from its father and mother through the seminal fluid that separates from them. Such generation requires another source, as well as something issuing from both sources. All of this is impossible with respect to Allah, Exalted is He. He is One, so He has no equal who could be His consort and counterpart; and He is Al-Samad, from whom nothing issues. Each of these two attributes—His being One and His being Al-Samad—precludes His begetting, and precludes His being begotten with even greater force.

Just as generation among animals requires two sources—whether those sources are of the same kind as the offspring, as with animals born through reproduction, or of a different kind, as with animals generated otherwise—so too does generation among things other than animals. An example is fire generated by two fire-making implements, whether two pieces of wood, a stone and a piece of iron, or something else. Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“And by those that strike sparks.”

He, Exalted, also says:

“Have you considered the fire that you kindle?
Was it you who brought its tree into being, or are We its Maker?
We have made it a reminder and a provision for travelers.”

He, Exalted, also says:

“He puts forth a comparison for Us, forgetting his own creation. He says, ‘Who will give life to bones when they have crumbled away?’
Say, ‘He who brought them into being the first time will give them life. He has full knowledge of every creation—
He who made fire for you from the green tree, from which you then kindle your fires.’”

---

## Page 8846

Several Quran commentators have explained that there are two trees, one called markh and the other ‘afār. Whoever wishes to obtain fire from them cuts two twigs, like tooth-cleaning sticks, while both are still green and dripping water. The markh—the male—is then rubbed against the ‘afār—the female—and fire emerges from them by Allah’s permission, Exalted is He. The Arabs say, “Every tree contains fire, but markh and ‘afār have it in abundance.” Some people say, “Every tree contains fire except the jujube.”

“From which you then kindle your fires.”

These, then, are their fire-making implements.

The lexicographers, including al-Jawharī, have said: “The zand is the stick used to kindle fire, and it is the upper one. The zandah is the lower one, which has a hole in it; it is the female. Together, the two are called zandān.”

Those experienced in this explain that they rub the upper stick into the hole in the female, just as a male animal does with its female. This rubbing and friction release fine particles from both, from which fire is kindled. Fire is thus generated from the material of the male and the female, just as a child is generated from the substance of the man and the woman. Rubbing and striking the female implement with the male causes both to become hot, and each releases material from which fire is kindled. Similarly, when a male animal penetrates its female, chafing and rubbing her genitals with his, the heat of both intensifies, and each releases a substance that mingles with the other, producing offspring from the two. Fire is said to have “caught” in the material onto which the sparks are struck, which is

---

## Page 8847

like a womb for a child—namely, tinder, touchwood and similar materials that catch fire more readily than others—just as a woman conceives by a man. The fire may fail to catch, just as a woman may fail to conceive; and no spark may be produced, just as no semen may be discharged. Fire is not of the same kind as the two fire-making sticks; rather, it is generated from them, just as an animal is generated from water and clay. Animals are of two kinds: those produced through reproduction, such as humans, livestock and other creatures created from two parents; and those generated otherwise, such as creatures that arise from fruit and vinegar, lice generated from the dirt on human skin, mice, fleas and other creatures created from water and earth.

People have disagreed concerning the animals, plants, minerals, rain, fire kindled with fire-making sticks, and other things that Allah creates: are the very entities of these bodies brought into existence, with one kind transformed into another—as semen is transformed into a clinging clot and then a lump of flesh—or is it only accidents that come into being, while the entities themselves, which are substances, remain with different attributes through the four states He brings about in them: aggregation, separation, motion and rest? There are two views.

Some hold that bodies are composed either of individual, indivisible substances, as many speculative theologians maintain, or of infinitely many substances, as is reported of al-Nazzām.

---

## Page 8848

Thus, those who hold that bodies are composed of substances say that Allah does not bring into being anything that subsists in itself, but only accidents: aggregation, separation, motion, rest and other accidents.

Those among them who hold that substances were brought into existence say that Allah created them initially, and that everything He brings into being thereafter consists only of accidents within them; Allah does not create any further substances. This is the position of most of the Muʿtazilah, Jahmiyyah, Ashʿariyyah and others like them. Some of their leading figures suppose that this is the position of the Muslims and claim a Muslim consensus on it. Yet none of the early generations of the Muslim community held this view, nor did the majority of the community. Rather, the majority of the community—even groups among the speculative theologians—reject the indivisible substance and the composition of bodies from substances. Ibn Kullāb, the leading authority for his followers, was among those who rejected the indivisible substance. Abū Bakr ibn Fūrak mentioned this in his work on Ibn Kullāb’s doctrines and his disagreements with al-Ashʿarī. Likewise, rejection of the indivisible substance is the position of the Hishāmiyyah, the Dirāriyyah, and many of the Karrāmiyyah and Najjāriyyah as well.

Those who hold that bodies are composed of individual substances are generally known to maintain that substances are of the same nature. Indeed, they—or most of them—also say that bodies are of the same nature, because they are composed of substances of the same nature and differ only because their accidents differ. These are accidental attributes, not inseparable ones, and therefore do not negate sameness of nature. For two things are defined as being of the same nature when whatever is possible for one is possible for the other, whatever is necessary for one is necessary for the other, and whatever is impossible for one is impossible for the other.

They say that substances are of the same nature, so it is possible

---

## Page 8849

for each one to have whatever is possible for the other; whatever is necessary for one is necessary for the other, and whatever is impossible for one is impossible for the other. The same applies to bodies composed of substances. Thus, when they establish a judgment concerning one body, they say: “This holds for all bodies,” on the basis that they are of the same nature. Most rational people reject this, and their most accomplished thinkers have refuted the arguments advanced to establish this sameness of nature, as al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī and others have mentioned. This has been discussed at length elsewhere. In al-Ibānah (The Elucidation), al-Asharī included the assertion that bodies are of the same nature among the doctrines of the Mutazilah that he rejected.

These thinkers say that Allah singles out one of two bodies of the same nature for certain accidents, to the exclusion of the other, by His will alone, according to the principle of the Jahmiyyah, or for some other reason, as the Qadariyyah maintain. They also say that transformation from one genus into another is impossible: a body cannot become an accident, nor can one genus of accidents become another. Thus, if they were to say that bodies are created and that a created thing changes from one genus into another, this would entail transformation between genera.

They therefore say that what develops in the womb, the fruit produced on trees, and the fire produced by fire-strikers are substances that already existed in the material from which these things were created. Those substances remain, but their attributes have been changed through aggregation, separation, motion and rest.

---

## Page 8850

This is why, when Abū Abd Allāh al-Rāzī presented the proofs for “establishing the existence of the Maker,” he mentioned four approaches: the contingency of entities, their temporal origination, the contingency of attributes, and their temporal origination. The first three approaches are weak—indeed, invalid. For they described the entities whose origination or contingency, or whose attributes’ contingency, they asserted in ambiguous terms that do not distinguish the Creator from creation, and they offered no sound proof for their claims.

As for “the fourth approach”—arguing from the origination of things known to have come into existence—it is sound and is the approach of the Quran. Yet they fell woefully short in pursuing it, for, according to their own principles, they have witnessed no entities coming into existence, but only attributes. The Quran’s approach, by contrast, demonstrates that everything other than Allah is created and is a sign pointing to Him. The proofs and signs contained in the Quran, which these speculative theologians and philosophers have failed to reach, have been discussed at length elsewhere, as has the fact that whatever truth they possess is only a part of what the Quran establishes.

The point here is that, since their account of the beginning of creation rested on this principle—namely, affirming the existence of indivisible atoms—their account of resurrection was likewise built upon it. They thus divided into two positions. Some say that the substances cease to exist and are then brought back into existence. Others say that the parts disperse and are then gathered together. An objection was then raised against them concerning a human being eaten by an animal, and that

---

## Page 8851

animal was eaten by another human being. If those parts are restored to one, they cannot be restored to the other. A further objection was raised against them: the human body is constantly losing matter, so what is to be restored? Is it what was present at the time of death?

If that is the answer, it follows that the person will be restored in a frail condition, contrary to what the scriptural texts state. If some other body is meant, no one body has a stronger claim than another. Some of them therefore claimed that a human being has original constituent parts that never break down and contain nothing from the animal eaten by the second person. Yet rational people know that the human body itself breaks down entirely, with none of its matter remaining.

Thus, their account of resurrection helped strengthen the philosophers’ specious argument for denying bodily resurrection. It also led a group of speculative thinkers to hold that Allah creates another body to which the soul returns, and that the purpose is to bring bliss or punishment to the soul, whether this occurs in the body or elsewhere. This, too, contradicts the explicit scriptural texts affirming the restoration of this very body.

This is what is set out in al-Rāzī’s books. On the major questions concerning the foundations of religion, neither his books nor those of his peers contain the correct position that accords with revelation and reason—the position with which Allah sent the Messenger and which was held by the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars. Instead, he presents the discussions of heretical philosophers and those of innovating speculative theologians who built upon the principles of the Jahmiyyah and the Qadariyyah concerning creation and resurrection, the beginning and the final return. Both approaches are unsound, since they constructed their account upon unsound premises. As for the position held by

---

## Page 8852

the early generations and most rational people—that bodies change from one state to another—he attributes it only to philosophers and physicians. This view—that Allah creates the bodies whose coming into being we observe by changing and transforming them from one body into another—is held by the early generations, all the jurists, and the majority. Hence the jurists discuss whether an impure substance becomes pure through transformation, as when excrement turns into ash, or a pig or something else turns into salt, and similar cases.

Allah transforms the semen in the womb into a clinging clot, then into a lump of flesh. Likewise, fruit is created by transforming the material He brings forth from the tree—its moisture—together with air, the water that falls upon it, and other materials that He turns into fruit by His will and power. Likewise, He splits the seed, and the materials He creates from it turn into an ear of grain, a tree, or something else. This is how He—glorified and exalted be He—creates what He creates. Thus, He created Adam from clay, transforming the very substance of the clay into bone, flesh, and the other parts of the body. Likewise, He transforms the lump of flesh into bones and other bodily parts.

Allah the Exalted says:

“We certainly created man from an extract of clay.
Then We placed him as a sperm-drop in a secure lodging.
Then We made the sperm-drop into a clinging clot, and We made the clot into a lump of flesh, and We made the lump into bones, and We clothed the bones with flesh; then We brought him into being as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.
Then, after that, you will surely die.
Then, on the Day of Resurrection, you will surely be raised.”

Likewise, He creates fire by transforming some of the kindling into fire, as the Exalted says:

“He who made for you fire from the green tree.”

Allah turned those very particles that came from the green tree into fire, without there having been any fire in the green tree to begin with—just as there had originally been no fruit in the tree and no embryo in the woman’s womb. Rather, He created this existing thing from the material of something else, transforming that material into it and adding other materials to it. The same applies to resurrection: He restores a person after his entire body has decayed except for the tailbone, as established in an authentic report from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who said:

When He restores a person to life in the second creation, that existence will not be like this one. No foul bodily waste will be discharged by the people of Paradise, as established in an authentic report from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who said:

“The people of Paradise will neither urinate nor defecate, neither spit nor blow their noses. Only perspiration like musk will come from them.”

In the two authentic collections, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is reported to have said:

“People will be gathered barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised.” Then he recited: “As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it—a promise binding upon Us. We shall surely do so.”

Thus, they will return with their foreskins, not circumcised.

Al-Hasan al-Basrī and Mujāhid said: “Just as He first created you in this world when you were nothing, so you will return alive on the Day of Resurrection.” Qatādah said: “He first created them

## Page 8854

from dust, and to dust they return.” As the Most High said:

“From it We created you, into it We shall return you, and from it We shall bring you forth once again.”

“And the earth—We spread it out and placed firmly anchored mountains upon it,”

up to His words:

The term “restoration” thus entails an original and something restored. This applies equally to the restoration of bodies and of accidents, as in repeating a prayer or other acts. For:

## Page 8858

is it described without qualification as something like it. Rather, the Most High says:

“Say, ‘If mankind and jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce its like.’”

Whenever the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) uttered a statement, he would repeat it three times. It may nevertheless be called its like in a qualified sense. Thus, someone reporting another person’s words may say, “This is how so-and-so spoke,” meaning that he said something like this. One also says, “He did this ʿawdan ʿalā badʾ (a repetition after an initial act),” when he does something a second time after the first. Related expressions are al-biʾr al-badī (a newly dug well) and al-biʾr al-ʿādī (a well dug again): the former is one dug for the first time, and the latter one dug again. The latter designation is not derived from the name ʿĀd, as has been claimed.

One says, “I asked him to repeat something, and he repeated it,” when asking him to do it a second time. From this comes the word ʿādah (habit). The expressions ʿādahu, iʿtādahu, and taʿawwadahu mean that something became a habit for him. One also says, “He accustomed his dog to hunting, and it became accustomed to it.” This derives from muʿāwadah, which means returning to the original activity. A brave man is described as muʿāwid (one who returns to the fray), because he never tires of combat. One says, “His fever returned,” and, “He returned to him with the question,” meaning that he asked him repeatedly. People are said to engage in taʿāwud (returning to one another), in war or otherwise, when each side returns to the other. Al-ʿuwwād, pronounced with an initial u-vowel, denotes food served again after some of it has already been eaten. And ʿawādi means ʿud (“Return!”), just as nazāli means inzil (“Come down!”).

In all these cases, the term “repetition” is used with regard to the reality in question: the reality present on the second occasion is the same as on the first, even though the individual instances are distinct. Hence, one may say, “It is like it,” or, “This is that very thing,” and both are correct. By “reality,” I mean that which is specific to that individual instance; what is meant is not what is shared between

---

## Page 8859

the agents. For someone who performs an act like another person’s is not said to have repeated it, but rather to have imitated or resembled him. By contrast, when someone performs an act a second time like the one he performed initially, he is said to have repeated his act. Likewise, someone who repeats another person’s words is said to have repeated them, whereas someone who composes similar words is not said to have repeated them. One also says, “It was read before this person, and he repeated it before that person,” and, “This person reads—that is, studies—and this person repeats.” Had these been different words merely resembling the original, one would not describe him as repeating them.

Similarly, someone who breaks a ring or another fashioned object is told, “Restore it as it was,” and someone who demolishes a house is told, “Restore it as it was.” By contrast, someone who builds another house like it is not called a restorer. Of the restored thing, one may say, “This is the very same thing as before,” or, “This resembles the original in every respect,” and use similar expressions indicating that it is identical to the original in one respect and like it in another.

This dispels the objections raised concerning this matter, such as the assertion, “Repetition can occur only if that same time is repeated,” and similar claims involving things whose repetition plain reason rules out. Rather, a thing is repeated by bringing forth its like, even though some speculative theologians maintain that there is no difference whatsoever in any respect.

The restoration of which Allah has informed us is restoration in the sense intelligible in this discourse. It is what both the polytheists and the Muslims understood from the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), and it is what the word “restoration” denotes. What is restored is the very same thing as the original. Although there is a difference between what restoration entails and what the initial creation entails, that difference does not preclude

the restoration of the original. Accordingly, consider a person who has turned to dust, from which plants then grow and are eaten by another person, and so on; or a person who is eaten by another person or an animal, and that animal eats yet another person. He is thus restored from the material into which he was transformed. If a thousand dead people decompose in a single grave and all become dust, they will be restored and rise from that grave. in its second form does not involve His creating them through transformations of this kind. Whoever supposes that restoration requires restoring the foods that were transformed into their bodies is mistaken.

Thus, if one person eats another, the latter merely becomes nourishment for him, like any other food; there is no need to restore that food. It is well known that nourishment enters the stomach as food and drink, then becomes chyle, resembling bread soaked in broth, then chyme, resembling a thin flour soup. It is then cooked into blood, which Allah Most High distributes throughout the body. Every part of the body receives its share, and the blood is transformed into the likeness of the part concerned: into bone, flesh, or sweat. This process of nourishment resembles their transformation at the beginning of creation: a drop of fluid, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh.

Just as He, glorified be He, does not need, when restoring them, to turn each of them into a drop of fluid, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, so too He does not need to turn their nourishment into bread, fruit, and meat, then into chyle and chyme, then into blood, and then into bones, flesh, and veins. Rather, He restores this body in another form for a second creation unlike this creation, as He says:

“and recreate you in forms you do not know.”

In doing so, He has no need for any of the transformations that occurred in the first creation.

## Page 8862

And this makes clear the answer to his statement, “The body is continually breaking down.” The body’s breakdown is no more remarkable than the transformation of a drop of fluid into a clinging clot, and of a clinging clot into a lump of flesh, each differing in nature from the other. In the body undergoing breakdown, however, the replacement parts resemble and match the earlier ones. If restoring the body does not require its transformation from one nature into another, still less does it require the changes caused by its breakdown.

It is well known that someone who sees a person in his youth and then sees him in old age knows that this is the same person, despite this transformation. The same applies to all other animals and plants. Someone who has been away from a tree for some time and then returns and finds it knows that it is the same tree, even though breakdown and transformation occur in all other animals and plants just as they do in the human body.

No rational person, in believing that this tree is the same tree, that this horse is the one he had years ago, or that this person is the one he saw twenty years ago, needs to suppose that some original parts have remained without breaking down. Such a thought does not even occur to anyone. Nor, when rational people say, “This is the same one,” do they mean only those parts that are neither known nor distinguishable from others. Rather, they refer to the whole tree, horse, or person, even though each may once have been small and then grown.

Nor can it be said that it is the same solely because the rational soul remains one and the same, as alleged by those who claim that the second body is not that first body, but that the purpose is instead to recompense the soul with bliss or torment

consists of fresh dates, grapes, or the like—together with drink that is water or contains water, for a hundred years without changing, then, with still greater reason, He, glorified and exalted is He, has the power to make food and drink remain unchanged in the next creation. Section

The point here is that generation necessarily requires two sources. Anyone who supposes that the air itself between the two fire-striking implements turns into fire through being heated, without any material coming off them and turning into fire, is mistaken. This is because no fire is produced unless friction releases material from them; friction alone does not produce fire.

Moreover, people strike sparks onto something beneath the two implements, such as sūfān and hirāq (tinder materials), and the fire falls onto it. Only something heavy falls. Were there no heavy particle from the fire-striking implements—the iron and the stone—the fire would not fall. If the air alone had turned into fire, it would not descend, for air naturally rises rather than falls. Yet after the material released has turned into fire, the air near it may turn into fire, either as smoke or as flame.

---

## Page 8866

The point is that things produced through generation were created from two sources, just as Adam was created from dust and water. Nothing—neither animal nor plant—is created from pure dust unmixed with water. All plants likewise arise from two sources, and the Messiah was created from Mary and Gabriel’s breath.

As the Exalted says:

“And Mary, daughter of ʿImrān, who guarded her private part, and We breathed into it of Our Spirit.”

He also says:

“And she who guarded her private part, and We breathed into her of Our Spirit.”

And He says:

“So We sent to her Our Spirit, and he appeared before her as a man in perfect form. She said, ‘I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are mindful of Him.’ He said, ‘I am only a messenger from your Lord, to grant you a pure boy.’”

The Quranic commentators have mentioned that Gabriel breathed into the neck opening of her garment. The jayb is the opening around the neck, not what some ordinary people call a jayb: a pocket at the front of a garment for keeping dirhams and the like. When Allah commanded Moses to put his hand into his jayb, it was this opening, known by that name in the Arabic language.

Abū al-Faraj and others mentioned two views: was the breath blown into the neck opening of the garment, or into the private part? Those who adopted the first view understood it to mean the opening of her garment. Those who said that it meant the passage through which a child is born said that the pronoun “it” refers to something not explicitly mentioned, since he breathed into her garment, not into her private part. This interpretation has no merit; rather, it departs from the explicit wording of the Quran.

If this report is established, it does not contradict the Quran; if it is not established, it deserves no consideration. For those who reported that Gabriel breathed into the neck opening of her garment meant that he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—did not

---

## Page 8867

uncover her body. Likewise, when Gabriel came to the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—while ʿĀ’isha was undressed, he would not look at her in that state. Thus, he breathed into the neck opening of Mary’s garment, and the breath reached her private part. What was intended was precisely to breathe into her private part, as Allah states in two verses. Otherwise, breathing only into the garment, without the breath reaching her private part, would contradict the Quran and would have no effect in bringing about a child. None of the leading Muslim scholars said this, nor has anyone transmitted it from any recognized scholar of the early generations.

The point here is that the Messiah was created from two sources: Gabriel’s breath and his mother Mary. This breathing was not the breathing that takes place after four months have passed, when the fetus is a lump of flesh. That is breathing into a body that has already been created, whereas when Gabriel breathed, the Messiah had not yet been created, nor had Mary conceived. She conceived him only after the breathing, as shown by His words:

“He said, ‘I am only a messenger from your Lord, to grant you a pure boy.’”

“So she conceived him and withdrew with him to a distant place.”

When Gabriel breathed into her, she conceived him. This is why the Messiah was described as “a spirit from Him,” with reference to this breathing. Allah, glorified is He, has made clear that the messenger who is His spirit—Gabriel—is the spirit who addressed her and said, “I am only a messenger from your Lord, to grant you a pure boy.” Thus, His words, “We breathed into her,” or “into it of Our Spirit,” mean: from this spirit, who is Gabriel. Jesus is a spirit from this spirit, and so he is a spirit from Allah in this

---

## Page 8868

respect, and “from” indicates the point of origin.

The point here is that something may arise from two sources through the transformation of the matter between them. When they meet, there is matter between them which undergoes transformation through the force of their friction against one another; some of its particles must therefore be lost. This is like fire being generated between two fire-making implements when stone is struck against iron, or wood against wood, such as wood from the markh and ʿafār trees. Through the force of the movement produced by striking one against the other, some of their particles are transformed, and the air between them grows hot and becomes fire. Whenever the two implements are struck against one another, they lose particles through the force of friction. Thus, this fire results from the transformation of the air and those particles, caused by striking one fire-making implement against the other.

The same applies to the light produced when rays are reflected onto something facing a luminous source, such as the sun or fire. The terms “light” and “illumination” are sometimes applied to a body existing in its own right, such as the flame at the top of a lamp. This can arise only from matter that turns into fire, such as wood or oil; the air also turns into fire. The air, too, can turn into fire only through a loss of material from the burning fuel or from the two fire-making implements.

At other times, “light,” “illumination,” and “radiance” refer to the rays falling upon the ground and walls from the sun or fire. This is an accident, not a body existing in its own right: it must inhere in a substrate capable of receiving it. Thus, rays require both a luminous body and something facing it onto which they can be reflected.

---

## Page 8869

The same applies to the fire produced in a lamp’s wick when it is placed in a fire, or when wood is placed in a fire. The fire first transforms the material—oil or wood—so that the surrounding air grows hot and turns into fire. This transformation occurs only after some of the material has been lost.

The same applies to air that fans a fire, as when wind blows and the fire blazes in the wood, or when bellows or the like are used to blow air. The air being blown continues to kindle the fire because the material sustaining it, such as wood and charcoal, is capable of turning into fire, and because the strong movement of the air carries the fire to material capable of receiving it. The air near the fire may also be transformed, for flame is air that has turned into fire, like the flame in a lamp’s wick. Thus, when it is extinguished, it becomes smoke: air mixed with fire, just as vapour is air mixed with water, and dust is air mixed with earth.

Vapour may also be called smoke. An instance of this is the saying of the Most High:

“Then He turned towards the heaven while it was smoke.”

The Quran commentators explained this as water vapour, as stated in the transmitted reports:

“Allah created the heavens from water vapour.”

This is the smoke in question. Smoke is air mixed with something hot. It may contain no water, in which case it is simply smoke; or it may contain water, in which case it is both smoke and vapour, like the vapour rising from a cooking pot. Smoke may also be called vapour. Thus, someone who fumigates himself with fragrant incense is said to have tabakhkhara (“used vapour”), even though no moisture is present; rather, the fragrant smoke is called vapour.

Al-Jawharī said: “Water vapour is what rises from water like smoke. Bakhūr, pronounced with a short a in the first syllable, is what is used for fumigation.” However, the air turns into fire only

---

## Page 8870

after the material that has turned into fire, such as wood or oil, has been consumed. Thus, fire is generated only from material, just as animals are generated only from material.

Section

The point is that whenever the term “generation” is applied to independently subsisting entities, it necessarily involves two sources and the separation of a part from the source.

When satiety and the quenching of thirst are described as generated, or when the departure of the soul and similar accidents are so described, every use of this term necessarily involves two sources. An accident, however, requires a subject in which to subsist; it does not require material that turns into an accident. Bodies, by contrast, are created only from materials that turn into bodies, changing into another kind—as when semen turns into a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, and in other instances of the creation of animals and plants.

As for what comes from a single source, such as Eve’s creation from Adam’s shortest rib, although she was created from material taken from Adam, this is not called generation. This is why it is not said that Adam begot Eve, nor that he is Eve’s father. Rather, Allah created Eve from Adam, just as He created Adam from clay.

---

## Page 8871

As for the Messiah, it is said that Mary gave birth to him, and he is called “the Messiah, son of Mary.” Thus, the Messiah was a part of Mary and was created after the spirit was breathed into Mary’s private part, as the Most High said:

“And Mary, daughter of ʿImrān, who guarded her private part, into which We breathed of Our spirit. She believed in the words of her Lord and His Scriptures, and was among the devoutly obedient.”

And in the other verse:

“We breathed into her of Our spirit and made her and her son a sign for all the worlds.”

As for Eve, Allah created her from material taken from Adam, just as Adam was created from earthly material: water, dust, and the wind that dried it until it became sounding clay. Hence, it is not said that Adam begot Eve, nor that dust begot Adam. Yet it is said of the Messiah that Mary gave birth to him, for he came from two sources: Mary and the breath that Gabriel blew into her. Allah the Most High said:

“Then We sent to her Our spirit, who appeared before her as a man in perfect form.”

“She said, ‘I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you fear Him.’”

“He said, ‘I am only the messenger of your Lord, to grant you a pure boy.’”

“She said, ‘How can I have a boy when no man has touched me, nor have I been unchaste?’”

“He said, ‘So it will be. Your Lord has said: “It is easy for Me. We shall make him a sign for people and a mercy from Us. It is a matter already decreed.”’”

“So she conceived him and withdrew with him to a distant place.”

And so the account continues. She conceived him only after the breathing; she did not carry him for a time without any breathing, only for the spirit of life then to be breathed into him, as happens with other human beings. Thus, there is a difference between the breathing that brings about conception and the breathing that imparts the spirit of life.

---

## Page 8872

It is thus clear that any entity subsisting in its own right that is said to be generated from another can arise only from material issuing from that parent, and only from two sources. The Lord Most High is al-Samad, so nothing can issue from Him. Moreover, He—glorified be He—has no consort, so He cannot have a child.

As for expressions concerning the generation of accidents, such as saying that rays are generated, knowledge is generated by thought, satiety by eating, or heat by movement, and the like, this is not the generation of independently subsisting entities. Nevertheless, it necessarily requires a subject in which to inhere and two sources.

Thus, the Christians’ statement that the Messiah is the son of Allah—exalted is Allah above that—necessarily entails their saying that Mary is Allah’s consort. They thereby attribute to Him a wife and consort, just as they attribute a child to Him. Whatever meaning they give to his being His son, the notion of a wife is to be understood in that same sense. The proofs requiring that He be declared free of having a consort likewise require that He be declared free of having a child. If they describe Him in terms even further removed from what befits Him, they are necessarily committed to describing Him in terms that are less remote. This has been discussed at length in refuting the Christians.

Section

“He neither begets nor is born,”

and in His words:

“Indeed, it is out of their falsehood that they say,
‘Allah has begotten,’ and indeed they

## Page 8873

are liars,” and in His words:

Thus, the Christian scholars explain their statement, “He is the son of Allah,” by what they have stated: that the Word is the Son. All three sects agree on this. The falsity of their claim is evident to clear reason on several grounds:

First:

Nothing in the words of the prophets calls any attribute of Allah a son—neither His speech nor any other attribute. Their calling an attribute of Allah a son therefore distorts the words of the prophets, taking them out of their proper context. As for the statement they transmit from the Messiah, “Baptize the people in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit,” he did not mean by “the Son” Allah’s attribute that is His Word, nor by “the Holy Spirit” His life. This meaning is nowhere intended in the words of the prophets, as has been explained at length in refuting the Christians.

The second ground:

Is this Word, which is the Son, an attribute of Allah subsisting in Him, or is it a self-subsisting substance? If it is His attribute, their doctrine is invalid on several grounds.

First:

An attribute cannot be a god who creates, provides sustenance, gives life, and causes death. Yet, according to them, the Messiah is a god who creates, provides sustenance, gives life, and causes death. If that which clothed itself in him is not a god, then he is all the more certainly not a god.

Second:

An attribute cannot subsist in anything other than the one it qualifies, and therefore cannot be separate from Him. If they say, “Allah’s speech descended upon him,” or say, “He is the Word,” or anything similar, this is something he shares with all the other prophets.

---

## Page 8880

Third:

An attribute cannot unite with something and clothe itself in it unless the one it qualifies does so as well. The Father himself would then be the Messiah, yet the Christians agree that the Messiah is not the Father. Their doctrine is self-contradictory: its parts invalidate one another. They make him a god who creates and provides sustenance, but do not make him the Father, who is God, while saying, “There is one God.”

Some of their theologians, such as Yahyā ibn ʿAdī, have likened this to a man described as a physician, an accountant, and a scribe, with different functions corresponding to each attribute. The response is: this is true, but their doctrine is not analogous to it. If you say that the Lord exists, lives, and knows, and that each attribute has its own implications, then plainly, if it is the essence bearing these attributes that enters into union, all the attributes accompany it. When Zayd, the physician, accountant, and scribe, puts on a coat of mail, all these attributes remain inherent in him. If, however, it is one attribute rather than another that clothes itself in something, the same untenable consequence returns.

If they say, “It is the essence together with one attribute rather than another that clothes itself in something,” this necessarily entails separating the two attributes, which is impossible. Attributes that subsist in a single subject and are inseparable from it cannot be separated from one another. Some attributes of created beings may cease to exist while the others remain, unlike the attributes of the Lord, blessed and exalted is He.

Fourth:

The Messiah himself is neither Allah’s words nor any of His attributes. Rather, he was created by Allah’s word. He was called a Word because he was created through “Be,” without the usual manner of conception. As the Exalted says:

“Indeed, the likeness of Jesus before Allah is as that of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, ‘Be,’ and he was.”

And the Exalted says: “That is Jesus

son of Mary—the word of truth about which they dispute.”

Thus, when Christians say that the Messiah is the Creator, they are in error both in making an attribute a creator and in making him that very attribute, whereas he was merely created through the word. The response is that this is false on several grounds.

First: Our attributes come into being through our learning, reflection, thought, and reasoning. The Lord’s word and His knowledge, however, are eternal and inseparable from His essence. They therefore cannot be described as generated, unless someone claims that every attribute inseparable from its bearer is generated from it and is its son. Such a claim is plainly among the most untenable, both rationally and linguistically. A person’s life, capacity for speech, and other inseparable attributes are not said to be generated from him or to be his son. Moreover, this would entail that the Lord’s life is likewise His son and generated from Him, as is His power. Otherwise, what distinguishes the generation of knowledge from the generation of life, power, and His other attributes?

Second: If this is a case of the generation of substances and self-subsisting entities, it must proceed from two sources, and a part must issue from the source. Our knowledge and speech, however, are not self-subsisting entities. If, on the other hand, it is an attribute subsisting in its bearer and an accident inhering in a subject, like our knowledge and speech, then this too can only be generated from two sources, and it must have a subject in which it is generated.

Knowledge and speech arise in any one of us only through antecedent premises, which serve as foundations for what follows from them. Knowledge and speech then come to exist in a subject in which they did not previously exist.

If you say that the Lord’s knowledge is like this, it follows that He comes to know things after not knowing them, and that His essence comes to speak after He was not speaking. Besides constituting unbelief according to the vast majority of peoples—Muslims, Christians, and others—this is also invalid according to plain reason. A being that lacks knowledge cannot make itself knowledgeable without someone to teach it, and it is impossible for Allah Most High to learn from His creation. Likewise, a being incapable of speech cannot become capable of it without someone making it capable. Nor does any individual generate all his own knowledge. Rather, certain knowledge is created within him which he cannot reject; when he reflects upon it, he acquires further knowledge.

No human being says that a person generates all his own knowledge. Nor does anyone say that he makes himself able to speak after being unable to do so. Rather, the One who enables him to speak is the One who has caused all things to speak.

If they say that the Lord generates some of His knowledge and some of His speech, but not all of it, then it becomes invalid to call knowledge—which is the Word, taken without qualification—the Son. The term “Son” would then designate only some of His knowledge or some of His speech. Yet they claim that the Messiah is the Word and the hypostasis of knowledge without qualification. Not all of that is generated from Him, nor is all of it called a son, as all rational people agree.

Third: Calling a knowledgeable person’s knowledge and speech his offspring is unknown in any of the widely known languages, and it is rationally invalid. His knowledge and speech are like his power and his knowledge. If

He does not say that knowledge is his son or offspring, just as he does not say that satiety and the quenching of thirst are his sons or offspring. This concerns the generation of accidents and qualities inhering in a human being; these are not called his offspring or sons.

Anyone who metaphorically speaks of the “little daughters of his thought” is using an expression like “little daughters of the road” for side paths, “son of the road” for a traveler, or “son of water” for a waterbird.
