the early generations; indeed, what is reliably reported from them contradicts these doctrines.” Thus, because the theologians displayed considerable shortcomings and ignorance concerning the realities of the religious sciences, while in rational matters they sometimes agreed with the philosophers in their falsehoods and sometimes opposed them in their truths, the advantage in their debates shifted from one side to the other. Nevertheless, the theologians are more correct overall in rational questions concerning divine matters and universals, just as they are closer to the revealed teachings than the philosophers. Consequently, when these people, who have learned what the philosophers know, hear the prophets’ reports about the angels, the Throne, the Kursī, Paradise, and Hell—while supposing that nothing exists beyond what they and the philosophers know—they become bewildered and reinterpret the prophets’ words to fit what they know, although there is no evidence for this, nor do they have, for this

---

## Page 8940

denial, any knowledge; for absence of knowledge is not knowledge of absence. Their denial is like a physician’s denial of the jinn because nothing in the practice of medicine establishes their existence. Yet nothing in medical knowledge disproves their existence either. Likewise, you find someone who has mastered a branch of knowledge and thereby distinguished himself from ordinary people who do not know it, yet continues, out of ignorance, to deny whatever he does not know. Human beings go astray more through what they reject and deny without knowledge than through what they affirm and believe.

Allah Most High says:

“Rather, they have denied what they do not fully comprehend and whose fulfillment has not yet come to them.”

This is because human beings generally possess sound senses and reason, so when they affirm something and believe it, it is true. For this reason, mass-transmitted reports are accepted from people of every kind: they report what they have seen and heard, and a vast multitude will not all be mistaken about such matters or deliberately lie about them. Once it is known that they have neither colluded over their report nor derived it from one another—as doctrines and opinions are passed down from earlier to later generations—and that the matter is not one about which people ordinarily err, their truthfulness is known with certainty. A person reporting something either deliberately lies or makes a mistake, and both possibilities are ruled out in mass-transmitted reports. The opposite holds for what people deny and reject: most, or many, of them deny what they do not know and reject what they do not fully comprehend.

Thus, when these people, who suppose that existing things are confined to what these philosophers know, hear what the prophets have reported about the Throne and the Kursī, they say: “The Throne is

---

## Page 8941

the ninth celestial sphere, and the Kursī is the eighth.” We have discussed this in “The Question of Encompassment” and demonstrated, on both rational and scriptural grounds, the ignorance of those who say this.

When someone of this kind hears them mention the angels, he supposes that they are the intellects and souls posited by the philosophers, or the forces within bodies. Likewise, he imagines that the jinn and devils are accidents inhering in souls, since this is the extent of his knowledge. He also accepts what Ibn Sīnā and others like him maintain: that extraordinary phenomena in this world are caused by celestial, natural, or psychic powers. He places the prophets’ miracles in the category of psychic powers, regarding them as belonging to the same kind as sorcery, except that the sorcerer intends evil whereas the prophet intends good.

All this stems from ignorance of the universal principles encompassing existing things and their kinds, and from ignorance of what the Messenger brought. Their knowledge of the universal sciences and metaphysics extends no further than what the ancient philosophers knew, together with additions received from certain speculative theologians or adherents of religious faith.

For this reason, the discussions of metaphysics and universal principles by later philosophers, such as Ibn Sīnā and others like him, were superior to those of their predecessors. This also explains why Greek philosophy became congenial to heretical innovators among the adherents of religious faiths: it contained an admixture of religious teaching. Thus the heretical Banū ‘Ubayd embraced it, taking the Intellect and the Soul from these polytheistic Sabian philosophers, and Light and Darkness from the Magians. They themselves called them “the Preceder” and “the Follower.” Likewise, heretics claiming affiliation with Sufism and devotion to God, such as Ibn Sab‘īn and others like him, followed

## Page 8942

a path on which, they claimed, they combined religious teaching with philosophy. Yet they are heretics who do not belong to the seventy-two sects. Both groups have been discussed at length elsewhere. The purpose here is to discuss the terms “occupying space” and “direction.” These philosophically inclined speculative theologians came to disagree about the angels: do they occupy space or not?

Those who inclined toward philosophy, holding that the angels are the intellects and souls posited by the philosophers and that these do not occupy space, said that the angels do not occupy space—especially since a group of philosophers did not limit their number to ten intellects and nine souls, as

---

## Page 8943

is commonly attributed to the Peripatetics. Rather, they maintained that there was no proof ruling out a greater number. Seeing that prophetic revelations had spoken of the multitude of angels, they sought to establish their multitude through a philosophical method, as did Abū al-Barakāt, author of al-Mu'tabar, and al-Rāzī in al-Matālib al-'Āliyah, among others.

As for the speculative theologians, they say that every contingent thing, everything that has come into being, or every created thing either occupies space or subsists in something that occupies space. Many of them say that every existent either occupies space or subsists in something that occupies space, and that no existent can be conceived otherwise. Various groups engaged in speculative theology and rational inquiry have maintained this.

When philosophically inclined thinkers such as Ibn Sīnā and his followers, al-Shahrastānī, al-Rāzī, and others sought to establish the existence of something that is not of this kind, their principal support was their affirmation of universals, such as shared humanity and shared animality. Since these are universals only in the mind, their opponents did not dispute this with them. Rather, they disputed their affirmation of something existing outside the mind, subsisting in itself, yet entirely imperceptible to the senses—indeed, something that cannot even be conceived.

They said to them: “What is intellectually apprehended is in the intellect. But whatever exists and subsists in itself must be capable of being perceived by the senses, even if we do not perceive it in this world, just as we do not perceive the jinn, the angels, and other such beings. It must therefore be perceptible to beings other than ourselves, such as the angels and jinn, and be perceived after death, or in the Hereafter, or

---

## Page 8944

be perceived in this world by some people but not others, such as the prophets who saw the angels and heard their speech.”

This approach—that everything subsisting in itself can be seen—is the one followed by leading rational thinkers such as Ibn Kullāb and others. Ibn al-Zāghūnī and others also followed it.

As for the claim that every existent can be seen or perceived through all five senses, as maintained by al-Ashʿarī and those who agree with him, such as al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā, Abū al-Maʿālī, and others, this approach is rejected by the overwhelming majority of rational thinkers. Indeed, they say that its invalidity is self-evident once it is fully understood, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

The same applies to their dispute concerning the human spirit, which departs from a person at death according to the majority, who hold that it is an entity subsisting in itself, neither an accident of the body, such as life and the like, nor a part of the body, such as the air exhaled from it. Many speculative theologians, however, have claimed that it is an accident subsisting in the body or one of its parts. Yet this contradicts the Quran, the Sunnah, the consensus of the early and later generations, the position of the overwhelming majority of rational thinkers among all nations, and rational proofs. This is one of the points the philosophers have used to assert their superiority over many speculative theologians.

Al-Qādī Abū Bakr said that most speculative theologians hold that the spirit is one of the accidents

---

## Page 8945

and this is our position, provided that by “spirit” he does not mean the soul. For he said:

“The spirit present in the body is of two kinds: one is the life subsisting in it, and the other is breath. Breath is air that spreads through it.”

What is meant by breath is the particles of air released through the pores and expelled in breathing. This is the view of al-Isfarāyīnī and others. Ibn Fūrak said that it is what flows through the cavities of the organs. Abū al-Maʿālī disagreed with them—and rightly so—saying:

“The spirit consists of subtle bodies interwoven with perceptible bodies. Allah has established the customary order whereby bodies remain alive so long as these subtle bodies remain interwoven with them. When they separate from them, death follows life, in accordance with that continuing customary order.”

The position of the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, the rest of the early generations of the Muslim community, and the leading scholars of the Sunnah is that the spirit is an entity subsisting in itself, which departs from the body and experiences bliss or punishment. It is neither the body nor any part of it, such as the breath mentioned above.

Since Imam Ahmad explicitly affirmed this, as did other imams, his followers did not disagree on this point. Some of them, however, such as al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā, claimed that it is a body and that it is the air moving back and forth through the body’s passages, in agreement with one of the two meanings mentioned by Ibn al-Bāqillānī. Since these views were among the weakest, many people used them to gain the upper hand over their proponents.

---

## Page 8946

The point here is that those who hold that the spirit is an entity subsisting in itself, distinct from the body, its parts, and its accidents, disagreed over whether it is a body occupying space. They held two views, just as they disagreed concerning the angels. The speculative theologians among them say that it is a body, whereas the philosophers say that it is an intellectual substance, not a body.

We have already indicated that what the philosophers call intellectual substances exist only in the mind. Their designation of entities as “abstract” and “separate” originally derives from the human soul: since it separates from the body at death and becomes detached from it, they called it “separate” and “abstract.” They then posited the intellects and souls they affirm, calling them “separate” and “abstract” entities on that basis. By something “separate from matter,” they mean something that is neither a body nor subsists in a body. The soul, however, is connected to the body through governing it, whereas the intellect has no connection whatsoever with bodies.

There is no doubt that the vast majority of rational people affirm a distinction between the body and the spirit that departs from it. People generally call the latter a spirit and the former a body. Yet the word “body” in ordinary Arabic does not have the same meaning as “body” in the technical terminology of the speculative theologians. Rather, as explained earlier, it means the bodily frame: the dense body, or its bulk. The spirit does not resemble the body in bulk and density, and is therefore not called a body.

Thus, whoever holds that angels, spirits, and the like are not bodies in the ordinary linguistic sense is correct in this. The Lord of all worlds is all the more entitled not to be described as a body, for the distinction between spirits and bodies is well established in ordinary language.

---

## Page 8947

As for the speculative theologians and philosophers who employ technical terminology, they give “body” a broader meaning: anything that can be indicated through the senses, described as being here or there, or admit of three dimensions, and the like.

Likewise, in their terminology, “that which occupies space” means a body, and includes the indivisible atom according to those who affirm its existence. The linguistic meaning of “body” has already been explained. As for *mutahayyiz*, Allah Most High says:

“And whoever turns his back to them that day—unless maneuvering for battle or joining another company—has indeed incurred Allah’s wrath.”

Al-Jawharī said:

“*Al-hawz* means gathering. Anyone who takes something into his possession is said to have *hāzahu*, with the verbal nouns *hawz* and *hiyāzah*; *ihtāzahu* is also used. *Al-hawz* and *al-hayyiz* mean gentle driving. One says *hāza al-ibila*, with the present-tense forms *yahūzuhā* and *yahīzuhā*, meaning that he drove the camels. *Hawwaza al-ibila* means that he drove the camels to water. Al-Asma‘ī said: ‘When the camels graze far from water, the first night on which you direct them towards water is called the night of *al-hawz*.’ *Tahawwazat al-hayyah* and *tahayyazat* mean that the snake writhed.

“One says: ‘Why do you writhe like a snake?’ This is expressed both as *tatahawwazu tahawwuza al-hayyah* and *tatahayyazu tahayyuza al-hayyah*. Sībawayh said: ‘It follows the pattern *tafa‘‘ul*, from *huztu al-shay’a*—I gathered the thing.’ Al-Qatāmī said:

She drew away from me, fearing I would be her guest,
As a viper withdraws, fearing one who would strike.

“He means: this old woman moves away from me and draws back, fearing that I will stay with her as a guest.

---

## Page 8948

Al-hayyiz denotes the appurtenances adjoining a house, and every distinct area is a hayyiz. Its root originally contains the letter wāw (w). Hayz is a shortened pronunciation of hayyiz, just as hayn is of hayyin (‘easy’), and layn of layyin (‘soft’). Its plural is ahyāz. Al-hawzah means an area. Inhāza ‘anhu means ‘he turned aside from it.’ When people are said to have inhāzū, they have left their position for another. Of one’s allies, one says that they ‘withdrew from the enemy’ or ‘turned aside’; of enemies, that they ‘were routed’ and ‘turned their backs in flight.’ When two parties in battle are said to have tahāwazā, each has withdrawn from the other.”

These statements by the lexicographers concerning this word and its root imply that tahayyuz, inhiyāz, tahawwuz, and similar expressions involve moving from one location to another. This is narrower than merely being contained by something that exists. Thus, in the meaning of hawz, they take into account movement from one quarter to another. Hence they say, “Huztu al-māl” (I gathered the wealth into my possession) and “Huztu al-ibil” (I drove the camels together). This involves moving them from one quarter to another. They therefore do not call something fixed in its position—such as a mountain, the sun, or the moon—mutahayyiz, “occupying space.”

A broader sense is to understand “occupying space” as being surrounded by an actually existing spatial region. Anything surrounded by something else would then be described as occupying space. On this understanding, whatever lies between heaven and earth occupies space. Indeed, everything in the universe occupies space except the universe’s surface, which nothing surrounds: that does not occupy space. Likewise, the universe as a whole does not occupy space in this sense, since it is not within another universe surrounding it.

The speculative theologians, however, intend something broader by “occupying space.” For them, a spatial region is broader than a place: the entire universe is in a spatial region, but it is not in a place.

---

## Page 8949

and, in their view, something that occupies space need not be contained by anything else, nor need it have an actually existing spatial region. Rather, anything that can be pointed to and has distinguishable parts occupies space according to them.

They then disagree about what occupies space: is it composed of indivisible atoms, or of matter and form? Or is it composed of neither? Their disagreement concerning bodies has already been discussed.

In their view, a body occupies space, and nothing that occupies space falls outside the category of body except the indivisible atom, according to those who affirm its existence. Many or most of these thinkers believe that everything occupying space is composite—that is, it admits division into indivisible parts. Some even imagine that this is the consensus of the Muslims. Most of them maintain that things occupying space are identical in definition and essential reality.

Anyone who understands spatial occupation in this sense must declare Allah Most High free of occupying space in this sense. If he says, “The angels occupy space in this sense,” or, “The soul occupies space in this sense,” the majority of rational people, Muslims and others, dispute his claim. Indeed, no one among the early generations of the Muslim community or its leading scholars is known to have said that the angels occupy space in this sense, nor did they use any expression conveying this meaning. Likewise, none of the early generations said that the human soul, which departs from a person at death, occupies space in this sense, nor did anyone use an expression conveying this meaning concerning it.

If, then, ascribing this kind of spatial occupation to the angels and the soul is an innovation in religion and rationally false, then it must likewise be an innovation and a falsehood when ascribed to the Lord of

---

## Page 8950

the worlds, all the more so. From this it becomes clear that most of what the philosophers and these speculative theologians say about human souls and the angels is false. What, then, of what they say about the Lord of the worlds?

Thus, the books that set out the positions of these two groups on these great questions—concerning the Lord of the worlds, His angels, human souls, the Hereafter, and prophethood—contain no position that accords with reason and revelation. They know neither what the early generations and the leading scholars said on these matters nor what the Quran and Sunnah indicate. Bewilderment therefore prevails even among their most accomplished thinkers: when they reach the end of their inquiry, they have attained no knowledge, because the statements of both groups that they have examined contain falsehood on both sides.

For this reason, Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī said near the end of his life:

“I have reflected on the methods of speculative theology and the approaches of philosophy, and I have not found them to heal the ailing or quench thirst. I have found the most direct path to be the way of the Quran. Read, concerning affirmation:

‘To Him ascends good speech, and righteous work raises it.’

‘The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.’

And read, concerning negation:

‘There is nothing like Him.’

‘They do not encompass Him in knowledge.’

Whoever undergoes what I have undergone will come to know what I know.”

As for someone who believes that what occupies space is whatever is distinct from something else and stands apart from it, and that it is not

## Page 8951

a requirement that it be composed of discrete parts or admit of separation and division: if he says, “The Lord occupies space in this sense,” meaning that He is distinct from His creatures, he intends a sound meaning. Using this expression, however, is an innovation and introduces confusion, for the meaning he intends is not the linguistic meaning of “occupying space”; rather, it is a technical usage adopted by him and his group. Rational thinkers dispute this technical meaning, so the expression can convey a false meaning from which the Lord must be declared free. A person may not use an expression that conveys a false meaning to someone else, thereby leading that person to understand that false meaning, without explaining what he intends.

Indeed, consider these speculative theologians who mean by “that which occupies space” something composed of indivisible parts—that is, something that admits of division. When they say, “Every contingent being, or every originated being, or every created being, is either something that occupies space or something subsisting in what occupies space,” the great majority of rational thinkers disagree with this classification. No leading Muslim scholar has agreed with them on this classification: neither the Companions, nor those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment, nor any other leading Muslim scholars.

How much more so, then, when one of them says, “Everything that exists either occupies space or subsists in something that occupies space,” intending by “that which occupies space” what these theologians intend! His statement is then further removed from revelation and reason than theirs. This is why their later thinkers demanded that they provide proof that these are the only possibilities. The error of these theologians is not on account of the intelligible substances posited by the philosophers, for the falsity of those has likewise been established by clear reason.

---

## Page 8952

And what these philosophers say about the rational soul—that it cannot be pointed to, cannot be described as moving or being at rest, ascending or descending, and is neither within the world nor outside it—is likewise, in the judgment of the great majority of rational thinkers, even more false than what those speculative theologians say. This applies especially to the claim made by some of them—such as Ibn Sīnā and his like—that it knows nothing of particulars, but knows only universals. This is a blatant denial of the obvious: the soul knows its own body and knows everything it sees, smells, hears, and tastes through the body, as well as what it seeks, commands, loves, and hates, and everything else with which it engages through its knowledge and action. How, then, can it be said that it does not know particular things, but knows only universals?

Likewise, their claim that its connection to the body is merely one of governance and direction, like a king’s governance of his kingdom, is utterly unsound. A king manages the affairs of his kingdom, issuing commands and prohibitions, but he cannot direct his subjects by his own will and power unless they themselves act by their own will and power. Nor does the king experience the pleasure that any one of them experiences, or suffer the pain that he suffers. The relationship between the soul and the body is not like this. Rather, Allah has established between them such union and harmony that no known counterpart can serve as an analogy.

Yet the soul’s entry into the body does not resemble the entry of any observable physical body into another. Its entry into the body is not like that of water and similar liquids into vessels. These liquids touch only the vessels’ inner surfaces, not their inner substance or outer surfaces. They come into contact only with

---

## Page 8953

the vessels at the liquids’ outer edges, not their centres. This is not the case with the soul and the body. Rather, the soul is connected with every part of the body, inwardly and outwardly. Likewise, its entry into the body is not like the entry of food and drink into the body of someone who consumes them: these pass through known channels and undergo transformation, among their other properties. Nor does the soul flow through the body as blood does, for blood is present in some parts of the body but not others.

In short, none of the proposed analogies involves every part of one thing being connected with the other, as is the case with the soul and the body. Nevertheless, the soul is within the body and has entered it. It leaves the body at death and is drawn out gradually, emerging from it little by little. It does not leave it as a king leaves the city he governs. Because people have witnessed nothing comparable to the soul, they find it difficult to express its true nature.

This should alert them to the fact that they do not know the true nature of the Lord of all worlds, nor have they conceived how He is—glorified and exalted is He—and that the attributes ascribed to Him are as befits Him, majestic is His glory. For the soul, which is itself one of His servants, is described as ascending when a person sleeps and prostrating beneath the Throne, while still remaining in that person’s body, without having left it altogether. In sleep, a person senses the activities of his soul—activities that affect his body.

Thus, the ascent attributed to the soul does not resemble the ascent of observable things. When these ascend to a place, they leave their former place entirely, and their movement

---

## Page 8954

upward is a movement from one place to another. The soul’s movement in its ascent and prostration is not like this.

Thus, when His Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—describes the Lord, glorified is He, as descending to the lowest heaven every night, drawing near to the pilgrims on the afternoon of Arafah, speaking to Moses on the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree, and rising towards heaven while it was smoke, saying to it and to the earth, “Come willingly or unwillingly,” to which they replied, “We come willingly”—it does not follow that these actions are of the same kind as the descent we observe in visible entities, such that one could say that they necessarily entail vacating one place and occupying another.

The soul’s descent and ascent do not entail this, so how much less would this follow in the case of the Lord of all worlds? Likewise, the angels have an ascent and descent of this kind.

It is therefore impermissible to deny any of the names and attributes that Allah and His Messenger have affirmed, or to liken them to the attributes of created beings. This is particularly clear in the case of created beings we do not observe: the names and attributes established for them are not like those of the creatures we do observe. How much more, then, does this apply to the Lord of all worlds, who is far further removed from resembling any created being than one created being is from resembling another? Every created being bears a greater resemblance to another created being unlike itself than the Creator bears to any created being. Glorified and exalted is He, far above what the wrongdoers say.

## Page 8955

What we have pointed out helps make clear that the classifications of existing things presented by the author of al-Muhassil and others like him, according to the views of the philosophers and speculative theologians, are all incomplete. Each of these two groups falls short of its predecessors.

As for the speculative theologians, their classifications do not follow the approach indicated by the Quran and Sunnah and followed by the early generations of the Muslim community. Likewise, these philosophers who follow Aristotle did not follow the approach of the great philosophers of antiquity. Those earlier philosophers held that this world came into being. They maintained that above this world there is another world, which they described in some of the same terms the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—used to describe Paradise. They also affirmed bodily resurrection, as can be found in the statements of Socrates, Thales, and other leading philosophers. It has been reported that Aristotle was the first among them to maintain that the world has no beginning.

## Page 8959

that he said:

The point is that knowing what the Messenger brought and what he intended by the wording of the Quran and hadith is the foundation of knowledge, faith, happiness, and salvation. Next comes knowing what people have said on these matters, so that one can distinguish meanings consistent with the Messenger’s teaching from those that contradict it.

Terms are of two kinds: those found in the speech of Allah and His Messenger, and those not found in their speech. One should understand the meaning of the first kind and make that meaning the foundation, then ascertain what people mean by the second kind and assess it against the first.

This is the way of those who follow guidance and the Sunnah. Those who follow misguidance and innovation take the opposite approach: they make the terms they have introduced, and their meanings, the foundation, subordinating what Allah and His Messenger have said to their own formulations. Through reinterpretation and distortion, they force the revealed words to conform to their own meanings. They say, “We interpret the Quran through reason and language.” What they mean is that they adopt a meaning on the basis of their own reasoning and opinion, then interpret the Quran accordingly, using whatever interpretations and explanations they can devise, which involve displacing words from their proper meanings. Hence Imam Ahmad said: “Most of people’s errors arise from reinterpretation and analogical reasoning.”

He also said: “Anyone speaking on jurisprudence should avoid these two foundations: ambiguous formulations and analogical reasoning.” This approach is shared by all proponents of innovation, great and small.

for this is the way of the Jahmiyyah, the Mu‘tazilah, and those philosophers and heretical Bātiniyyah who engage in reinterpretation.

The others say that he did not intend to evoke imaginative representations, but rather intended a meaning that could be understood through reinterpretation.

They said: Tafsīr brings something out of obscurity into clarity, whereas ta’wīl shifts speech from its ordinary sense to a meaning whose establishment requires evidence, without which the apparent meaning of the wording would not be abandoned. These scholars mention only the first and second meanings of ta’wīl; they do not mention its meaning in the language of the Quran. It has already been established that ta’wīl in the Quran is the actual reality to which the speech ultimately refers, even when that accords with the meaning apparent from the wording. Indeed, nowhere in the Quran is the term ta’wīl known to signify something contrary to what the wording indicates, unlike the convention of later scholars.

Speech is of two kinds: directive and informative. Directive speech comprises commands, prohibitions, and permissions. The ta’wīl of a command or prohibition is the actual performance of what is commanded or the actual abandonment of what is forbidden.

Thus, in the Sahīh, ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say while bowing and prostrating: ‘Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You.

He means that they are more knowledgeable about the ta’wīl of what Allah has commanded and forbidden: they recognize the actual, concrete actions He has commanded and the prohibited actions He has forbidden. The explanation of His speech is not itself what exists in external reality; rather, it clarifies His speech, expounds it, and reveals its meaning. Thus, tafsīr belongs to the realm of speech: speech is explained through other speech that clarifies it. Ta’wīl, however, consists in doing what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden; it does not belong to the realm of speech.

The second kind is informative speech, such as the Lord’s statements about Himself—exalted is He—concerning His names and attributes, and His statements about the promises and warnings He has mentioned to His servants. This is the ta’wīl mentioned in His words:

## Page 8980

And the claim of al-Zamakhsharī and others that “‘He rose over something’ means ‘he possessed it’” is a bare assertion, unsupported by any example from Arab speech. Even if such usage were conceded, this meaning would still be invalid when applied to Allah’s rising over the Throne. For He has stated that He created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne. He has also stated that the Throne existed before the creation of the heavens and the earth, as both the Quran and the Sunnah indicate. Thus, from the moment He created the Throne, He owned it and held dominion over it. How, then, could His rising over it have occurred after the creation of the heavens and the earth?

Moreover, He owns everything and holds dominion over it, so the Throne would not be singled out for His rising over it. This is not like singling it out in connection with His lordship when He says:

“Lord of the Magnificent Throne.”

The Throne may be singled out because of its magnificence, but the same expression may also be applied to all other created things. Thus, one may say, “Lord of the Throne and Lord of all things.” Rising over, however, applies specifically to the Throne. It is therefore not said, “He rose over the Throne and over all things.” Nor has any Muslim used this expression with reference to all things, nor is such usage found in the Quran or the Sunnah. By contrast, the expression of lordship is used both specifically of the Throne and generally of all things. The same applies to creation and similar expressions that admit both specific and general application, as in His words, exalted is He:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created—created man from a clinging substance.”

Rising over is therefore an expression specific to the Throne; it is not applied to anything else, either specifically or generally. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

The purpose here is simply to demonstrate the correctness of the statement of the early generations:

“What ‘rising over’ means is known.”

unlike those who assign this expression ten-odd meanings, as mentioned by Ibn ‘Arabī al-Ma‘āfirī.

This is why these expressions admit ambiguity. Someone who has partners says, “We have done such-and-such, and We indeed do such-and-such.” This is impossible in the case of Allah Most High. The same applies to His words:

All these instances of istiwāʾ (being established upon something) entail the dependence of what is above upon what is beneath it: were that which supports it absent, it would fall. Allah Most High, however, has no need of the Throne or anything else. Rather, He, glorified is He, bears the Throne and its bearers by His power. It has been reported that they were only able to bear the Throne when He commanded them to say: “There is no power nor strength except through Allah.”

Thus, the term istiwāʾ is ambiguous: when applied to created beings, it entails meanings from which Allah is utterly free. We know its meaning—elevation and evenness—but we do not know the manner unique to the Lord, whereby He is established above the Throne without any need of it. Rather, the Throne needs Him, and everything depends upon Him in every respect. Among existing things, we have never known anything to be established upon something else while having no need of it, with that which is beneath it instead depending upon what is above it. It is therefore ambiguous in this respect.

The two expressions and their meanings have an element in common, as well as a distinguishing element intended in each case. We do not know the distinguishing reality unique to the Lord. Thus, we know it in one respect and do not know it in another. The latter is its ultimate reality, while the former is its explanation.

The same applies to what Allah has told us about the food, drink, and clothing in Paradise, such as milk, honey, wine, and water. We know of no milk except that produced by livestock

Rather, it has a reality different from theirs. This belongs to the ultimate reality that we do not know. Ibn ʿAbbās said:

As for interpretation in the sense of the reality as it actually exists, none but Allah knows that. Yet it may be said that this relative ambiguity is not the ambiguity mentioned in the Quran, for Allah has stated that none but He knows its interpretation. Rather, this is like the verses that many people find difficult because they do not understand their meaning, while others do. Two answers may therefore be given:

The first is that the verse admits two readings: one in which the reader pauses at His words, “except Allah,” and another in which the reader pauses at His words, “and those firmly grounded in knowledge.” Both readings are true. The first refers to what is inherently ambiguous, knowledge of whose ultimate reality Allah has reserved for Himself. The second refers to what is relatively ambiguous, whose explanation is known to those firmly grounded in knowledge; that explanation is its interpretation. Similar instances occur in the Quran, as in His words: “Though their plotting was

---

## Page 8986

such as to move mountains.” The expression “to move” has two well-known readings, one negative and the other affirmative, and each reading conveys a sound meaning.

Likewise, the well-known reading is:

“And beware of a trial that will not afflict exclusively those among you who have done wrong.”

A group of the early generations read it as: “It will surely afflict those among you who have done wrong exclusively.” Both readings are true. The person who transgresses Allah’s limits is a wrongdoer. Someone who fails to oppose him may be considered not to be a wrongdoer because he did not participate in his wrongdoing; alternatively, he may be considered a wrongdoer because he neglected his duty to oppose it. His words are to be understood accordingly:

“When they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil and seized the wrongdoers with a terrible punishment because of their disobedience.”

Thus, Allah saved those who forbade evil. As for those who disliked the sin and said, “Why do you admonish a people,” the majority hold that they were saved, because they disliked it and opposed it to the extent of their ability. As for someone who entirely refrains from opposing wrongdoing, he is a wrongdoer who will be punished, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When people see wrongdoing and do not change it, Allah may soon afflict them all with a punishment from Him.”

This hadith accords with the verse.

The point here is that both negation and affirmation can be valid when considered from two different perspectives. Thus, His words, “It will not afflict exclusively those among you who have done wrong,” mean that it will not be restricted to the transgressors, but will also encompass those who witnessed wrongdoing and did not change it. As for whoever reads, “It will surely afflict those among you who have done wrong

---

## Page 8987

exclusively,” he includes those who failed to oppose wrongdoing despite being able to do so. It may also mean that they are punished in this world but resurrected according to their intentions, like the army that marches against the House and is swallowed up in its entirety, while anyone compelled to accompany it will be gathered according to his intention.

The second answer:

It is to affirm definitively that the ambiguity mentioned in the Quran is the intrinsic ambiguity inseparable from these passages, whose ultimate reality none but Allah knows. As for relative ambiguity, when people use the term in this sense, they mean that they discussed passages whose meaning was unclear and difficult for some people, and that the Jahmiyyah based their arguments on what they found unclear and difficult—even if it did not belong to those ambiguous passages whose ultimate reality none but Allah knows. Something may often be unclear to one person without being unclear to another.

Imam Ahmad’s words may also be understood as referring exclusively to what is intrinsically and necessarily ambiguous, without intending relative ambiguity in any part of his statement. His words, “interpreted it contrary to its true import,” mean: contrary to the reality to which it actually refers, even though none but Allah knows that reality. Those endowed with knowledge know that this is the reality intended, so the passage is no longer obscure to them or open to another meaning.

For this reason, ambiguity occurs in statements concerning either Allah or the Hereafter, and none but Allah knows the ultimate reality of all this. Indeed, the clear passages of the Quran may also be said to have an ultimate reality, just as the ambiguous passages do. As He says:

“Are they waiting for anything but its fulfillment?”

Nevertheless, none but Allah knows the timing and manner of that fulfillment. It may instead be said that this ultimate reality pertains to the ambiguous passages, since they concern the promise

## Page 8988

and the warning, all of which is ambiguous. Moreover, not every verse that some people consider ambiguous necessarily belongs to the ambiguous passages.

do not refer here to the general perfection and mutual consistency shared by all the verses of the Quran, as mentioned in His words:

and:

Here He describes the entire Book as mutually consistent: its parts agree rather than differ, each confirming the others. This is the opposite of the contradiction and disagreement mentioned in His words:

and:

“Turned away from it is whoever is turned away.”

This mutual consistency encompasses the whole Quran, just as the perfection of its verses encompasses it in its entirety. Yet in the passage under discussion, He says:

“Some of its verses are clear—they are the foundation of the Book—and others are ambiguous.”

Thus He describes some of it as clear and some as ambiguous. The term therefore has two meanings. It also has a third, relative meaning: one may say, “This has become unclear to us,” as the Children of Israel said:

even though the cows themselves are distinct and distinguishable from one another. This is a case of confusing truth

## Page 8989

with falsehood, as in the words of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) in the hadith:

This is what those who hold that people firmly grounded in knowledge know the ta’wīl intended: they regarded the ambiguous passages of the Quran as belonging to this category—things that are unclear to some people but not to others. There are distinctions between the two things that prevent their being confused, and some people recognize these distinctions. This understanding is sound in itself and cannot be denied. Undoubtedly, those firmly grounded in knowledge understand what is unclear to others.

This may be one reading of the verse, as discussed earlier concerning its admitting two readings. On this reading, however, the term ta’wīl means explanation. The reason is that they know its ta’wīl in general terms, just as they know the ta’wīl of the clear passages. Thus, they have a general knowledge of the Reckoning, the Balance, the Bridge, reward, punishment, and the other things about which Allah and His Messenger have informed us. They therefore know the ta’wīl—what takes place in external reality—in this general sense

## Page 8990

but they do not know it in detail, for they do not know how it is or what its true reality is, since it is unlike what they have known and witnessed in this world. On the reading that denies them this knowledge, may it also be said that the clear passages have a ta’wīl whose details they do not know? Alternatively, it may be said that they do know the ta’wīl of the clear passages, but do not know the time, place, or manner of its realization.

Many of the early generations said: “The clear passages are those to be acted upon, while the ambiguous passages are those to be believed in but not acted upon.” Thus, many transmitted reports state: “We act upon its clear passages and believe in its ambiguous passages.” Likewise, Ibn Mas‘ūd and others are reported to have said concerning the words of the Most High:

He said: “They regard as lawful what it declares lawful, regard as unlawful what it declares unlawful, act upon its clear passages, and believe in its ambiguous passages.”

The statements of the early generations on this subject indicate that ambiguity is relative: something may be unclear to one person but not to another. The first view is, and Allah knows best, derived from His words:

Here He contrasts what is abolished with what is made firm. Yet He, glorified be He, meant only the abolition of what Satan had cast, not the abrogation of what He Himself had revealed. They nevertheless classified abrogated passages in general as ambiguous because they resemble other passages in recitation and composition

## Page 8992

and in being Allah’s speech, Quran, and miraculous, as well as in other respects, although their meaning has been abrogated. This explains what is incumbent upon the entire community: they must know in detail what is to be acted upon so that they may act upon it. Although knowledge of these matters may be commendable or a communal obligation, it is not an individual obligation, unlike knowledge of what must be acted upon. Every person must therefore know in detail the actions required of him, but is not required to have detailed knowledge of matters that do not require action.

its parts confirming one another, there would be nothing objectionable in following that. Nor does its parts confirming one another preclude seeking its interpretation. Thus, those firmly grounded in knowledge know what is intended by the ambiguous passages just as they know what is intended by the clear passages. ## Page 8995

Ahmad’s remarks in his refutation of the heretics and the Jahmiyyah concerning the ambiguous passages of the Quran about which they entertained doubts and which they misinterpreted, together with his statement that the Jahmiyyah interpreted three ambiguous verses, followed by his explanation of their meaning, demonstrate that, in his view, scholars know the meaning of the ambiguous passages. The clear passages are superior to them, yet He has explained their meaning to His servants. Thus, people have come to know it. What is false is to claim both that the Quran indicates this and that no one knows it.

Furthermore, if the Messenger did not understand the matters of knowledge that Allah conveyed in the Quran, this would provide the heretics with one of their strongest grounds for attacking him. It would support their claim that he either did not understand these matters or understood them but did not explain them. Indeed, this position entails that he did not know them, since whatever Allah alone knows is known neither to the Prophet nor to anyone else.

In short, the abundant evidence establishes with certainty the falsity of the claim that the Quran contains verses whose meaning neither the Messenger nor anyone else knows.

---

## Page 9004

Certainly, the Quran may contain verses whose meanings are unknown to many scholars, let alone others. This is not tied to any particular verse; rather, one person may find obscure what another understands. Sometimes this is because the wording is unfamiliar; sometimes because its meaning is confused with another; sometimes because a misconception within a person prevents him from recognizing the truth; sometimes because he has not reflected deeply enough; and sometimes for other reasons. It must therefore be affirmed with certainty that, regarding His words:

“No one knows its interpretation except Allah and those firmly grounded in knowledge. They say, ‘We believe in it.’”

the correct view is that “those firmly grounded in knowledge” is conjoined to “Allah,” with “and” coordinating one noun phrase with another. Or both views may be correct, corresponding to two readings, with “interpretation” referring to one thing when knowledge of it is denied and another when such knowledge is affirmed. If, however, the correct view is that “and” begins a new sentence, then the interpretation whose knowledge is denied to anyone other than Allah must refer to the modalities that He alone knows. This, however, is open to question.

It is reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said, “I am among those firmly grounded in knowledge who know its interpretation.” It is also reported from him that those firmly grounded in knowledge do not know its interpretation. And it is reported that he said:

“Explanation of the Quran is of four kinds: an explanation that the Arabs understand through their own language; an explanation that no one is excused for not knowing; an explanation known to scholars; and an explanation known only to Allah—whoever claims to know it is a liar.”

This statement reconciles the two views. It shows that scholars know aspects of its explanation that others do not, and that it contains matters known only to Allah. But anyone who holds that the correct view is to pause at His words “except Allah,” while taking ‘interpretation’ to mean explanation, is unquestionably mistaken.

---

## Page 9005

As for interpretation in its third sense—diverting an expression from its more likely meaning to a less likely one—this technical usage was not yet known in the time of the Companions, nor even among the Successors or the four imams. Nor was this terminology current during the first three generations. Indeed, I know of none of them who restricted the word “interpretation” to this meaning. However, when this restricted usage became widespread among many later scholars, they assumed that this was what “interpretation” meant in the verse. They consequently came to believe that the ambiguous passages of the Quran had meanings contrary to what is understood from them. Thereafter, they divided their religion and split into sects. Yet the ambiguous passages in question, which occasioned the revelation of the verse, do not outwardly indicate any unsound meaning; rather, the error lies in the hearer’s understanding.

Admittedly, it may be said that this wording alone does not fully explain what is intended. But there is a difference between its not indicating the intended meaning and its indicating the opposite of that meaning. It is the latter that is denied. Indeed, nothing in the Quran indicates falsehood at all, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Yet many people claim that the apparent wording of a verse conveys a particular meaning—either a meaning they themselves believe, or a false meaning that therefore requires reinterpretation. Their claim is false: the verse indicates neither their belief nor that false meaning. This is exceedingly common. These are the people who hold that the Quran frequently requires interpretation in its newly introduced sense: diverting an expression from what it signifies to something contrary to what it signifies.

---

## Page 9006

Among the evidence cited by those who maintain that those firmly grounded in knowledge know the interpretation is the report established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī and elsewhere, from Ibn ‘Abbās:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, supplicated for him, saying: ‘O Allah, grant him understanding of the religion and teach him interpretation.’”

Thus, he prayed for him to have knowledge of interpretation without qualification. Ibn ‘Abbās explained the entire Quran. Mujāhid said: “I went through the Quran with Ibn ‘Abbās from beginning to end, stopping him at every verse and asking him about it.” Ibn ‘Abbās used to say: “I am among those firmly grounded in knowledge who know its interpretation.”

Moreover, reports transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him, through numerous independent chains establish that he discussed all the meanings of the Quran, both its commands and its accounts. His discussions of Allah’s names and attributes, promises of reward and warnings of punishment, and narratives, as well as his discussions of commands, prohibitions, and rulings, demonstrate that he addressed all the meanings of the Quran.

Ibn Mas‘ūd also said: “There is no verse in the Book of Allah but that I know what it was revealed about.”

Furthermore, they agree that the interpretation of the verses concerning rulings is known; these number some five hundred verses. The rest of the Quran speaks of Allah and His names and attributes; of the Last Day, Paradise, and Hell; or of narratives and the ultimate fate of the believers and the disbelievers. If this constitutes the ambiguous portion whose meaning is known only to Allah,

---

## Page 9007

then no one knows the meaning of most of the Quran—neither the Messenger nor anyone in the community. Clearly, this is a blatant denial of the obvious.

Moreover, it is well known that understanding the interpretation of dreams is more difficult than understanding the interpretation of spoken accounts. The way a dream points to its interpretation is subtle and obscure, beyond the grasp of most people, unlike the way words indicate their meaning. If Allah has taught His servants to interpret what they see in dreams, then all the more would He teach them the interpretation of the clear Arabic speech He reveals to His prophets. Jacob said to Joseph:

“Thus will your Lord choose you and teach you the interpretation of dreams.”

Joseph said:

“My Lord, You have granted me authority and taught me the interpretation of dreams.”

He also said:

“No food will come to you as your provision but I will inform you of its interpretation before it reaches you.”

Furthermore, Allah has censured the disbelievers, saying:

“Or do they say, ‘He has fabricated it’? Say, ‘Then produce a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful.’”

“Rather, they have denied what they do not fully comprehend, and whose fulfilment has not yet come to them.”

He also said:

“And on the Day We gather from every nation a company of those who denied Our signs, they will be kept in order.”

“Until, when they arrive, He will say, ‘Did you deny My signs without fully comprehending them? Or what was it that you were doing?’”

This is a censure of anyone who denies what he does not fully comprehend.

---

## Page 9008

Thus, among the differing views people have expressed concerning the explanation and interpretation of the Quran, no one may accept one view rather than another without knowledge, nor reject any of them without fully comprehending it. This is possible only if he knows the true meaning intended by the verse, thereby knowing that whatever contradicts it is false, and so rejecting the falsehood he fully comprehends. But if he does not know its meaning and does not fully comprehend any of these views, he may not reject any of them, even though some of these contradictory views are certainly false. On that basis, someone who denies the Quran would be no different from someone who rejects contradictory views, and someone who denies the truth would be no different from someone who rejects falsehood. The falsity of a necessary consequence demonstrates the falsity of the premise that entails it.

Moreover, if he proceeds on his belief that only Allah knows the meanings of verses conveying information, he must reject the claims of everyone who cites such a Quranic verse as evidence for any matter concerning belief in Allah and the Last Day, as well as everyone who explains such verses. The same consequence necessarily follows regarding the hadiths of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

If he says, “The ambiguous passages comprise only some of those conveying information,” he must provide a clear distinction between Quranic verses whose meanings can be known and those whose meanings cannot be known—not by an angel brought near to Allah, nor a prophet sent by Him, nor any of the Companions, nor anyone else. Yet it is well known that no one can provide a dividing criterion between passages whose meanings some people can know and those whose meanings no one can know. Whatever criterion he might propose would prove untenable. It is therefore clear that the ambiguous passages are not those

---

## Page 9009

whose meaning no one can know. This is an independent proof concerning this question.

Moreover, His statements,

“They have not fully comprehended it,”

and,

“Did you deny My signs without fully comprehending them?”

reproach them for their lack of comprehension together with their denial. If everyone were equally unable to comprehend the ambiguous passages, there would be no point in reproaching them for this particular failing; the reproach would concern their denial alone. It would be tantamount to saying, “Did you deny what you have not fully comprehended, when none but Allah can fully comprehend it?” Yet someone who denies what Allah alone knows has more excuse than someone who denies what people can know. Thus, if those firmly grounded in knowledge did not fully comprehend these signs, omitting this description would make the reproach stronger than including it.

This becomes clear from another consideration, which also constitutes evidence concerning this question: Allah reproaches those who deviate for their ignorance and evil intent. They pursue the ambiguous passages, seeking their interpretation, although none knows their interpretation except those firmly grounded in knowledge—and they are not among them. They seek discord, not knowledge and truth. This resembles His statement, exalted is He:

“Had Allah known any good in them, He would have made them hear. But even if He had made them hear, they would have turned away in aversion.”

Here, “He would have made them hear” means enabling them to understand the Quran. That is, had Allah known that they had good intentions and were receptive to the truth, He would have enabled them to understand the Quran. Yet even if He had enabled them to understand it, they would have turned away from faith and acceptance of the truth because of their evil intent. Thus, they are ignorant and wrongdoing. Likewise, those whose hearts are inclined to deviation are

---

## Page 9010

blamed for their evil intent while seeking knowledge for which they are not qualified. The fact that these people are reproached for seeking such knowledge and denied it does not mean that blame attaches to someone whose intention is good and whom Allah has made firmly grounded in knowledge.

If it is objected:

Most of the early generations held that those firmly grounded in knowledge do not know the interpretation, as did most scholars of language. This is reported from Ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUrwah, Qatādah, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, al-Farrāʾ, Abū ʿUbayd, Thaʿlab, and Ibn al-Anbārī. Ibn al-Anbārī said: In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, it is: “Its interpretation is with Allah alone; and those firmly grounded in knowledge.” In the reading of Ubayy and Ibn ʿAbbās, it is: “And those firmly grounded in knowledge say.”

He said: Allah has revealed in His Book matters whose knowledge He has reserved exclusively for Himself, as in His statement, exalted is He:

“Say: Its knowledge is with Allah alone.”

And His statement:

“And many generations in between.”

Thus, He revealed the unambiguous passages so that the believer might believe in them and attain felicity, while the disbeliever might reject them and suffer misery. Ibn al-Anbārī said: The person who transmitted the other opinion from Mujāhid was Ibn Abī Najīh, and his transmission of Quranic commentary from Mujāhid is not sound.

The response is:

The claim that most of the early generations held this view is made without knowledge. It is not established that any of the Companions said that those firmly grounded in knowledge do not know the interpretation of the ambiguous passages. Ibn Abī Mulaykah reported from ʿĀʾishah that she said:

“Their firmness in knowledge lay in believing in its unambiguous and ambiguous passages, though they did not understand it.”

---

## Page 9011

Yet al-Bukhārī narrated the Prophetic hadith on this subject through Ibn Abī Mulaykah, from al-Qāsim, from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, without this addition. Nor did Ibn Abī Mulaykah mention hearing this addition from al-Qāsim. Rather, what is established from the Companions is that those firmly grounded in knowledge understand the ambiguous passages, as shown by the previously mentioned report of Muʿādh ibn Jabal on this subject. Similar reports are also transmitted from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and others. The readings attributed to Ibn Masʿūd and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb have no known chain of transmission by which they could serve as evidence. What is well known from Ibn Masʿūd is that he used to say:

“There is no verse in Allah’s Book without my knowing what it was revealed about and what was intended by it.”

Abū ʿAbd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī said:

“Those who taught us the Quran—ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, and others—told us that whenever they learned ten verses from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, they would not proceed beyond them until they understood the knowledge and practice they contained.”

This is widely known and has been transmitted from scholars of hadith and Quranic commentary generally. It has a known chain of transmission, unlike the readings attributed to those two Companions. Likewise, Ibn ʿAbbās is known to have said: “I am among those firmly grounded in knowledge who know its interpretation.” It is also authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed that he be granted knowledge of the interpretation of the Book. How, then, could he not know its interpretation?

Moreover, ʿAbd Allāh’s reading, “Its interpretation is with Allah alone,” does not contradict this view, for only Allah can bring about its actual fulfillment. As He, exalted is He, says:

“Are they waiting for anything but its fulfillment? On the Day its fulfillment comes”

And He says:

“Rather, they have denied what they have not fully grasped, and whose fulfillment has not yet come to them.”

---

## Page 9012

It is widely reported from the early scholars generally that promises and warnings belong to the ambiguous passages. Their interpretation is the actual fulfillment of what has been promised, and that rests with Allah: none but He can bring it about. The Quran does not say, “Knowledge of its interpretation is with Allah alone,” as it says concerning the Hour:

“They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive? Say, ‘Knowledge of it is only with my Lord. None but He will reveal it at its appointed time. It weighs heavily upon the heavens and the earth. It will come upon you only suddenly.’ They ask you as though you were well informed about it. Say, ‘Knowledge of it is only with Allah, but most people do not know.’”

“Say, ‘I have no power to benefit or harm myself, except as Allah wills. Had I known the unseen, I would have acquired much good, and no harm would have touched me.’”

Likewise, when Pharaoh said to Moses:

“What, then, of the former generations?”

“He said, ‘Knowledge of them is with my Lord, in a record. My Lord neither errs nor forgets.’”

Thus, if Ibn Mas‘ūd’s reading excluded those firmly grounded in knowledge from possessing this knowledge, it would have read, “Knowledge of its interpretation is with Allah alone,” rather than, “Its interpretation is with Allah alone.” The latter is indisputably true.

As for the other reading attributed to Ubayy and Ibn ‘Abbās, statements contradicting it have been transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbās. The disciple most closely associated with him in Quranic commentary was Mujāhid, whose commentary most leading scholars rely upon, including al-Thawrī, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and al-Bukhārī. Al-Thawrī said, “If a Quranic commentary reaches you from Mujāhid, that is sufficient for you.” Most of the commentary al-Shāfi‘ī transmits in his books comes through Ibn ‘Uyaynah, from Ibn Abī Najīh, from Mujāhid. Likewise, al-Bukhārī, in his Sahīh, relies on this

---

## Page 9013

commentary. The claim that Ibn Abī Najīh’s transmission from Mujāhid is not authentic is answered as follows:

The commentary transmitted by Ibn Abī Najīh from Mujāhid is among the most authentic Quranic commentaries. Indeed, no commentary available to Quranic scholars surpasses it in authenticity; others may, at most, equal it. Moreover, it is corroborated by Mujāhid’s statement: “I went through the Quran with Ibn ‘Abbās, stopping him at every verse and asking him about it.”

Furthermore, Ubayy ibn Ka‘b (may Allah be pleased with him) was known to explain the ambiguous passages of the Quran. For example, he explained Allah’s words:

“Then We sent to her Our Spirit,”

and His words:

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth,”

and:

“And when your Lord took,”

as well as other passages. These explanations are well known through chains of transmission from him and are more firmly established than this reading, for which no chain of transmission is known. He would also answer questions about ambiguous meanings in the Quran, as when ‘Umar questioned him; he was also asked about the Night of Decree.

As for his statement, “Allah revealed what is stated in general terms so that the believer might believe in it,” the response is: This is true. But does the Quran, the Sunnah, or any statement of the early scholars say that the prophets, angels, and Companions do not understand that general wording? Or do the scholars agree that the meaning of what is stated in general terms in the Quran is understood, and that what remains unspecified in it is recognized? Such is the example given concerning the time of the Hour. All Muslims understand the meaning of Allah’s words concerning the Hour: that it will certainly come, and that Allah alone knows its time and has disclosed it to no one. Hence, “the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said

---

## Page 9014

in response to the questioner—who appeared to be an unknown Bedouin and asked him about the Hour, ‘When will the Hour be?’—‘The one questioned about it knows no more than the questioner.’” He did not say that no one understands the words revealed concerning it. Rather, such a claim contradicts the consensus of Muslims, indeed of all rational people. Allah’s statements concerning the Hour and its signs are clear and intelligible, and their meaning is understood. The same applies to His words:

“And many generations in between.”

The intended meaning of these words is known: Allah created many generations whose number none but He knows. As He says:

“And none knows the forces of your Lord except Him.”

What in any of this indicates that no one—neither the angels, nor the prophets, nor the Companions, nor anyone else—understands the meaning of what Allah has told us concerning faith in Allah and the Last Day?

As for what was related from ‘Urwah, it is known from reports transmitted through him that he did not interpret most verses of the Quran, apart from a few whose explanations he related from ‘Ā’ishah. Clearly, if ‘Urwah did not know the interpretation, it does not follow that others did not know it, such as the Rightly Guided Caliphs and the scholars among the Companions, including Ibn Mas‘ūd, Ubayy ibn Ka‘b, Ibn ‘Abbās, and others.

As for the linguists who say that those firmly grounded in knowledge do not know the meaning of the ambiguous passages, they contradict themselves in this. All of them discuss the interpretation of everything in the Quran and elaborate extensively on it, to the point that every one of them has advanced interpretations without precedent, which are erroneous. And Ibn al-Anbārī, who

---

## Page 9015

went to great lengths to defend that view, is among those who discuss the meanings of the ambiguous verses most extensively. He advances interpretations of them that have not been transmitted from any of the early generations, and supports his explanations of the Quran by appealing to rare Arabic usages. His purpose is to refute Ibn Qutaybah, yet he is no more knowledgeable about the meanings of the Quran and hadith, no more faithful to the Sunnah, nor more discerning in these matters than Ibn Qutaybah. Although Ibn al-Anbārī had an exceptionally extensive knowledge of Arabic committed to memory, understanding the texts is a different discipline from memorizing the words of the language.

He and others criticized Ibn Qutaybah for challenging some of Abū ʿUbayd’s explanations of unfamiliar expressions in hadith. Ibn Qutaybah, however, explained his reasons for doing so and followed the approach of other scholars like him. He and his peers are sometimes right and sometimes wrong.

If none but Allah knows the meaning of the ambiguous passages, then all these scholars are speaking presumptuously about Allah, discussing something that there is no way to know. But if their explanations of the meanings of the ambiguous passages are correct—even concerning a single word—then their error becomes evident when they say: “None but Allah knows the meaning of the ambiguous passages, and no created being knows it.” Let whoever defends their view choose one of these two alternatives.

It is well known that much of their explanation of the ambiguous passages is correct, while some of it is mistaken. It is therefore known with certainty that their interpretation of this verse is among their errors, for they have correctly interpreted many ambiguous passages. The same applies to the report from Qatādah that those firmly grounded in knowledge do not know the interpretation of the ambiguous passages, for his book

---

## Page 9016

on Quranic exegesis is among the best-known works, and its transmission from him is reliably established through the narrations of Ma‘mar and Sa‘īd ibn Abī ‘Arūbah. For this reason, most authors of Quranic commentaries cite his views, since they are authentically transmitted from him. Yet the entire Quran—both its clear and its ambiguous passages—is explained in it.

What made the statement that none but Allah knows the interpretation of the ambiguous passages widespread among Ahl al-Sunnah was the emergence of false interpretations advanced by the people of innovation, such as the Jahmiyyah and the Qadariyyah among the Mu‘tazilah and others. They began interpreting the Quran according to their own unsound opinions. This is a well-known approach among the people of innovation: they explain the Quran according to their own rational judgments and linguistic interpretations. Thus, the Quranic commentaries of the Mu‘tazilah are filled with interpretations of the texts affirming the divine attributes and decree that depart from what Allah and His Messenger intended. It was these corrupt interpretations that the early generations and the leading scholars condemned, as Imam Ahmad stated in his refutation of the heretics and the Jahmiyyah concerning the ambiguous passages of the Quran about which they entertained doubts and which they interpreted contrary to their true meaning. This, then, is the kind of interpretation that the early generations and the leading scholars condemned.

After them came people who affiliated themselves with the Sunnah without a thorough knowledge of it or of what contradicts it. They supposed that none but Allah knows the meaning of the ambiguous passages. They also assumed that “interpretation” bore the meaning assigned to it in the terminology of later scholars: diverting an expression from its more likely meaning to a less likely one. Thus, in one place they assert and defend the view that, as for the ambiguous passages, no one knows

---

## Page 9017

their meaning except Allah. Yet they contradict themselves in several ways.

First, they say that the texts are to be understood according to their apparent meanings, and they do not go beyond those meanings. Accordingly, they reject every interpretation that conflicts with the apparent meaning and affirm that meaning. At the same time, however, they say that the text has an interpretation known only to Allah, while “interpretation,” as they understand it, contradicts the apparent meaning. How, then, can it have an interpretation contrary to its apparent meaning when they have already affirmed that apparent meaning? Their opponents in debate challenged them on this point; indeed, Ibn ‘Aqīl challenged his own teacher, the judge Abū Ya‘lā, over it.

Another contradiction is that we find that whenever any of these people are confronted with a text that contradicts their position, whether on a fundamental or a subsidiary question, they invariably interpret it in strained, contrived ways that amount to distorting words from their proper places—the same sort of interpretations that the Jahmiyyah and Qadariyyah give to texts that contradict their views. How can this be reconciled with their statement, “None but Allah Most High knows the meanings of the ambiguous texts”?

Consider what you find in their books of their debates with the Mu‘tazilah concerning the divine attributes, the Quran, and divine decree. When the Mu‘tazilah support their own position by citing verses that contradict these people’s position, such as His words:

“And He does not approve of disbelief for His servants.”

“No vision can encompass Him.”

“And when your Lord said to the angels”

and similar verses, observe how they interpret these texts in ways that are mostly unsound

## Page 9018

though some contain truth. If their interpretations are correct, this demonstrates that those firmly grounded in knowledge know the interpretation of the ambiguous texts, thus exposing their contradiction. If they are false, that leaves them even further from the truth.

Consider Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the imam of Ahl al-Sunnah, who remained steadfast during the inquisition and became a standard by which Muslims distinguish adherents of the Sunnah from adherents of innovation. When he composed his book, “Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah,” concerning the ambiguous passages of the Quran about which they expressed doubts and which they misinterpreted, he discussed their meanings verse by verse. These were the passages pursued by those who deviated, seeking discord and seeking their interpretation. He clarified and explained their meanings to expose the unsoundness of those deviant interpretations.

He established through rational and scriptural proofs that Allah can be seen, that the Quran is uncreated, and that Allah is above the Throne. He refuted the rational and scriptural arguments advanced by those who denied these matters, and clarified the meanings of the verses he himself called ambiguous, explaining them verse by verse.

Likewise, when they debated him and cited scriptural texts against him, he explained them verse by verse and hadith by hadith, exposing the unsoundness of the interpretations given by those who deviated and clarifying their meanings himself. Ahmad did not say that none but Allah understands the meanings of these verses and hadiths, nor did anyone say this to him. Rather, all the groups agree that their meanings can be known; they disagree only over what is intended, just as they disagree over verses containing commands and prohibitions.

Similarly, Ahmad would explain the ambiguous verses and hadiths cited as evidence by those who deviated among the Khawārij

## Page 9019

and others, such as the Prophet’s saying:

“No adulterer commits adultery while he is a believer; no thief steals while he is a believer; and no drinker drinks wine while he is a believer,”

and similar reports.

Yet no one, whether from Ahl al-Sunnah or from these groups, ever said concerning the texts he himself cited, or those his opponent cited against him: “These are verses and hadiths whose meanings no human being knows, so refrain from citing them as evidence.”

Imam Ahmad rejected the approach of the people of innovation who explain the Quran according to their own opinions and interpretations, without drawing upon the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or the statements of the Companions and the Successors. The Companions conveyed the meanings of the Quran to the Successors just as they conveyed its wording; they transmitted the one just as they transmitted the other. The people of innovation, however, interpret the texts in ways that contradict what Allah and His Messenger intended, claiming that this is the interpretation known to those firmly grounded in knowledge. Their claim is false, especially in the case of the interpretations of the heretical Qarmatians and Bātiniyyah. The same applies to the adherents of newly introduced speculative theology among the Jahmiyyah, Qadariyyah, and others.

These latter, however, acknowledge that they do not know the interpretation. The most they can say is: “The apparent meaning of this verse is not intended, but such-and-such may be intended, or such-and-such.” Even if one of them assigns it a particular interpretation, he does not know that it is

what Allah and His Messenger intended. Rather, in their view, Allah and His Messenger may have intended something else. Such are the interpretations they offer for scriptural texts, as in their explanations of His words:

the saying, “Our Lord descends”; and His words:

and other such texts. The most they can say is: “This may mean such-and-such; that meaning is also possible,” and so forth. This is not knowledge of the interpretation. If, in addition, their discussions of rational matters contain such sophistry and obfuscation that they provide no proof of the truth, then these people possess neither knowledge based on revelation nor knowledge based on reason. ## Page 9021

neither understand nor reason, in numerous passages of His Book. They devise vague, ambiguous terms encompassing both truth and falsehood, then treat these as clear, foundational principles.
