Imam Ahmad likewise said this. Ibn al-Anbārī also said:

“A clear text admits of only one interpretation; an ambiguous text is open to competing interpretations.”

The response, then, is that the entire Muslim community, its earlier and later generations alike, discusses meanings of the Quran that admit of multiple interpretations. Indeed, those who champion the view that people firmly grounded in knowledge do not know the meaning of ambiguous texts are themselves among those who discuss it most extensively.

---

## Page 9022

And the imams, such as al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and those before them, all discuss texts that admit of several meanings, giving preference to some meanings over others on the basis of evidence, in all foundational and subsidiary questions of knowledge. No Muslim scholar is known to have said of a text cited as evidence in a particular issue: “No one knows what this means, so it cannot be used as evidence.” Were anyone to say this, the same could be said in reply to him. If, in the well-known disputes among the imams, someone claims that the text he cites is clear and its meaning known, whereas the other text is ambiguous and no one knows its meaning, his claim can be met with an identical counterclaim.

This differs from our saying: “Some texts have a plain, clear, evident meaning, admitting of only one interpretation and leaving no room for uncertainty; others contain obscurity and ambiguity, but those firmly grounded in knowledge know their meaning.” This is a sound explanation. On this understanding, disagreement over ambiguous texts indicates that the meaning of all of them can be known. Whoever maintains that their meaning can be known sets out his evidence for this. Moreover, what the earlier and later generations have said about ambiguous texts indicates that the meaning of all of them can be known.

As for those who say that ambiguous texts are the abrogated texts, the meaning of an abrogated text is known. This view is reported from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, al-Suddī, and others. Yet Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Qatāda are the very people reported as saying that those firmly grounded in knowledge do not know its interpretation. It is known with certainty, by the consensus of Muslims, that those firmly grounded in knowledge know both the meaning of an abrogated text and that it has been abrogated. Thus, this report from them contradicts the other report and shows that the latter is false, if the former is true; otherwise, the two reports conflict

---

## Page 9023

in what they attribute to them. What is reported from them is that those firmly grounded in knowledge know the meaning of ambiguous texts.

The second view is reported from Jābir ibn Abd Allāh, who said: “Clear texts are those whose interpretation scholars know, while ambiguous texts are those whose knowledge is beyond the reach of scholars, such as the coming of the Hour.”

It is well known that Muslims agree that no one but Allah knows when the Hour will come. If this is what is intended by the term “interpretation,” then the meaning is that no one but Allah knows the time of its realization. This is true, but it does not indicate that the meaning of the discourse concerning it is unknown. Likewise, if “interpretation” means the actual realities of things, and it is said that no one but Allah knows how those realities are, we have already discussed this. It has also been noted that, according to those who pause at His words:

“And no one knows its interpretation except Allah,”

this is what “interpretation” must mean. But to understand “interpretation” as explanation and knowledge of the meaning, while pausing at “except Allah,” is unquestionably wrong and contrary to the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of Muslims.

Those among later scholars who say this contradict themselves: they make this statement and also say things that contradict it. This view conflicts with faith in Allah and His Messenger in many ways and necessarily impugns the Messenger’s mission. Undoubtedly, those who expressed it did not reflect upon its implications or its true nature. Rather, they stated it without qualification, their principal aim being to rebut the interpretations that the people of innovation give to ambiguous texts.

Their intended aim is sound, and every Muslim agrees with them on it. But we do not counter one falsehood with another, nor refute one innovation with another, nor should one reject the interpretation

---

## Page 9024

of the Quran offered by the people of falsehood by saying: “The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Companions did not know the interpretation of the ambiguous passages of the Quran.” This impugns the Messenger and the early generations of the Muslim community in a way that may be more serious than a particular group’s mistaken interpretation of some verses. A sensible person does not build a palace by demolishing a city.

The third view is that the ambiguous passages are the disconnected letters at the beginning of certain surahs. This is reported from Ibn Abbās. On this view, the disconnected letters do not constitute complete utterances, whether nominal or verbal sentences. Rather, they are names pronounced in their pausal forms. This is why they have no grammatical inflection: inflection arises only when words are joined in a syntactic construction. They are simply pronounced in their pausal forms, as when one says: alif, bā, tā, thā. Hence they are written as letter symbols, not as the names pronounced, for in speech they are names.

Thus, when al-Khalīl asked his companions how to pronounce the letter zāy in Zayd, they said, “Zā.” He replied, “You have pronounced its name; the letter itself is pronounced ‘zahhi.’” Thus, in speech they are names, while in writing they are disconnected letters: (a-l-m). They are not written out as alif, lām, mīm, as the names are written in the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Whoever recites the Quran with correct articulation will receive ten good deeds for every letter. I do not mean that Alif-Lām-Mīm is one letter; rather, alif is a letter, lām is a letter, and mīm is a letter.”

In the usage of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions, the term harf encompasses what grammarians call nouns, verbs, and particles. Hence Sībawayh said when classifying speech:

---

## Page 9025

“A noun, a verb, and a particle conveying a meaning, which is neither a noun nor a verb.”

Since linguistic usage recognizes both nouns and verbs as falling under the term harf, he distinguished this third category, which grammarians call a particle, by describing it as conveying a meaning while being neither a noun nor a verb. These are the meaning-bearing units from which speech is composed. As for the letters of the alphabet, they are written simply as individual letter symbols and pronounced without grammatical inflection. They are described as neither inflected nor indeclinable, since these descriptions apply only to words in syntactic combination.

If, according to this view, everything apart from these letters is clear, then the purpose has been achieved: the sole aim is to understand the speech of Allah and the speech of His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Furthermore, it may be said that most people have discussed the meaning of these letters. If their meaning is known, then the meaning of the ambiguous passages is known. If their meaning is unknown, and they constitute the ambiguous passages, then the meaning of everything else is known. That is what we seek to establish.

Moreover, Allah Most High says:

“Some of its verses are clear—they are the foundation of the Book—and others are ambiguous.”

According to the majority of scholars, these letters are not counted as verses; only the Kufan scholars count them as such.

The authentically reported occasion for the revelation of this verse indicates that passages other than these letters are also ambiguous. Nevertheless, this view accords with what is reported of the Jews seeking to determine spans of time from the letters of the alphabet.

---

## Page 9026

Fourth: The ambiguous passages are those whose meanings are unclear, as Mujāhid said. This accords with the view of most scholars, all of whom discuss the interpretation of these ambiguous passages and explain their meaning.

Fifth: The ambiguous passages are those whose wording recurs. This was stated by ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam. He explained that the clear passages are the accounts of the prophets that Allah Most High relates in His Book, setting them out in detail and explaining them. The ambiguous passages are those whose wording differs when these accounts are repeated. Thus, in one passage concerning Noah, He says:

“Load into it,”

and elsewhere:

“Put aboard it.”

Concerning Moses’ staff, He says:

“And suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly,”

and elsewhere:

“And suddenly it was a serpent, plain to see.”

The proponent of this view thus understood ambiguity as variation in wording while the meaning remains the same, as when someone who has memorized the Quran confuses one wording with another. Some scholars have written works on this kind of ambiguity: since the same account has a similar meaning in both passages, the reciter confuses one wording with the other. Such resemblance undoubtedly does not preclude knowing the meanings. Nor is it said of such passages that only those firmly grounded in knowledge know their interpretation. Thus, if this view is correct, it supports our position; if it is weak, it does not undermine it.

Sixth: It is whatever requires clarification, as reported from Ahmad.

Seventh: It is whatever admits multiple interpretations, as reported from al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad. It has also been reported that Abū al-Dardā’, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “You do not attain the full measure of

---

## Page 9027

understanding until you recognize that the Quran admits multiple interpretations.” Scholars have composed works on “Multiple Meanings and Corresponding Usages.” “Corresponding usages” refers to a word whose meaning is the same in two or more passages, while “multiple meanings” refers to a word whose meaning differs. This is comparable to the distinction between univocal and equivocal terms, although the two classifications differ in a way that calls for fuller discussion elsewhere.

It has also been said: “They correspond in wording, but their meanings differ,” which would make them akin to equivocal terms. This is not so; rather, the correct understanding of “multiple meanings and corresponding usages” is the first explanation.

Muslims, both earlier and later generations, have discussed these different meanings, passages requiring clarification, and passages admitting multiple interpretations. It is therefore known with certainty that Muslims agree that scholars can understand the meanings of the entire Quran. It is also clear that anyone who says that the Quran contains passages whose meaning no one understands or knows except Allah contradicts the consensus of the Muslim community, as well as the Book and the Sunnah.

Eighth: The ambiguous passages are the narratives and parables. Their meaning, too, can be known.

Ninth: They are those passages that are to be believed but not acted upon. Their meaning, too, can be known.

Tenth: Some later scholars say that the ambiguous passages are the verses and hadiths concerning the divine attributes. Their meaning, too, can be known. For, concerning most of the verses on the attributes, there is agreement

---

## Page 9028

among Muslims that their meaning can be known. As for those whose meaning people have disputed, the early generations condemned only the Jahmiyyah’s interpretations of them and denied that people know the manner of the attributes.

As Mālik said: “The meaning of rising over is known; its manner is unknown; belief in it is obligatory; and asking about it is an innovation.” The other imams of the Sunnah said likewise.

Thus, there is a distinction between the known meaning and the unknown manner. If the manner is called “interpretation,” it is permissible to say: “None but Allah knows this interpretation,” as we explained earlier.

But if understanding and explaining the meaning is called “interpretation,” just as understanding the other verses of the Quran is called “interpretation,” and it is claimed that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), Gabriel, the Companions, and the Successors did not know the meaning of His words:

“The Most Merciful rose over the Throne,”

nor the meaning of His words:

“What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?”

nor the meaning of His words:

“Allah is angry with them,”

but that these were to them like speech in a foreign language that an Arab does not understand.

Likewise, if it is said that, to them, the words of the Most High:

“They have not accorded Allah His due reverence. The whole earth will be in His grasp on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be rolled up in His right hand,”

and His words:

“Vision cannot encompass Him, but He encompasses all vision,”

and His words:

“Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing,”

and His words:

“Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him,”

and His words:

“That is because they followed what angered Allah and disliked what pleased Him,”

and His words:

“And do good; indeed, Allah loves those who do good,”

and His words:

“And say, ‘Act, for Allah will see your deeds, as will His Messenger and the believers,’”

and His words:

---

## Page 9029

“Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Quran,”

and His words:

“Then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of Allah,”

and His words:

“When he came to it, he was called: ‘Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it,’”

and His words:

“Are they waiting for anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, along with the angels?”

and His words:

“And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank,”

and His words:

“Are they waiting for anything but that the angels should come to them, or your Lord should come, or some of your Lord’s signs should come?”

and His words:

“Then He turned towards the heaven while it was smoke,”

and His words:

“His command, when He wills something, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is,”

and other such verses.

Whoever claims that Gabriel and Muhammad—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon them both—the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, the imams of the Muslims, and the community understood none of the meanings of these verses; that Allah alone possessed knowledge of their meanings, just as He alone knows the time of the Hour; and that they merely recited words whose meaning they did not understand, like someone reading speech of which he understands nothing—has falsely attributed this to them. The mass-transmitted reports from them establish the opposite: they understood these passages just as they understood the rest of the Quran.

Although His servants cannot encompass the true reality of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, nor exhaust His praise, this does not prevent them from knowing whatever He, glorified and exalted, has taught them of His names and attributes. Likewise, knowing that He has knowledge of all things and power over all things does not require them to know the manner of His knowledge and power. And knowing that He truly exists does not require them to know the manner of His essence.

---

## Page 9030

This is among the evidence that those firmly grounded in knowledge know the ta’wīl (interpretation). For everyone agrees that they know the interpretation of the clear verses, yet it is known that they do not know the manner of what Allah has said about Himself in those verses. This shows that not knowing the manner does not preclude knowing the interpretation—that is, explaining the words and clarifying their meaning. Rather, they know the interpretation of both the clear and the ambiguous passages, without knowing the manner of the Lord’s being in either case.

If it is said, “This undermines the distinction you have drawn between ta’wīl meaning explanation and ta’wīl as used in the Book of Allah Most High,” the reply is: It does not undermine that distinction. Knowing the explanation and meaning of an expression, and conceiving it in the mind, is different from knowing the reality existing outside the mind to which those words refer. A thing has an existence in external reality, an existence in the mind, an existence in speech, and an existence in writing. Speech consists of words bearing a meaning in the mind, and those words are recorded in writing. Understanding the words, conceiving their meaning in the mind, and expressing it verbally are distinct from the reality existing outside the mind. Not everyone who knows the former knows the particular reality of the latter.

An example of this is that the People of the Book know the descriptions and accounts of Muhammad—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—contained in their scriptures. This is knowledge of the words, their meaning, and their explanation. Their ta’wīl, however, is Muhammad himself, who was sent as a messenger. Thus, knowing him as a particular individual is knowing the ta’wīl of

---

## Page 9031

those words. Likewise, a person may know about Hajj and its sacred sites—the House, the Mosque, Minā, ‘Arafah, and Muzdalifah—and understand what these names mean, without knowing the actual places until he sees them. He then recognizes that the Kaaba he sees is the one mentioned in His words:

“Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by mankind.”

Likewise, the land of ‘Arafāt is what is mentioned in His words:

“When you depart from ‘Arafāt, remember Allah.”

Likewise, the Sacred Monument is Muzdalifah, which lies between the two mountain passes of ‘Arafah and the valley of Muhassir. He recognizes it as the place mentioned in His words:

“Remember Allah at the Sacred Monument.”

Similarly, a man may have a dream, and an interpreter may tell him its interpretation, which he understands and conceives in his mind. For example, the interpreter may say, “This indicates that such-and-such happened, and that such-and-such will happen.” Then, when that happens, it is the ta’wīl of the dream. Its ta’wīl is not his knowledge of it, his mental conception of it, or his words about it. Hence Joseph, the man of truth, said:

“This is the fulfilment of my dream of long ago.”

He also said:

“No food will come to you as your provision without my informing you of its interpretation before it reaches you.”

Thus, he informed them both of the ta’wīl before the ta’wīl came to pass; informing them was not itself the ta’wīl. The Prophet—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—therefore knows the ta’wīl even though it has not yet occurred, and even if he does not know when it will occur. Likewise, we know the ta’wīl of the promises and warnings Allah has mentioned in the Quran, even though we do not know when this ta’wīl will occur—the ta’wīl mentioned in His words, glorified and exalted is He:

“Are they waiting for anything but its fulfilment? On the Day its fulfilment comes…”

And He, Most High, said:

“Every announcement has its appointed time.”

---

## Page 9032

Thus we know the fulfilment of Allah’s announcement: it is the reality of which Allah has informed us. We do not know when it will occur, and we may not know its nature or extent. This applies equally to the fulfilment of the clear and the less clear passages. As Allah, Most High, says:

“Say, ‘He has the power to send punishment upon you from above you or from beneath your feet, or to divide you into factions and make you taste one another’s violence.’”

The Prophet—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—said, “It will certainly happen, but its fulfilment has not yet come.” Its fulfilment was therefore known—namely, the occurrence of discord and strife—even though it was not known when it would occur. A person may not know its nature or reality, but when it occurs, someone with knowledge recognizes that this is the fulfilment indicated by the verse. Someone else may not recognize this, or may forget it after having once known it, and thus fail to recognize that this is the fulfilment of the Quran. For when His words, Most High, were revealed:

“Beware of a trial that will not afflict only the wrongdoers among you,”

al-Zubayr said: “For a long time we recited this verse, and I did not think we were among those it concerned. Yet we turned out to be the very people it meant: ‘Beware of a trial that will not afflict only the wrongdoers among you.’”

Furthermore, in His Book Allah has censured those who hear the Quran without understanding its meaning, and those who do not reflect upon it. He has praised those who hear and understand it. He, Most High, says:

“Among them are those who listen to you, until, when they leave your presence…”

—and the rest of the verse. He tells us that they would ask the people of knowledge, “What did the Messenger say just now?” This indicates that the knowledgeable Companions understood meanings in the words of Allah’s Messenger—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—that others did not understand. These are those firmly grounded in knowledge

---

## Page 9033

who know the meanings of the Quran, both its clear and its less clear passages. This is like His saying, Most High:

“These parables We set forth for people, but none understand them except those with knowledge.”

This indicates that those with knowledge understand them, even though others do not. Many of the early generations regarded the parables as the less clear passages. Indeed, parables fit this description more closely than other passages because of the resemblance between what is being compared and what it is compared to. Understanding their meaning is knowing their interpretation, which those firmly grounded in knowledge know, unlike others. Similar to this is His saying, Most High:

“Those who have been given knowledge see that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth and guides to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.”

Had they not understood the meaning of what was revealed, how could they have known whether it was true or false? Can words whose meaning has not been grasped be judged true or false? He, Most High, also says:

“Do they not reflect upon the Quran, or are there locks upon their hearts?”

And He says:

“Do they not reflect upon the Quran? Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have found much inconsistency in it.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Have they not reflected upon the Word, or has something come to them that never came to their forefathers?”

And He, Most High, says:

“So give good tidings to My servants who listen to what is said and follow the best of it.”

And He says:

“And those who, when reminded of the verses of their Lord, do not respond to them as though deaf and blind.”

And He says:

“Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Quran so that you may understand.”

And He says:

“A Book whose verses have been perfected, then set out in detail, from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware.”

And He says: “A Book

---

## Page 9034

whose verses have been set out in detail—an Arabic Quran for people who know, bringing good tidings and warning,” up to His words: “and between us and you is a barrier.”

If much or most of the Quran were beyond anyone’s understanding, then only part of it could be reflected upon and understood. This contradicts what the Quran indicates, particularly concerning most of what the polytheists denied: verses conveying information, reports about the Last Day or Paradise and Hell, the denial that Allah has partners or children, and His being named the Most Merciful. Their objections were therefore mostly to what He told them about Allah’s attributes—both what is denied of Him and what is affirmed of Him—and what He told them about the Last Day. Allah has censured those who do not understand, comprehend, or reflect upon these things.

It is thus clear that Allah commands people to understand these things and reflect upon them. He, Most High, says:

“And among them are those who listen to you. But can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not understand? And among them are those who look at you. But can you guide the blind, even though they do not see?”

And He says:

“And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed coverings over their hearts lest they understand it, and deafness in their ears,” to the end of the verse.

And He, Most High, says:

“When you recite the Quran, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier. And We place coverings over their hearts lest they understand it, and deafness in their ears,” to the end of the verse.

Some have argued that Allah has never denied anyone other than Himself knowledge of anything

And the angels said:

The Companions frequently said, “Allah and His Messenger know best.” And in the well-known hadith:

“I ask You by every name belonging to You, by which You have named Yourself, or which You have revealed in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or kept to Yourself in Your knowledge of the unseen.”

Allah, Most High, has said:

Foremost among disputes are disputes over the meanings of the Quran. So if the Messenger did not know its meanings

---

## Page 9036

it would be impossible to refer disputes to him. The Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, and all the leading scholars of the religion agreed that the Sunnah explains and clarifies the Quran, indicates its meaning, and sets out in detail what it expresses in general terms. It elucidates the Quran’s undetailed statements, whether commands or reports.

Allah, Most High, said:

“Mankind was one community; then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners,” up to His words: “concerning that over which they differed.”

Among the gravest disagreements are those concerning matters of belief conveyed through revelation about Allah and the Last Day. The Book must therefore judge between people concerning their disagreements over these matters. It could not serve as a judge if its meaning could not be known. Allah has provided evidence pointing to its meaning. Otherwise, a judge who explains what is in his mind passes no judgment at all. Likewise, if it is said that He judges by the Book, His judgment is decisive, distinguishing truth from falsehood; and this can only be achieved through clarification. Allah, Most High, said of the Quran:

“Indeed, it is a decisive word.”

That is, it distinguishes truth from falsehood. How, then, could it be decisive if there were no way to know its meaning?

Furthermore, Allah said:

“And among them are unlettered people who know nothing of the Scripture beyond its recitation; they do nothing but conjecture.”

He censured those who know nothing of the Book beyond its recitation, just as He censured those who distort its meaning and speak falsely. Allah, Most High, said:

“Do you then hope that they will believe you, when a group of them used to hear the words of Allah and then distort them after

---

## Page 9037

they had understood it, knowing full well what they were doing?” up to His words:

“Will you not then understand?”

This is one of the two groups. Then Allah, Most High, said:

“And among them are unlettered people who know nothing of the Scripture beyond its recitation”—that is, merely reciting it—“and they do nothing but conjecture.”

Then He censured those who fabricate writings, claiming that they are from Allah when they are not. He said:

“So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands,” up to His words: “they earn.”

These three categories encompass the people of misguidance and religious innovation. For the people of innovation whom Allah and His Messenger censured are of two types:

The first knows the truth but deliberately opposes it.

The second is ignorant and follows others.

The first group invent things that contradict the Book of Allah and claim that they are from Allah: either fabricated hadiths or false explanations and interpretations of the revealed texts. They bolster these with their appeals to opinion and reason, seeking leadership and material gain. These people write the Scripture with their own hands to exchange it for a paltry price. Woe to them for the falsehood their hands have written, and woe to them for the money they earn from it.

When confronted with passages from the divine scriptures and told, “These contradict your views,” they distort the words from their proper places through corrupt interpretations. Allah, Most High, said:

“Do you then hope that they will believe you, when a group of them used to hear the words of Allah and then distort them after they had understood them, knowing full well what they were doing?”

---

## Page 9038

As for the second type—the ignorant—they are the unlettered people who know nothing of the Scripture beyond its recitation and do nothing but conjecture.

Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda explained His words:

“And among them are unlettered people,”

as referring to those who do not know the meanings of the Scripture. They memorize and recite it without understanding and do not know what it contains. His words:

“Beyond its recitation,”

mean recitation alone: they have no understanding of the Scripture, but merely confine themselves to what they hear being recited to them. This was the explanation given by al-Kisāʾī and al-Zajjāj. Likewise, Ibn al-Sāʾib said that they cannot properly read or write the Scripture; “beyond its recitation” means only what their scholars relate to them.

Abū Rawq and Abū ʿUbayda said that it means reciting from memory, without reading from books. According to this interpretation, the recitation is that of the unlettered people themselves; according to the other, it is what they hear their scholars recite. Both interpretations are correct, and the verse encompasses both. For He, glorified and exalted, said:

“They know nothing of the Scripture.”

He did not say that they neither recite nor listen. Then He said:

“Beyond its recitation.”

This is a disconnected exception: rather, they know recitations, whether through their own recitation or by listening to others recite. If the exception is taken as connected, the implied meaning would be: they have no knowledge of the Scripture except a knowledge of recitations—not a knowledge of mere recitation without understanding.

Amānī is the plural of umniyya, meaning recitation. This meaning also occurs in His words, Most High:

“We never sent any messenger or prophet before you but that, when he recited, Satan cast something into his recitation. But Allah abolishes what Satan casts, then Allah makes His verses firm. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

The poet said:

---

## Page 9039

He recited Allah’s Book at the beginning of the night;
By its end, he had met his destined death.

Ummiyyūn (unlettered people) is derived from umma (community). Some say it refers to the community and the condition of ordinary people; thus an ummī is an ordinary person without discernment. Al-Zajjāj said: “He retains the disposition of a community that has not received instruction, remaining in his natural state.” Others said that it is derived from umma, because writing was practiced by men rather than women, and because such a person remains as his mother bore him.

The correct view is that it is derived from umma, just as ʿāmmī (commoner) is derived from ʿāmma (the common people), who have not distinguished themselves from the populace through the qualities that set the elite apart. Likewise, an unlettered person has not distinguished himself from the community through the reading and writing that distinguish its elite. The term ummī is applied to someone who cannot read or write a book. It is also applied to people who have no Book revealed by Allah to read, even though they may read and write material that was not revealed.

In this sense, all the Arabs were unlettered, for they had no Book revealed by Allah. Allah Most High said:

“And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered, ‘Have you submitted yourselves?’ If they submit, they are rightly guided.”

He also said:

“It is He who sent among the unlettered a Messenger from among themselves.”

Many Arabs could write and read written texts, yet they were all unlettered. When the Quran was revealed to them, they were no longer unlettered in the sense of being unable to recite a Book from memory. Rather, they recited the Quran from memory, and their gospels were in their breasts. They remained unlettered, however, in the sense that they had no need to write down their religion; rather, their Quran was preserved in their hearts

---

## Page 9040

as recorded in the Sahīh from ʿIyād ibn Himār al-Mujāshiʿī, who reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When I created My servants, I created them upright in faith”—and later in the same hadith—“I shall test you and test others through you. I have sent down to you a Book that water cannot wash away, which you recite asleep and awake.”

Our community is therefore unlike the People of the Book, who do not preserve their scriptures in their hearts. Even if every written copy of the Quran were lost, the Quran would remain preserved in the hearts of this community. In this respect, the Muslims remain an unlettered community even after the Quran’s revelation and their memorization of it.

As recorded in the Sahīh from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah Most High be pleased with them both, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“We are an unlettered community: we neither calculate nor write. The month is like this and like this.”

He did not say, “We neither read a book nor memorize.” Rather, he said, “We neither write nor calculate.” Our religion therefore does not require writing and calculation, unlike the practice of the People of the Book, who determine the times for their fasting and its ending through written records and calculation. Their religion depends on books: if these were lost, they would not know their religion. This is why most adherents of the Sunnah are found to memorize the Quran and hadith to a greater extent than the people of innovation. The people of innovation resemble the People of the Book in certain respects.

As for His words:

“So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet,”

he is unlettered in this respect: he neither writes nor reads what is in books—not in the sense that he cannot recite from memory. Indeed, he had memorized the Quran with the utmost mastery. In the terminology of the jurists, an ummī (unlettered person) is the opposite of a reciter, not the opposite of someone who writes, as in the first sense; and by it they mean

---

## Page 9041

in most cases, someone who cannot recite al-Fātihah properly. Thus, His words, exalted is He:

“Among them are unlettered people who know the Book only through recitation”

mean that they know the Book only as a recitation whose meaning they do not understand. This includes someone who has not previously learned to write or read and whose knowledge comes only from hearing recitations, as Ibn al-Sā’ib said. It also includes someone who recites it from memory but does not read it from a written copy, as Abū Rawq and Abū ʿUbaydah said.

It may be said that His words, “do not know the Book,” mean writing: that they cannot write and can only recite. It also includes someone who can write and recite but does not understand what he reads and writes. As Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah said, they are unfamiliar with the meanings of the Book: they know it through memorization and recitation, without understanding, and do not know what it contains.

The Book here means the revealed Book, namely the Torah; it does not mean writing, for He said:

“They do nothing but conjecture.”

This indicates that He denied them knowledge of the Book’s meanings. A man’s inability to write with his own hand does not necessarily mean that he has no knowledge and merely conjectures. Indeed, many who write with their own hands do not understand what they write, while many who do not write understand the meanings of what others write.

Moreover, Allah mentioned this in a passage censuring them. Yet there is nothing blameworthy in a man’s inability to write if he fulfills his obligations. Rather, the blame lies in his failure to understand

---

## Page 9042

the Book revealed to him, whether he writes and reads it or neither writes nor reads it. As the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“This is a time when knowledge will be taken away.”

Ziyād ibn Labīd asked him, “How can knowledge be taken away when we have recited the Quran? By Allah, we will certainly continue to recite it and teach our wives to recite it.”

He replied, “I had thought you among the most knowledgeable people of Medina! Do not the Jews and Christians possess the Torah and the Gospel? Yet what benefit do they derive from them?”

This is a well-known hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhī and others.

Moreover, Allah, exalted is He, said before this:

“A group of them used to hear Allah’s words, then distort them after understanding them, knowingly.”

Those people understood it and then distorted it. They are blameworthy whether or not they memorized it in their hearts, wrote it down, and recited it both from memory and from a written text. It was therefore fitting to mention those who do not understand it: those who know it only through recitation. For Allah sent down the Quran as a mutually consistent Book with recurring themes. He sets out categories and parallels within it: its comprehensive treatment of the categories gives it its recurrent character, while its presentation of parallels makes it mutually consistent.

Even if these people write and read, they are nonetheless unlettered people among the People of the Book. Likewise, we describe someone of this kind as unlettered, unschooled, and a layman, even if he has memorized the Quran and can read a written text, when he does not understand its meaning.

Since Allah censured those who know the Book only through recitation without understanding its meanings, just as He censured those who knowingly distort words from their proper places after understanding them, this indicates that both kinds are blameworthy: the ignorant person who

---

## Page 9043

does not understand the meanings of the texts, and the liar who distorts words from their proper places. This is the condition of the people of religious innovation, who fall into one of two categories:

Either a man who distorts words from their proper places, speaks according to his own opinion, and interprets the text in a way he attributes to Allah. Such people write the Book with their own hands and say that it is from Allah. They claim that the doctrines they have invented are the truth, what the Messenger brought, what the early generations followed, and so forth. Then they distort the texts that contradict those doctrines. If they do this deliberately, knowing that what they are doing contradicts the Messenger, they are of the same kind as these Jews. This occurs among many heretics, and in certain matters among others as well. As for those whose intention is to follow the Messenger inwardly and outwardly, but who err in what they write and how they interpret, they are not of the same kind.

Nevertheless, their errors have given rise to falsehood of that kind. As the saying goes:

“When a scholar slips, others slip along with him.”

This is the condition of those in this community who adopt mistaken interpretations.

Or an unlettered man who merely follows others, knowing nothing of the Book except what he hears from them or recites himself, and knowing it only through recitation. Allah has censured him for this. It is thus clear that Allah censures those who neither know the meanings of the Quran, nor reflect upon it, nor understand it, just as the Quran explicitly censures them in numerous places. It is therefore impossible to say:

“Most of the Quran, or much of it, is known to no created being beyond mere recitation—neither Gabriel, nor Muhammad, nor the Companions, nor anyone

---

## Page 9044

among the Muslims.” For this would liken them to those people in the very matter for which Allah censured them.

If it is asked: “Is it not obligatory for every Muslim to know the meaning of every verse?”

The answer is: Yes, but knowing the meanings of all the verses is a collective obligation, while every Muslim must know what is indispensable for him. Allah censured those people because their knowledge of the Book does not extend beyond its recitation: they do not know its meanings and have nothing but conjecture. This resembles His saying:

“They are indeed in doubt about it, full of misgivings.”

It may be objected that some commentators have explained “except amānī” as meaning nothing but the lies and falsehoods they utter with their mouths. This interpretation has been reported from some of the early generations and was adopted by al-Farrā’. He said: “Amānī means fabricated lies.” An Arab once said to Ibn Da’b while he was relating an account: “Is this something you have transmitted, or something you have made up?”—that is, fabricated. Thus, amānī was understood to mean the things their scholars wrote on their own authority and then attributed to Allah, such as altering the description of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Others said that amānī refers to the false and groundless hopes they entertain concerning Allah, as in their statements:

“The Fire will not touch us except for a few days.”

“None will enter Paradise unless they are Jews or Christians.”

“We are Allah’s children and His beloved.”

This interpretation, too, has been reported from some of the early generations.

The answer is: Both interpretations are weak; the first interpretation is correct, because He, glorified be He, said:

---

## Page 9045

“Among them are unlettered people who know nothing of the Book except its recitation.”

This exception must be either connected or disconnected. If it is connected, neither lies nor the heart’s wishes can be excepted from the Book. If it is disconnected, such an exception applies only to something comparable to what is mentioned and resembling it in some respects. It thus belongs to a shared category that is not expressed in the wording, rather than to the category explicitly mentioned.

For this reason, a disconnected exception is not valid where an elliptical exception is valid. An example is His saying:

“They will not taste death therein,”

followed by:

“Except the first death.”

This is a disconnected exception, because it is appropriate to say: “They will taste nothing but the first death.” Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly, but only through trade by mutual consent.”

For it is appropriate to say: “Do not consume one another’s wealth except through trade.” Similarly, He says:

“They have no knowledge of it, but follow only conjecture; they certainly did not kill him.”

It is appropriate to say: “They have nothing but conjecture to follow.”

Here, then, when He says, “They know nothing of the Book except its recitation,” it is appropriate to say: “They know it only as recitation.” For they know it as something they recite and hear. It is not appropriate to say: “They know nothing but what their hearts wish for,” or: “They know nothing but lies.” They also knew things that were true: not everything they learned from their scholars was false. By contrast, someone who does not understand the meaning of the Book knows nothing but its recitation.

Moreover, these false hopes which they entertained in their hearts and voiced with their tongues

---

## Page 9046

—as in His saying, “Those are their wishful hopes”—were shared by all of them. Thus, the unlettered among them cannot be singled out for censure on this account. Their being unlettered has no bearing on such censure, nor does their lack of knowledge of the Book. Rather, someone who knows these hopes to be false deserves greater censure for them than someone who does not know that they are false. Hence, when Allah censured them for these hopes, He spoke generally rather than singling out a particular group. He Most High said:

“They say, ‘None will enter Paradise unless they are Jews or Christians.’ Those are their wishful hopes.”

And so the verse continues.

Moreover, He said:

“They do nothing but conjecture.”

This shows that He censured them for lacking knowledge and having nothing but conjecture. This is the condition of someone ignorant of the meanings of the Book, not someone who knows that he is lying. It is therefore clear that this group is not the group who utter lies and falsehoods. Had that been intended, the wording would have been, “They utter nothing but false hopes,” rather than, “They know nothing of the Book except its recitation.”

Rather, that other group consists of those who distort words from their proper places and twist their tongues when reciting the Book so that you may think what they recite belongs to the Book, although it does not. They say, “This is from Allah,” although it is not from Allah, and they write the Book with their own hands to obtain a paltry price for it. They distort the meanings of the Book and alter its wording for those unfamiliar with it, lying both in their speech and in their writing.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“You will surely follow the ways of those before you, matching them as precisely as one arrow-feather matches another, so that even if they entered a burrow

---

## Page 9047

of a lizard, you would enter it.” They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, do you mean the Jews and Christians?” He replied, “Who else?”

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) also said:

“My nation will surely follow the ways of the nations before it, span by span and cubit by cubit.” They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, do you mean the Persians and Romans?” He replied, “Who else but those peoples?”

This proves that there will be people in this nation who resemble the People of the Book in the conduct for which Allah censured them in this verse. This is a truth that has been witnessed. Allah Most High said:

“We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth. Is it not enough that your Lord is a witness over all things?”

Whoever reflects on what Allah and His Messenger have foretold will see that many of these things—indeed, most of them—have already occurred. This indicates to him that the remainder will also occur.

Section

It has thus become clear that one must seek knowledge of the Book and wisdom that Allah revealed to His Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), and understand their intended meaning, as did the Companions, those who followed them in goodness, and those who followed their path. Allah and His Messenger have explained everything people need in their religion with complete clarity. How much more, then, the fundamentals of monotheism and faith! Once what the Messenger explained is known, one then examines the statements of

---

## Page 9048

people and what they intended by them, then measures them against the Book and the Sunnah. Sound reason always agrees with the Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) and never contradicts him, for the Balance accompanies the Book, and Allah sent down the Book in truth, and the Balance.

People’s intellects, however, may fall short of comprehending the details of what he brought. The Messenger therefore brings them what they were unable to discover and were perplexed about—not what their reason knows to be false. The messengers (may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon them) convey matters that bewilder reason, not matters that reason deems impossible. This is the path of guidance, the Sunnah, and knowledge. The path of misguidance, innovation, and ignorance is the reverse: to devise an innovation based on men’s opinions and interpretations, then subordinate what the Messenger brought to it, distorting his words and interpreting them to accord with the principles they have laid down.

In reality, you find that these people neither rely on what the Messenger brought nor receive guidance from him. Rather, they accept whatever agrees with their views and use it as supporting evidence, not as their foundation. Whatever contradicts them, they reinterpret, like those who distort words from their proper places, or refrain from determining its meaning, like those who know nothing of the Book beyond mere recitation.

These people may not know what the Messenger brought, whether through inability or negligence. Such knowledge requires two premises: that the Messenger said such-and-such, and that he intended such-and-such by it. As for the first, most of them have no doubt that he brought the Quran, although some extremists among the people of innovation doubt parts of it. As for the hadiths, however, most people of innovation are ignorant of them. They suppose that these were transmitted by individual narrators whom they consider capable of lying and making mistakes. Nor do they know of the multiplicity of

---

## Page 9049

their transmission routes, the qualities of their narrators, and the grounds warranting belief in them to the extent that hadith scholars do. These scholars have absolute certainty concerning most of the authentic hadith texts in the two Sahīh collections, as we have explained at length elsewhere.

As for the second premise, they may not know the meanings of the Quran and hadith. Some of them say that evidence conveyed through words cannot yield certainty about the speaker’s intent. We have explained the falsity of this claim at length elsewhere.

In interpreting the Quran and hadith, many of them consult only what those who share their doctrine say, adopting their interpretations. They cite as evidence the texts that agree with them and reinterpret those that contradict them. For many of them, following a revealed text was never, in reality, their foundation at all. This applies to the major innovations, such as those of the Rāfidah and the Jahmiyyah. The originator of Rāfidī doctrine was a heretic who began by deliberately telling outright lies that he knew to be lies, like those Jews whom Allah describes as knowingly fabricating lies about Him. Then others came after them who supposed that what those earlier people had fabricated was true, yet remained in doubt about it. As the Most High says:

“Indeed, those who inherited the Scripture after them are in disquieting doubt about it.”

Likewise, the Jahmiyyah have no textual evidence whatsoever for denying the divine attributes, Allah’s being above the Throne, and similar matters—not a verse, a hadith, or a report from the Companions,

---

## Page 9050

rather, the one who originated this did not intend to follow the prophets. He invented it just as others instituted idol worship and other religions of the unbelievers, knowing that these contradicted the messengers—as was mentioned concerning those Jews who altered their religion. It then spread among people who did not know its origins.

This differs from the innovation of the Khawārij, which originated in their understanding of the Quran: they misunderstood it, but their intention was to follow the Quran inwardly and outwardly. They are not heretics. Likewise, the fundamental aim of the Qadariyyah was to uphold the commands and prohibitions, promises and warnings brought by the messengers, and they follow the passages of the Quran that indicate these things. The fundamental intention of ‘Amr ibn ‘Ubayd and those like him was not to oppose the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, unlike the originator of Rāfidī doctrine.

Likewise, the doctrine of irjā’ was introduced by people whose intention was to regard all who face the qiblah in prayer as believers, not unbelievers. They opposed the Khawārij and the Mu‘tazilah, but ended up at the opposite extreme.

Similarly, moderate Shiism—which consists of regarding ‘Alī as superior and giving him precedence over others, and similar views—was not an invention of heretics. This differs from the claim that he was explicitly designated and was infallible: the one who invented that was a hypocrite and a heretic.

---

## Page 9051

For this reason, ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Yūsuf ibn Asbāt, and others said: “The fundamental sects of innovation are four: the Shī‘ah, the Khawārij, the Qadariyyah, and the Murji’ah.”

They said: “The Jahmiyyah are not among the seventy-two sects.” Likewise, Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Hāmid reported two views on this matter from the scholars of Ahmad’s school, this being one of them.

By this they meant the unqualified Jahmī doctrine held by Jahm himself and those who followed him in it: denying the names as well as the attributes, such that Allah is not called by any of His most beautiful names, nor designated a thing, an existent, or anything else. The only name Jahm is reported to have used for Him is “Powerful.” Since all the names are applied to created beings, he claimed that they entailed likening Allah to creation, unlike “Powerful.” For he was the leading figure of the Jabriyyah, and in his view, a servant possesses neither power nor action, and none but Allah is called powerful. This is why he is reported to have called Allah “Powerful.”

Worse than him are those who deny the names and attributes—the heretics among the philosophers and the Qarmatians. Thus, all the imams regarded these people as heretics and hypocrites. Indeed, their inward unbelief is greater than the unbelief of the Jews and Christians. There is no doubt that they are not among the seventy-two sects. If they outwardly profess Islam, the most that can be said of them is that they are hypocrites, like the hypocrites who lived in the time of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Those hypocrites were closer to Islam than these people, for they observed the outward ordinances of Islam, whereas these people have

---

## Page 9052

advocated abolishing them: no fasting, no prayer, no pilgrimage, and no zakat. However, it may be said that the proof conveyed by the prophetic message had been established more fully against the former than against the latter.

As for those who adopt some Jahmī doctrines, such as the Mu‘tazilah and others who adhere to Islam inwardly and outwardly, they undoubtedly belong to the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The same applies to those who are better than them, such as the Kullābiyyah and the Karrāmiyyah. It also applies to the Shī‘ah who give preference to ‘Alī, and those among them who affirm explicit designation and infallibility while believing inwardly and outwardly in the prophethood of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and supposing that what they follow is the religion of Islam. These are people of error and ignorance, but they are not outside the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, they are among those who divided their religion and became sects.

Most of these people follow the ambiguous passages of the Quran, seeking discord and seeking their interpretation, just as some hypocrites and disbelievers do. Hence, a group of Quranic commentators, including al-Rabī‘ ibn Anas, said: “They are the Christians, such as the Christians of Najrān.” Another group, including al-Kalbī, said: “They are the Jews.” Another group, including Ibn Jurayj, said: “They are the hypocrites.” Another group, including al-Hasan, said: “They are the Khawārij.” And another group, including Qatādah, said: “They are the Khawārij and the Shī‘ah.”

Whenever Qatādah recited this verse:

“As for those

---

## Page 9053

in whose hearts is deviation,” he would say: “If they are not the Harūriyyah and the Saba’iyyah, then I do not know who they are.” The Saba’iyyah are named after ‘Abd Allāh ibn Saba’, the leader of the Rāfidah.

Section

The correct meaning—namely, denying that He has any equal, partner, or rival—is indicated by His words, glorified is He, “One”; His words, “And there is none comparable to Him”; His words, “Do you know of any equal to Him?”; and similar passages. Thus, the correct meanings are established by the Quran and Sunnah, and reason also points to them.

Someone may say: “Al-Ahad (the One), al-Samad (the Self-Sufficient), or another such designation means that which neither divides nor separates, or which is not composite,” and so forth. If these expressions mean that He is not susceptible to separation or division, this is true. But if they mean that He cannot be pointed to in any way, or convey something akin to what they mean by an indivisible atom—namely, that nothing of Him can be pointed to as distinct from anything else—then, according to most rational people, such a thing cannot exist; it is merely postulated in the mind. We know that wherever the Arabs use the words al-wāhid and al-ahad (one), whether in negation or affirmation, they do not intend this meaning.

Thus, in His words, exalted is He:

“And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection,”

He did not intend the meaning by which they have explained al-wāhid and al-ahad. The same applies to His words: “And if there is only one

---

## Page 9054

then she shall have half.” Likewise, His words:

“And there is none comparable to Him.”

The meaning is that no one whatsoever is comparable to Him. If “one” denotes something in which nothing can be distinguished from anything else, and nothing can be pointed to separately from anything else, then nothing that exists is “one” except what they claim concerning the indivisible atom and the Lord of the worlds. In that case, He would not have denied that any existing thing could be comparable to the Lord, since it would not fall within the designation “anyone.”

We have discussed this at considerable length in our treatment of the rational and scriptural arguments advanced by those who deny the divine attributes—the Jahmiyyah and their followers—in our book entitled Bayān Talbīs al-Jahmiyyah fī Ta’sīs Bida‘ihim al-Kalāmiyyah (Exposing the Jahmiyyah’s Deception in Establishing Their Innovations in Speculative Theology).

Thus, when the Jahmiyyah invoked the name al-Wāhid (the One) to argue before the early generations—including Imam Ahmad and others—for denying the divine attributes, Ahmad said:

“They said, ‘You will never affirm Allah’s oneness until you say: Allah existed, and nothing else existed.’ We replied, ‘We do say that Allah existed and nothing else existed. But when we say that Allah has always possessed all His attributes, are we not describing one God?’

“We offered them an illustration, saying: ‘Tell us about this date palm: does it not have a trunk, frond bases, fibre, fronds, leaflets, and a palm heart? Yet it is designated as one thing and called a date palm with all its attributes. Likewise Allah—to whom belongs the highest description—is, with all His attributes, one God. We do not say that there was ever a time when He had no power, until He created power for Himself. Nor do we say that there was ever a time when He did not know, until

---

## Page 9055

He created knowledge for Himself. Rather, we say that He has always been All-Knowing, All-Powerful, and Sovereign, without saying when or how.’”

This is further clarified by the occasions for the revelation of this surah mentioned by the Quranic commentators, which support this understanding. They mention several occasions.

The first is the previously cited report from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the polytheists said to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Tell us the lineage of your Lord.” Then this surah was revealed.

The second is the report:

“'Āmir ibn al-Tufayl said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘To what are you calling us, O Muhammad?’ He replied, ‘To Allah.’ He said, ‘Then describe Him to me. Is He made of gold, silver, or iron?’ Then this surah was revealed.”

This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbās through Abū Zabyān and Abū Sālih, both reporting from him.

The third is that some Jews said this, asking, “Of what kind is He? From whom did He inherit the world, and to whom will He bequeath it?” Then this surah was revealed. This was stated by Qatādah and al-Dahhāk. Al-Dahhāk, Qatādah, and Muqātil said:

“Some Jewish rabbis came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said, ‘O Muhammad, describe your Lord to us, so that perhaps we may believe in you. Allah revealed His description in the Torah, so tell us about Him. Of what is He made, and of what kind is He? Is He made of gold, copper, brass, iron, or silver? Does He eat and drink? From whom did He inherit the world, and to whom will He bequeath it?’ Then Allah revealed this surah.”

It is devoted exclusively to describing Allah.

---

## Page 9056

The fourth is what al-Dahhāk narrated from Ibn ‘Abbās:

“A delegation from Najrān came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with seven bishops from Banū al-Hārith ibn Ka‘b, among them al-Sayyid and al-‘Āqib. They said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘Describe your Lord to us. What is He made of?’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, replied, ‘My Lord is not made of anything, and He is distinct from all things.’ Then Allah Most High revealed: ‘Say: He is Allah, One.’”

These people were asking whether He belonged to any kind of created being and whether He was made from some substance. Allah Most High therefore explained that He is One, belonging to no kind of created being, and that He is al-Samad, not made from any substance. Rather, He is al-Samad; He neither begets nor is begotten.

If He denies that He was begotten from a parent’s substance, then there is all the more reason to deny that He is made from any other substance. For the substance of one born from material like his own is more perfect than that of one created from a different material—as Adam was created from clay. The substance from which his children were created is therefore superior to the substance from which he himself was created. This is why his creation was more wondrous.

If, then, the Lord is declared free of originating from the higher substance, He is all the more emphatically declared free of originating from the lower substance. Likewise, if He is far above having anyone equal to Him, then He is all the more certainly above having anyone superior to Him.

This further demonstrates that this surah encompasses every form of declaring Allah free of imperfection and praising Him, through both negation and affirmation. This is why it is equivalent to one-third of the Quran. His being al-Samad affirms perfection incompatible with any deficiency, while His oneness affirms that He alone possesses that perfection,

---

## Page 9057

and likewise, if He declares Himself above begetting—whereby the substance of offspring, the noblest of substances, would issue from Him—then He is all the more emphatically above having the substance of anything other than offspring issue from Him. And if He declares Himself above having substances from which creatures are made issue from Him, then He is all the more emphatically above having waste products issue from Him that are unfit to serve as such material.

A human being produces the substance of offspring, as well as substances from which other things arise, as lice, worms, and other creatures are created from his sweat and bodily moisture. Mucus, saliva, and other things also issue from him. Allah has freed the people of Paradise from having any of these things issue from them. The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, reported that they neither urinate nor defecate, neither spit nor blow their noses; that what issues from them is like the perspiration of musk; and that they have intercourse with a male organ that never becomes concealed and desire that never ceases, without semen or death. If one of them desires a child, its gestation and birth take place in a short time.

This therefore entails His declaring Himself above having offspring or having anything issue from Him as it does from created beings. This, too, is part of the full meaning of al-Samad, as explained earlier: He is the One from whom nothing issues. Likewise, His declaring Himself above being begotten—and thus above originating from another like Himself—means that He is all the more emphatically above originating from any other substance. It has already been stated in the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka‘b that everything born will die

---

## Page 9058

and nothing dies without leaving an inheritance. Allah Most High neither dies nor leaves an inheritance. This refutes the Jews’ question: “From whom did He inherit the world, and to whom will He bequeath it?” Likewise, it is reported that the Christians asked: “Describe your Lord to us. What is He made of?” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, replied: “My Lord is not made from anything, and He is distinct from all things.” Likewise, the polytheists and the Jews asked: “Is He made of silver, gold, or iron?” This was because they were accustomed to the gods they worshipped besides Allah having materials from which they were made. The idols of idol-worshippers are made of gold, silver, iron, and other materials.

There are also those who worship human beings, whether those human beings did not command them to worship them or did command them to do so. These include those who worship the Messiah and ‘Uzayr, and Pharaoh’s people, to whom he said:

“I am your lord, the most high,”

and:

“I know of no god for you other than myself.”

He also said to Moses:

“If you take a god other than me, I will certainly have you imprisoned.”

Another example is the man whom Allah had given a share of sovereignty, who disputed with Abraham concerning his Lord. When Abraham said, “My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death,” he replied, “I give life and cause death.” Another is the Dajjāl, who claims divinity. From the creation of Adam until the Hour is established, there is no trial greater than the trial of the Dajjāl. There are also those who said:

“Never abandon your gods; never abandon Wadd, Suwā‘, Yaghūth, Ya‘ūq, or Nasr.”

Several of the early generations stated that these were the names of righteous men who had lived among them. When they died, the people remained by their graves, then made statues of them, and then, after that,

---

## Page 9059

they worshipped them. This was how idols first came to be worshipped. These idols subsequently passed to the Arabs. Al-Bukhārī related this in his Sahīh from Ibn ‘Abbās, who said:

“The idols that had been among Noah’s people later appeared among the Arabs. Wadd belonged to Kalb at Dūmat al-Jandal; Suwā‘ belonged to Hudhayl; Yaghūth belonged to Murād, then to Banū Ghutayf at al-Jurf near Saba’; Ya‘ūq belonged to Hamdān; and Nasr belonged to Himyar, to the family of Dhū al-Kalā‘. These were the names of righteous men from Noah’s people. When they died, Satan prompted their people to erect monuments at the places where they used to sit and to name them after those men. They did so, but the monuments were not worshipped until that generation had died out and knowledge had been lost. Then they were worshipped.”

Noah, peace be upon him, remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty, calling them to worship Allah alone. He was the first messenger whom Allah sent to the people of the earth, as is established in the Sahīh. Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the last of the messengers. Both messengers were sent to polytheists who worshipped these idols, which were fashioned in the likenesses of righteous human beings. The purpose of worshipping them was to worship those righteous people.

The same is true of the polytheists among the People of the Book and among the innovators and misguided members of this community: this is the ultimate extent of their polytheism. Christians make images in their churches of the human beings they venerate besides Jesus and his mother, such as Saint George and other saints. They worship these images, petition them, invoke them, and offer

---

## Page 9060

sacrifices to them and make vows to them, saying, “These remind us of those righteous people.”

The devils lead them astray just as they used to lead the polytheists astray. Sometimes a devil assumes the likeness of the person being invoked and worshipped, so the one invoking him thinks that he has come, or supposes that Allah has fashioned an angel in his likeness. A Christian, for example, may invoke Saint George or someone else while in captivity or other circumstances, and then see him coming through the air. The same happens to others. They have asked some of their patriarchs about this: how could he be present in all these places? The answer was: “These are angels whom Allah creates in his likeness to help whoever invokes him.” In reality, these are devils who have led the polytheists astray.

The same happens to many people of innovation, misguidance, and polytheism who claim to belong to this community. One of them invokes his revered shaykh and seeks his aid, though the shaykh is dead; or he seeks his aid at his grave, petitions him, and may make a vow to him or do something similar. He then sees that person coming to him through the air, warding off some harm he fears, answering some question he has asked him, or doing something of that kind. If the shaykh is alive, he thinks that the shaykh himself has come. Indeed, I know groups of such people who go to the very shaykh whose aid they sought, having seen him come to them through the air, and tell him about it.

One group goes to one shaykh, and another group to another. Sometimes the shaykh himself knows nothing of the incident. If he craves leadership, he remains silent and gives them the impression that he himself came to their aid. If he has some truthfulness, but is ignorant and misguided, he says:

“This is an angel whom Allah has fashioned in

---

## Page 9061

my likeness.” He regards this as one of the miraculous gifts granted to the righteous and uses it to justify those who seek aid from the righteous and take them as lords, claiming that when people seek their aid, Allah sends angels in their likeness to help those who invoke them.

Thus, I know more than one prominent shaykh possessed of truthfulness, asceticism, and devotion to worship who, supposing this to be one of the miraculous gifts granted to the righteous, began instructing his disciples:

“If any of you has a need, let him seek my aid, call upon me for help, and ask for my counsel.” He would also say, “After my death, I shall do what I used to do during my lifetime.”

Yet he does not know that these are devils who have assumed his likeness to mislead him and his followers, making associating partners with Allah, invoking others besides Allah, and seeking their aid seem good to them. Nor does he realize that they may cast into his heart the words, “After your death, we shall do for your companions what we used to do for them during your lifetime.” He supposes this to be a divine communication cast into his heart, and so instructs his companions accordingly.

I know someone among these people whom devils used to serve during his lifetime in various ways, such as speaking to his companions who sought his aid, helping them, and so forth. After he died, they began appearing to individual followers in the shaykh’s likeness, giving them the impression that he had not died, and sending his companions messages purporting to be from him.

One of this shaykh’s followers used to meet with me. He was ascetic and devoted to worship, and loved both me and this shaykh. He thought that this was among the miraculous gifts granted to the righteous and that the shaykh had not died. He told me about the words the shaykh had sent him after his death and read them aloud; they proved to be the speech of devils

---

## Page 9062

indeed. More than one person I know has told me that they sought my aid and saw me in the air, coming to them and rescuing them from their distress. One had been surrounded by Armenian Christians who intended to seize him. Another had been surrounded by the enemy while carrying confidential letters from well-wishers; had they discovered what he was carrying, they would have killed him. There were other such cases.

I told them that I knew absolutely nothing of what had happened, and swore to this so that they would not suppose I was concealing it as miraculous gifts are concealed. I already knew that what they had done was not prescribed by Islam, but was rather associating partners with Allah and a religious innovation. Later, it became clear to me—and I explained to them—that these were devils assuming the likeness of the person whose aid was sought.

More than one follower of the shaykhs has told me that similar things happened to those who sought their aid. A great many people have related that they sought aid from the living and the dead and witnessed similar things. Such accounts became so widespread that it came to be known that these manifestations were the work of devils.

Devils lead a person astray as far as they can. If he knows nothing of the religion of Islam, they draw him into blatant association of partners with Allah and outright disbelief. They command him not to remember Allah, but to prostrate to the devil and offer sacrifices to him. They also command him to eat carrion and blood and to commit indecent acts.

This happens frequently in lands of outright disbelief, and in lands where disbelief prevails and Islam is weak. It also happens in some Muslim cities, in places whose inhabitants are weak in faith. Indeed, it has occurred in Egypt and Syria in forms that would take a long time to describe. Its occurrence in the lands of the East, before the emergence of

---

## Page 9063

Islam among the Tatars, was very frequent. The more Islam spread among them and they came to understand its true nature, the less influence the devils had among them. If a person is Muslim but chooses indecency and wrongdoing, they assist him in wrongdoing and indecency. This is exceedingly common—more common than the preceding kind—in lands whose inhabitants combine Islam with pre-Islamic ignorance, and righteousness with wickedness.

A shaykh may possess faith and religious devotion, yet have little understanding of the true nature of what Allah sent His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to convey. He may know in general that the friends of Allah receive miraculous gifts, without knowing that perfect friendship with Allah consists in faith, mindfulness of Him, and following the Messengers inwardly and outwardly. Or he may know this in general, yet lack sufficient understanding of the realities of inward faith and the outward prescriptions of Islam to distinguish states that come from the Most Merciful from those arising from the self or from devils. Dreams likewise fall into three categories: dreams from Allah; dreams reflecting what a person thinks about while awake and then sees in sleep; and dreams from Satan. The same applies to spiritual states.

If his understanding of the true nature of Muhammad’s religion, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is limited, the devils instruct him to do something he does not recognize as wrong. Sometimes they carry one of these people through the air, have him stand at ‘Arafāt, and then return him to his own land, still wearing his ordinary clothes. He has not entered the state of pilgrimage consecration upon coming abreast of the prescribed boundary points, uncovered his head, or removed the clothing that a person in that state must remove. Nor do they let him, after standing at ‘Arafāt, perform tawāf al-ifādah (the pilgrimage circumambulation), stone the pillars, and complete his Hajj. Rather, he supposes that merely standing there—as he has done—

---

## Page 9064

is an act of worship. This stems from his limited knowledge of Islam. Had he known the religion of Islam, he would have known that what he has done is not worship of Allah, and that anyone who regards this as lawful is an apostate who must be put to death. Indeed, Muslims agree that one must enter the state of pilgrimage consecration at the prescribed boundary point, and that someone in that state may not wear such clothing without a valid excuse. Standing at ‘Arafāt alone is not sufficient; the pilgrimage circumambulation is indispensable, by the agreement of the Muslims. He must also proceed to the Sacred Monument and stone Jamrat al-‘Aqabah. There is disagreement over whether this is an essential pillar or an obligation whose omission can be compensated for by a sacrificial offering. He must also stone the pillars during the days at Minā, by the agreement of the Muslims.

The jinn may carry one of these people to visit Jerusalem or elsewhere, fly with him through the air, and walk with him through water. They may make him see that he has been taken to the city of the friends of Allah, and may even make him see himself eating the fruits of Paradise and drinking from its rivers. All this, and similar things, I know to have happened to people I know. But this is an extensive subject, and this is not the place to discuss it at length.

The point is simply that polytheism in the world originated in the worship of righteous human beings and their images, with those people being the intended objects of worship. Some forms of polytheism originated in the worship of heavenly bodies—the sun, the moon, or others—and idols were fashioned as talismans for those heavenly bodies. The polytheism of Abraham’s people—and Allah knows best—was of this kind, or some of it was. Other forms of polytheism originated in the worship of angels or jinn, for whom idols were erected. Otherwise, the idols themselves

---

## Page 9065

were not worshipped for their own sake as inanimate objects, but for reasons that prompted such worship. The Arabs’ polytheism was predominantly of the first kind, though it included elements of all these kinds. For ‘Amr ibn Luhayy was the first to alter the religion of Abraham—peace be upon him. He had travelled to Syria and seen that the people of al-Balqā’ had idols through which they sought to obtain benefits and avert harm. He then did the same in Mecca, when Khuzā‘ah were the custodians of the House before Quraysh, and he was the chief of Khuzā‘ah. In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is reported to have said:

“I saw ‘Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qam‘ah ibn Khindif dragging his entrails—that is, his intestines—in the Fire. He was the first to alter the religion of Abraham, set votive camels free to roam, and slit the ears of she-camels to mark their consecration.”

The polytheism of Noah’s people was likewise—and Allah knows best—though it began with the worship of righteous people. Satan leads people from this to other forms of polytheism.
