Rather, their aims were disbelief, associating partners with Allah, and opposing Islam as far as they could. All their followers were people of innovation and misguidance. Thus, during their rule, the Christians seized most of Syria. Then Allah raised up Sunni rulers such as Nūr al-Dīn, Salāh al-Dīn and his brothers, together with their followers. They reconquered the Muslim lands and waged jihad against the disbelievers and hypocrites.

---

## Page 9106

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade prayer at sunrise and sunset because the polytheists prostrate to the sun at those times, and Satan accompanies it. Although a Muslim praying does not intend to prostrate to the sun, the prohibition serves to block the means to polytheism, lest he imitate the polytheists in practices peculiar to them and thereby be led into polytheism. Hence, he forbade deliberately choosing these two times for prayer. This is Ibn ʿUmar’s wording in the two Sahīh collections. Deliberately setting out to pray at these times is therefore forbidden.

However, if an occasion arises for which prayer is prescribed—such as the prayer upon entering a mosque, the eclipse prayer, prostration upon recitation, the two units of prayer following circumambulation, or repeating a prayer with the local imam—there is a well-known disagreement among the scholars concerning these acts. The stronger view is that they are permissible and recommended, for they are good deeds involving no evil, and their opportunity is lost if they are left undone. The prohibition concerns deliberately setting out to pray at that time, because this resembles the disbelievers’ deliberate prostration at that time. When a prayer has no particular occasion, a person has chosen to perform it at that time, even if he did not choose the time for its own sake. By contrast, a prayer prompted by a particular occasion is performed because of that occasion; the time has no bearing on it whatsoever.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also issued a general prohibition against praying in graveyards, saying:

“The whole earth is a place of prayer, except graveyards and bathhouses.”

This was narrated by the compilers of the Sunan collections. It has been transmitted both with a connected chain to the Prophet and as a direct attribution to him by a Successor. The hadith masters have judged the connected version to be correct. Bathhouses are a refuge for devils, while prayer in graveyards was forbidden

---

## Page 9107

because it involves imitating those who take graves as places of worship, even though the person praying may not intend to pray there because of any special merit of that spot, but may simply happen to do so.

Nevertheless, this involves resembling those who do intend that, so he forbade it. Likewise, he forbade prayer without a particular occasion at sunrise and sunset, even when a person does not seek any special merit in that time, because it involves resembling those who do seek special merit in it—namely, the polytheists. His prohibition of prayer at those times is thus like his prohibition of prayer in that place.

The polytheism that has led most of the children of Adam astray originated in, and found its greatest expression in, the worship of human beings and statues fashioned in their likeness. The polytheists were accustomed to gods who begot and were born, who inherited and were inherited from, and who were made of one thing or another. They therefore asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about the God he worshipped: “What is He made of? Is He made of this or that? From whom did He inherit the world, and to whom will He bequeath it?”

So Allah Most High said:

“Say: He is Allah, the One;
Allah, the Eternal Refuge.
He neither begets nor is born,
nor is there anyone equivalent to Him.”

In the hadith of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, it says: “For no one is born but will die, and no one inherits but will be inherited from.”

That is to say, all those worshipped besides Allah have been born, such as the Messiah, Uzayr and other righteous people, along with their images, and the likes of the Pharaohs who claimed divinity. Such a being is born and will die. Even if he inherited his possessions from someone else, when he dies someone else will inherit from him. But Allah, glorified is He, is Ever-Living: He does not die, nor is He inherited from. Glorified and exalted is He. Allah knows best, and may Allah bless Muhammad.

---

## Page 9108

Surah al-Falaq (Daybreak)

Shaykh al-Islām, champion of the Sunnah and suppressor of innovation, Taqī al-Dīn Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may the Lord benefit us through his knowledge—also said the following, among the writings he composed in the Citadel:

Section: On the words,

“Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak.”

Allah Most High says:

“The Cleaver of grain and fruit stones.”

And He Most High says:

“The Cleaver of daybreak, who has made the night for rest.”

Falaq (splitting open) is a verbal noun used in a passive sense, just as qabd (seizing) can mean “that which is seized.” Thus, everything the Lord has split open is falaq. Al-Hasan said: “Falaq is everything that splits open to reveal something, such as daybreak, grain, and fruit stones.”

Al-Zajjāj said: “If you reflect on creation, it will become clear to you that most of it comes into being through splitting open

---

## Page 9109

as when the earth splits open to yield vegetation and clouds to release rain.”

Many Quran commentators have said that falaq means daybreak. Thus one says, “This is clearer than daybreak,” using either falaq al-subh or faraq al-subh. Others have said that falaq means all creation.

As for the claim that it is a valley in Hell, a tree in Hell, or one of the names of Hell, its soundness is not established either by the meaning of the word or by any report from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Nor is there any wisdom in singling out His lordship over such a thing. This is unlike saying “the Lord of creation,” “the Lord of everything that splits open,” or “the Lord of the light He brings forth for His servants by day.” Singling these out for mention reveals the greatness of the Lord in whom refuge is sought.

If falaq is understood to have both a general and a particular meaning, then with its general reference to creation, I seek refuge “from the evil of what He has created”; and with its particular reference to daylight, I seek refuge “from the evil of darkness when it settles.”

For “that which darkens” has been interpreted as the night, as in His words:

“Establish prayer from the sun’s decline until the darkness of the night.”

This is the view of most Quran commentators and scholars of the Arabic language. They said that “settles” means “enters into everything.”

Al-Zajjāj said: “Ghāsiq means that which is cold. Night is called ghāsiq because it is colder than day.”

Al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasā’ī related from ‘Ā’ishah that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, looked at the moon and said: “‘Ā’ishah, seek refuge in Allah from its evil, for it is the darkening one when it settles.”

It is also related

---

## Page 9110

from Abū Hurayrah in a report traced back to the Prophet: “The darkening one is the star.” Ibn Zayd said that it is the Pleiades. Diseases and plagues would become more prevalent when they set and subside when they rose. Some people have thought that this prophetic report conflicts with the interpretation that it means the night, so they treated it as a separate interpretation and explained its “settling” as its coming to rest.

Ibn Qutaybah said: “It is also said that the darkening one is the moon when it is eclipsed and turns black, and that ‘settles’ means that it enters an eclipse.”

This interpretation is weak. What the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said cannot be opposed by anyone else’s words, for he speaks only the truth. He did not instruct ‘Ā’ishah to seek refuge from the moon when it was eclipsed, but when it was visible. Allah Most High says:

“We made the night and the day two signs. We erased the sign of the night and made the sign of the day illuminating.”

The moon is the sign of the night. Likewise, the stars rise and become visible at night. His instruction to seek refuge from this is therefore an instruction to seek refuge from the sign of the night, which indicates it and marks its presence. The presence of an indicator necessarily entails the presence of what it indicates. Thus, when the evil of the moon is present, the evil of the night is present. The moon also has effects that other things do not, so there is all the more reason to seek refuge from the evil arising from it.

This is like his statement concerning the mosque founded upon piety:

“It is this mosque of mine.”

Yet the verse unquestionably includes the Mosque of Qubā’. Likewise, he said of those gathered beneath the cloak:

“These are the members of my household.”

Yet the Quran includes his wives within his household. Such singling out is because what is singled out has a greater claim to the description. Thus, of all things present at night, the moon most warrants seeking refuge from its evil. Night is dark, and roaming through it are the devils

---

## Page 9111

of humankind and the jinn to an extent they do not by day. Various evils occur at night that do not occur by day: unbelief, wickedness, disobedience, sorcery, theft, betrayal, indecencies, and other such things. Evil is always associated with darkness. Allah made the night solely for human beings to be still and rest, yet the devils among humankind and the jinn commit evils during it that they cannot commit by day. They seek aid through the moon and invocation of it, and through the moon and its worship. Abū Ma‘shar al-Balkhī has a work entitled “Mushaf al-Qamar” (The Scripture of the Moon), in which he mentions matters of unbelief and sorcery that warrant seeking refuge from it.

Thus, Allah, glorified be He, mentioned seeking refuge from the evil of creation in general, then specifically enjoined seeking refuge from the evil of the darkening one when it settles—the time whose evil is widespread. He then singled out sorcery and envy. Sorcery proceeds from wicked souls, but with the aid of such things as blowing upon knots. Envy also proceeds from wicked souls, whether through the evil eye or through wrongdoing committed with the tongue or hand. Of sorcery, He specifically mentioned those who blow upon knots, who are women. The envier is usually a man, although an envier may be either a man or a woman.

The evil proceeding from the wicked souls of men and women is external to a person; it is not within his heart, unlike the whisperer who withdraws. In Surah al-Nās, He mentioned “the whisperer who withdraws,” for he is the source of deeds

---

## Page 9112

that are blameworthy: unbelief, wickedness, and disobedience. Thus, this surah teaches seeking refuge from the evil of the harmful deeds a person engages in—unbelief, wickedness, and disobedience. This also includes seeking refuge from the evil of one’s own soul.

Surah al-Falaq teaches seeking refuge from the evil of created things, both generally and specifically. Hence, it says, “the Lord of daybreak,” whereas this surah says, “the Lord of humankind.” For He who brings forth the dawn with light removes the evil in darkness through the goodness in His light. And He who splits the grain and fruit-stone after they have formed removes the evil in the knots of those who blow upon them. Indeed, splitting the grain and fruit-stone is a greater act than untying the knots of those who blow upon them.

Likewise, envy arises from a person’s narrowness of spirit and avarice: his heart does not open to Allah’s bestowal of favor upon him. The Lord of daybreak removes the harm caused by the envier’s narrowness of spirit and avarice.

He, glorified be He, splits nothing open except to bring forth good. He brings forth the dawn with its guiding light and the blazing lamp upon which His servants’ well-being depends. He splits the grain and fruit-stone to bring forth the various fruits and foods that sustain people and their animals. Human beings need to obtain the benefits of guidance and provision, and these are brought about through such splitting open. The Lord who has split things open for people to bring forth what benefits them is the One in whom refuge is sought from whatever harms them. Thus, He is asked to complete His favor by warding off harmful things from His servant, upon whom He first bestowed His blessings.

Splitting one thing open to bring forth another demonstrates perfect power and the bringing forth of something from its opposite, just as He brings forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living. This, too, is a kind of splitting open. Thus, He, glorified be He, is able to ward off a harmful opposite by means of a beneficial one.

## Page 9113

Surah al-Nās

He—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

On “Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of humankind,” through to the end of the surah.

Concerning His words:

“From the evil of the retreating whisperer, who whispers into the hearts of humankind, from among jinn and humankind.”

There are several interpretations. Ibn al-Jawzī mentioned only two, omitting the third, which is the correct one: “from among jinn and humankind” identifies the whisperer. That is, those who whisper into people’s hearts may be either jinn or human beings. Allah Most High has told us that He appointed enemies for every prophet—devils from among humankind and jinn, inspiring one another with embellished speech to deceive. This inspiration of theirs is their whispering. A whisperer need not be hidden from sight; rather, he may be seen. Allah Most High says:

“Then Satan whispered to them to expose to them what had been hidden from them of their nakedness. He said, ‘Your Lord has only forbidden you this tree to prevent you from becoming angels or becoming immortal.’ And he swore to them, ‘I am truly a sincere adviser to you both.’”

This is speech whose speaker is known, not something cast into the heart from an unknown source. Iblīs had been commanded to prostrate before Adam, but he refused and was arrogant. Thus, he was not someone unknown to Adam. He and his offspring see the children of Adam from where they cannot see them; Adam himself, however, did see him.

---

## Page 9114

Many human beings may also see devils and jinn, but these possess a capacity for concealment and hiding that human beings do not. Allah Most High says:

“When Satan made their deeds seem fair to them and said, ‘No one among humankind can overcome you today, and I am your protector.’ But when the two forces came within sight of each other, he turned on his heels and said, ‘I am free of you.’”

Works of Quranic commentary and prophetic biography relate that Satan came to them in the form of a human being. Likewise, Allah says:

“Like Satan when he says to a person, ‘Disbelieve!’ Then, when he disbelieves, he says, ‘I am free of you. I fear Allah, Lord of all worlds.’”

In the hadith of Abū Dharr, the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said, “We seek refuge in Allah from the devils among humankind and jinn.” Abū Dharr said, “I asked, ‘Are there devils among human beings?’ He replied, ‘Yes, worse than the devils among the jinn.’”

The soul, too, whispers, as Allah Most High says:

“We certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him.”

Here, a person’s own soul whispers to him, as in the expression “inner speech.” The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Allah has pardoned my community for what passes through their minds, so long as they neither speak of it nor act upon it.”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded it in their Sahīh collections. Thus, those who whisper into people’s hearts are their own souls, the devils among the jinn, and the devils among humankind. “The retreating whisperer” encompasses whispering by both jinn and human beings. Otherwise,

---

## Page 9115

what sense would there be in seeking refuge only from the whispering of the jinn, when the whispering of one’s own soul and of human devils is also harmful, and may be more harmful than that of the jinn?

As for al-Farrā’s statement that “from the evil of the whisperer who whispers into the hearts of people” refers to both groups—jinn and humankind—and that Allah called the jinn “people” just as He called them “men” and “a company,” this is a weak interpretation. The word “people” is too familiar, clear, and well known to require subdivision into jinn and humankind. Allah Most High has used the word “people” in numerous passages.

Moreover, describing him as whispering into the hearts of both groups would serve to clarify and explain. Yet people do not know that the jinn are subject to whispering; this can only be known through a transmitted report, and there is no such report here. Furthermore, He says:

“From among jinn and people.”

How, then, can the word “people” encompass both jinn and people? How can one of two contrasting categories also be a subdivision of the other? This interpretation makes people a category contrasted with the jinn, while making the jinn a kind of people. This is like saying, “The noblest Arabs, from among non-Arabs and Arabs.” Would anyone say such a thing?

Allah Most High’s calling them “men” does not prove that they are called “people.” Even supposing one could say, “Some people from among the jinn came,” that would be a qualified expression, just as one says, “a human being made of clay and spurting fluid.” It does not follow that they fall within the unqualified term “people.” Allah Most High has said:

“O people, fear your Lord, who created you from a soul

---

## Page 9116

that was one, and created from it its mate.” All people, then, were created from Adam and Eve, even though Allah, glorified be He, addresses both jinn and humankind, and the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was sent to both kinds. Yet the word “people” does not encompass the jinn; rather, He says, “O company of jinn and humankind.”

Likewise, al-Zajjāj’s statement that the meaning is “from the evil of the whisperer”—meaning the jinn—“and from the evil of people” is weak, although it is more plausible than the first interpretation. For the evil of the jinn is greater than that of humankind. How, then, could He prescribe seeking refuge from all people without qualification, while prescribing refuge from only some of the jinn?

Moreover, if the whisperer who withdraws is only from among the jinn, there is no need for the words “from among jinn” and “from among people.” Why, then, single out the whispering of the jinn as something from which to seek refuge, to the exclusion of human whispering?

Furthermore, when a noun precedes a coordinated term, it is preferable to coordinate that term with the nearer noun, just as it is preferable for a pronoun to refer to the nearer antecedent—unless there is evidence requiring coordination with the more distant noun. Thus, coordinating “people” here with “jinn,” with which it is paired, is preferable to coordinating it with “the whisperer.”

---

## Page 9117

It is enough to note that all Muslims have recited this surah since the time of their Prophet, yet these two interpretations have been reported only from certain grammarians. The statements transmitted from the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness contain nothing of the kind. Rather, they contain only the interpretation we have defended. Thus, in Maʿmar’s Tafsīr, Qatāda comments on the words “from among jinn and humankind”:

“There are devils among the jinn and devils among humankind, so we seek refuge in Allah from the devils among humankind and the jinn.”

Qatāda thus explained that the meaning is to seek refuge from the devils among humankind and the jinn. Ibn Wahb also narrated that ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said concerning His words, “the whisperer who withdraws”:

“The one who withdraws is one who sometimes whispers and sometimes withdraws, whether from among the jinn or humankind.”

Ibn Zayd thus explained that the whisperer who withdraws may belong to either kind. It used to be said: “Human devils are harder on people than devils among the jinn: a devil among the jinn whispers without your seeing him, whereas this one confronts you face to face.”

Ibn Jurayj said concerning “from among jinn and humankind”:

“There are only two whisperers: a whisperer from among the jinn, who is ‘the one who withdraws,’ and a whisperer from a person’s own self, referred to in His words, ‘and humankind.’”

Although this third interpretation resembles al-Zajjāj’s, it is better than his, for it takes the whispering that comes from a person’s own self to be what is meant by “humankind.” Its meaning is therefore better. Ibn Abī Hātim recorded all three accounts in his Tafsīr.

---

## Page 9118

Furthermore, He mentions in the verse “the Lord of humankind,” “the Sovereign of humankind,” and “the God of humankind.” If the intent is that people should seek refuge in their Lord, Sovereign, and God from the evil of whatever whispers in their breasts, then it is He from whom they seek the good that benefits them and protection against the evil that harms them. Whispering is the root of every evil that harms them, for it is the starting point of disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience.

The Lord’s punishments are only for their sins. If a person has no sin, everything that befalls him is a blessing for him. If he is tried with something painful, Allah raises his rank and rewards him—assuming a complete absence of sins. This, however, is not their actual condition, for every child of Adam sins, and the best of those who sin are those who repent. The Most High has said:

“But man undertook it. Indeed, he was unjust and ignorant.”

“So that Allah may punish the hypocrites, men and women, and the polytheists, men and women, and turn in mercy to the believers, men and women.”

Thus, repentance is the ultimate goal of believers, from the prophets to those below them. Allah Most High said:

“Then Adam received words from his Lord, and He accepted his repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepter of repentance, the Most Merciful.”

Noah said:

“My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You for that of which I have no knowledge. Unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers.”

Abraham and Ishmael said:

“Our Lord, make us both submissive to You, and from our descendants a community submissive to You. Show us our rites and accept our repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepter of repentance, the Most Merciful.”

Moses said:

“You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy on us. You are the best of those who forgive.”

Our Prophet’s supplications of this kind are numerous and well known.

---

## Page 9119

Thus, whispering is the origin of every evil. If they have sought refuge in their Lord, Sovereign, and God from its evil, this includes the whispering of both jinn and humans. Any other evil they suffer at human hands befalls them only because of their sins: it is recompense for their deeds, like the harm inflicted by jinn through means other than whispering, or the punishments sent down from heaven. Here, they have not sought refuge from the evil of created beings without qualification, as they have in Surah al-Falaq, but from evil whose origin lies within their own souls.

Even if mentioning “the Lord of humankind,” “the Sovereign of humankind,” and “the God of humankind” means that they seek refuge in Him so that He may protect them and protect others from them—and this is the broader of the two meanings—that is achieved by His protecting them from the evil of the whisperer who whispers in people’s breasts. For it is he who whispers to them to wrong one another, lead one another astray, and assist one another in sin and transgression.

No evil, then, befalls one human at the hands of another except that it originates with the retreating whisperer. By contrast, when the harm people inflict on one another arises not from whispering but from the revelation with which Allah sent His angels, it is just—as in carrying out the prescribed punishments, fighting the disbelievers, and exacting retribution from wrongdoers. These actions involve harm and pain for human wrongdoers, but they proceed from Allah’s revelation, not from whispering. They are a blessing from Allah for His servants, even for the person punished. For if he is punished, that punishment is an expiation for him if he is a believer; otherwise, it lessens his punishment in the Hereafter compared with the punishment of someone who was not punished in this world.

---

## Page 9120

This is why Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was a mercy to all creation: because of the general good brought about through him and the happiness in this world and the Hereafter attained by those who believed in him; because he was himself a mercy, which people could accept, while whoever refused it wronged only himself; and because he restrained the disbelievers and hypocrites, reducing their evil and preventing them from doing what they would have done without him. He killed some of them, and their early deaths were better, both for them and for others, than their living longer in disbelief. Thus, Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was a mercy to all creation in every respect. One therefore does not seek refuge from him, or from others like him among the prophets and their believing followers, although they too are human and inflict harm, punishment, and pain upon their enemies.

Thus, seeking refuge from people concerns only what the whisperer instigates in them. On this understanding, one seeks refuge in the Lord of humankind, the Sovereign of humankind, the God of humankind, from the evil of the whisperer who whispers to the person seeking refuge, and from the evil of the whisperer who whispers to everyone else, so that no evil reaches that person through them. If people's evil comes only from the whisperer, then seeking refuge from the evil of the one who whispers to them achieves the intended purpose, cuts off evil at its source, and is closer to justice. It also excludes Allah's prophets and His allies from being among those whose evil one seeks refuge from, and from being coupled with the retreating whisperer. Such a coupling would imply the superiority of jinn over humans, something no rational person would assert.

If it is objected:

“If all evil originates with the retreating whisperer, then there is no need

---

## Page 9121

to mention seeking refuge from human whispering, since it follows from the whispering of the jinn.”

The reply is:

Rather, whispering is of two kinds: one comes from the jinn, and the other from human souls. As He says:

“We have certainly created man and know what his soul whispers to him.”

Evil thus comes from both sources. Humans have their devils just as the jinn have theirs. Waswasah (whispering) is akin to washwashah (hushed speech), written with the dotted letter shīn. One says, “So-and-so yuwashwishu (whispers to) so-and-so,” or “washwashahu (he whispered to him),” when he speaks secretly into his ear. Waswasah is used similarly; hence the expression waswasat al-huliyy (the soft jingling of jewelry). However, the form with the undotted letter sīn has a more specific meaning.

The Lord of humankind is the One who nurtures them through His power, will, and governance. He is the Lord of all worlds, the Creator of them all and of their deeds.

“The Sovereign of humankind”

is the One who commands and forbids them. A sovereign exercises authority through speech. Inanimate things have no sovereign, since they cannot understand speech addressed to them, but they do have an owner. Sovereignty applies only to those who understand their sovereign. Animals understand one another, as He says:

“We have been taught the language of birds.”

“An ant said, ‘O ants!’”

Thus, animals may have a sovereign of their own kind or of another kind, as Solomon was their sovereign.

The God is the One worshipped, to whom all intentions and deeds are directed, as has already been explained at length.

It has also been said that humankind are singled out for mention because they are the ones seeking refuge, or because they are

---

## Page 9122

those from whose evil refuge is sought. Abū al-Faraj mentioned both explanations, but neither has a sound basis, for the whispering of the jinn is greater, yet He did not mention them. Rather, He mentioned humankind because they are the ones seeking refuge. They seek refuge in their Lord, who protects them; in their Sovereign, who commands and forbids them; and in their God, whom they worship, from the evil of the one who stands between them and worshipping Him. They also seek refuge from the evil of the whispering that arises in human souls, whether from humans or jinn, for it is the root of the evil that proceeds from them and the evil that befalls them.

Section

This clarifies some aspects of this prayer for refuge and the one preceding it. As the hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, state, those seeking refuge have never sought it with anything like these two. Whispering is the root of all disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience, and thus the root of all evil. Whenever a person is protected from its evil, he is protected from the punishment of Hell, the punishment of the grave, the trials of life and death, and the trial of the false messiah, the Dajjāl. All these come about through whispering. He is also protected from Allah’s punishment in this world and the Hereafter, for he is punished only for sins, whose origin lies in whispering.

Furthermore, if the verse also encompasses the whispering of others, so that His words,

“From the evil of the whisperer,”

constitute seeking refuge from the whispering that assails him and that which assails people because of him, then he is protected from their wrongdoing. And if

---

## Page 9123

only the whispering that assails him is intended, they are given power over him only because of his sins, which arise from that whispering. Allah Most High says:

“When a calamity befell you, although you had inflicted twice as much, did you say, ‘How did this happen?’ Say, ‘It is from your own selves.’”

He also says:

“Whatever calamity befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned.”

And He says:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever ill befalls you is from yourself.”

Whispering is a kind of speech and discourse. Thus, regarding His words, “what his soul whispers to him,” the Quran commentators explained: “what his soul says to him.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has pardoned my community for what passes through their minds, so long as they neither speak of it nor act upon it.”

This speech is of two kinds: declarative and non-declarative. Declarative speech concerns either the past or the future. The whisperer reminds a person of the past; concerning the future, he tells him of things that the person himself will do, or things that will happen by Allah’s decree or through someone else’s actions. These are vain hopes and false promises. Non-declarative speech consists of commands, prohibitions, and permissions.

At times Satan whispers evil, and at other times he causes a person to forget what is good. This happens through the inner talk with which he preoccupies him. Allah Most High says concerning forgetfulness:

---

## Page 9124

“And if Satan causes you to forget, then once you remember, do not sit with the wrongdoing people.”

Moses’ young attendant said:

“I forgot the fish, and none but Satan made me forget it.”

Allah Most High says:

“But Satan made him forget the remembrance of his lord.”

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When the caller gives the call to prayer, Satan turns and flees, passing wind so that he cannot hear the call. When the call is over, he returns. When the call to begin the prayer is given, he flees again; when it is over, he returns and intrudes between a person and his own thoughts, saying, ‘Remember such-and-such; remember such-and-such,’ bringing up things he had not been thinking of, until the man no longer knows how many units he has prayed.”

Thus Satan reminded him of past matters about which he had spoken inwardly to himself—things already in his mind, whether his own actions or other matters. Through these distractions, the worshipper forgot how many units he had prayed and no longer knew their number. Forgetfulness displaced what he had been keeping in mind and occupied his mind with something else, until he forgot the first matter.

As for Satan’s telling him about the future through promises and vain hopes, an example is Allah’s statement:

“And Satan will say, when the matter has been decided, ‘Allah gave you a true promise. I too promised you, but I failed you. I had no authority over you except that I called you and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves.’”

This verse contains both his command and his promise. Allah Most High also says:

“Whoever takes Satan as an ally instead of Allah has indeed suffered a manifest loss.”

“He makes them promises and fills them with vain hopes, but Satan promises them nothing but delusion.”

“Those people will have Hell as their refuge

---

## Page 9125

and will find no escape from it.” Allah Most High says:

“Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to commit indecency, while Allah promises you forgiveness from Himself and bounty. Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.”

This verse, too, mentions his command and his promise. When Moses killed the Copt, he said:

“This is Satan’s doing. He is indeed an enemy who clearly leads astray.”

Several Companions, including Abū Bakr and Ibn Masʿūd, said concerning opinions they reached through their independent judgment: “If it is correct, it is from Allah; and if it is mistaken, it is from me and from Satan.”

Thus, they attributed beliefs instilled in the mind that do not accord with the truth to Satan, even though the person holding them incurs no sin because he has exerted his utmost effort. Likewise, a person incurs no sin because of Satan’s whisperings during prayer or because of his own inward thoughts. The believers said:

“Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake.”

And Allah said: “I have granted this.” Forgetting the truth is from Satan, and error is from Satan. Allah Most High says:

“When you see those who engage in offensive discourse concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they turn to another subject. And if Satan causes you to forget, then once you remember, do not sit with the wrongdoing people.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it must pray it when he remembers it.”

When he and his Companions slept through the prayer during the Khaybar expedition, he told them:

“Move on, for this is a place where a devil came to us.”

He also said:

“Satan came to Bilāl and began lulling him as one lulls a child, until he fell asleep.”

---

## Page 9126

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had entrusted Bilāl with waking them at dawn. Sleep that prevents a person from fulfilling what he has been commanded to do, and drowsiness, are from Satan, though they are excused. Hence it has been said: “Drowsiness in a gathering for the remembrance of Allah is from Satan.” Likewise, nocturnal emissions during sleep are from Satan, yet a sleeping person is not held accountable.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Dreams are of three kinds: a dream from Allah, a dream from Satan, and a dream in which a person sees during sleep what he has been thinking about while awake.”

It has also been said that these are the words of Ibn Sīrīn. Nevertheless, the division of dreams into two kinds—one from Allah and another from Satan—is undoubtedly authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

These two kinds arise from the whisperings of the self and the whisperings of Satan, and both are excused, for a sleeping person is exempt from accountability. Satan’s whispering veils the heart like a fleeting image in the imagination, causing a person to forget the faith he possesses until he becomes blind to the truth and falls into falsehood. If he is among those who fear Allah, his condition is as Allah describes:

“Indeed, when those who fear Allah are touched by a suggestion from Satan, they remember, and at once they see clearly.”

For Satan has touched them with a passing influence that veils the heart. It may be thin or thick, but it is a covering over the heart that prevents it from seeing the truth. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When a servant commits a sin, a black spot is marked on his heart. If he repents, desists, and seeks forgiveness, his heart is polished clean. But if he continues to sin, it grows until it covers his heart. That is

---

## Page 9127

the rust of which Allah Most High said:

‘No! Rather, their hearts have been covered with rust by what they used to earn.’”

But Satan’s passing influence differs from the rust caused by sins: the latter is a punishment for sin. The veil over the heart is subtler than that, as in the authentic hadith in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A veil comes over my heart, and I seek Allah’s forgiveness seventy times a day.”

Satan casts evil into the soul, while the angel casts good into it. It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There is not one of you who has not been assigned a companion from among the angels and a companion from among the jinn.”

They asked, “Even you, O Messenger of Allah?”

He replied, “Even me, but Allah has aided me against him, so he has submitted.” In another version: “So he commands me only to do good.”

That is, he surrendered and yielded. Ibn ʿUyaynah used to narrate it as fa-aslamu (“so I am safe”), with a final u vowel, saying, “Satan does not embrace Islam.” However, the wording in the other version, “So he commands me only to do good,” indicates that he no longer commanded him to do evil. This is his submission, even if it is a figurative reference to his subjugation and abasement rather than to his belief in Allah.

It is like a man who subdues his visible enemy and takes him captive. The vanquished enemy knows that his conqueror recognizes the evil he suggests to him and will not accept it, but will instead punish him for it. Being overpowered, he is therefore compelled to suggest only good to him, out of humiliation and helplessness, not out of righteousness or religious devotion. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“But Allah has aided me against him, so he commands me only to do good.”

Ibn Masʿūd said, “There is a prompting from the angel and a prompting from Satan. The angel’s prompting is a promise of good

---

## Page 9128

and an affirmation of the truth. Satan’s prompting is a threat of evil and a denial of the truth.”

Allah Most High has said:

“It is only Satan who frightens you with his allies.”

That is, his allies frighten you through the terrifying whispers he casts into your hearts, like a human devil who instils fear of the enemy, spreading alarm and discouraging others.

The opposite of this is expressed in His words:

“When your Lord revealed to the angels, ‘I am with you, so strengthen those who believe. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve.’”

Allah Most High also said:

And He said:

Making someone steadfast means rendering him firm rather than doubtful. This is achieved by instilling what strengthens him: affirmation of the truth and a promise of good. As Ibn Masʿūd said, “The angel’s prompting is a promise of good and an affirmation of the truth.” Whenever the heart knows that what the Messenger has conveyed is true, it believes him. When it knows that Allah has promised it confirmation, it trusts Allah’s promise and becomes steadfast.

Such steadfastness is brought about through words, just as one person reassures another about a matter in which he has become unsettled, telling him that he is right and explaining what assures him that he will be granted victory, so that he becomes steadfast. It may also be brought about through action, by holding the heart firm until it becomes steady, just as one person holds another until he becomes steady.

It is reported in a hadith that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever asks to be appointed a judge and seeks help in obtaining it will be left to his own devices. Whoever neither asks to be appointed a judge nor seeks help in obtaining it, Allah will send down an angel to guide him aright.”

Thus, this angel makes him sound in speech through what he instils

---

## Page 9129

in his heart: an affirmation of the truth and a promise of good.

Allah Most High has said:

“He is the One who bestows blessings upon you, and His angels pray for you, to bring you out of darkness into light.”

This shows that these blessings are a means of bringing them out of darkness into light. He has mentioned His bringing the believers out of darkness into light in several verses, such as His words:

“Allah is the Protector of those who believe. He brings them out of darkness into light. As for those who disbelieve, their protectors are false gods, who bring them out of light into darkness.”

It is stated in the hadith:

“Allah bestows blessings upon those who teach people what is good, and His angels pray for them.”

This is because, by teaching what is good, such a person brings people out of darkness into light, and the reward corresponds to the deed. Thus, the Messenger is the most deserving of these blessings in their fullest measure, as Allah Most High said:

“Indeed, Allah bestows blessings upon the Prophet, and His angels pray for him.”

Salāh (prayer) is supplication, whether conveyed through good words that imply supplication or expressed in an explicit supplicatory formula. The angels supplicate for the believers, as authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The angels continue to pray for any one of you as long as he remains in his place of prayer, saying, ‘O Allah, forgive him; O Allah, have mercy on him,’ so long as he does not invalidate his ablution.”

He thus explained that their prayer consists of their saying, “O Allah, forgive him; O Allah, have mercy on him.” A transmitted report states:

“The Lord offers salāh, saying, ‘My mercy has preceded—or prevailed over—My anger.’”

---

## Page 9130

And these words of His—glory be to Him—are both a statement and a performative utterance, conveying that mercy precedes anger and prevails over it. He—glory be to Him—does not call upon another to act, as the angels and other creatures call upon Him. Rather, He expresses what He calls for through His command, His word, and His oath, as when He says:

“I shall surely do such-and-such.”

And:

“Be—and it is.”

His saying, “I shall surely do such-and-such,” is an oath on His part, as in His words:

“I will surely fill Hell with you and those who follow you.”

And:

“But My word has come to pass: I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together.”

And:

“Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession in the land, just as He granted succession to those before them; that He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them; and that He will surely replace their fear with security.”

And:

“Allah has decreed: ‘I and My messengers will surely prevail.’ Indeed, Allah is Powerful, Almighty.”

This is a promise reinforced by an oath, unlike His words:

“We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe in the life of this world.”

This is a promise and a statement containing no oath, though it is emphasized by the particle lām, which can mark the response to an oath. His words:

“Allah has promised you abundant spoils that you will take.”

And:

“And when Allah promised you one of the two groups.”

And similar expressions are promises without further reinforcement.

Allah Most High has said:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except through revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who then reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills.”

He thus states that He gives revelation to human beings, sometimes through revelation from Himself, and at other times by sending a messenger, whereupon whatever He wills is revealed to the messenger by His permission.

---

## Page 9131

And the angels are Allah’s messengers. The word malak (angel) itself conveys the meaning of bearing a message. Its original form is mal’ak, on the pattern maf‘al, but frequent usage led to its being simplified: the hamza’s vowel was transferred to the preceding unvowelled consonant, and the hamza was dropped. Malāk is derived from ma’luk and mal’ak, with the hamza preceding the lām in the first and the lām preceding the hamza in the second; both mean “message.” Alūka likewise means “message,” with the hamza preceding the lām. The poet said:

“Convey to al-Nu‘mān this message from me:
My confinement and my waiting have grown long.”

Here the hamza comes first. In malak, however, the lām precedes the hamza, and this derivation is preferable. Its counterpart in greater derivation is lāka, yalūku (to chew or roll something in the mouth), as in chewing over words or champing a bridle-bit; the hamza is stronger than the wāw. Next comes, in intermediate derivation, akala, ya’kulu (to eat). For a person chews what he takes into himself—whether food, speech, or knowledge—which enters his inner being and nourishes him.

‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd said: “Every host loves to have people attend his banquet, and Allah’s banquet is the Quran.” The word ādib means a host, and ma’duba means the hospitality offered: the food prepared for a guest. He thus explained that Allah has entertained His servants with the words He sent down to them. These are the nourishment and sustenance of their hearts. Their hearts benefit from them and need them even more than the body benefits from and needs its food.

And ‘Alī—may Allah be pleased with him—said: “The godly scholars are those who nourish people with wisdom

---

## Page 9132

and nurture them through it.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I spend the night with my Lord, who feeds me and gives me drink.”

Allah Most High has told us that the Quran is a healing for what is in the hearts. Yet people’s hearts and bodies need nourishment even more than they need healing. In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The guidance and knowledge with which Allah has sent me are like rain falling upon land. One part retained the water and produced abundant pasture and grass. Another part retained the water, so people drank from it and used it for watering and cultivation. Another part was merely barren, level ground that neither retained water nor produced pasture. Such is the likeness of one who gains understanding of Allah’s religion and benefits from the guidance and knowledge with which Allah has sent me, and the likeness of one who pays it no heed and does not accept Allah’s guidance with which I was sent.”

He thus explained that what he was sent with is to hearts what water is to the earth: sometimes it drinks it in and produces growth, sometimes it retains it, and sometimes it does neither. The earth drinks water and is nourished by it until it yields its bounty. Allah Most High has also told us that it is a spirit through which hearts come to life. He said:

“And thus We have revealed to you a spirit by Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor faith, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. And indeed, you guide to a straight path.”

Since what He reveals to His servants is sometimes conveyed through an angel and sometimes without an intermediary, this applies to all believers without exception; it is not exclusive to the prophets. He said:

---

## Page 9133

exalted is He:

“We inspired the mother of Moses: ‘Nurse him.’”

And He, Most High, said:

“And when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and My Messenger, they said, ‘We believe, so bear witness that we are Muslims.’”

Since He has said:

“And your Lord inspired the bees…”

to the end of the verse, thereby stating that He inspires them, human beings are all the more fitting recipients of inspiration. He, Most High, also said:

“And He imparted to each heaven its command.”

And He, Most High, said:

“By the soul and Him who fashioned it, then inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness.”

Thus He, glorified is He, inspires the soul with wickedness and righteousness. Wickedness comes through Satan, as an inspiration in the form of whispering, while righteousness comes through an angel, as an inspiration in the form of revelation. The former commands wickedness, while the latter commands righteousness; a command must necessarily be accompanied by an assertion.

In customary usage, however, the word “inspiration,” when used without qualification, does not mean whispering. This verse is among the indications that a distinction is to be made between revelatory inspiration and whispering. If what is commanded is mindfulness of Allah, it is revelatory inspiration; if it is wickedness, it is Satan’s whispering.

The criterion distinguishing praiseworthy inspiration from blameworthy whispering is therefore the Book and the Sunnah. If what is cast into the soul is something that the Book and the Sunnah identify as mindfulness of Allah, it is praiseworthy inspiration. If they identify it as wickedness, it is blameworthy whispering. This distinction holds consistently, without exception. Abū Hāzim mentioned a distinction between the whispering of the soul and that of Satan, saying:

“Whatever is disliked

---

## Page 9134

by your soul for yourself comes from Satan, so seek refuge in Allah from it. Whatever your soul desires for yourself comes from your soul, so restrain it from that.”

Speculative thinkers have discussed the knowledge that arises in the heart following reflection and inference. They have mentioned three positions on this, as related by Abū Hāmid in his al-Mustasfā and by others: the position of the Jahmiyyah, that of the Qadariyyah, and that of the philosophers.

Many speculative theologians mention only two positions: those of the Jahmiyyah and the Qadariyyah. This is because their books recount the views known to them of those whom they know to have discussed this matter, and these are the only groups they know. The question is a subsidiary issue of divine decree, for whatever arises in a soul comes into existence within it; thus, the positions concerning it are like those concerning similar occurrences.

The position of Jahm and those who agree with him, such as Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī and many later affirmationists, is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah in holding that Allah is the Creator of everything and that Allah creates the actions of His servants. Yet he affirms neither causes, nor efficacious power, nor wisdom behind the Lord’s actions. He therefore denied the intrinsic natures and powers present in things, and denied causes and wise purposes. For this reason, he assigned no cause to anything. Rather, he says, “This comes about through Allah’s creation and power.” They mentioned no cause for it, and they speak truthfully in

---

## Page 9135

attributing it to His decree and affirming that He is its Creator, contrary to the Qadariyyah. Yet complete understanding requires affirming and knowing the causes.

As for the Qadariyyah among the Muʿtazilah and others, they based their account on their principle that everything resulting from a servant’s action is itself his action and is not attributed to anyone else—such as becoming satiated, having one’s thirst quenched, the departure of the soul, and similar effects. They therefore said: “This knowledge results from the servant’s reflection or his recollection of that reflection.”

The philosophers based their account on their principle that forms arise through emanation from the active intellect when the receptive matter is suitably prepared. They therefore said: “It arises in human souls through emanation from the active intellect when the soul is prepared by bringing the two premises to mind.” This position is erroneous. The preceding position is closer to the truth, and the first is closer still. Yet none of them accurately explains the matter.

The reality is that Allah has assigned to human beings angels and devils that cast good and evil into their hearts. True knowledge is good, while false beliefs are evil. As Ibn Masʿūd said:

“The angel’s prompting affirms the truth, while Satan’s prompting denies the truth.”

Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said concerning the judge:

“Allah sent down to him an angel to guide him aright.”

Likewise, Allah has informed us that angels impart inspiration to human beings, even though human beings are unaware that it comes from an angel, just as they are unaware of the whispering devil.

---

## Page 9136

But Allah has informed us that He speaks to human beings through revelation, or through an angel who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills; the third way is to speak from behind a veil. Some commentators have said that revelation here means revelation in dreams, and Abū al-Faraj mentioned no other interpretation. Yet this is not so. Dreams sometimes come from Allah, sometimes from one’s own self, and sometimes from Satan. The same applies to what is cast into one’s heart while awake. The prophets, however, are protected from error both while awake and in dreams.

For this reason, the prophets’ dreams are revelation, as Ibn ‘Abbās and ‘Ubayd ibn ‘Umayr stated, citing His words:

“I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you.”

Not everyone who sees a dream receives revelation through it. Likewise, not everyone into whose heart something is cast receives revelation through it. A person’s soul may be in a more perfect state while awake than while asleep—as with someone praying and communing privately with his Lord. If he may receive revelation while asleep, why should he not receive it while awake, just as Allah revealed to the mother of Moses, the disciples, and the bees? Nevertheless, no one may declare without qualification that what occurs within him is revelation, whether awake or in a dream, unless there is evidence establishing this, for whisperings prevail among people. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 9137

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

Section: On Surahs al-Falaq and al-Nās

The interpretations of al-falaq vary in scope, from general to specific. It has been interpreted as creation in general; as everything in creation that is split open, such as daybreak, grain, and date stones—which encompasses most of creation; and as daybreak specifically. As for interpreting it as the Fire, or a pit or tree within it, this requires revealed evidence.

As for al-ghāsiq (the darkening one), a hadith narrated from ‘Ā’ishah and traced back to the Prophet is recorded in the collections of al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasā’ī:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, looked at the moon and said to her: ‘O ‘Ā’ishah, seek refuge in Allah from this, for this is the darkening one when it enters.’”

Ibn Qutaybah said: “Al-ghāsiq is the moon when it is eclipsed and turns dark, and waqaba means that it enters an eclipse.”

The well-known interpretation among Quranic commentators and linguists is that al-ghāsiq means the night, and waqaba means that it enters

---

## Page 9138

into everything, bringing darkness. Al-ghasaq means darkness. Al-Zajjāj said that al-ghāsiq means cold, and that night is therefore called ghāsiq because it is colder than day. Alternatively, al-ghasaq is said to mean flowing and enveloping: the darkness of night flows over and envelops the earth. If al-ghāsiq is interpreted as the moon, its “entering” may mean its entering an eclipse. There is no contradiction between interpreting it as the night and as the moon, for the moon is the sign of the night. There are thus three levels: night in general, then the moon in general, then the moon during an eclipse.

This accords with what was mentioned concerning the One in whom refuge is sought. The broad interpretation of al-falaq as creation corresponds to “from the evil of what He has created,” while its specific interpretation as daybreak—the emergence of light—corresponds to “the darkening one when it enters,” meaning the onset of darkness.

Ibn Zayd said: “Al-ghāsiq is the Pleiades when they set.” Illnesses and plagues used to become more frequent when they set, though they may also occur when they rise. It seems—and Allah knows best—that part of the wisdom behind this is that light is of the nature of good, and darkness of the nature of evil. Evils arising from the soul occur at night that do not occur during the day. The moon also has an influence on the earth, especially during an eclipse, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“They are two signs by which Allah strikes fear into His servants.”

Fear is only aroused when a cause for fear comes into being, and that occurs only when there is a cause of punishment or reason to expect it. It is thus known that an eclipse is an occasion on which punishment may befall the inhabitants of the earth;

---

## Page 9139

and for this reason, prolonged prayer, charity, the freeing of slaves, and supplication were prescribed during an eclipse to avert punishment, and likewise during other signs that mark the onset of punishment, such as earthquakes, the appearance of celestial bodies, and the like. The moon is the nearest of the celestial bodies that affect the earth through moisture, dryness, and other means.

For this reason, those who sought benefit and harm from celestial bodies based their judgments about events on the moon’s course. When it was in its exaltation, as in Cancer, they considered the time auspicious; when it was in Scorpio, its fall, they considered it inauspicious. Such was its place in their knowledge, and likewise in their practice of magic and other arts: the moon was the nearest source of influence. They even compiled the “Scripture of the Moon” for worshipping it and glorifying it.

Thus, the things from which refuge is sought in this surah follow a perfect order, proceeding from the most general, highest, and farthest to the most specific, nearest, and lowest. They are divided into four categories.

First: the evil of created things in general. Al-Hasan’s statement that this means Iblīs and his offspring, and the statement of others that it means Hell, refer to spiritual and corporeal things that are pure evil for us.

Second: the evil of the darkening one when it enters. This includes whatever in the higher world affects the lower world: the night, the celestial bodies within it, such as the Pleiades, and its ruler, the moon. It also includes the magic of blending (1), which is the highest and most elevated form of magic.

## Page 9140

Third: the evil of those who blow on knots—the sorceresses who take form through actions involving physical bodies.

Fourth: the envious person—that is, souls that inflict harm out of folly. This encompasses all causes of evil. Then, in “Surah al-Nās,” He specifically addresses the evil arising from jinn and humans, who are harmful spirits.

Section

The connection between the two surahs becomes apparent from another perspective: what one seeks refuge from is evil, just as what one seeks is good. Evil arises either from a person’s own actions or from something other than his actions. The origin of his doing evil is whispering, which sometimes comes from jinn and sometimes from humans. Cutting off evil at its root and source is better than repelling it after it has occurred.

Thus, when a person is granted refuge from the evil of the whisperer who whispers into people’s hearts, he has been granted refuge from the evil of disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience. This concerns his own actions, but the verse also encompasses the wrongdoing of others toward him. This surah therefore concerns evil arising from a person’s actions. As for evil arising from others, that is addressed in Surah (al-Falaq), which contains the seeking of refuge from the evil of created things, both generally and specifically. And Allah knows best.
